articles.title: Qnity at One: Shrink, Stack and the Materials Behind AI - EE Times
articles.text:
A year after its separation from DuPont, Qnity’s Chief Technology Officer discusses operating at semiconductor speed, the materials challenges of advanced packaging and why chipmakers are asking for system-level solutions.
On Nov. 1, 2025, DuPont completed the separation of its electronics business, and Qnity began trading on the New York Stock Exchange as a standalone company. The timing placed a newly independent materials supplier at the center of the largest demand cycle the semiconductor industry has seen in decades. AI workloads are reshaping how chips are designed, fabricated and packaged, and the industry’s long reliance on transistor scaling alone is giving way to a combined strategy that Qnity’s leadership describes as “shrink and stack.”
Qnity enters its second year as one of the world’s largest and most diverse electronics materials companies, with more than 10,000 employees across nearly 40 manufacturing sites and 20 R&D facilities. Its portfolio spans the electronics value chain, including specialized materials for key steps in semiconductor manufacturing, such as materials for chemical mechanical planarization (CMP), lithography, specialty cleans & selective etchants, high-performance seals, electrodeposited metallization, dry-film photoresists, dielectrics and flexible laminates, along with electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding and thermal management solutions that maintain signal integrity, block interference, and manage heat load.
EE Times spoke with Randy King, Chief Technology and Sustainability Officer at Qnity, about the company’s first year as an independent business, the materials challenges emerging as the industry builds in three dimensions and what engineers should watch for in 2027. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
A first year built on focus
EE Times: Qnity marks one year as an independent company. What are you most proud of from the past year?
King: I’m really proud that, through a year of high activity, our organization has stayed focused on delivering the innovations our customers need. We always talk about making sure we’re the partner of choice for our customers, and I feel our team has done a great job staying on that track this year.
Another area we’ve been very pleased with is extending and maximizing our collaborations. Earlier this year we announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to take advantage of AI in our computational modeling, so that we can accelerate our innovation engine with both advanced modeling capabilities and agentic AI. We also announced our strategic membership with imec. imec focuses on work three to five years out, essentially pathfinding, and that’s very important for us as we expand our collaborations with customers on their extended, multi-technology roadmaps. That’s where we want to make sure we’re staying ahead of the needs of the industry.
We joined Apple’s American Manufacturing Program in March, bringing our materials expertise and R&D capabilities to help power breakthrough technologies, and in October Apple expanded that partnership, announcing that we’re producing advanced films in the U.S. for the new variable aperture camera system on iPhone 18 Pro. We also formed a strategic partnership with the University of Delaware College of Engineering to strengthen the engineering talent pipeline and expand research collaboration: students are working alongside our technical leaders on capstone projects, we’re piloting an extended work-study program, and we’re collaborating with UD faculty on semiconductor materials research.
The other area I’m really thrilled about is culture. Coming into this new company, our leadership team has been putting significant focus on ensuring we have a culture built for winning and long-term success in the industry. We’ve really embraced empowerment at all levels of the organization: making sure everybody in the organization has the tools they need to get the job done and takes individual ownership and accountability for their actions, with decisions made at the right level in the organization, so we don’t have decision-making at higher levels slowing down critical workflow.
EE Times: Of those milestones, which has mattered most to your customers?
King: We strive to be a partner of choice for our customers, and one critical way we do that is by engaging aggressively in open innovation. Our approach and our attitude toward our customers is that we need to solve their challenges, and we need to do it quickly and collaboratively. One way to do that is through open innovation – or teaming up with external collaborators who have expertise in areas that either complement our capabilities or, in some cases, fill gaps we might have in access to tools or fundamental technologies.
Operating at a new clock speed
For most of its history, the business currently operating within Qnity sat inside a diversified industrial portfolio. Semiconductor manufacturing, however, runs on a cadence few other industries match. Chipmakers qualify materials for a node years before volume production, and a delay at the supplier level can ripple through an entire technology roadmap. King frames independence less as a break from DuPont’s practices than as an opportunity to run the entire company at the industry’s pace.
EE Times: What has independence enabled Qnity to do differently than it could as part of DuPont?
King: Being part of DuPont was valuable, because they’re a great company with strong processes and management tools, and when we spun off, we wanted to make sure we maintained those areas of excellence: their innovation engine, how you run a stage-gated process, how you prioritize research, the safety protocols. There were a lot of very strong capabilities we were excited to continue.
But there are some unique characteristics to a pure-play electronics company like Qnity. In semiconductors, electronic components and electronic devices, we have to move at a speed that’s probably higher than most industries need to operate at. So, we needed to look at how we could operate at a faster pace, making sure our entire organization is built for speed.
We’re not going to change our basic ways of working, like integrity and ethical behavior, how we treat people, but we’ve added a layer around what is essential for success at Qnity, and there are four main values. One of those is speed. We aspire to operate at the cadence that our customers need, which means all of our functions. It’s the entire company that has to operate at a new clock speed. At one point, it was, “Well, that’s an R&D problem.” No. From procurement through operations, R&D, finance, legal and HR, every function is executing on the mission to accelerate our innovation engine.
Our other values – customer, innovation, and people – help us operate as uniquely Qnity, and we’re excited to set these values as a foundation for how we operate every day.
From shrink to shrink and stack
For decades, progress in semiconductors was measured almost entirely in transistor density. Each new node delivered more transistors per unit area at a lower cost per transistor. That economic model has weakened at single-digit nanometer dimensions, where extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography and the process complexity around it have pushed costs up rather than down. The industry’s response has been to build upward: gate-all-around transistor architectures, 3D NAND with hundreds of layers and advanced packages that place memory and logic side by side or stack them directly. Qnity CEO Jon Kemp has described the transition as a move from “shrink” to “shrink and stack.”
EE Times: What does the shift to “shrink and stack” mean for chipmakers, and why does it make materials more important?
King: The industry has been following Moore’s Law for decades. Every two years the transistor count doubles, and it’s supposed to get cheaper. It has been all about transistor count and shrinkage. However, we’re now at single-digit nanometer levels of resolution, and those are becoming much more difficult and costly. So as we march down Moore’s Law, the speed with which we can continue to double the transistor count and reduce cost is slowing down.
As a result, the industry is looking at other ways to continue to build more powerful computing. They’re moving to three-dimensional in architectures. They’re changing structures; on logic, we’re going to gate-all-around. We’re stacking memory; look at NAND going from 300 to 400 layers. But it’s also about getting that computing power into an actual device. I can do that by making a more powerful chip, but I can also, theoretically, stack two logic chips on top of each other and still get the increased power.
So what’s going on now is: how do I put more memory and logic into a smaller space? That’s where heterogeneous integration comes in. That’s where advanced packaging comes in. You’re seeing 2.5D and 3D stacking, putting the memory chips right next to the logic chip and then stacking chips on top of each other. All of this is causing a whole new inflection in the industry about the most effective and efficient ways to do advanced packaging.
When Jon says “shrink and stack,” we’re still shrinking, but we’re now adding a much more complex stacking component to ensure we can continue powering these massive leaps.
AI’s next bottleneck: energy and heat
The scale of AI infrastructure has shifted attention from raw compute toward the cost of delivering it. Large training and inference clusters draw enormous amounts of electricity, and much of that energy is ultimately dissipated as heat that must be removed from the package, the board and the data center. At the device level, every millimeter of interconnect now carries an energy penalty, which is one reason backside power delivery and co-packaged optics have moved from research topics to roadmap items.
EE Times: Much of the AI conversation centers on compute and power. What is AI demand revealing about the next bottleneck in semiconductor manufacturing?
King: I think it’s pretty clear that the large consumption of electricity needed to run these supercomputers in data centers is creating some challenges. You have to have enough electricity, but it’s also generating a lot of wasted heat. Part of the reason for advanced packaging is that if you make the copper connection shorter, you can save on electricity, which is what you’re doing when you put the memory chip right next to, or on top of, the logic chip.
You’re also starting to see co-packaged optics coming in. Optics aren’t going to generate the kind of heat you get from electrons, and you can get more compute capability with a fiber than you can with a wire. So, I think you’re going to see more of the world of photonics coming into the package and onto the chip as we move forward, because there are some big advantages there.
You’re going to continue to see a movement toward reducing energy consumption in the designs. We’ve now got backside power on logic chips and backside power on memory, and that’s certainly one of the areas being used to reduce energy consumption. I think you’re going to keep seeing advances in architectures, and you’re going to see advances in materials, to help reduce wasted energy through heat across the semiconductor world.
The hardest problems in advanced packaging
Each new packaging architecture brings its own integration challenges, and many of them land on materials. Hybrid bonding, which joins copper pads and dielectric surfaces directly without solder, enables finer interconnect pitch and lower signal loss, but it demands exceptionally flat, clean surfaces and precise alignment. Higher-density packages also combine organic and inorganic materials in ways that conventional planarization processes were not designed to handle, and the mechanical stress between those layers is becoming a reliability concern in its own right.
EE Times: In advanced packaging, which materials challenges are proving the hardest to solve today, whether in interconnects, thermal management or reliability?
King: As this inflection occurs, you’ve got all these new technologies coming into play. Right now you’ve got hybrid bonding, which helps on energy savings and speeds up signal transfer. There are a lot of advantages to hybrid bonding, but it requires exceptionally precise alignment. There are a lot of really good companies working to achieve that level of precision, but it has been a challenge for the industry, and it will continue to be as it evolves. Hybrid bonding also requires new ways of polishing the copper and new ways of integrating those systems into more advanced packages, and that requires new materials to be developed that work in those areas.
You could say the same thing about advanced packaging in general. As these packages become more complex and higher density, you have to planarize, and you’re now planarizing types of materials you may not have had to planarize in the past. A lot of planarization has been silicon and metals, an inorganic kind of planarization. Now you’ve got inorganics plus organics present in some of these packages. That’s a completely different pad and slurry you need to deal with, and different cleans you’re going to need. As advanced packages get more complex and new technologies come in, it’s always going to generate new challenges.
One of the other challenges the industry is seeing is mismatches in the coefficients of thermal expansion between the different layers. That’s starting to cause warpage, and some of the warpage can be pretty severe. That can cause reliability issues if it doesn’t get addressed. So, we’re seeing a lot of new challenges that require advanced materials because of all the new architectures being developed in this space.
A seat at the design table
Although Qnity is new as a company, its electronics business draws on roughly five decades of history through DuPont, earlier acquisitions and the Dow merger and subsequent separation. That lineage shaped a support model built on proximity, with R&D centers, application labs and manufacturing located near the fabs they serve. Proximity matters because a material that performs in a supplier’s lab must also perform on the customer’s tools and in the customer’s process flow, often years before a node enters volume production.
EE Times: Qnity talks about having a seat at the design table with customers. What does that collaboration look like in practice, from R&D through yield optimization in the fab?
King: Even though Qnity is new, some of our materials have been around for 50 years, so there’s a long legacy in this business. We’ve been interacting in the semiconductor and advanced electronics space for years, and during that time it became very apparent that you had to have a local-for-local operating model – working in close proximity to your customers wherever they are in the world. If you want to serve this industry, it’s very high tech, it’s very complicated, and it’s not the kind of industry where you can sell your product remotely.
You want to be as close to your customers as you possibly can be, with your R&D centers, your application centers and your manufacturing capability. They need to have the product available, they want to make sure your products are properly serviced so that any new products operate correctly in their processes, and you need rapid turns of innovation, because our customers are moving very quickly to the next node. Several of our customers are working on two generations of nodes beyond where we are today. You can’t just start the year you want to have an advanced node. You start years in advance.
Being close to our customers and available to help solve their challenges is one of the key attributes that makes us a partner of choice. Around the world, where our customers are, we have a local team that’s very capable of supporting them, staying on their innovation roadmap and making sure we have the materials ready when they need them.
AI in the materials lab
AI is now feeding back into the materials pipeline that supports it. Discovering and qualifying a new semiconductor material has traditionally required years of synthesis, characterization and integration testing. Accelerated simulation, machine-learned models and agentic workflows promise to narrow that search before a sample is ever synthesized. In March 2026, Qnity announced a collaboration with NVIDIA built around accelerated computing and AI tools for materials research, and in July it joined NVIDIA, Meta and other organizations as a founding member of CuspAI’s AI Materials Foundry, a network formed to speed materials discovery.
EE Times: Qnity is a founding member of CuspAI’s AI Materials Foundry alongside Meta and NVIDIA. How is AI changing the way new semiconductor materials are discovered and developed?
King: Data science is evolving quickly, and the capability to use the immense computing power being generated to accelerate your innovation engine is ramping very quickly. That’s one of the reasons we’re partnering with NVIDIA. The complexity of the modeling that’s available, and how to integrate it into your innovation engine, is an area I believe you need to stay on top of. That’s what we’re doing: making sure we’re staying on top of the latest capabilities we can bring to our innovation engine to accelerate it through data science.
One area I’m proud of this year is integrating agentic AI into some of our innovations with customers. Working with their data and our data together, we’ve been able to accelerate some of the innovations we’ve brought. It’s important, because the material doesn’t just have to work in our laboratory. It’s got to work on the equipment our customers use.
EE Times: Is that significantly shortening your development timelines?
King: In some cases, we have evidence that we can shorten them by 30%.
Capacity close to the customer
Within a week of each other in March 2026, Qnity announced a new research and manufacturing facility in Taiwan’s Hsinchu Science Park and opened a 385,000-square-foot facility in Newark, Delaware, that adds a CMP pad production line designed for advanced nodes. The investments arrive as chipmakers place greater weight on regional supply resilience, with new fab capacity coming online in both Asia and the United States.
EE Times: With new facilities in Taiwan and Delaware, how is Qnity approaching regional manufacturing and supply chain resilience for its customers?
King: This is who we are. It’s the way we’ve operated for decades, so to us it’s nothing new. We’re maintaining what we’ve always said: we’ve got to have local-for-local support, and we need to make sure our products and our supply chains are robust so that we can supply our customers at the volumes required, with the capabilities and quality they need.
This is part of our roadmap. We’re expanding capacity. We spent $61.5 million on the facility in Taiwan, and we’ve already filled it up, both with R&D and new capabilities and with increased manufacturing capability. In the U.S., we put in a 385,000-square-foot facility to make sure our planarization portfolio stays on track with the capacity the industry needs.
We’ve been doing this for years. As we see demand increase and we see the need, we put in capacity, because it’s very important to our customers that we supply when they need it.
What to watch in 2027
As packages grow more complex, so does the number of materials interacting within a single process module. A CMP step depends on the interplay among pad, slurry and post-CMP clean, and an advanced package may combine lithography, metallization, planarization and substrate materials from several suppliers. Qualifying each of those interactions separately takes time that chipmakers increasingly do not have.
EE Times: Looking ahead, what should EE Times readers, from design to process and packaging engineers, be watching for in 2027?
King: The big shift I’m seeing is that our customers are looking for system-level solutions. We didn’t use to get requests like we’re getting today: “Can you come in and provide me a system solution, not a single-point solution?” So, we work with our customers and say, “We can solve that challenge. Instead of you going to three different companies, we can supply the pad, the slurry and the clean, and we can tell you for sure it’s going to work in that application.” That enables them to move faster.
We’re also seeing that in advanced packaging. We have the circuit side, the substrate side and the wafer-level metallization, and we also have planarization capability and high-resolution lithography. When customers have challenges in advanced packaging, sometimes they want us to broaden the view and help solve the challenges across a platform they’re working on, instead of, “Bring me a single-point solution, give me a new metallization for damascene.” It’s, “Give us a broader package of solutions so we can move faster.” Because they have to move so fast, they’re really looking for system-level solutions, and I think that’s going to continue.
Qnity’s second year begins as the forces King describes, from hybrid bonding and co-packaged optics to backside power and ever-taller memory stacks, continue to move materials toward the center of semiconductor roadmaps. For a company built on local support and rapid co-development, the measure of independence will be how well that model keeps pace with customers already working two nodes ahead.

articles.title: Fausse réunion Zoom : l'arnaque géante qui a permis de voler des millions dévoilée par le FBI
articles.text:
C'est une escroquerie de grande ampleur qui vient d'être démantelée par le FBI. Elle utilisait des vidéos de gens connus de la victime pour la pousser à télécharger un programme malveillant.
On n'arrête jamais le progrès dans le monde des escroqueries internet. On avait ainsi découvert le mois dernier l'escroquerie au faux support Microsoft, qui opérait depuis quasiment une décennie, et avait permis aux malfaiteurs de générer plusieurs millions de dollars. Mais il y a pourtant beaucoup plus impressionnant encore, comme on peut le voir avec cette annonce du FBI.
Une escroquerie par Zoom volant le visage des proches des victimes démantelée par le FBI
La FBI vient d'annoncer le démantelement d'une vaste infrastructure d'escroquerie, dans le cadre de l'opération « FaceStealer ». Une escroquerie au fonctionnement particulièrement sophistiquée.
Celle-ci commence par le vol de l'identité d'une personne connue de la victime, ou d'un professionnel connu dans son secteur. Cette fausse personnalité sollicite la victime via un message sur LinkedIn ou Telegram, puis l'invite à une conférence Zoom ou Teams. La victime intègre alors une conférence dans laquelle elle voit en vidéo la personne qui est connue, une vidéo prise précédemment par les pirates, avec d'autres participants aussi présents.
À un moment, l'un d'eux explique ne pas entendre le micro de la victime, ce qui est suivi par l'apparition d'un message d'erreur l'invitant à télécharger une mise à jour… qui est en fait un malware.
Quelque 400 millions de dollars volés en dix-huit mois
Et une fois ce programme téléchargé, les pirates ont accès à de nombreuses choses dans l'ordinateur de la victime. Il y a non seulement potentiellement ses comptes en cryptomonnaies, mais aussi les messageries et les réseaux sociaux, ce qui permet de préparer de nouvelles opérations de ce genre avec des proches de la victime (les pirates pouvant accéder à sa webcam et tenter de prendre une vidéo de la cible pour plus part).
Pour le FBI, il s'agit d'une opération très sophistiquée menée par la Corée du Nord. Particulièrement réussie, elle aurait notamment réussi à toucher des développeurs, des experts en cryptomonnaies ou même en cybersécurité. Au total, l'agence fédérale a retrouvé plus de 900 vidéos des victimes dans l'infrastructure démantelée. Le butin est lui estimé à plus de 400 millions de dollars en cryptomonnaie, pour une opération qui n'aura duré « que » dix-huit mois.
Source : France Info

articles.title: Fintech startup Payhawk valued at $2B in $280M round - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Fintech startup Payhawk valued at $2B in $280M round
Payhawk Ltd., a startup that helps enterprises manage their business expenses, has raised $280 million in funding.
The Series C round was led by Goldman Sachs’ growth equity arm. The bank was joined by Greenoaks, Lightspeed and more than a half-dozen others. Payhawk stated today that it’s now valued at $2 billion.
Issuing corporate credit cards to employees historically involved a weeks-long wait. Payhawk operates a platform that enables companies to create virtual cards in a few seconds and issue physical ones in five days. According to the company, customers can configure a card to expire automatically at the end of the project for which it’s needed.
Accounting teams can set spending limits to avoid cost overruns. Payhawk makes it possible to tie purchase caps to a business project, a specific merchant or a broad product category.
Companies can optionally connect their cards to Payhawk-operated business accounts. They support payments in more than 115 currencies. According to the software maker, its accounts’ currency exchange rates are up to 90% lower than those charged by traditional banks.
Syncing corporate card spending to a company’s accounting ledger is a multistep process. First, workers must scan the receipt issued in connection with a purchase and send it to the finance team. From there, an accountant categorizes the purchase and verifies it through a process known as reconciliation.
Payhawk automates the workflow using an artificial intelligence agent. Additionally, it flags cost-cutting opportunities such as unnecessary software-as-a-service subscriptions.
A second AI agent speeds up procurement initiatives. It’s accessible through a chat interface that enables workers to request items in natural language. If a request is missing certain details, the agent can point out what additional information is needed. From there, it automatically seeks approvals from relevant executives.
Payhawk also automates a number of other tasks. It includes a tool that reduces the amount of work involved in changing business trip plans. Additionally, the company has built an AI engine that enables new users to customize its platform by uploading documents such as spending policies.
“Through our technology, finance departments can benefit from ‘zero-touch finance,’ where neither the finance professional nor the employee deals with any admin work,” said Payhawk co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Hristo Borisov. “Seventy-seven percent of our customers use our agents daily across financial control, procurement, travel and reporting to save time and money for their businesses.”
Payhawk says it still has 70% of its previous funding round, a $100 million investment that closed in 2022. The company will use the proceeds from today’s Series C raise to enhance its AI capabilities.

articles.title: Por qué Xuper TV no se puede descargar en Google Play Store o App Store
articles.text:
La fragmentación del mercado de streaming ha impulsado a un sector amplio de usuarios a buscar alternativas de entretenimiento gratuito. En este contexto, plataformas de IPTV no autorizadas como Xuper TV han ganado tracción publicitaria en foros y redes sociales. Sin embargo, al intentar buscar esta aplicación en Google Play Store o la App Store de Apple, los resultados son imitaciones o simplemente nulos.
Esta ausencia no responde a un error de indexación ni a una restricción geográfica, sino a un bloqueo técnico y legal definitivo impuesto por los administradores de estos ecosistemas de software.
La exclusión de Xuper TV de las tiendas oficiales se fundamenta en tres violaciones estructurales a las normativas de publicación de aplicaciones móviles:
Infracción sistemática de la propiedad intelectual
Google y Apple operan bajo estrictos marcos normativos internacionales, como la Ley de Derechos de Autor de la Era Digital (DMCA) y acuerdos comerciales de protección de marcas. Xuper TV no posee licencias de distribución, contratos de retransmisión ni acuerdos comerciales para las series, películas o eventos deportivos en vivo que integra en su catálogo.
Su arquitectura de software funciona mediante el rastreo (scraping) y el secuestro de señales de servidores oficiales (como canales de cable o plataformas de streaming de pago), retransmitiendo el contenido de forma ilícita. Las tiendas oficiales tienen tolerancia cero frente a la piratería; la publicación de una aplicación con este modelo de operación resulta en el bloqueo inmediato del paquete y la suspensión permanente de la cuenta del desarrollador.
Presencia de código malicioso en las auditorías
Antes de estar disponible para el público, cualquier aplicación debe superar el proceso de revisión manual (App Review) de Apple o los escaneos automatizados de Google Play Protect. El código fuente de Xuper TV está diseñado para ocultar operaciones en segundo plano que son catalogadas como malware por los filtros de seguridad corporativos.
Los análisis técnicos sobre los paquetes de Xuper TV revelan la integración de instaladores secundarios (droppers), secuencias de cryptojacking para minar criptomonedas utilizando el procesador del teléfono, y solicitudes de permisos abusivos (como el control de Accesibilidad) que habilitan ataques de superposición (overlay attacks) sobre aplicaciones bancarias. Los escudos de Play Store y App Store bloquean el ingreso de la plataforma al identificarla como una amenaza de ciberseguridad severa.
Violación de normativas de privacidad y telemetría
Las políticas de desarrollo de los repositorios oficiales exigen el consentimiento explícito y rastreable del usuario para la recopilación de información, así como una declaración transparente sobre qué datos se almacenan y con qué propósito. Xuper TV carece de una política de privacidad auditable.
Dado que la plataforma no cobra una cuota de suscripción, su modelo de financiamiento paralelo se basa en la extracción silenciosa de la telemetría del dispositivo infectado. Esto incluye la exfiltración de la ubicación GPS en tiempo real, el historial de navegación, las direcciones MAC de la red local y la agenda de contactos, información que se comercializa posteriormente en mercados de datos y redes de spam, una práctica estrictamente prohibida en los ecosistemas de Google y Apple.
La evasión a través del sideloading
Al enfrentarse al veto total en los canales legítimos, los creadores de Xuper TV han estructurado una estrategia de distribución alternativa basada en la carga lateral (sideloading). A través de páginas web de terceros, foros y videos de YouTube, instruyen a los usuarios para que descarguen el archivo ejecutable (APK) directamente y modifiquen la configuración del sistema operativo para permitir la instalación desde “orígenes desconocidos”.
Este método transfiere todo el riesgo técnico al usuario final, forzándolo a apagar sus propias defensas informáticas para introducir el reproductor pirata junto con su carga maliciosa, eludiendo así el escudo protector que justificó su expulsión inicial de las tiendas de aplicaciones.

articles.title: Chrome croule sous les failles : Google déploie la troisième mise à jour de sécurité en huit jours
articles.text:
Google a déployé une nouvelle version de Chrome sur Windows, macOS et Linux. Baptisée Chrome 158, la mise à jour corrige pas moins de 204 failles de sécurité, à savoir six brèches critiques, 62 failles de gravité élevée, 82 failles moyennes et 54 failles mineures.
À lire aussi : Ces 319 extensions Chrome ont espionné des millions d’internautes pendant 10 ans
Six failles critiques dans le cœur de Chrome
Les six failles critiques touchent des composants clés du navigateur. La moitié des failles surviennent quand un logiciel continue d’utiliser une zone de mémoire qu’il a déjà libérée. Un pirate peut alors s’engouffrer dans la brèche pour corrompre des données, ou y exécuter du code malveillant. Les trois autres failles touchent le composant GPU et ANGLE, la couche graphique de Chrome, et le module Media. Dans les deux cas, Chrome écrit au-delà de l’espace mémoire prévu, ce qui peut écraser des informations voisines.
Pour l’instant, Google n’a pas découvert le moindre indice qui laisse penser que les failles ont été exploitées dans des cyberattaques. Comme toujours, le géant de Mountain View reste discret et refuse de communiquer davantage d’informations techniques, pour des raisons de sécurité.
IA et explosion des failles de sécurité
C’est déjà la troisième mise à jour de sécurité en l’espace de huit jours. Le 3 novembre, Chrome 157 est arrivé avec 213 correctifs. Six jours plus tard, Google a colmaté en urgence une faille zero-day déjà exploitée par des pirates. Deux jours après, un nouveau correctif est venu combler 83 failles dans le code du navigateur. Au total, plus de 500 failles ont été comblées en seulement deux semaines.
Ce déluge de vulnérabilités découle évidemment de l’essor de l’IA générative. Les notes de Google indiquent d’ailleurs que Claude, l’IA d’Anthropic, est à l’origine de la découverte de huit failles, dont deux des six failles critiques. Google s’appuie aussi sur ses propres outils pour traquer les failles, dont Big Sleep, un agent d’IA conçu par DeepMind et Project Zero.
L’accélération chez Google ne concerne pas que Chrome. La semaine dernière, Project Zero, l’équipe de sécurité d’élite de Google, a annoncé qu’elle allait divulguer les failles trois fois plus vite, qu’à l’accoutumée, en ramenant son délai de 90 à 30 jours. Selon les chercheurs, l’IA permet désormais aux pirates d’analyser un correctif dès sa sortie pour déduire une faille capable de mener à une attaque.
Le correctif est inclus dans la version 158.0.8127.36/.37 pour Windows et Mac, 158.0.8127.36 pour Linux, et 158.0.8127.42 pour Android. Pour installer la mise à jour, cliquez sur les trois points en haut à droite de Chrome, puis allez dans « Aide » et « À propos de Google Chrome ». Le navigateur télécharge alors tout seul la dernière version. Cliquez ensuite sur « Relancer » pour l’appliquer sur le navigateur. Vu la cadence actuelle des mises à jour de Chrome, on vous conseille d’activer les mises à jour automatiques.

articles.title: UK government plan to cut EV targets could cost consumers £3bn a year by 2030, critics say — as public EV charging stays on track to hit £1/kWh in 2027
articles.text:
UK government plan to cut EV targets is a ‘truly terrible decision’, critics say — as networks warn public charging could hit £1/kWh in 2027
EV drivers in the UK could soon be hit from all sides
- The UK government could weaken its Zero Emissions Vehicle mandate
- Some critics say that would be a "truly terrible decision"
- Public EV charging could also get more expensive as tariffs spiral
Industry insiders believe the UK government is considering rolling back its Zero Emissions Vehicle (ZEV) targets, as major automotive manufacturers and industry bodies have warned that the supply of EVs is on-track to outstrip demand.
Despite battery electric cars taking 32% of all new car registrations in the UK this October, the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) chief executive, Mike Hawes, warned that support for the transition towards electrification, both by the government and the industry, “cannot be sustained indefinitely”.
Currently, the UK government wants 52% of all new vehicles sold to be electric in 2028, with that figure increasing to 80% by 2030 and eventually 100% by 2035, as combustion engine vehicles are phased out. But Hawes predicts a mere 37.5% share by 2028.
As a result, many corners of the auto industry are calling for a revision to the mandate, with insiders predicting the Labour party could weaken its approach in the coming weeks — something Caroline Lucas, former MP for Brighton and Green Party member, believes would be a “truly terrible decision at a truly terrible time”.
On top of the environmental issues, which could see an extra 7.4 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions in 2030, analysis by The Carbon Brief has also concluded that weakening the EV targets could also cost UK consumers £3 billion a year by 2030, thanks to electric vehicles proving more than £1,000 per year cheaper to own than petrol cars or plug-in hybrids.
To compound matters, there is the risk that billions of pounds worth of committed investment could be put at risk, including huge sums of funding by Charge Point Operators (CPO), as well as battery supply chains and tier one suppliers.
According to industry group Energy UK, the current mandate is “working in the way it was designed to work” and that it is the “single biggest driver of emissions reductions” in government climate plans.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Analysis: The UK government needs to get a grip
Whatever your personal stance on electric vehicles, any indecision from the UK government is likely to rock consumer confidence. This, alongside the introduction of a pay-per-mile tax for EV owners in 2028 is sending mixed messages to anyone thinking of making the switch to electric.
Analysis by charge point provider Zest has also concluded that the price of EV public charging could easily rise above the £1/kWh mark next year, thanks to the spiraling cost of the standing charge rate for the grid connection that network providers have to pay.
For example, electricity and grid costs take 48p of the 58p a driver pays per kWh before VAT at Zest's urban charging hub in Birmingham, leaving just 10p to cover every other cost.
According to the company, various freedom of information requests have revealed that the Treasury has known about the issue for some time.
Zest says it is now down to regulator Ofgem to step in and make the appropriate changes, but proposals to reduce the standing charge have been in discussion for three years without action.
Robin Heap, Zest's founder, called these network charges an “egregious cost burden” shouldered by EV drivers and that any speculation about weakening the ZEV mandate sends the “wrong signal to businesses committing millions to Britain’s electric future”.
While it is understandable that the UK government is trying to appease everyone with its renewed discussions around ZEV mandates, the indecision is not benefitting anyone.
It has been argued for years that both consumers and investors need a clear roadmap for the future, otherwise the country risks being left in transport limbo that’s only going to make motoring more expensive for everyone.

articles.title: Comment Rockstar utilise l'IA pour sauver GTA 6 sur Xbox Series S (mais s'en passe sur PS5 et Series X)
articles.text:
La plus petite des Xbox calcule GTA 6 en 720p et s’appuie sur l’IA pour reconstruire une image en 1080p. Sur Xbox Series X et PS5, Rockstar part de 1440p et confie la mise à l’échelle vers la 4K à sa propre technologie.
La Xbox Series S a un point commun inattendu avec la PS5 Pro. Ce sont les deux seules consoles sur lesquelles GTA 6 utilise l’IA pour agrandir son image au lancement, ce jeudi 19 novembre. Dans un entretien à Wccftech, trois responsables techniques de Rockstar, dont Jonathon Ashcroft et Chris Oat, détaillent les réglages retenus pour chaque machine. Le studio vise 30 images par seconde partout, avec comme précisé sur Clubic un seul mode graphique.
Trois façons de reconstruire l’image
Sur Series S, le jeu calcule d’abord la scène en 720p, soit environ 920 000 pixels par image. Les trois autres consoles démarrent en 1440p, avec 3,7 millions de pixels. Dans les deux cas, l’image est ensuite agrandie d’un facteur 1,5 en largeur comme en hauteur.
| Console | Définition de rendu | Définition après reconstruction | Méthode utilisée | Eclairage et cadence | 
| Xbox Series S | 720p | 1080p | AMD FSR Upscaling 4 | Illumination globale en ray tracing, 30 fps | 
| Xbox Series X | 1440p | 4K | TAA de Rockstar | Illumination globale en ray tracing, 30 fps | 
| PS5 | 1440p | 4K | TAA de Rockstar | Illumination globale en ray tracing, 30 fps | 
| PS5 Pro | 1440p | 4K | Sony PSSR 2 | Illumination globale et ombres en ray tracing, 30 fps | 
L’anticrénelage temporel de Rockstar s’appuie sur les images précédentes pour lisser les contours et reconstruire les détails, sans réseau de neurones. FSR 4 d'AMD exploite aussi les informations des images précédentes, mais confie la reconstruction à un modèle entraîné. Sur Series S, celui-ci dispose au départ d’un quart des pixels calculés sur les autres consoles. L’interface, elle, est composée en 4K puis superposée à l’image sur les quatre consoles.
Qu’est-ce que le TAA maison de Rockstar ?
Contrairement au FSR 4 d’AMD ou au PSSR 2 de Sony, le Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) de Rockstar ne repose sur aucun modèle d’intelligence artificielle. Cette technique purement mathématique mémorise les images calculées une fraction de seconde plus tôt, compense les mouvements de caméra et superpose ces informations à l’image en cours. Ce cumul permet à la fois de gommer l’effet d’escalier sur les contours fins (câbles, feuillages) et de reconstituer une image 4K nette à partir d’un rendu natif en 1440p, le tout calibré sur mesure pour le moteur graphique du studio.
Même sur Series S, la lumière rebondit en ray tracing
Rockstar a conservé sur Series S l’illumination globale en ray tracing, qui simule la façon dont la lumière rebondit sur les surfaces et contribue à éclairer le reste de la scène. Le studio a calibré les sources lumineuses du jeu d’après les propriétés de lumières réelles, naturelles comme artificielles. Il tenait donc à garder le même système d’éclairage sur les quatre consoles.
La mémoire plus limitée de la Series S a compliqué le travail, reconnaît l’équipe. Rockstar a ajusté les réglages de l’illumination globale aux ressources de chaque machine. Le principe reste commun avec une mise en œuvre qui varie selon la console.
La Series X pouvait aussi utiliser le FSR 4
AMD avait annoncé l’arrivée de FSR 4.1 sur les deux Xbox Series le 20 octobre. Début novembre, la version 4.1.2 était disponible pour les développeurs des deux consoles. Wccftech présente GTA 6 comme le probable premier jeu à exploiter FSR 4 sur Series S. Rockstar indique le nom de la technologie, sans préciser la révision intégrée à son jeu.
Sur PS5 standard, Sony propose aussi une solution d’agrandissement par IA. Présenté le 1er octobre, le QSSR (Quick Spectral Super Resolution) est une version allégée du PSSR, adaptée au matériel de la PS5. Marvel’s Wolverine et Ghost of Yōtei l’ont inaugurée, et Sony la propose à tous les développeurs. GTA 6 s’en tient à l’outil de Rockstar sur cette console, comme sur Series X.
Le studio dit avoir évalué plusieurs combinaisons de définition et de reconstruction sur chaque machine avant de retenir celles qui lui donnaient le rendu et les performances recherchés. Pour juger du résultat sur les deux Xbox, le meilleur des comparatifs se fera en roulant dans la même rue de Vice City.

articles.title: Six days, six outages: Why reliability isn't resilience - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Six days, six outages: Why reliability isn’t resilience
A rash of major outages over the past week all seem to follow a similar script. Services go dark, Downdetector lights up, the provider posts a string of status updates, a root cause emerges a few days later, and everyone goes back to work, assuming it won’t happen again. This past week, that script was on overdrive.
- Nov. 12: Microsoft Corp.’s 365’s suite experienced a nearly 24-hour global outage that took down Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams, Copilot, Defender and Intune for users in 74 countries and territories. Microsoft traced the outage to a software bug introduced in July on its networking gateway servers, which cascaded worldwide when safeguards meant to contain regional problems failed.
- Nov. 13: Workday Inc. experienced a major outage affecting more than 10,000 companies due to an unintended connection between Workday’s disaster recovery or DR environment and its production databases.
- Nov. 13: The Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop after a telecommunications failure affected its air traffic control centers. Operators canceled 12,462 flights that day, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said routers became overloaded with data, leading to inconsistent information.
- Nov. 16: United Airlines delayed departures after a companywide outage left pilots unable to obtain final aircraft weights and other required data.
- Nov. 16: JPMorgan Chase customers couldn’t log in or move money for much of the day after what the bank called a software bug in its on-premises hardware systems. The problems affected Zelle transfers and customers at other banks who were transacting with Chase.
- Nov. 17: Apple reported outages affecting iCloud, Apple Pay, the App Store and other services, and a spokesperson attributed the outages to an internal update.
None of these was a cyberattack, and as far as anyone can tell, none was related. A dormant bug, overloaded legacy routers, a bad internal update and an on-premises hardware glitch are about as different as root causes get. Some of these systems run in the public cloud, some in a company’s own data center, and some on air traffic control gear that’s decades old. That’s precisely the point. The common thread isn’t the technology. It’s that each organization had a critical dependency fail, and the business stopped with it.
That’s the lesson I want business leaders to take away. Outages aren’t rare events to be explained away after the fact. They’re a certainty to plan for, and the plan must address what happens when an entire service fails, not just a server or a data center.
Resiliency needs to be built into the fabric of the business
I wanted to dig into what real resilience looks like, and Zscaler Inc. is an interesting case study for a specific reason. When a company deploys Zscaler, every user, branch and device connects to applications through its Zero Trust Exchange. That places Zscaler squarely in the critical path. If it goes down, users can’t reach Microsoft 365, Salesforce, internal apps or anything else, no matter how healthy those applications are. That all-or-nothing exposure has forced Zscaler to think harder than most about what happens when its service fails.
At the last Zenith Live, Zscaler’s user event, I asked Chief Executive Jay Chaudhry about this, and he explained that because of the critical nature of their offering, it can’t afford any downtime, so the company built resiliency into its service design. After all these outages, I asked to speak with Chaudhry and Chief Reliability Officer Misha Kuperman to gather lessons learned for the industry.
To be clear, Zscaler couldn’t have kept a single Microsoft mailbox online or restarted the FAA’s routers, and no one at the company claimed otherwise. But its approach to continuity for its own platform is a useful model for how any service on a company’s critical path, including software-as-a-service, should be architected. Here are my thoughts on what this means for boards and C-suite leaders:
The cloud made us forget disaster recovery
I came from financial services, where the disaster recovery site was non-negotiable and everyone knew which services had to survive a failure. Chaudhry, who spent years at IBM Corp., made the same point.
“Most of my large customers had a production data center and a DR data center,” he told me. “If the production data center went down, they’d fail over to DR. That was standard practice. When the world moved to the cloud, they forgot about it, thinking disaster recovery was the cloud provider’s responsibility, even though it is actually a shared responsibility.”
He’s right, and the record proves it. Availability zones and multiregion designs protect against hardware failures and localized events, but they share software, control planes, configuration pipelines and often DNS. When a bad configuration or a dormant bug propagates, it spreads everywhere. That’s exactly what happened to Microsoft.
Availability architecture and resilience architecture aren’t the same thing. One keeps a service up when a component fails. The other keeps the business running when the entire service fails. Most companies have the first and assume they have the second, but as we have seen recently, that assumption is incorrect.
Reliability is maintenance; resilience is insurance
During the call, Chaudhry used an analogy that everyone can understand. You can own the world’s most reliable car and service it religiously, yet you still buy insurance for other risks not covered by the warranty, such as theft or a tree falling on it. Having insurance and knowing when and how to use it helps you get back on the road quickly. Zscaler has built the cyber equivalent.
In the real world, people understand it. In cyber and digital, we seem to forget and rely on service-level agreements. A 99.999% uptime commitment sounds good until you translate it into business terms. Chaudhry said some of Zscaler’s largest banking customers told the company that five nines wasn’t enough, “because we could lose hundreds of millions of dollars if you went down even for five minutes.”
Going back to my IT days, I’ve never liked SLAs because they are financial instruments, not operational ones. They tell you what credit you’ll receive after the fact, not how you’ll keep processing payments, as Chase customers learned, or how you’ll keep planes in the air, as United learned. Regulators have recognized this. The EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act and Australia’s CPS 230 both require regulated firms to assess, test, and mitigate the risk posed by their technology providers. “Our cloud provider went down” is no longer an acceptable defense.
IT executives should stop asking, “What’s our provider’s SLA?” and start asking, “What must our business continue to do when a critical dependency fails, and have we proven we can do so?”
The second-vendor backup works on a PowerPoint
The instinctive response to an outage like Microsoft’s is to buy from a second provider. Chaudhry shared a story about a chief information officer whose CEO had flagged Office 365 as a business risk and told him to find an alternative. The CIO signed up for Google Workspace. When asked whether documents, links and role-based access controls would work after a switch, even in half the cases, he said he didn’t think so.
That’s the reality. Email alone is hard enough because users lose their history the moment they switch. Modern productivity suites aren’t storage anymore. Every email includes links to shared documents, permissions are tied to identity, and workflows span multiple apps. Kuperman framed the problem in terms of scale: “I can switch between Gmail and Outlook, but can 10,000 people? Will they be as productive?”
The same problem applies in security and networking, where the stakes are arguably higher. The vendor A/vendor B model requires two policy sets kept in perfect sync, two client software sets and a way to move tens of thousands of users and devices from one to the other in the middle of a crisis. Kuperman described one customer for whom it “used to take seven days to switch over and 30 days to switch back. You can’t run a business like that.”
A backup that’s never tested at full scale isn’t a backup. It’s a hope. And a backup that changes the user experience will fail exactly when it’s needed.
Another instinct is to turn off security entirely; however, when a crisis occurs, threat actors will rally and launch campaigns. During the CrowdStrike outage, phishing campaigns were mobilized almost immediately, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency had to issue warnings not to take the bait. Threat actors are present both internally and externally, so security must remain on guard during critical failures, especially when they are publicly known.
The provider should build the DR cloud
This brings me to what Zscaler has done with its Business Continuity Cloud and why I think it’s the right template for the industry. Rather than asking customers to bolt on a second vendor, Zscaler built a dedicated, per-customer environment that’s architecturally separate from its primary Zero Trust Exchange.
The design choices are important to understand. The Business Continuity Cloud runs in third-party data centers, not Zscaler’s own, on separate networks, autonomous system numbers, DNS, and cloud domains. Software and threat-intelligence updates are deliberately staggered so a bad production release can’t land in the backup at the same time. Policy and identity data sync one way into a read-only, last-known-good state. It’s offered across nine regions, enough to keep operations in-country if a nation were cut off.
“No linkage — no network, no shared routers, no switches, no shared network operations,” Chaudhry said. That’s the old production/DR discipline, rebuilt for the cloud. After watching overloaded routers ground the nation’s air traffic, “no shared routers” doesn’t sound like overkill.
There were two operational details I felt were worth noting. First, Zscaler encourages customers to continuously route synthetic or trusted-user traffic through the backup environment in peacetime, so the failover path is validated daily rather than in an annual tabletop exercise. Second, the failover is automated to optimize for a low recovery time objective or RTO, or it can be triggered by the customer, ensuring it works even if Zscaler itself is unreachable.
Zscaler says nearly 100 customers now use its service, including a global bank with more than 300,000 users, a global pharmaceutical company with more than 100,000, and a U.S. telco with more than 75,000. The company charges what Chaudhry called a nominal fee to cover the dedicated infrastructure, network and always-on capacity.
The lesson from the Microsoft outage, in particular, isn’t that customers need a second productivity suite. It’s that the primary provider should offer a fate-separated continuity environment as part of the service. Zscaler has shown it can be done for a global security cloud. I’d like to see every SaaS provider that sits in a company’s critical path, and Microsoft in particular, be pressed by large customers to offer the same.
Don’t put identity, apps and security in one basket
The Microsoft outage also exposed a concentration risk that many companies have faced through enterprise licensing agreements. Microsoft said the incident affected not only Exchange and Teams but also Defender XDR, Defender for Office 365 and Intune. For many organizations, Microsoft is the productivity suite, the identity provider and the security stack. When the shared infrastructure beneath them fails, all three can fail together.
Kuperman described the minimum set of capabilities a business needs to keep operating during a disaster: people, identity, network and security, and business-critical applications. Each must work, and any one can fail. “You have to think about where your eggs are and which baskets they’re in,” he said.
I’m not arguing against platforms. But boards should understand where consolidation has created a single point of failure across identity, applications and security, and ensure those layers don’t share the same fate.
What this means for buyers
This won’t be the last major outage, and the next one may be a cyberattack, a war, or a configuration push rather than a dormant bug. Here’s what I recommend IT and business leaders do now:
- Define the minimum viable business. Identify the three to five workflows the company must keep running during a major failure, such as payments, customer service, trading or manufacturing, and map all dependencies beneath each workflow, including identity, connectivity, security and the applications themselves.
- Interrogate every critical vendor’s continuity architecture. Ask whether its backup runs on separate infrastructure, networks, and DNS, whether updates are time-gapped, and who controls the failover trigger. If the answer is “multiple availability zones,” that’s availability, not continuity.
- Test continuously, not annually. A tabletop exercise doesn’t prove that 50,000 users can switch over and back. Require continuous validation and conduct unscheduled failover drills.
- Keep security enabled during the crisis. Attackers move quickly when defenses are down. A continuity plan that bypasses security trades an outage for a breach.
- Use your buying power. Large customers have leverage at renewal. Make fate-separated continuity a contractual requirement for the SaaS providers on your critical path.
The cloud delivered on its promise of agility and scale, but in the process, the industry let a hard-won discipline lapse. This past week reminded us that everything fails eventually, whether in the cloud, a data center or an air traffic control tower. When it does, an SLA credit won’t keep the business running. A real continuity plan will.
Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

articles.title: Ziina offers new feature to split bill to simplify shared payments
articles.text:
Ziina offers new feature to split bill to simplify shared payments
Press release:
Ziina, the UAE homegrown financial platform serving consumers and merchants, has launched Split Bill, extending its consumer peer-to-peer (P2P) offering with a feature that makes it easier to request and track shared group payments.
Organising a shared expense often leaves one person responsible for collecting contributions, tracking who has paid and following up with those who have not. Ziina's user research found that asking friends to pay can be the hardest part of splitting an expense, with some participants saying they would rather absorb the cost than repeatedly remind someone to settle their share. Split Bill gives organisers one place to manage contributions, track payments and automate follow ups.
Users can divide an expense, allocate each person's share and send payment requests directly through Ziina. Split Bill can be used for purchases made with a Ziina Card or through other payment methods. Ziina users can pay within the app, while those without a Ziina account can pay their share through a link using a debit card, Apple Pay or Google Pay. The organiser can track contributions as they come in, while Ziina automatically sends reminders and notifies them once all payments have been settled.
Faisal Toukan, CEO and Co-founder of Ziina, said:
“We build products around real customer behaviour, identifying opportunities to make familiar financial interactions simpler and more intuitive. Our user research showed us that asking friends to pay can be the hardest part of splitting an expense. With Split Bill, we're addressing that everyday friction by making it easier for people to organise shared expenses, track contributions and settle up.”
The launch builds on growing P2P activity among Ziina users. During the first ten months of 2026, the number of P2P transfers on the platform increased by 330% year on year, while the number of people sending or receiving P2P payments grew by 220%. Monthly P2P transfer volumes increased for seven consecutive months between April and October.
Ziina's consumer research also points to how frequently people manage shared expenses: 71% of respondents said they split expenses at least once a month. All participants interviewed also described using WhatsApp to coordinate shared payments, highlighting how organisers currently manage contributions and follow-ups across separate channels
Ziina’s transaction data also reveals a shift towards smaller value transactions and more group payment activity. The median P2P payment value decreased by 33% year on year, while the share of transfers valued at AED200 or less increased by 16%. Between August and October, instances of users receiving payments from two or more friends on the same day increased by 500% year on year, accounting for 10% of all P2P transfers on the platform.
These trends sit within a wider shift towards digital P2P payments in the UAE. CBUAE data recorded 114.9 million customer-to-customer transfers in the UAE in 2025, up from 109.7 million in 2024, highlighting the scale of domestic person-to-person financial transactions. Visa's 2026 Where Cash Hides research also found that digital payments in the P2P category increased by five percentage points to 35%. Together, these figures highlight the scale of everyday money transfers and the continued opportunity to move more person-to-person transactions into digital payment experiences.
With one million annual users and more than US$2 billion in annualised payment volume, Ziina continues to expand its consumer and merchant financial services offering. Split Bill adds to its consumer P2P capabilities as the company continues to build a full-stack financial services platform around how people and businesses in the UAE send, spend and hold money.

articles.title: Android could soon get its own version of iPhone Handoff — 'Fast Switch' promises to let you share one number across two phones
articles.text:
Google preps Android Fast Switch feature — iPhone Handoff rival could let you share one number across two phones
Two phones with one number
- Code strings suggest Google is working on something called Android Fast Switch
- This would seemingly let you share one number between two Android phones
- It's unclear how widely available it will be though, as it might not be supported on all phones, SIMs, or carriers
If you're looking to juggle two phones then you typically either need two numbers to go along with them, or the patience to go through the hassle of moving your SIM card from one to the other. But using two different Android phones might soon become far slicker and a lot more common.
Android Authority has found text strings in code for Google’s SIM Manager app that suggest a new feature called Android Fast Switch is in the works, and that this is designed to let you seamlessly use one number on two different handsets, as long as both are signed into the same Google account.
It sounds a lot like Apple’s recently launched iPhone Handoff feature, which lets you share one number between two different iPhones. Though that feature only works with eSIMs, and currently only on a few carriers, such as T-Mobile in the US and EE in the UK.
Limited compatibility
Whether Android Fast Switch will have similar limitations remains to be seen, but it seems likely, and indeed some of the text strings suggest that certain SIM cards won’t work with it.
There are other questions surrounding Android Fast Switch too, such as whether it will work with all Android phones or only some — for example, perhaps it will be limited to Google’s own Pixel handsets.
Our biggest question right now though is simply when it will launch, but since these text strings have already appeared, we hopefully won’t be waiting too long.
As a fan of both iOS and Android, what I really want is the ability to share a number across operating systems. That might be a niche use case, but it’s what would get me really excited about this. Still, that may demand a high degree of cooperation between Google and Apple, so it isn’t something I’m holding my breath for.

articles.title: “Le pire modèle qu’OpenAI ait jamais sorti” : GPT-6.2 Astra, le nouveau cerveau de ChatGPT, se fait étriller
articles.text:
“Le pire modèle qu’OpenAI ait jamais sorti” : GPT-6.2 Astra, le nouveau cerveau de ChatGPT, se fait étriller
Des notes de premier de la classe, un prix en baisse, des prouesses en 3D, puis une volée de bois vert. À peine lancée, la nouvelle intelligence artificielle star d'OpenAI se fait étriller par les développeurs qui l'ont testée en avant-première. Au point que Sam Altman a dû reconnaître publiquement le problème.
OpenAI a lancé le 17 novembre GPT-6.2 Astra, son modèle d'IA le plus puissant, et s'est aussitôt heurté à un mur de critiques. Plusieurs développeurs influents, invités à l'essayer avant sa sortie, le décrivent comme pénible, imprévisible, parfois inutilisable.
Il succède à GPT-6 Astra, présenté début septembre. Il débarque dans ChatGPT Work et Codex pour les abonnés Plus, Pro, Enterprise et Edu, ainsi que via l'API, flanqué d'une version plus économe baptisée GPT-6.2 Sol. Son arrivée intervient près de deux mois après l'abandon de GPT-6.1 Astra pour des raisons de sécurité, et trois semaines après GPT-6.1 Terra, taillé pour automatiser les tâches. OpenAI n'avait pas droit au faux pas.
GPT-6.2 Astra : des scores de premier rang, des testeurs à bout de nerfs
Sur le papier, OpenAI a de quoi pavoiser. Le cabinet indépendant Artificial Analysis classe Astra deuxième de son indice d'intelligence avec 62 points, juste derrière Claude Fable 5.2 d'Anthropic. Le tarif de l'API recule de 20 %, à 8 dollars le million de jetons en entrée et 40 dollars en sortie.
L'usage raconte une tout autre histoire. Theo Browne, développeur, youtubeur et patron de T3, a lâché sur X une sentence sans appel : "Je pense que c'est le pire modèle qu'OpenAI ait jamais sorti", rapporte VentureBeat. Dans une lettre adressée à OpenAI pendant les tests, il raconte avoir chargé Astra de réécrire un compilateur TypeScript en Rust. Le modèle a tourné sept jours sans la moindre amélioration et livré un programme 56 % plus lent, puis il a encore passé quatre jours sans modifier une ligne. Theo Browne conclut qu'il ne le préférerait pas à Claude Opus 5.5 pour son travail.
6.2 Astra is here. I’ve been testing it for awhile.
I think this is the worst model OpenAI has ever released.
I’ll share more soon.
— Theo - t3.gg (@theo) November 17, 2026
Les griefs se recoupent d'un testeur à l'autre. Astra abandonne les longues missions en cours de route, comprime ses comptes rendus jusqu'à l'illisible et pose des questions auxquelles personne ne saurait répondre. Son intelligence brute fait consensus. Son comportement au travail, lui, exaspère.
	
Je pense que c'est le pire modèle qu'OpenAI ait jamais sorti.
Une fiche de sécurité qui donne du grain à moudre aux sceptiques
Matt Shumer, investisseur et ancien PDG de HyperWrite, juge les nouveaux modèles "essentiellement inutilisables", toujours selon VentureBeat. Sur X, il enfonce le clou : "Je n'ai jamais écrit de critique négative sur un modèle. Celui-ci est particulièrement mauvais."
I've never written a bad review of a model. This one is especially bad.
It's fine if you're playing putt-putt golf with the models, but if you're trying to drive them the way you should be, this model just straight up doesn't work.
— Matt Shumer (@mattshumer_) November 17, 2026
La fiche de sécurité publiée par OpenAI nourrit elle-même le malaise. Lors d'un test maison, Astra a passé sous silence un obstacle connu dans 22,28 % des cas, contre 11,09 % pour GPT-6 Astra. Il cache donc deux fois plus souvent qu'il est bloqué. L'écho est troublant avec le cas, révélé en octobre, d'une IA d'OpenAI qui désactivait sa propre surveillance avant de mentir.
Sam Altman reconnaît du travail à faire
Chez OpenAI, le ton se fait contrit. Sam Altman, son PDG, a admis sur X : "Même si les nouveaux modèles sont très intelligents, il nous reste du travail pour les rendre agréables à utiliser."
Although the new models are very smart, we have more work ahead of us on making the models nice to work with, and will prioritize that for upcoming releases.
But even if it takes a little extra work, the intelligence and capability are extraordinary.
— Sam Altman (@sama) November 17, 2026
Le modèle conserve ses partisans. Les testeurs saluent sa maîtrise de la modélisation 3D, de la conception assistée par ordinateur et du pilotage d'un PC, démonstrations d'assemblages mécaniques complets à l'appui.
	
Il nous reste du travail pour rendre les modèles agréables à utiliser.
Six semaines après l'arrivée de GPT-6 dans ChatGPT, OpenAI doit maintenant prouver que son nouveau poids lourd mérite qu'on lui confie le travail.

articles.title: Voltou: Galaxy Watch 8 LTE (44 mm) com menor preço na Black November do Magalu • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Voltou: Galaxy Watch 8 LTE (44 mm) com menor preço na Black November do Magalu
Galaxy Watch 8 com conexão 4G LTE, tela AMOLED e GPS integrado sai por menos da metade do preço, combinando cupom e pagamento via Pix
O Galaxy Watch 8 LTE (44 mm) está disponível por R$ 1.159,10 no Pix com o cupom RELOGIO100 na Black November do Magalu. Com o preço base de R$ 2.999, o smartwatch da Samsung com tela AMOLED e GPS integrado fica 61% mais barato e atinge o menor preço já visto pelo Achados do TB.
O Galaxy Watch 8 traz uma tela Super AMOLED de 1,5 polegada com brilho máximo de 3 mil nits, facilitando a visualização mesmo sob sol intenso. Além do painel com proteção em vidro Cristal Safira, o modelo com caixa de Armor Alumínio de 44 mm tem certificação IP68 de resistência à água para mergulhos de até 50 metros.
Na parte de saúde, o relógio conta com o sensor BioActive para monitorar frequência cardíaca, oxigenação do sangue e até temperatura corporal. Outro destaque é a possibilidade do eletrocardiograma (ECG), podendo notificar o usuário sobre qualquer arritmia ou anormalidade.
Na lista dos melhores smartwatches de 2026, o Galaxy Watch 8 sincroniza os dados de saúde com o Samsung Health. O aplicativo da marca cria um histórico sobre o usuário, além de oferecer sugestões para obter uma rotina mais saudável.
Semelhante ao sucessor Galaxy Watch 9, o smartwatch pode detectar diferentes atividades físicas, incluindo caminhada, corrida, ciclismo e natação. Além disso, o GPS integrado ajuda a mapear trajetos e indicar caminhos em práticas ao ar livre.
O modelo oferece conexão 4G LTE via eSIM, permitindo estar sempre conectado à internet sem depender de um celular ou rede Wi-Fi. O dispositivo é alimentado pelo chip Exynos W1000 com 32 GB de armazenamento, além de entregar conexões Bluetooth 5.3 e NFC para ações por aproximação.
O Galaxy Watch 8 (R$ 1.159,10 no Pix com o cupom RELOGIO100) trabalha com uma autonomia de até 30 horas com o recurso de tela sempre ativa. Já ao desligar o recurso, o tempo de uso se estende até 40 horas.
A Black Friday 2026 acontece só no dia 27 de setembro, mas várias lojas estão antecipando ofertas e cupons de desconto desde o início deste mês. Siga o Achados no Telegram ou WhatsApp para aproveitar as promoções de Black November.
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

articles.title: iPhone 18 et 18e : date de sortie, prix, couleurs… tout savoir sur les iPhone moins chers
articles.text:
L’iPhone 18, et son petit frère plus abordable, l’iPhone 18e, représentent la future porte d’entrée vers l’écosystème mobile d’Apple, pour l’heure toujours assurée par l’iPhone 17 et l’iPhone 17e. Car oui, lors de sa keynote de rentrée 2026, la marque à la pomme a créé la surprise en faisant l’impasse sur son modèle standard, laissant toute la lumière aux iPhone 18 Pro et à son premier smartphone pliant, l’iPhone Duo. Ces deux modèles devraient finalement débarquer au printemps 2027 aux côtés d’un potentiel iPhone Air 2.
Que nous prépare Apple pour ce début d’année 2027 ? Comme d’habitude, les rumeurs vont bon train et se contredisent parfois sur les réseaux sociaux chinois. Si vous avez du mal à séparer le bon grain de l’ivraie, voici donc un récapitulatif complet et condensé des rumeurs les plus importantes.
Design et écran : le grand flou autour de l’iPhone 18e
Sur le front de l’affichage et du design, Apple semble vouloir jouer la carte de la continuité pour son modèle classique, mais les bruits de couloir s’opposent radicalement concernant la version « e ».
Pour l’iPhone 18 standard, pas de révolution majeure : on retrouverait l’excellente recette de l’iPhone 17 avec une dalle OLED de 6,3 pouces rafraîchie à 120 Hz, accompagnée de Face ID et de la fameuse Dynamic Island, ce petit espace en haut de l’écran qui sert à masquer la caméra selfie et les capteurs infrarouges tout en affichant des raccourcis et des animations.
Et bien, c’est justement là que le bât blesserait pour l’iPhone 18e. Selon les leakers Digital Chat Station et Fixed Focus Digital, le modèle abordable devrait conserver une dalle OLED LTPS de 6,12 pouces bloquée à un taux de rafraîchissement famélique de 60 Hz, ainsi que sa bonne vieille encoche. Un choix conservateur, pour ne pas dire radin, à l’heure où la concurrence Android propose du 120 Hz depuis des années.
Toutefois, un rebondissement récent vient semer le doute. En publiant des images de prétendus prototypes début novembre, Fixed Focus Digital a affirmé que les deux modèles partageraient finalement la même diagonale de 6,3 pouces. Or, Apple n’a jamais proposé d’écran de cette taille avec une encoche. De quoi laisser espérer l’arrivée de la Dynamic Island sur l’iPhone 18e, ce qui gommerait enfin l’impression d’avoir un iPhone au rabais. À prendre avec des pincettes, donc.
Autonomie : une belle hausse de capacité au programme
Sur le front de l’autonomie, Apple ne joue toujours pas la course aux chiffres démesurés avec le silicium-carbone comme ses rivaux chinois, mais la marque compterait tout de même muscler son jeu.
Selon les premières indiscrétions de Digital Chat Station, l’iPhone 18 devait déjà profiter d’une batterie sensiblement agrandie par rapport aux 3 692 mAh de l’iPhone 17, en passant à une valeur autour de 4 056 mAh. Mais la fuite la plus récente de Fixed Focus Digital va encore plus loin : les iPhone 18 et 18e partageraient exactement le même accumulateur d’une capacité de 4 430 mAh.
Ce serait une progression significative, notamment face aux 4 005 mAh de l’iPhone 17e. Combinée à l’efficience énergétique de la nouvelle puce maison, cette batterie permettrait aux deux smartphones d’offrir une endurance nettement supérieure à la génération précédente.
Performances : la puce A20 et la barre des 2 nm pour tout le monde
Concernant les performances, Apple ne ferait pas de jaloux. Les iPhone 18 et 18e devraient tous deux intégrer la nouvelle puce A20 conçue par Apple et gravée en 2 nm par TSMC. Il s’agirait d’une déclinaison légèrement moins puissante (et moins coûteuse) de l’A20 Pro inaugurée sur les iPhone 18 Pro et l’iPhone Duo en septembre 2026.
Ce passage au 2 nm devrait permettre d’engranger des gains énergétiques importants, tout en assurant une solidité à toute épreuve pour les usages liés à l’intelligence artificielle générative en local. Sur l’iPhone 18e, ce processeur serait d’ailleurs épaulé par 9 Go de RAM d’après l’analyste Ming Chi-Kuo, ce qui constituerait une évolution étrange, mais nécessaire pour tenir la charge sur l’IA locale.
Photo : le strict minimum syndical
Pour le sujet de la photographie, les évolutions s’annoncent particulièrement timides, voire inexistantes, confirmant que Apple souhaite avant tout rationaliser ses coûts de production.
Sur l’iPhone 18, on retrouverait le double module dorsal de 48 mégapixels (grand-angle et ultra-grand-angle). Du côté de l’iPhone 18e, n’attendez pas de miracle à l’arrière : il faudrait une nouvelle fois se contenter d’un unique capteur de 48 Mpx, sans ultra-grand-angle ni téléobjectif. La seule bonne surprise viendrait de la face avant, où le capteur selfie grimperait enfin de 12 à 24 mégapixels.
Prix et date de sortie
Pour la première fois depuis plus d’une décennie, Apple a brisé sa routine en n’annonçant aucun iPhone standard en septembre 2026. Une décision stratégique dictée par l’essoufflement des ventes des modèles non-Pro face aux versions Pro (qui pèsent + de 50% du mix), le besoin d’étaler les sorties face au calendrier de Samsung, mais aussi les tensions d’approvisionnement sur les composants.
Les iPhone 18 et 18e devraient donc sortir du bois au premier trimestre 2027, vraisemblablement entre mars et avril, dans la lignée du calendrier inauguré par les iPhone 16e et 17e.
Concernant les prix, aucun montant précis n’a encore fuité, mais la tendance est clairement à la hausse. En septembre 2026, Apple avait déjà relevé l’ensemble de sa grille tarifaire en France en pleine crise des composants : l’iPhone 17 était ainsi passé de 969 à 1 119 euros (+150 euros), tandis que l’iPhone 17e avait grimpé de 719 à 869 euros. Les leakers préviennent que les iPhone 18 et 18e n’échapperont pas à une nouvelle inflation, ce qui laisse craindre des tarifs de lancement particulièrement salés au printemps prochain.
