articles.title: GTA 6: Auf diese 4 Aspekte der Open World solltet ihr beim ersten Spielen achten
articles.text:
GTA 6: Auf diese 4 Aspekte der Open World solltet ihr beim ersten Spielen achten
Wenn ihr nach all dem langen Warten endlich in Grand Theft Auto 6 den fiktiven Bundesstaat Leonida erkunden könnt, richtet sich euer Blick wahrscheinlich erstmal auf die schiere Opulenz der Bilder: die feinen Lichteffekte in den Nächten von Vice City, die flirrende Hitze über den Sümpfen oder die realistisch modellierten Charaktere. Doch der eigentliche Generationssprung von GTA 6 steckt nicht in höheren Texturauflösungen oder noch besseren Partikeleffekten – so imposant das alles auch sein mag.
Die wirklich interessanten Neuerungen sind hinter der glänzenden Oberfläche zu finden. Im unsichtbaren Räderwerk von Rockstars hauseigener Rage-Engine. Wer das Spiel nicht nur als reine Action-Kulisse durchrast, sondern zwischendurch stehen bleibt und genau beobachtet, entdeckt ein eng verzahntes Zusammenspiel aus verschiedenen Systemen, die das Spiel besonders lebendig erscheinen lassen. Auf diese vier technischen Aspekte lohnt es sich beim ersten Streifzug besonders zu achten.
GTA 6: Künstliche Intelligenz statt Zufallsgenerator
In der Debatte um Games und Künstliche Intelligenz wird die KI oft mit generativen Werkzeugen gleichgesetzt, die Entwickler nutzen, um etwa Artwork zu erstellen oder Level zu designen. Rockstar Games aber sagt, dass sie KI nicht auf diese Weise eingesetzt haben, jede Straße, jedes Kleidungsstück und jedes Artwork sei handgefertigt.
Der technologische Sprung ist stattdessen in der System- und Verhaltens-KI zu finden, die die Kulissen des Spiels zum Leben erweckt. Aus veröffentlichten Patenten des Publishers geht hervor, wie Rockstar klassische, starre Skript-Schleifen und Entscheidungsbäume durch mehrstufige Modelle und dynamische Gewichtungen ablöst.
Das werdet ihr etwa im überarbeiteten Fahndungssystem erleben können. Während die Polizei in früheren Serienteilen oft wie telepathisch vernetzte Verfolger agierten, die immer genau wussten, wo ihr gerade seid, setzt GTA 6 stärker auf zeugenbasierte Meldungen und taktische Einkreisung. Beim Spielen könnt ihr beobachten, wie Informationen durch die Spielwelt wandern: Wer hat eine Tat tatsächlich gesehen? Wann greift ein Passant zum Telefon? Und genügt es, ungesehen um die Ecke zu biegen und das Fahrzeug zu wechseln, damit Suchtrupps zunächst nur das alte Kennzeichen verfolgen?
Ebenso interessant ist das Gedächtnis der Open World. Das Spiel bewertet, ob Überfälle sauber und professionell ablaufen oder in unsinnigem Blutvergießen enden. Diese Einstufung wirkt sich darauf aus, wie nervös Ladenbesitzer, Passanten und Sicherheitskräfte auf die von euch gesteuerten Protagonisten Jason Duval und Lucia Caminos reagieren. Statt eines binären Gut-Böse-Schemas entsteht ein kleinteiliges Netz aus Konsequenzen, das bestimmte Stadtteile nach wiederholten Eskalationen spürbar angespannter wirken lässt.
NPCs als eigenständige Akteure in GTA 6
An belebten Knotenpunkten wie Vice Beach oder den Einkaufsmeilen von Downtown drängen sich deutlich mehr NPCs, also Non-Player-Characters, gleichzeitig als es in früheren Teilen von GTA noch der Fall war. Diese größeren Menschenmengen wären jedoch kaum der Rede wert, wenn alle Passanten nach demselben Muster agieren und reagieren würden. Denn gerade in Videospielen ist Mehr nur selten auch Besser. 
Die bemerkbare Neuerung in GTA 6 erkennt ihr daran, wie diese NPCs situativ und individuell reagieren. Fällt ein Schuss oder kracht ein Wagen in eine Absperrung, flüchten Umstehende nicht mehr wie eine synchronisierte Herde in dieselbe Richtung. Je nach Entfernung, Blickfeld und Charaktereigenschaften, suchen manche hinter Mauern Deckung, andere erstarren kurz oder zücken ihr Smartphone, um das Geschehen für die spielinterne Social-Media-Plattform live zu streamen.
Ein genauer Blick auf die Bewegungsabläufe verrät zudem, wie eng Animation und Physik mittlerweile verschmolzen sind. Durch modernes Motion Matching und eine weiterentwickelte Version der Euphoria-Physik-Engine reagieren NPCs nicht mehr mit vorgefertigten Standard-Animationen auf Rempler, Stürze oder Treffer. Im Spiel lohnt es sich daher, auf kleine Alltagsmomente zu achten: Stolpert ein abgelenkter Passant über eine Bordsteinkante, stützt er sich instinktiv an der nächsten Hauswand ab. Auf Treppenstufen passen sich Fußstellung und Körperschwerpunkt fließend an die Neigung an.
Auch sind die Dialoge und Monologe der NPCs inzwischen deutlich komplexer. Die Charaktere sprechen kontextabhängige Dialogzeilen, passend zur Tageszeit, dem Wetter, der Umgebung oder dem Zustand eurer Spielfigur. Ein verschwitztes Shirt nach einem Sprint, Schmutz an der Kleidung oder ein plötzlicher Platzregen schlagen sich unmittelbar in Kommentaren und Handlungen nieder. So wirken die Bewohner Leonidas weniger wie austauschbare Statisten und mehr wie Nachbarn mit eigenem Tagesrhythmus.
Berufsverkehr und mehr
Jahrelang war der Straßenverkehr in Open-World-Spielen kaum mehr als eine bewegliche Hindernisbahn auf unsichtbaren Schienen. In GTA 6 steuert eine hierarchische Wegfindungs-KI die Verkehrsströme auf Basis von Tageszeit, Straßenzustand und aktuellen Störungen. Gleichzeitig weisen die zugrunde liegenden Systeme den einzelnen Fahrern unterschiedliche Persönlichkeitsmerkmale wie Geduld, Risikobereitschaft oder Aggressivität zu.
Wer sich auf eine vielbefahrene Kreuzung stellt oder einen kleineren Blechschaden provoziert, kann diese Profile unmittelbar studieren: Vorsichtige Fahrer vergrößern bei Störungen den Sicherheitsabstand und scheren behutsam aus, während ungeduldige Hitzköpfe riskant die Spur wechseln, hupen oder sich lautstarke Wortgefechte liefern. Hinzu kommen spürbare Rushhour-Wellen am Morgen und am späten Nachmittag, in denen Hauptverkehrsadern tatsächlich verstopfen und sich Einsatzfahrzeuge mit Blaulicht erst eine Gasse bahnen müssen.
Ergänzt wird das Verkehrsbild durch bodenständige Logistik- und Fahrzeugmechaniken. Lieferwagen folgen nachvollziehbaren Routen, Fahrzeuge verfügen über Diebstahlsicherungen, die das spontane Knacken teurer Sportwagen erschweren, und Tank- sowie Ladestationen binden Autos stärker in den Alltag der Spielwelt ein. Der Verkehr ist damit kein bloßer Hintergrund mehr, sondern ein unberechenbarer taktischer Faktor bei jeder Flucht.
Wetter als Spielmechanik
Das fiktive Gegenstück zu Florida bietet sich für drastische Wetterumschwünge freilich sehr gut an. In GTA 6 dient das Klima nicht nur dazu, die Atmosphäre des Spiels zu verändern, sondern hat schon nahezu Simulations-Charakter. Volumetrische Wolkentürme, die nicht nur Textur-Tapete sind, ziehen über den Himmel und erzeugen lokale Mikroklimata – es kann also an der Küste stürmen, während wenige Kilometer landeinwärts noch die Sonne scheint.
Besonders aufmerksam solltet ihr dabei auf das Zusammenspiel zwischen Wind, Wasser und Fahrzeugphysik achten. Starke Böen rütteln nicht nur Palmen und Leuchtreklamen durch, sondern türmen Wellen auf, erschweren den Landeanflug mit leichten Flugzeugen und beeinflussen sogar das Fahrverhalten von schnellen Sportwagen. Setzt tropischer Platzregen ein, sammeln sich Pfützen auf dem Asphalt, der Bremsweg verlängert sich und die Sichtweite sinkt stark.
Und natürlich wirkt sich das Wettersystem auch auf die Charaktere in der Spielwelt aus: Fußgänger spannen Regenschirme auf oder flüchten unter Vordächer, Autofahrer drosseln bei Nässe ihr Tempo und selbst die Tierwelt in den Feuchtgebieten passt ihr Verhalten an die Witterung an. All das lohnt es sich zu beobachten.
Die spannendsten Momente von GTA 6 erlebt ihr also nicht unbedingt bei wilden Verfolgungsjagden und lauten Schusswechseln. Auch nicht in den Missionen, die mitunter sogar etwas monoton werden können. Sondern in den scheinbar nebensächlichen Momenten dazwischen. Wenn ein plötzlich aufziehender Küstensturm den Feierabendverkehr ausbremst, ein ungeduldiger Fahrer ein riskantes Überholmanöver wagt, Passanten einen Unfall direkt mit dem Smartphone festhalten und eine Streife aufgrund von Zeugenaussagen die Fahndung beginnt. Genau in diesen ungeskripteten Kettenreaktionen könnt ihr eine Welt erleben, die dank ihrer vielen Systeme so lebendig wirkt wie kaum eine andere zuvor.

articles.title: MS Dhoni's startup investments: 13 companies he has backed
articles.text:
Inside MS Dhoni’s startup playbook: 13 companies backed by Captain Cool
From Garuda Aerospace to SolarSquare, explore 13 startups backed by MS Dhoni across fintech, electric mobility, gaming and clean energy.
MS Dhoni's retirement from the Indian Premier League (IPL) as a player marks the end of an important chapter in his cricketing career. On November 17, 2026, Chennai Super Kings (CSK) announced that Dhoni would take up the role of team mentor from the 2027 season.
However, cricket is not the only field where Dhoni has built a presence. Over the years, the former Indian captain has invested in several Indian startups through personal investments and his family office, Midas Deals.
His investment portfolio spans fintech, drone technology, electric mobility, food, gaming, digital entertainment and renewable energy.
Here are 13 startups and companies backed by MS Dhoni.
1. Garuda Aerospace
Founded in 2015 by Agnishwar Jayaprakash, Chennai-based Garuda Aerospace develops drones for agriculture, defence, infrastructure and industrial applications. Dhoni invested in the company in June 2022 and became its brand ambassador. In February 2024, he acquired a 1.1% stake for Rs 4 crore.
2. Khatabook
Founded in 2018, Bengaluru-based Khatabook is a fintech platform that helps small businesses and merchants manage digital bookkeeping and daily transactions. Dhoni invested in the startup in March 2020 and also became its brand ambassador. The investment amount was not disclosed.
3. CARS24
CARS24 is a Gurugram-based online marketplace for buying and selling pre-owned vehicles. Founded in 2015, the company uses technology to simplify vehicle valuation, inspection and transactions. Dhoni invested in the startup in August 2019 as part of its Series D funding round.
4. HomeLane
Founded in 2014, HomeLane is a Bengaluru-based home interior design company that helps homeowners plan and customise their living spaces. Its services include modular kitchens, wardrobes and complete home interiors. Dhoni invested in the company in August 2021, although the investment amount was not disclosed.
5. EMotorad
Pune-based EMotorad manufactures electric bicycles for urban commuting and recreational use. Founded in 2020, the company aims to make electric mobility more accessible. Dhoni invested an undisclosed amount in the startup in April 2024 in exchange for equity and also became its brand ambassador.
6. Shaka Harry
Shaka Harry is a plant-based protein and alternative meat brand based in Bengaluru. It develops plant-based food products for consumers looking for alternatives to conventional meat. Dhoni invested in the company in 2022, although the financial details of the investment were not disclosed.
7. 7InkBrews
Mumbai-based 7InkBrews operates in the food and beverage industry. Dhoni became a co-founder, shareholder and brand ambassador of the company in April 2021. Its consumer brand, Copter7, offers chocolates and beverages inspired by Dhoni's iconic helicopter shot and jersey number seven.
8. Tagda Raho
Tagda Raho is a fitness startup that combines traditional Indian exercise techniques with modern fitness practices. Based in Bengaluru, the company promotes indigenous workout methods and fitness equipment. Dhoni invested in the startup in November 2023.
9. ACKO
ACKO is a digital-first insurance company offering products across motor, health and travel insurance. The company uses technology to simplify insurance purchases and claims. In July 2025, Dhoni joined ACKO as an investor and brand ambassador through his family office.
10. Kuku
Kuku is a Bengaluru-based digital storytelling platform operating across audio entertainment, educational content and short-form video. Its products include Kuku FM, Kuku TV and Guru. In March 2026, Dhoni invested in the company and became the brand ambassador for its microdrama platform, Kuku TV. The investment amount was not disclosed.
11. LightFury Games
LightFury Games is a gaming startup developing cricket-based gaming experiences for digital audiences. In 2025, the company raised $11 million in a funding round involving investors such as Blume Ventures, V3 Ventures, MIXI and Times Internet. Dhoni participated as a strategic investor alongside cricketers Jasprit Bumrah, Hardik Pandya and Ravindra Jadeja.
12. SolarSquare
SolarSquare is a rooftop solar company that provides residential solar installation and related services. Founded in 2015, the company helps households adopt solar energy solutions. In July 2026, Dhoni invested in the startup through his family office, Midas Deals, and joined as its brand ambassador as part of its $53 million Series C funding round.
13. BluSmart
BluSmart was an electric mobility startup that operated an all-electric ride-hailing service and EV charging infrastructure. Dhoni's family office invested in the company during its pre-Series B funding round in June 2024. However, the company suspended its ride-hailing operations in 2025 following financial and regulatory challenges.
Final thoughts
MS Dhoni's investments reflect his growing involvement in India's startup ecosystem beyond professional cricket. His portfolio spans businesses working in financial technology, electric mobility, drone manufacturing, digital entertainment and clean energy.
While the investment amounts and ownership details remain undisclosed for several companies, his involvement demonstrates how sports personalities are increasingly participating in India's entrepreneurial ecosystem.
As Dhoni transitions from an IPL player to a mentor, his business interests offer another perspective on his journey beyond the cricket field.

articles.title: Introducing workload recovery and expanded infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Introducing workload recovery and expanded infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
Large training jobs can fail even when every node looks healthy. A GPU with a subtle fault can pass its stress tests and still return wrong values. When a job stalls on an NCCL timeout, it keeps its GPUs, and Slurm still shows it as running. If a device plugin crashes on one node, the job fails with an error that never mentions the plugin. Teams usually find these problems only after the loss diverges or the job fails, and by then the compute is spent. Each of these failures lowers goodput, the share of your cluster’s time that goes to useful training. Today, we’re introducing workload recovery and infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod that catch these failures sooner and raise the goodput of your training workloads.
SageMaker HyperPod already handles nodes that report hardware faults. The health monitoring agent (HMA) watches each node for GPU errors, deep health checks test nodes during provisioning, and automatic node recovery reboots or replaces faulty hardware. These features look at one node’s hardware at a time. They can’t tell whether the GPUs train correctly, whether a job is still making progress, or whether the Kubernetes components a job depends on are working.
In this post, we walk through the three new capabilities that catch these failures. For each one, we show how to set it up and what it reports when it finds a problem:
- MultiNodeTrainingValidation is a new deep health check for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). When HyperPod provisions an instance, or when you run the check on demand, it trains a small model on the instance and then across instances of the same type. The instance fails if the loss becomes NaN or infinite, or training doesn’t finish in time.
- The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches the Kubernetes layer of an EKS cluster for problems such as crash-looping device plugins, missing DaemonSets, and tainted nodes. When a job fails, it reports the pods and nodes involved as Kubernetes events and Amazon CloudWatch logs.
- Hung job detection finds Slurm jobs that have stopped making progress. An agent on each node watches the job’s output and GPU activity, or log patterns that you define. It writes an event to CloudWatch and can cancel the job so that Slurm requeues it.
Why node health alone isn’t enough
The existing HyperPod resiliency features check a single node at a time. The health monitoring agent (HMA) watches each node for GPU errors such as Xid and NVLink faults, Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) errors, and kernel errors. The InstanceStress deep health check runs DCGM level 4 diagnostics and tests each instance’s GPUs, GPU memory, NVLink, and EFA devices. The InstanceConnectivity check runs NCCL tests across GPU instances, or NCCOM tests on AWS Trainium. Together, these confirm that each node’s hardware works. They don’t show whether the GPUs compute correctly, whether a job is still making progress, or whether the cluster’s Kubernetes components are healthy. Three kinds of failure get past them:
- Numerical faults – A GPU can pass every hardware test and still compute wrong results. The first sign is often NaN or infinite loss in a production run. Meta attributed 6 of the 419 unexpected interruptions in its 54-day Llama 3 405B pre-training run to silent data corruption (The Llama 3 Herd of Models).
- Hung jobs – An NCCL timeout, a stalled data pipeline, or a deadlock can stop a job without ending it. The job keeps its GPUs and their memory, and Slurm reports it as running until someone checks the loss curve or the log.
- Cluster-level failures – Some failures happen in Kubernetes, not in a node’s hardware. A device plugin crash-loops, a required DaemonSet never starts on a new node, or ranks on different nodes fall out of step in an NCCL collective. HMA checks each node on its own, so it doesn’t see these problems. When the job fails, the error often doesn’t say which pod or node caused it.
Solution overview
Each capability covers a different point in a training run. MultiNodeTrainingValidation runs when instances are provisioned, or on demand, and confirms that their GPUs train correctly. Hung job detection runs alongside each Slurm job and catches a job that has stopped making progress. The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches the cluster continuously and, when a job fails, reports the pods and nodes that were involved. The following table summarizes the three.
| Capability | What it catches | When it runs | Available on | 
| MultiNodeTrainingValidation deep health check | NaN or infinite loss, or training that doesn’t finish in time, on GPUs that pass hardware checks | When instances are created or updated, or on demand | EKS clusters, on supported EFA-enabled NVIDIA GPU instances | 
| HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent | Node condition changes, pod and DaemonSet failures, and failed training jobs, with the pods and nodes involved. NCCL communication state for jobs that opt in | Continuously | EKS clusters | 
| Hung job detection | Jobs that stop making progress but don’t exit | While each job runs | Slurm clusters | 
Hung job detection is new for Slurm clusters. On EKS clusters, HyperPod already detects hung jobs that run through the HyperPod training operator, and Ray Train jobs get hang detection by default. We describe both options in the hung job detection section.
Each capability targets a different source of lost goodput. Scheduling goodput is the share of time that all the resources a job needs are available. Runtime goodput is the share of that time in which the job makes forward progress. Program goodput is the share of the hardware’s peak performance that the job gets. The following table shows the effect of each capability.
| Capability | Scheduling goodput | Runtime goodput | Program goodput | 
| MultiNodeTrainingValidation | Instances that fail the training test are labeled and, with automatic node recovery, replaced, so jobs don’t start on hardware that produces invalid output | Fewer production runs lost to NaN or infinite loss from a faulty GPU | Flags instances whose training doesn’t finish within the time limit | 
| HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent | Reports nodes that lose GPUs or EFA devices, missing device plugins, and taints, so you can restore capacity sooner | Names the pods and nodes behind a failed job, so you find the cause and restart sooner | No direct effect | 
| Hung job detection | No direct effect | Flags a hung job in minutes instead of hours, and can cancel it so Slurm requeues it | No direct effect | 
Consider a pre-training job running on 32 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (256 NVIDIA H100 GPUs). If the job hangs at 1:00 AM and no one notices until 9:00 AM, it wastes 256 instance-hours or 2,048 GPU-hours. At the SageMaker HyperPod on-demand price of approximately $66 per instance-hour in US East (N. Virginia), the hang costs about $16,900. With a 15-minute hung job detection rule, HyperPod cancels the stalled job and Slurm requeues it. The hang costs about $530 instead, saving approximately $16,400.
Validate training correctness with the MultiNodeTrainingValidation deep health check
The MultiNodeTrainingValidation deep health check trains a fixed, known-good workload, first on each instance and then across instances. It catches GPUs that pass InstanceStress and InstanceConnectivity but produce NaN or infinite loss once they train together. If an instance fails, HyperPod labels it as failed and, with automatic node recovery turned on, reboots or replaces it. When the check runs during provisioning, this happens before your jobs can use the instance.
How it works
MultiNodeTrainingValidation adds two tests to the deep health check run:
- Tiny Megatron test: A short Megatron-LM training run on all GPUs of each instance.
- Megatron test: The same workload across instances of the same type, communicating over EFA.
Either test fails an instance if the training loss becomes NaN or infinite, or if training doesn’t finish within the time limit. The workload is fixed, so a failure points to the hardware rather than to a model or code change.
The following table shows how it fits with the other deep health checks.
| Check | What it runs | What it catches | 
| InstanceStress | GPU and NVLink count, DCGM level 4 diagnostics, and EFA latency and bandwidth tests (Neuron tests on Trainium) | Hardware that’s missing, failing, or unstable | 
| InstanceConnectivity | NCCL tests across GPU instances (NCCOM on Trainium) | Slow or broken communication between instances | 
| MultiNodeTrainingValidation | Tiny Megatron test on each instance, Megatron test across instances | GPUs that run but train incorrectly: NaN or infinite loss, or training that doesn’t finish in time | 
Prerequisites
You need the following:
- An Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon EKS.
- An instance group of a supported EFA-enabled NVIDIA GPU instance type, such as ml.p5.48xlarge. The Megatron test runs across instances of the same type.
Turn on MultiNodeTrainingValidation for an instance group
HyperPod runs deep health checks when it creates or updates instances. To include MultiNodeTrainingValidation, add it to OnStartDeepHealthChecks in the instance group configuration that you pass to create-cluster or update-cluster. We turned on all three checks:
To confirm the setting, run the following command:
The output lists the three checks:
Run MultiNodeTrainingValidation on demand
You can also check instances that are already in the cluster, for example before a long pre-training run. Use the StartClusterHealthCheck API:
To check specific instances instead of the whole group, add "InstanceIds": [...] to the configuration.
Check the results
HyperPod writes one line per test to the DeepHealthCheckResults/<id> log stream in your cluster’s CloudWatch log group, /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/<cluster-name>/<cluster-id>. Here’s the stream from our run on two ml.p5.48xlarge instances. TINY_MEGATRON and MEGATRON are the two MultiNodeTrainingValidation tests:
When the run finishes, each instance carries the result as a node label:
For the training details, read /var/log/aws/clusters/sagemaker-deep-health-check.log on the instance, for example through an AWS Systems Manager session. On the instance that ran rank 0, the log ends with a summary of the Megatron test:
The other instance’s log has a line for every iteration, with the loss and a running count of NaN iterations:
In our run, the loss fell from 11.57 to 3.62 over 300 iterations, with no NaN or skipped iterations, at about 507 milliseconds per iteration on 16 H100 GPUs.
How long MultiNodeTrainingValidation takes
On our two-node cluster, the full deep health check took 1 hour 28 minutes after the instances finished their lifecycle scripts. DCGM level 4 diagnostics took most of that. The two MultiNodeTrainingValidation tests added about 8 minutes. Instances can’t take workloads until the checks finish, so plan for this additional time when you add capacity.
| Test | Check | Time since previous result | 
| HARDWARE_CHECK | InstanceStress | 3 min | 
| DCGM (level 4) | InstanceStress | 74 min | 
| EFA | InstanceStress | 1 min | 
| TINY_MEGATRON | MultiNodeTrainingValidation | 4 min | 
| NCCL | InstanceConnectivity | 1 min | 
| MEGATRON (2 instances) | MultiNodeTrainingValidation | 4 min | 
Keep in mind that MultiNodeTrainingValidation tests the hardware with a fixed reference workload. A pass means the instances trained that workload correctly. It doesn’t guarantee that your own job will converge. We recommend running it on new capacity, on replacement instances, and before long pre-training runs.
Catch cluster-level failures with the HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent
HMA watches the hardware on each node, but many failures that stop a training job happen in Kubernetes. A device plugin can crash-loop until its node stops offering GPUs to the scheduler, or a taint can evict a job’s pods. The job error rarely names the pod or node involved, so engineers piece together what happened from kubectl output, per-rank logs, and timestamps.
The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches these resources from one place in the cluster. When something breaks, it tells you what changed and which nodes, pods, and jobs are affected. It reports through Kubernetes events and structured CloudWatch logs. The agent only reports. It doesn’t reboot nodes or restart jobs, because the cause might be in the workload. HMA and HyperPod node recovery still handle hardware faults, and the HyperPod training operator still handles job restarts.
How the agent works
The agent runs as a single pod per cluster in the aws-hyperpod namespace and prefers CPU nodes, so it doesn’t use GPU capacity. It watches the following:
- Nodes: The agent reports these changes: 
         
  - Condition changes such as NotReady or memory, disk, or PID pressure.
  - Fewer allocatable GPUs or EFA devices.
  - Lost NVIDIA capability labels.
  - Added, changed, or removed taints.
  - Missing HyperPod labels.
- Critical infrastructure pods: DaemonSet pods in kube-system, aws-hyperpod, and kubeflow, plus the training operator’s controller. The agent reports crash loops, restarts, container errors, and pods that stay not ready.
- DaemonSets: Required DaemonSets that are missing or have no available pods, rollouts that stall, and pods running on nodes that no longer allow them.
- Training jobs: HyperPodPyTorchJob, Kubeflow PyTorchJob (v1), and Kubeflow TrainJob (v2). When a job fails, the agent records the failure reason with the job’s pods and nodes.
- NCCL communication: For jobs that opt in, the state of the job’s NCCL communicators, read from NCCL’s built-in reliability, availability, and serviceability (RAS) subsystem.
The agent reports what it finds in two places:
- Kubernetes events on the affected node, pod, DaemonSet, or job. A Warning event marks a problem and a Normal event marks its recovery. You read them with kubectl get events and kubectl describe.
- Structured JSON logs in the cluster’s CloudWatch log group, which keep the history after Kubernetes events expire.
The following table lists the events you’re most likely to see.
| Event reason | Raised when | 
| TrainingJobFailed | A HyperPodPyTorchJob or Kubeflow job fails. The message includes the failure reason from the job’s operator. | 
| CriticalPodCrashLoop, CriticalPodRestarted | A device plugin, HMA, or another critical pod crash-loops or restarts. | 
| NecessaryDaemonSetMissing | A DaemonSet you declared as required is missing or has no available pods. | 
| NodeResourceDegraded | A node’s allocatable GPUs or EFA devices drop or disappear. | 
| NodeConditionDegraded | A node becomes NotReady or reports memory, disk, or PID pressure. | 
| NodeTaintAdded, NoExecuteTaintApplied | A node is tainted. For a NoExecute taint, the log lists the pods and jobs that might be evicted. | 
| DaemonSetMisscheduled | DaemonSet pods are running on nodes that no longer allow them. | 
| NodeRecovered, PodRecovered, DaemonSetRecovered | A problem reported earlier has cleared. | 
For the full list of events, see the documentation.
Prerequisites
You need the following:
- A SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon EKS.
- For an existing cluster, kubectl and Helm access to the cluster, and the HyperPod Helm chart from the sagemaker-hyperpod-cli repository.
- NCCL 2.24 or later in the training container, if you want to monitor NCCL communication.
Install and verify the agent
If your cluster already uses the HyperPod Helm chart, apply the agent’s custom resource definition (CRD) first, because Helm doesn’t install CRDs during an upgrade. Then upgrade the release with the agent turned on:
The upgrade also moves the other HyperPod components in the chart, such as HMA and the device plugins, to the chart’s current versions. To see what will change first, run the same command with --dry-run=server.
Check that the agent is running and that its health report exists:
The health report lists the HyperPod components that the agent tracks, such as HMA, and when their status last changed:
By default, HMA is the only required DaemonSet. If your cluster uses the device plugins from the HyperPod Helm chart, add them so that the agent reports a missing plugin. Also add the namespaces where your training jobs run, so that it can link pod failures to their jobs. Each list replaces its default, so keep the default entries. Save the following as krma-values.yaml:
Then apply it:
See what the agent reports
To see how the HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent handles an infrastructure failure, we deployed a small DaemonSet into aws-hyperpod, pinned it to one node, and made it exit a few seconds after starting. It behaves like a crash-looping device plugin without touching the real one. Within seconds, the agent raised events on the pod and the DaemonSet:
Next, we ran a two-node HyperPodPyTorchJob and made one rank exit during training. The agent raised a TrainingJobFailed event on the job:
It also wrote the failure to CloudWatch with the pods and nodes involved, so you don’t need to look them up from the job’s pod list:
The agent writes these logs to the cluster log group, /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/<cluster-name>/<cluster-id>, in streams named SageMakerClusterMonitoringAgent/<instance-group>/<instance-id>. It starts a new stream when it moves to another node, so filter by the stream prefix. For sample queries, see the documentation.
Monitor NCCL communication for a job
NCCL 2.24 and later include the reliability, availability, and serviceability (RAS) subsystem, a small listener in each NCCL process that reports the state of the job’s communicators. For jobs that opt in, the agent reads this report from every pod every 30 seconds.
By default, NCCL binds the RAS listener to localhost inside the pod, where the agent can’t reach it. To opt a job in, you bind the listener to the pod IP instead. That makes port 28028 reachable on the pod network, which NVIDIA’s documentation notes has security implications. Before you turn it on, apply a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy that allows TCP port 28028 only from the agent’s pod and still allows traffic between the job’s own pods. The agent’s documentation includes an example policy. Then set NCCL_RAS_ADDR in the training container:
To confirm the setting, turn on NCCL debug logging with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO and NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,RAS. Each rank then logs the address RAS listens on:
If the address is ::1 or 127.0.0.1, NCCL_RAS_ADDR isn’t set and the agent can’t reach the listener.
For each monitored job, the agent combines the per-pod results into a job-level state. The job is healthy when every pod returns a valid report, degraded when only some do, and unhealthy when none do. Unhealthy usually means the training processes have stopped.
The agent logs a summary after each polling cycle. In a run on two ml.p5.48xlarge instances, every cycle reported both training pods healthy, 30 seconds apart:
The agent also writes each RAS report to CloudWatch, so you can spot communicator problems while the job is still running. In our test, we made one rank of a two-node job stop calling all_reduce. The report from the next polling cycle showed the communicator out of step and named the rank, GPU, process, and node that had fallen behind:
Rank 1 is one operation behind rank 0, so start with rank 1’s GPU on node 10.0.2.22.
Detect and recover hung jobs on HyperPod Slurm clusters
A training job can hang without exiting. An NCCL timeout, a stalled data pipeline, or a deadlock can leave the job holding its GPUs while Slurm still shows it as running. It stays that way until someone notices that the loss or the log has stopped changing. Teams that run Slurm often build their own watchdog scripts and alarms to catch these jobs, and then need to maintain them.
Today, we’re launching hung job detection for SageMaker HyperPod Slurm clusters. It finds these jobs, writes an event to CloudWatch, and can cancel a hung job so that Slurm puts it back in the queue. You turn it on for each job with an environment variable that points to a small rules file. It needs no changes to your training scripts or containers, and it works with PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, and custom scripts.
How hung job detection works
Hung job detection runs as an agent on every node and is off by default. The agent watches only jobs that set the HYPERPOD_HANG_RULES environment variable to the path of a rules file. The rules file decides how the agent detects a hang:
- Default detection watches the job’s standard output and GPU activity. It declares a hang when the output stops for an extended period while the GPUs sit idle but still hold memory. That’s what a rendezvous hang looks like, when one node fails and the others wait at a barrier. It also declares a hang when the output stops for a longer period, whatever the GPUs are doing. In our test, the first case fired 15 minutes after the job’s last output.
- Custom rules watch your log for regular expressions that you choose. A progress rule declares a hang when a line such as your training step message doesn’t appear within its timeout. An error rule declares a hang as soon as a line such as an NCCL error appears. Custom rules replace default detection for that job.
|  | Default detection | Custom rules | 
| Turn on with | {“enabled”: true} | One or more enabled log_pattern rules | 
| Declares a hang when | Output stops while GPUs are idle but hold memory, or output stops for a longer period | A progress pattern doesn’t appear within its timeout, or an error pattern appears | 
| Misses | Jobs that keep their GPUs busy without making progress, such as a job stuck in a loop | Hangs your patterns don’t describe. If a pattern keeps matching, no hang is declared, even with idle GPUs | 
When the agent declares a hang, it writes a HANG_DETECTED event to CloudWatch. If the rules file sets the action to cancel, the agent also cancels the job and Slurm requeues it. With the default action, notify, the agent writes the event and leaves the job running.
Hung job detection is separate from auto-resume, which restarts jobs that exit after a hardware failure. Auto-resume handles jobs that crash and hung job detection handles jobs that keep running without making progress.
On HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS, HyperPod already detects hung jobs in two cases. The HyperPod training operator checks the logs of each HyperPodPyTorchJob against rules in the job specification and restarts the job when it hangs. The same rules can also restart a job whose throughput drops or whose loss spikes. You don’t need Ray for this. For Ray Train jobs, HyperPod hung job detection for Ray watches every worker by default, with no changes to your code.
Prerequisites
You need the following:
- A SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Slurm.
- A HyperPod Slurm AMI released on or after November 10, 2026, which includes hung job detection. Clusters created on or after that date already have it. To check an existing cluster without updating it, run srun --help on a cluster node. If the output lists --no-hang-detection, the cluster supports hung job detection. If it doesn’t, update the cluster software first. The update replaces each instance’s root volume, so back up anything stored there before you update.
- A rules file that every compute node in the job can read at the same path. The agent reads the file from that path on each node. Shared storage such as Amazon FSx for Lustre or Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) is a straightforward option. To keep rules files in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), copy them to the same path on every node, for example in your lifecycle script. If you plan to use a directory such as /opt/slurm, first confirm that it’s shared across nodes rather than local to each one.
Turn on hung job detection
Create a rules file on shared storage. The smallest valid file turns on default detection:
The agent uses whatever rules file a job points to and doesn’t check who owns it. Anyone who can edit the file, or replace it in its directory, can change detection for every job that uses it, including making the agent cancel those jobs. The chmod 600 in the example keeps a personal rules file private to its owner. For a file that a team shares, use chmod 644 so the team can read it and only its maintainer can edit it. In both cases, make the parent directory writable only by its owner so nobody can swap the file.
Then point the job at the rules file when you submit it:
To use one rules file for many jobs, you can also set HYPERPOD_HANG_RULES in a shell profile or a site-wide profile script.
When a monitored job starts, the first lines of its output show that the agent registered it:
These lines also appear when the rules file is invalid, so check CloudWatch for a CONFIG_ERROR event too, as described in the next section.
Add custom rules to track training progress
Default detection can’t catch a job that keeps its GPUs busy without making progress, so we recommend at least one rule that watches for your training steps or epochs. The following rules file cancels the job if no epoch finishes for 45 minutes, or as soon as an NCCL error appears:
The fields work as follows:
- Set enabled to true on each rule. Rules are off by default.
- start_timeout_minutes is how long the job can run before the pattern first appears. Set it longer than the time your job needs to load the model, compile, and restore a checkpoint.
- timeout_minutes is how long the pattern can stay absent after that. Set it longer than the biggest normal gap, including checkpoint saves and evaluation.
- stop_pattern turns the rule off when it matches, so work after training ends isn’t flagged.
- fault_on_match marks an error pattern. One match means the job is hung.
By default, the agent reads the job’s Slurm output file. To watch a different file, set monitoring.log_file. To cut false positives, set metric_evaluation_data_points on a rule so that several 10-second checks in a row must fail before the agent declares a hang. A rules file can have up to 20 rules and be up to 1 MB.
Start with "action": "notify" while you tune timeouts and patterns, and switch to cancel once the events match real hangs.
View hung job detection events in CloudWatch
HyperPod writes detection events from the controller node to the cluster’s CloudWatch log group, /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/<cluster-name>/<cluster-id>, in the stream SageMakerHangJobDetectionEvents/<controller-instance-group>/<controller-instance-id>. Events for every job land in this stream, whichever node the job ran on. To find the events for one job, filter by its job ID:
We tested each detection method on a HyperPod Slurm cluster with two ml.p5.48xlarge instances. The first test job allocated GPU memory and then stopped producing output. Default detection flagged it 15 minutes after its last output:
The layer field shows which method fired: signal_evaluator for default detection, or pattern_evaluator for a custom rule. In a second test, a progress rule with a 2-minute timeout fired 2 minutes after the job’s last step. In a third, an error rule fired about one second after the job printed an NCCL error line. Because that rules file used cancel, the agent also wrote a HANG_ACTION_TAKEN event with the action Slurm took (we’ve left out the time, level, and msg fields):
Slurm put the job back in the queue, and the requeued run started about 2.5 minutes later. sacct shows both runs:
Slurm requeues a job up to the cluster’s MaxBatchRequeue limit, which was 5 on our cluster. A job submitted with #SBATCH --no-requeue reported "action": "cancel" instead and stayed canceled. With notify, there’s no HANG_ACTION_TAKEN event. The agent follows HANG_DETECTED with a record that says Hang notification sent, no automatic action taken.
If a rules file is missing or invalid, the agent doesn’t monitor the job and writes a CONFIG_ERROR event instead. Here’s the event for a rules file with a JSON syntax error:
The job ran to completion without monitoring, and nothing appeared in sbatch, squeue, or the job’s output. Test a new rules file with a short job and check for this event before you use it for production jobs.
With notify, the job keeps running until someone acts on the event. To get an alert, create a CloudWatch metric filter for HANG_DETECTED events and an alarm that notifies an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic:
Turn off hung job detection
To turn off detection for a job that would otherwise inherit HYPERPOD_HANG_RULES, add --no-hang-detection to srun, or to sbatch to cover every step in the job. To turn it off for every job that uses a rules file, set "enabled": false in the file. Running jobs keep their current settings, and the change applies to jobs you submit afterward.
Conclusion
Node health is essential to reliable distributed training, but it does not provide a complete picture of workload health. MultiNodeTrainingValidation detects instances that pass hardware diagnostics but produce invalid training results. The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent connects Kubernetes infrastructure failures to the jobs, pods, and nodes involved. Hung job detection identifies Slurm jobs that remain active after they stop making progress and can return them to the queue automatically.
Together, these capabilities help you detect failures earlier, shorten investigations, and raise goodput by reducing the GPU time spent on workloads that can’t make useful progress. Use MultiNodeTrainingValidation when adding or revalidating capacity, run the HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent continuously on supported Amazon EKS clusters, and begin hung job detection in notify mode before you switch to automatic cancellation. To get started, see the SageMaker HyperPod resiliency documentation for Amazon EKS and the hung job detection documentation for Slurm. To learn more, visit the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod product page.

articles.title: Waymo pulls driverless cars from highways nationwide after California ban
articles.text:
What just happened? Waymo has taken its driverless cars off all limited-access highways in the United States after California regulators ruled that the company's freeway operations posed a danger to the public. The California Department of Motor Vehicles ordered the suspension after three Waymo vehicles entered a closed construction zone on Highway 101 and another attempted to pass California Highway Patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing traffic on Interstate 280. The pullback temporarily ends Waymo's highway operations, nearly a year after the company began offering freeway rides to passengers in the San Francisco Bay Area.
The DMV directive requires Waymo to stop both operating and testing its driverless vehicles on all California freeways, citing "an imminent hazard to public safety." The order will remain in effect until the company takes "effective corrective actions," the agency said. It did not provide a timeline.
Waymo went beyond what the order required. Company spokesman Chris Pappas said the company pulled its vehicles off freeways nationwide that same day. He said the Highway 101 incident "did not involve any injuries or collisions" and that Waymo would review its vehicles' performance while they remain off the highways.
The two incidents highlight areas where the system struggles. On Highway 101, three separate vehicles entered a lane that had been closed for construction. On Interstate 280, a video posted on social media showed a Waymo car attempting to pass two California Highway Patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing traffic. In both cases, the software had to recognize a temporary change in road conditions, whether construction cones and lane closures or police directing traffic, and respond appropriately while traveling at freeway speeds.
Construction zones have caused problems for Waymo before. In June, the company recalled 4,000 robotaxis for a software update after vehicles in Phoenix and San Francisco drove into work zones. Earlier in the year, it also had to update software in thousands of its vehicles after some drove into flooded roads. In each case, the solution involved a software update to the fleet. California's order now requires Waymo to submit its next fix for regulatory review before its vehicles can return to freeways.
Matthew Wansley, a law professor at Yeshiva University's Cardozo School of Law who studies the regulation of self-driving technology, said that, in principle, freeways are "actually a simpler driving environment than local roads." There are no pedestrians, cyclists or cross traffic to track. Robotaxis have also encountered construction zones and police activity on city streets, he told The New York Times, but the consequences of such incidents are generally less severe.
"When you are doing it at highway speeds, the margin for error is a lot lower," Wansley said. "It's very hard to kill someone at 25 miles per hour. It's very easy to kill someone at 65 miles per hour."
Philip Koopman, a professor emeritus at Carnegie Mellon University who studies autonomous vehicle safety, said the state's response was more forceful than regulators have typically been in dealing with the industry.
"Pulling them back from freeways is more of a firm hand than we've seen before, which is a good thing because these are concerning incidents," Koopman said. Wansley and Koopman both said the restriction should help prevent further accidents and give Waymo time to improve its technology.
The ban also threatens Waymo's growth plans, with airport trips likely to take the biggest hit. Freeways provide the most direct routes to major airports, and Koopman said losing access to them cuts into one of the company's most valuable markets.
"Highways are an issue because they really need to get to airports, and if you can't go on highways, that's a real problem for the airport business," he said. "That's a huge fraction of the value they can unlock."
Riders can still reach the airport using surface streets, although the trip may be less convenient. "You can get to San Francisco airport on surface streets, but it's not a lot of fun," Koopman said.
Waymo has not said when it expects to return its vehicles to freeways, nor has it explained what changes it plans to propose to convince the DMV that its vehicles can safely handle closed lanes and police-directed traffic slowdowns at speeds of 65 miles per hour.

articles.title: Business development in the agentic AI era puts CPUs first - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
AI’s GPU focus meets a CPU reality check at Dell and AMD
Agentic AI is rewriting the business development playbook for chipmakers and server builders. Graphics processing units still grab the headlines, but as supercomputing and AI converge, the next wave of demand is landing on central processing units that must fit within data centers’ existing power budgets.
The shift has been building for years. Customers that hung more GPUs off a single CPU found they were starving expensive accelerators of data, leaving them idle, according to Scott Tease (pictured, left), vice president of business development for high-performance computing and sovereign AI at Advanced Micro Devices Inc.
“People have realized how important that CPU is in a GPU architecture. But beyond that, agentic is not necessarily just a GPU thing,” Tease said. “Agentic is going to be very CPU heavy because with agentic, what you’re looking at, you want to go very fast, but you also want concurrency.”
Tease and David Schmidt (right), vice president of PowerEdge product management at Dell Technologies Inc., spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the growing role of CPUs in agentic workloads and the challenges of balancing compute performance with data center power constraints. (* Disclosure below.)
Power limits reshape business development for compute
Dell and AMD have been building rack-scale AI platforms together, but power remains the binding constraint. When Dell began planning its portfolio 2.5 years ago, enterprise customers expected rack power requirements to remain at 15 to 20 kilowatts and said they often ran out of power before filling a rack, according to Schmidt. Dell responded with the PowerEdge R9825, a 3U server built on AMD’s sixth-generation EPYC 9006 processors.
“It’s been optimized for power efficiency and cooling efficiency,” Schmidt said. “That means we’re using less power to cool the system overall, and that’s power that we can return to our customers.”
That efficiency compounds at refresh time. A single EPYC 9006 server can take 13 legacy machines out of production while cutting the system power needed for cooling by 80 percent, Schmidt noted. Tease sees reclaimed power feeding agentic workloads, where agents could turn one researcher’s ideas into thousands of compute jobs.
“Same number of researchers, massive increase in the amount of compute. Agentic is going to continue to drive more and more IT, and we’ve got to find a way to power it,” Tease said.
Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of SC26:

articles.title: Elon Musk says: 'I'm not MAGA' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Elon Musk, who spent $277 million to get Donald Trump reelected president in 2024 and who, during that campaign, declared himself “dark MAGA” and who, after the election, was subsequently photographed sporting a cartoonishly large MAGA hat while visiting the Oval Office, has some news for Americans: None of that necessarily makes him MAGA.
“I’m not MAGA,” Musk declared Wednesday during a conversation with Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times DealBook Summit. Musk joined the conversation via video call, as he is currently in China, joining President Trump for the APEC summit.
“Well, at least I’m not like … I’m not sure what MAGA means,” he backtracked. “If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.”
The comments were made amidst a broader question about how Musk felt in the wake of this year’s midterms, during which a “blue wave” led to Democratic victories throughout the country. Musk, notably, spent a gargantuan amount of money (reportedly some $445 million) to support Republican candidates. Musk admitted Wednesday that such vast political spending might not have been a good use of his money.
“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seen much for it,” he said. “Or maybe it would have been much worse without that. But it certainly shows that, you know, American elections are not just about money.”
During his conversation with Sorkin, Musk also seemed to lean away from his viral edgelord persona and claimed that he held no extreme views. He said: “I don’t think I have like, you know, any kind of extreme political views.”
Sorkin pushed Musk on this a little, noting that some people found his views on immigration extreme, to which Musk said: “Like what?” Mild laughter spread throughout the audience.
Ironically, the last time Musk spoke at DealBook, in 2023, he was in the middle of a very public battle with his social media site X’s advertisers. Critics had accused Musk of platforming a typhoon of hateful content on his site, and advertisers were threatening to walk over it. In response, Musk famously told Sorkin that he hoped those advertisers would “go f—” themselves.
Now Musk has an entirely new set of concerns. Democratic lawmakers in various committees have signaled that they may investigate Musk and his business activities as they probe potential corruption throughout the Trump administration.
Specifically, officials have said they’re interested in scrutinizing Musk’s role in DOGE, the “government efficiency” initiative that Musk launched inside the White House at the start of Trump’s new term, as well as Starlink’s activities in Ukraine, where the company has been accused of throttling the military’s access to its internet service.
Sorkin broached some of the potential concerns for the Tesla CEO: “You hear people like the chairman of the oversight committee saying, ‘Lawyer up,’ and you hear the president saying, ‘If I have to give him a pardon’ — meaning you — ‘I’ll give him a pardon.’”
Musk replied: “I don’t think I need a pardon by the way, because I haven’t committed any crimes.”
Musk then made one of those controversial statements he’s known for, appearing to compare an incoming Texas official to Lavrentiy Beria, the top head of the Soviet secret police under Josef Stalin.
“The incoming Texas, you know, House Majority Leader, said that I should go to prison,” Musk said. “I’m like, the guy’s trying to, you know channel Beria from, like, Stalin, where it’s, you know, show me the man, I’ll show you the crime type of thing.”
It’s not clear who (or what) Musk was talking about. Texas doesn’t have a House Majority Leader. However, he may have been referencing Gene Wu, who is the incoming chair of the Texas House Democratic caucus and who has suggested that Musk be investigated for potential criminal activity.
“Hopefully, in this country, you still need to do an actual crime before you go to prison,” Musk added.

articles.title: 9 best iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch apps according to Apple — from ElevenReader to Cosmos
articles.text:
These are the best iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch apps of 2026 — according to Apple
An app for almost every need
- Apple has announced its App Store App of the Year finalists
- Three apps have been selected for iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch, respectively
- The winners will be announced in the coming weeks
Apple has just revealed its finalists for the best iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch apps of the year, so if you’ve been itching to install something new, there should be something here that’s worth a look.
On iPhone, the finalists include ElevenReader, which lets you listen to books, articles, PDFs, and any other text read in a natural-sounding AI voice.
There’s also (Not Boring) Camera, which simulates an old-school camera with customizable film-inspired looks, and Raylie, which tells you which side of a plane to sit on for the best view, and what sights to expect during your flight, such as sunsets and landmarks.
Over on iPad, the finalists include Cosmos, which lets you create and collaborate on an inspiring mood board. Then there’s Kiddopia, which includes over 3,000 games aimed at teaching children math, language, and more. Finally, there’s Mockup, which helps you sketch, wireframe, and prototype apps and websites.
Track your health, your stress, and the lunar calendar
For Apple Watch, the finalists include Bevel, which takes your health and fitness data and uses it to provide AI-powered, actionable insights.
There’s also Moonlitt, which includes a lunar calendar and will alert you about upcoming lunar events, such as eclipses. And there’s StressWatch, which is an AI-powered stress monitor, designed to show you your stress levels in real time, so you can change your habits to lessen your stress.
These nine apps were selected by global App Store editors for exemplifying “the very best in technical innovation, user experience, and design,” and while the winners will be announced in the coming weeks, any of these finalists should be worth a download if they sound appealing to you.

articles.title: GTA 6 : Free muscle son réseau pour faire face au lancement
articles.text:
Le lancement de la décennie dans le jeu vidéo, GTA 6, a lieu ce soir. Et pour y faire face, Free a mis les moyens !
Même si vous n'êtes pas un gamer, vous n'être sûrement pas passé à côté de cette nouvelle : GTA 6 va sortir officiellement ce soir à minuit, en France. Une sortie extrêmement attendue, puisque l'on dénombre, à quelques heures de ce lancement, un volume de précommandes numériques de près de 16 millions - et c'est sans compter toutes les précommandes en version boîte. Autant dire qu'il va y avoir des téléchargements massifs, que vont devoir gérer les opérateurs des télécommunications.
Free annonce avoir renforcé sa bande passante en prévision du lancement de GTA 6
À partir de ce soir, à minuit, ceux qui veulent jouer à GTA VI vont télécharger près de 212 Go de données. Et vu la popularité folle de ce jeu vidéo, sûrement déjà celui de la décennie, Free a annoncé avoir renforcé sa bande passante.
Des équipes spécifiques sont par ailleurs mobilisées pour l'occasion. L'objectif est de permettre le téléchargement sans souci de tous ceux qui le souhaitent, sans pour autant gêner les autres utilisateurs du réseau.
Un gel du réseau programmé pour les 18 et 19 novembre
Il faut dire que l'on a déjà un exemple avec Orange, qui a enregistré quelque 150 000 prétéléchargements depuis leur ouverture, le 10 novembre. Résultat, le trafic a été doublé par rapport à ce qui est habituellement observable. Le leader français du secteur a pour autant affirmé avoir réussi à gérer sans incident ce trafic exceptionnel.
Du côté de chez Free, selon nos confrères de Frandroid, on a aussi décidé exceptionnellement d'un gel du réseau ce 18 novembre ainsi que le 19 novembre. L'idée est de ne pas programmer d'intervention technique non urgente ou d'opérations de maintenance, qui sont autant de possibilités de créer une panne du fait d'une manipulation. De quoi tenir le choc ce soir ?
Source : Univers Freebox

articles.title: Anthropic raises $81.3B in IPO, surpasses SpaceX's record offering
articles.text:
Anthropic raises $81.3B in IPO, surpasses SpaceX's record offering
Anthropic's IPO surpasses SpaceX's $75 billion offering. The company reported $16.2 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, up from $1.16 billion in the same period last year, even as its reported net loss widened.
Artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic has raised $81.3 billion through its initial public offering (IPO), making it the largest stock market offering on record and surpassing Elon Musk-led space company SpaceX's $75 billion IPO.
Anthropic priced its shares at $83 apiece, above the previously indicated range of $70-78 per share. The company is set to make its Nasdaq debut on Thursday, November 19, at a valuation of approximately $1.5 trillion.
According to the company's statement, the offering comprised 980 million shares, including 956.4 million shares sold by Anthropic and 23.6 million shares sold by its seven co-founders. The founders' share sale is worth approximately $1.96 billion.
Anthropic's IPO will serve as a litmus test for AI companies, with its stock market debut offering an indication of investor appetite for the sector.
The company is also raising $26 billion through a separate private placement, taking the combined value of the IPO and private placement to $107.3 billion.
Co-founded by Dario Amodei and others in 2021, Anthropic reported revenue of $16.29 billion in the first half of 2026, while its net loss widened to $80.75 billion, according to its regulatory filing. In comparison, the company reported revenue of $1.16 billion and a net loss of $12.97 billion in the first half of 2025.
Anthropic’s growth has been remarkable, with annual revenue rising from $41 million in 2023 to $4.59 billion in 2025.
In its IPO filing, Anthropic said, “We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history. If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach and solve problems that have resisted generations of human efforts.”
“Anthropic aims to realise these while navigating and preventing the risks that come with a technological revolution this fast and this powerful.”
Edited by Megha Reddy

articles.title: Netflix CEO admits app may bury stuff you want to watch under stuff you don’t
articles.text:
The streaming wars, or the battle to be the top streaming company, are ongoing, according to Ted Sarandos, a co-CEO of what many would consider today’s frontrunner.
When it comes to subscribers, no streaming service has more than Netflix, which reported having over 325 million subscribers as of January.
But in an interview with Bloomberg published today, Sarandos noted that people are still spending significant time watching traditional broadcast TV.
“The streaming wars are continuing as we go. Half of television engagement in the United States is still linear, old television,” he said, without specifying the source of the statistic. According to analysis from Nielsen, streaming represented 49.6 percent of TV viewing in August, with 36.4 percent coming from broadcast and cable. That still suggests a sizable amount of viewing time for streaming providers to target.
Netflix wants more hits
As Netflix seeks to strengthen its lead against rivals like YouTube and Skydance, there’s extra pressure for it to deliver hit shows and movies.
During the Peak TV era, Netflix drove subscribers by offering exclusive hit shows and movies, like House of Cards, Orange Is the New Black, and Beasts of No Nation (2015). Like many of its rivals, Netflix’s reputation for consistently delivering must-watch series and movies has weakened in the 2020s as streaming customers have become inundated with content and struggle to navigate the vast streaming landscape to find relevant content.
Sarandos said:
I think as Netflix has grown and matured and the business has grown and matured around us, that hit rate really matters. And you’ve got to get ahead of ‘are we on a path to continue [and] maintain that hit rate in the US particularly, but everywhere in the world?’ And I’d say the business is working everywhere in the world, including the US, but we should be doing better in the US than we were. And we’ve got to really focus on our ability to do that.
The CEO said that Netflix is focusing on “the ambition of storytelling” rather than “chasing everything that people just happen to spend five seconds on television on” or relying on AI-generated content.

articles.title: Nvidia says it’s ‘absurd’ to assume that company predicted the agentic moment during Vera’s development – ‘product intuition’ helped drive CPU design, superior memory bandwidth will play critical role in future AI agents, CPU head claims
articles.text:
Nvidia says it’s ‘absurd’ to assume it predicted the agentic moment during Vera’s development – ‘product intuition’ helped drive CPU design, superior memory bandwidth will play critical role in future AI agents, CPU boss claims
It turns out Nvidia doesn’t have a crystal ball, either.
One criticism that has emerged of Nvidia’s Vera CPU, driven by AMD, is that Nvidia – and, to a lesser degree, Arm with its AGI CPU – couldn’t have developed an “agentic CPU,” as the chip is often characterized in Nvidia’s marketing materials. Ian Finder, the head of Nvidia’s data center CPU business, pushed back on that criticism in a recent conversation with Tom’s Hardware Premium at SC26, calling the notion that Nvidia somehow knew about the agentic wave four years ago when Vera development began "absurd."
“There's a conviction around the design philosophy of the part, right? Am I going to sit here and tell you that we have this magic crystal ball around the agentic moment? That would be absurd, right?” Finder said. “But what we do have as a company, and I think this has been proven out in our track record, is [that] we have design intuition.”
Instead of specifically designing Vera for agentic workloads, which would be impossible without a way to see several years into the future, Finder characterized the part by its codesign with Nvidia’s accelerators, something that the team has continued to work on since its first Grace data center CPU. Coming from the assumption that data centers and AI workloads are accelerated (and they largely are), Finder says the co-design approach on the CPU can start in a “conceptually simple space, like what kind of CPU do we need to keep the accelerator fed and happy?”
Although conceptually simple, Finder continually looped back to a particular word to describe aspects of Vera and, to a lesser extent, Grace. “Opinionated” is the word he used, which in the broader context of Vera’s design, shows up in two places. Grace, Finder says, introduced an opinionated memory system with Nvidia’s Scalable Coherency Fabric, while Vera extends that memory system while adding an opinionated microarchitecture, Nvidia’s Olympus core.
The picture Finder paints is one of Nvidia starting from scratch in this space, contrasting it with the “legacy constraints” of, presumably, Intel and AMD in particular, who have large pools of customers with specific needs. As we described in our original breakdown of the Olympus architecture in Vera, Nvidia’s goal doesn’t seem to be to steal market share from AMD and Intel, but rather to grab market share in a CPU space that’s vastly accelerating on the back of AI agents.
This “clean sheet of paper” approach, and Nvidia’s codesign, led to some natural assumptions about what the CPU should do. “If we have silicon that needs really, really great single-thread performance, [and] we also need concurrency, then we need to get there with IPC instead of frequency. We need to make sure we have good loaded memory latency. We need to make sure we have a lot of bandwidth, and you start to design something on a clean sheet of paper that's not encumbered by dollar-per-core economics.”
Although Finder was clear that Vera’s design didn’t explicitly center around the agents we see today, there were early indications of the workload. “To say that four years ago, when we started putting pen to paper on Vera, [that] we absolutely saw the agentic moment, would [not] be... something I would claim, but we were starting to see the beginnings of tool calling and things like that. We certainly knew what we needed from a head node, and we knew the overall shape of this problem.”
As you can see in our Vera CPU benchmarking, the chip doesn’t excel at every workload. And, from the data you can see in our recent AMD EPYC Venice benchmarking, the AMD camp has reclaimed some top spots in several benchmarks. Finder suggests that the superior memory bandwidth of Vera will play a much bigger role in the agentic future as these systems evolve to take better advantage of the compute available.
Taking full advantage of the CPU
We need to rewind for just a moment. When the agentic wave hit earlier this year, some characterized the demand as a shift away from GPUs and toward CPUs. That is incorrect. Rather, as is becoming increasingly clear as these agentic workloads progress, these loops can’t take full advantage of the GPUs in a GPU-centric environment, with GPUs often oversubscribed on host nodes. The solution isn’t to get rid of GPUs, of course, nor is it to stop buying them. Rather, it’s to also buy enough CPUs to properly leverage that compute.
A portion of the AI industry is focused on tackling the problem of fully utilizing the GPU, Nvidia included. GPUs shouldn’t sit idle for very long (if at all) with the demand today, and they don’t. The challenge today is spinning up these agent sandboxes quickly, within milliseconds, so that the CPU isn’t sitting idle, either.
Finder provided an example of using a coding agent. If you’ve used a coding agent before, you’re probably familiar with this process. After prompting, the model will make several small tool calls to read and locate files, passing back to the model in between. These are tiny calls, almost negligible, and the vast majority of the time is spent in the model on the GPU. Then, it may start compiling and testing the project, which is much more bound by the CPU. The GPU, Finder says, isn't sitting idle during that time. It’s being leveraged for another purpose. Finder suggests “that very same thing is going to happen on the CPU.”
“The idea that we're just going to say, ‘OK, the CPU can just chill out here, and we're just going to wait,’ that's not going to happen,” Finder said. “What's going to happen is we're going to pack multiple environments together, and we're going to subscribe the socket.”
This “very interesting computer science problem,” as Finder described it, is being investigated by AI startups such as Daytona and E2B to spin up and close down agentic sandboxes in milliseconds. And serving more agents will naturally put pressure on the memory system, which is an area where Vera has an edge. “We built a product that does really, really well without such optimizations, but as a design point that really will lean into them when the industry starts to catch up to this,” Finder said.
Vera is a fascinating chip, regardless of what you think of it and how it’s presented in marketing materials (from Nvidia itself or elsewhere). Although Grace was the starting point internally, Vera has ridden the wave of agentic to become a much bigger player in the world of CPUs, and Nvidia has already announced that it will follow up with its Rosa CPU featuring the new Rigel microarchitecture. Vera is an opinionated CPU indeed, and time will tell if that opinion is correct.
Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

articles.title: GTA VI ya está disponible en Oceanía y Asia: así se puede jugar antes de su llegada a Latinoamérica
articles.text:
Jugadores de varios países ya pueden descargar y acceder a Grand Theft Auto VI en sus consolas de videojuegos. El lanzamiento escalonado de Rockstar Games ya habilitó el juego en Oceanía y buena parte de Asia.
GTA VI se activa a la 12:00 a.m del 19 de noviembre en cada región, así que la disponibilidad avanza de este a oeste. Mientras usuarios de Nueva Zelanda, Australia, Japón, Corea del Sur, China, Singapur, Filipinas e India ya pueden iniciar la partida, en Colombia, Perú, Argentina y México aún rige la espera.
En qué países ya se puede descargar y jugar GTA VI
Los primeros jugadores con acceso a GTA VI fueron los de Nueva Zelanda, donde el título se habilitó en la madrugada del 18 de noviembre en la mayoría de países de Latinoamérica. Fiyi llegó una hora después. Luego se sumaron las ciudades australianas de Sídney y Melbourne, seguidas por Japón y Corea del Sur.
Algunas horas después se habilitó el juego en China, Singapur y Filipinas. India completa el grupo de territorios que ya pueden jugar la nueva entrega de Rockstar Games que llega luego de trece años de espera.
Qué países serán los próximos en recibir el GTA VI
El siguiente turno corresponde a Emiratos Árabes Unidos. Después llegará el estreno para los países de Europa Central, entre ellos España, Francia, Alemania e Italia. El despliegue en el continente europeo continuará en Reino Unido y Portugal.
La diferencia de husos horarios convierte el lanzamiento en un proceso que se extiende durante varias horas, aunque la fecha oficial de salida para todos los territorios es el jueves 19 de noviembre de 2026.
La modalidad de estreno implica que la disponibilidad depende del horario de cada tienda digital y de la región configurada en la consola. Rockstar Games anunció el lanzamiento para PlayStation 5 y Xbox Series X|S, sin una fecha confirmada para computadores.
A qué hora estará activo GTA VI en diferentes países de Latinoamérica
GTA VI quedará habilitado a las 00:00 del jueves 19 de noviembre en Colombia y Perú. Ambos países comparten el mismo huso horario, así que los jugadores podrán iniciar la descarga o abrir el juego al mismo tiempo.
En Argentina, GTA VI llegará primero que Colombia y Perú. México tendrá horarios distintos según el estado. En Ciudad de México y las zonas que operan bajo el horario central, la activación llegará después que Colombia y Perú. En Quintana Roo, que comparte el horario de Colombia, el juego estará disponible al mismo tiempo.
La predescarga está disponible desde el 10 de noviembre para quienes compraron la edición digital. El videojuego requiere hasta 212 GB de espacio libre en la unidad SSD, así que conviene completar la instalación antes de la medianoche para evitar demoras cuando se active el acceso.
En PlayStation 5, la descarga se gestiona desde la biblioteca o la PlayStation Store. En Xbox Series X|S, el archivo queda disponible desde la Xbox Store después de que el usuario complete la reserva. Las ediciones físicas requerirán conexión a internet, porque incluirán un código de descarga en lugar de un disco.
Qué se conoce sobre la historia de GTA VI
La nueva entrega de la franquicia llevará la acción al estado ficticio de Leonida, con una versión contemporánea de Vice City como uno de los escenarios centrales. Rockstar presentó a Lucia y Jason como los protagonistas de una historia que incluye robos, persecuciones, actividades criminales y una representación satírica de las redes sociales.
Los tráileres oficiales muestran playas, autopistas, zonas urbanas y áreas naturales inspiradas en Florida, Estados Unidos. La campaña principal podría durar cerca de 50 horas y reunir alrededor de 100 misiones distribuidas en cinco capítulos.
Terminar todo el juego podría requerir hasta 200 horas. Entre las misiones figuran la identificación de más de 170 especies animales en Leonida, sumado a desafíos y eventos que aparecen de forma variable durante la partida.

articles.title: Black da Amazon: AirPods Pro 3 com Tradução ao Vivo surge em 10x sem juros • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Black da Amazon: AirPods Pro 3 com Tradução ao Vivo surge em 10x sem juros
AirPods Pro 3 têm Tradução ao Vivo e ANC aprimorado; fones wireless da Apple saem 27% mais baratos em rara oferta no prazo, faltando pouco para a Black Friday 2026
Os AirPods Pro 3 estão saindo por R$ 1.979 em até 10x sem juros na Amazon. Os fones de ouvido da Apple, com recurso de Tradução ao Vivo e ANC aprimorado, recebem desconto de 27% sobre o preço original de R$ 2.699.
Esta é uma rara oportunidade de comprar estes fones no prazo e no precinho, faltando poucos dias para a Black Friday 2026.
Um dos destaques dos AirPods Pro 3, que estão entre os melhores fones wireless do mercado, é o recurso de Tradução ao Vivo. Ele é ativado por gestos e traduz o idioma ouvido para o do usuário; a resposta é exibida na tela do celular, mas só funciona com iPhones.
O cancelamento ativo de ruído (ANC) foi melhorado nesta geração, ao abafar mais ruídos externos e oferecer os modos de uso Ambiente e Adaptável. A função não isola totalmente sons importantes, como os de trânsito, por motivos de segurança.
Os fones possuem um sensor que mede a frequência cardíaca, permitindo assim que o wearable ofereça, por meio do iPhone, suporte a mais de 50 atividades físicas no app Fitness.
O chip H2, os drivers de alta amplitude e os amplificadores de alcance dinâmico fornecem qualidade superior em graves e agudos, e os alto-falantes melhorados oferecem experiência melhorada de áudio espacial.
A bateria dos fones entrega até 8 horas de áudio com o ANC ativado, enquanto o estojo compatível com MagSafe garante autonomia de um dia inteiro, segundo a Apple. A certificação IP57 confere proteção contra poeira, água e suor.
Os AirPods Pro 3 (R$ 1.979 em até 10x sem juros) têm conectividade Bluetooth 5.3 e o kit inclui ponteiras de silicone de diferentes tamanhos, para um melhor ajuste nas orelhas do usuário.
A edição 2026 da Black November tem previsão de durar até o dia 30 de novembro, passando pelo evento principal, a Black Friday que ocorre em 27/11. Até lá, o varejo continuará oferecendo cupons de ofertas em eletrônicos com condições especiais.
