articles.title: Your Proton VPN's iPhone app has just changed its look — here's all you need to know
articles.text:
Your Proton VPN's iPhone app has just changed its look — here's all you need to know
Proton VPN 8.0 is finally on the App Store, and it brings a brand-new globe map, a tougher kill switch, and a new engine under the hood
- Proton VPN 8.0 is now rolling out on the App Store for iPhone, iPad users
- The most visible change is a new interactive globe map
- Under the hood, there's a new VPN engine and a tougher kill switch
Proton VPN's iPhone app looks a little different this week. Version 8.0 landed on the App Store on November 9, and the first thing you'll notice is a brand-new interactive globe map.
We first reported on the update earlier this month, when Proton published the 8.0.0 build on GitHub before it had reached the App Store. Now it's available to anyone running iOS 17 or later.
Proton VPN already sits among the best VPN services we've tested, and since last December, it has climbed to third place in our ranking. This release gives iPhone and iPad owners a fresh way to pick a server, plus some meaningful security upgrades.
Proton VPN – best for privacy 
Based in Switzerland, this privacy-first VPN offers good speeds, advanced anti-censorship features, and a server network that spans 145 countries around the world — including across Africa and Asia, where other providers tend to struggle. While its free VPN plan is handy, it comes with limitations. The good news is that upgrading to a premium subscription will cost you only the equivalent of $2.99 per month.
What's new in Proton VPN 8.0 for iOS
The biggest visual change is the interactive globe. When zoomed in, the view of your current country appears flat, but once you zoom out, you'll find a spinnable globe with Proton's many servers marked out for easy access.
It's the latest step in a steady refresh of the iOS app. Proton overhauled the home screen in April 2025, and a later quality-of-life update moved map pins from the middle of each country to the actual city.
The rest of the 8.0 changelog is less visible but arguably more important:
- Proton protocols: a new Rust-based VPN engine built for stability and censorship resistance.
- Advanced kill switch: blocks all internet traffic unless you're connected to Proton VPN.
- Better kill switch connectivity: you can now reach local network devices and use Apple CarPlay with the kill switch on.
- Persistent NetShield stats: your ad-blocker counts no longer reset between sessions.
NEW: Leave No Trace — A weekly newsletter on digital privacy and online surveillance.
Leave No Trace investigates the companies and governments putting our digital freedom at risk — and the people fighting back.
📩 Subscribe now to get every edition delivered to your inbox every Friday, launching this September.
What it means for you
The globe should make it easier to see where Proton's VPN servers are and where your traffic is exiting, rather than scrolling a flat list of countries.
The new engine matters more in the long run. Proton protocols replace the wireguard-go code that Proton says never sat well with Swift, the language behind its iOS app.
The advanced kill switch is the one to watch if you never want a single packet leaving your iPhone unprotected. Unlike the standard version, it stays active even after you restart your device. Proton does warn that some DNS requests from Apple's own services may still bypass the VPN.
When is it coming to other apps?
Proton hasn't said yet.
Proton protocols are already stable on Windows, and the globe map appeared in beta builds across Proton's major apps in August. But the latest stable Android release, from late October, makes no mention of it.

articles.title: Edge AI Moves Agricultural Intelligence from the Cloud to the Field - EE Times
articles.text:
An agricultural robot moving through a field must do more than collect information: It must interpret what its sensors detect, decide what to do, and potentially act before it reaches the next plant. Sending data to a remote computer for analysis is not always practical, particularly when connectivity is unreliable or decisions must be made immediately.
Xin “Rex” Sun, director of the Peltier Institute for Advancement in Agricultural Technology at North Dakota State University, is confronting that problem in research on AI-assisted crop monitoring.
His laboratory is developing a field platform equipped with sensors that could diagnose crop problems and eventually support interventions. The research involves powerful computing systems, but Sun wants the resulting applications to run on equipment that farmers can use in their fields.
“Edge AI will be the go-to approach, because if the technology can’t run on a robot, combine, or tractor, it’s of little use to farmers,” Sun said. “Farmers aren’t sitting in laboratories doing research. They need technology that works in the field.”
His team uses Nvidia GPUs for demanding research workloads, alongside smaller computing platforms such as Raspberry Pi and Arduino for other functions. The distinction illustrates a fundamental design choice: Different tasks require different amounts and types of processing.
As agricultural machinery becomes more autonomous, equipment manufacturers must make those choices across increasingly complex systems. The challenge is no longer simply getting an AI model to recognize something; it’s giving a machine enough intelligence to respond appropriately without exceeding its power budget or compromising safety.
From sensing to acting
Nvidia’s Chen Su, head of edge AI product marketing, said in written responses to EE Times that agricultural systems are moving beyond individual applications such as crop classification, weed detection, and plant health monitoring.
“Many systems are evolving from single-purpose vision applications into multi-workload edge AI platforms that run perception, crop analysis, localization, navigation, obstacle avoidance, and control together,” Su said.
A precision sprayer, for example, must identify a target and activate the appropriate mechanism at the right moment. A more autonomous machine must also determine its location, navigate the field, detect obstacles, and coordinate its movements with the agricultural operation.
These workloads place different demands on processors. According to Su, the computing requirements depend on sensor count and type, model complexity, machine speed, reaction times, and the number of simultaneous tasks.
The need for onboard processing goes beyond the limited connectivity common in rural areas. Even with a reliable network connection, sending information to the cloud and waiting for a response can introduce unacceptable delays when a machine is moving.
Su described the architectural change as a move from “sense and report” toward “sense, decide, and act.”
That requires more capable onboard computing, sensor fusion, real-time control, and software for developing and validating autonomous systems. Nvidia’s Jetson platforms target such embedded AI workloads, where computing performance must fit within constraints on size, power consumption, heat, and cost.
Not all of the processing needs to take place in one computer. Cameras and intelligent sensors can perform image processing, compression, filtering, and some object detection locally. A more powerful central processor can combine information from multiple sensors to support navigation and planning.
The cloud remains useful for training models, simulation, fleet management, and analytics. But Su expects the principal change over the coming years to be the emergence of complete autonomy stacks running onboard agricultural machines rather than individual AI features operating in isolation.
Matching intelligence to the machine
For NXP Semiconductors, the problem is not simply how to provide more computing power; it’s how to allocate processing across the functions of an agricultural machine.
According to Ramakrishna Karamsetty, senior director of product management for edge and physical AI hardware and software products at NXP, “agriculture is one of the toughest environments for computing.”
Karamsetty, who joined NXP after more than 25 years at Intel, pointed to differences in terrain, crops, climate, and connectivity. A system developed for a farm in Arizona may encounter entirely different conditions in Idaho, China, or India. “There is no one-size-fits-all solution,” he told EE Times.
The type of agricultural operation also determines the amount of intelligence required. Harvesting corn differs from picking delicate fruit, which requires evaluating color, ripeness, and other characteristics before harvesting. “Tasks that traditionally required a person to inspect and judge the crop need more intelligence at the edge,” Karamsetty said.
That doesn’t mean every agricultural machine requires a high-performance GPU, he said. Some functions can run on microcontrollers (MCUs), while others benefit from dedicated neural processing units (NPUs) or more powerful computing platforms.
Power consumption complicates the decision. Farm equipment must operate for extended periods, and its electronics must function within available thermal and electrical limits. Karamsetty argued that performance per watt can matter more than maximizing peak computing performance.
NXP is developing discrete and integrated NPUs intended to provide appropriately sized inference capabilities. The company’s broader strategy combines application processors, AI accelerators, and MCUs rather than treating inference as an isolated function.
Karamsetty described a processing pipeline in which application processors prepare information from cameras, LiDAR, and other sensors; NPUs execute AI inference; and MCUs handle control functions.
NXP calls its approach the Neural Axis Architecture, using the human nervous system as an analogy. Different processing layers take responsibility for planning, coordinating sensor information, and executing low-latency responses. The distinction becomes particularly important when AI is responsible for operating physical machinery.
Imagine a harvester moving through a cornfield, Karamsetty said. Its vision system is identifying crops and obstacles, while other components control the harvesting mechanism, steering, and braking. If AI inference slows down or encounters a problem, the machine must still be capable of stopping safely. “Safety functions must be isolated from AI inference and normal actuator functions so that an issue or delay in one does not compromise the other,” he said.
NXP’s approach is to integrate functional safety and security capabilities with its computing architecture. The objective is to prevent a problem in perception or an agricultural operation from compromising critical machine controls.
Software integration is another priority. Karamsetty said NXP wants developers to use a common software environment across MCUs, application processors, and NPUs rather than maintaining separate optimization and deployment processes for each processor type.
Beyond the proof of concept
The ability to adapt those models may ultimately matter as much as the processors running them. Agricultural conditions vary not only between regions but also within the same field over time. Lighting, dust, fog, weather, and changing crops can all affect how an AI system interprets sensor data.
Karamsetty envisages equipment manufacturers deploying models customized for particular locations, then managing updates remotely. A machine operating in one region might need a different model from an otherwise identical machine working elsewhere.
This could help manufacturers avoid developing entirely different equipment for every crop or environment. But it also introduces the challenge of validating and maintaining models across many locations. “I think the technology is at the point where cost-effective proofs of concept are possible, but that is not the same as having fully productized, widely deployable solutions,” Karamsetty said.
Commercial deployment requires more than successful demonstrations. Manufacturers must address functional safety, security, regulatory requirements, and reliability under conditions that may differ substantially from those used to develop the original model.
There’s also a question of ownership. Agricultural AI systems may increasingly rely on data collected from individual farms to improve their performance. Karamsetty sees a potential parallel with disputes over farmers’ rights to repair their own equipment.
Similar tensions could emerge if manufacturers use farmers’ data to customize models and subsequently charge those farmers for access to the resulting intelligence. “The ability to deploy customized models will be critical, especially while respecting farmers’ data privacy,” he said.
Karamsetty expects continued improvements in computing performance per watt, greater integration, and new semiconductor architectures. But he believes the larger competitive distinction may come from how manufacturers manage software and their relationships with equipment owners.
For agricultural autonomy, more computing power is only one part of the solution. The harder task is turning that power into dependable decisions that machines can execute safely, economically, and under the unpredictable conditions of working farms.

articles.title: « Un faux sentiment de secret » : face à l'IA, Google prend une décision qui divise le monde de la cybersécurité
articles.text:
Project Zero, l’équipe de chercheurs Google chargée de débusquer les failles de sécurité les plus préoccupantes, vient d’annoncer un changement majeur dans sa façon de travailler. À l’avenir, les fabricants auront beaucoup moins de temps pour corriger les brèches signalées par Google avant que celles-ci ne soient dévoilées auprès du grand public.
Quand Project Zero découvre une faille, l’équipe prévient d’abord l’éditeur concerné en étant le plus discret possible, afin d’éviter que des pirates cherchent à profiter de la situation. Jusqu’ici, le fabricant disposait de 90 jours pour corriger le problème dans son code informatique. S’il publiait un correctif à temps, il bénéficiait de 30 jours supplémentaires pour laisser aux utilisateurs le temps d’installer la mise à jour. Une fois ces délais écoulés, Google publiait tous les détails techniques de la faille. L’approche doit permettre de mettre la pression sur les éditeurs pour qu’ils corrigent vite le tir.
Trois fois moins de temps d’ici 2028
La nouvelle règle annoncée par Google doit accélérer tout le processus de divulgation des failles. L’éditeur a tiré un trait sur le délai supplémentaire de 30 jours. Dès le 2 février 2027, Google dévoilera publiquement les failles 60 jours après le signalement, au lieu de 90 jours.
Le géant américain va aller encore plus loin à partir du 3 janvier 2028 en raccourcissant ce délai à 30 jours, soit trois fois moins qu’aujourd’hui. Project Zero publiera les détails de la faille, même si aucun correctif n’est disponible, une fois le délai écoulé. Pour Google, l’intelligence artificielle a tout changé à la divulgation des failles.
« L’avènement de la découverte et de l’exploitation de vulnérabilités assistées par l’IA a changé le paysage des menaces, de sorte que le délai de correction encouragé par notre politique est clairement insuffisant », écrit Natalie Silvanovich, ingénieure chez Project Zero, dans un billet de blog.
Comme Google l’a déjà constaté, l’IA a fait exploser le nombre de failles découvertes par ses équipes. Les chercheurs de Google indiquent dénicher « plusieurs vulnérabilités par semaine dans des cibles où nous en trouvions autrefois quelques-unes par an ».
Un mode d’emploi pour les cybercriminels
Les pirates profitent évidemment de l’essor de l’intelligence artificielle. Avec l’IA, chaque mise à jour devient un mode d’emploi pour les pirates. En la décortiquant, ils découvrent la faille corrigée, puis s’en prennent à ceux qui n’ont pas encore mis à jour. C’est d’ailleurs de cette manière qu’une armée d’agents IA pirates s’attaque aux sites web français. Le délai de 30 jours, censé garder la faille secrète, ne protège donc plus personne. C’est pourquoi il a été abandonné.
Ce délai « n’a plus de sens dans un monde où les attaquants peuvent presque immédiatement déterminer les détails d’une faille à partir d’un correctif, et peut mettre les utilisateurs en danger en créant un faux sentiment de secret », explique Project Zero. En clair, il ne faut pas croire qu’une faille reste secrète le temps que tout le monde installe la mise à jour.
« Une vulnérabilité signalée aujourd’hui présente un risque immédiat beaucoup plus élevé pour les utilisateurs qu’une vulnérabilité signalée l’an dernier », prévient la chercheuse Natalie Silvanovich, qui pointe du doigt le « faux sentiment de secret » du précédent mode de fonctionnement.
Google assure avoir opté pour une transition progressive pour éviter de mettre les internautes en danger. Comme l’explique Project Zero, « la préoccupation majeure » de ses équipes était qu’un « changement immédiat de la politique puisse nuire aux utilisateurs en mettant à disposition des pirates des vulnérabilités non corrigées, pendant que les éditeurs améliorent leurs processus », explique Project Zero.
Qu’est-ce que ça change pour les utilisateurs ?
Pour les utilisateurs, ce changement de cap devrait se traduire par des mises à jour de sécurité plus fréquentes et plus rapides. Les éditeurs vont devoir corriger plus vite, sous peine de voir leurs failles exposées publiquement par Google. De votre côté, il faut simplement prendre la bonne habitude d’installer les mises à jour dès qu’elles sont disponibles, sur votre ordinateur comme sur votre smartphone.
Dans le milieu de la cybersécurité, la décision de Google ne fait du tout pas l’unanimité. Plusieurs experts craignent que les petites équipes ne puissent pas suivre le nouveau rythme imposé par Google.
« Une date limite ne fait pas apparaître un correctif comme par magie », souligne Katie Moussouris, PDG de Luta Security, auprès de Dark Reading.
De son côté, le chercheur Dustin Childs, de la Zero Day Initiative de Trend Micro, redoute de l’émergence de correctifs bâclés, développés et déployés à la hâte, « qui ne règlent pas entièrement la vulnérabilité ».
Google se veut rassurant et affirme que toutes les failles signalées par Project Zero en 2026 dans des projets open source ont été corrigées en 30 jours, sauf une, réparée en 31 jours. Pour Project Zero, les changements prévus ne devraient donc pas mettre les éditeurs et les constructeurs en difficulté. Google n’est pas le seul géant à serrer la vis. Anthropic, le laboratoire à l’origine de Claude, va lui aussi réduire son délai de divulgation à 30 jours pour les failles graves à partir de janvier.

articles.title: Introducing the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Introducing the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart gives you hundreds of open-weight foundation models you can deploy quickly. That choice is powerful, but it also creates a real question: Which model should you start with? Comparing models usually means reading model cards one at a time and hunting for benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions. Then you still must guess how each model will perform, and what it will cost, for your use case.
Today we are launching the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard, a new way to compare JumpStart models side by side on quality, speed, and cost, directly in Amazon SageMaker Studio. In this post, we explain what the leaderboard shows, define the key terms in plain language, and walk through how to go from a shortlist to a deployed model.
What is the JumpStart Model Leaderboard?
The leaderboard is a new view of the JumpStart base models page in SageMaker Studio, right next to the Categories and All models views. It uses the same search bar and filters you already know, and it opens on a leaderboard of large language models (LLMs). You see rankings immediately without answering setup questions first. For each model, it shows two kinds of information:
- Quality scores on three public benchmarks (BIG-Bench Hard, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU-Pro) that AWS runs itself, using the same evaluation setup for every model so the numbers are comparable.
- Performance and cost metrics that AWS measures by sending a standardized test workload to an endpoint using each JumpStart deployment configuration, so you see how fast a model responds and what it costs to run.
Because both kinds of numbers come from the same place and the same method, you can make a like-for-like comparison instead of stitching together data from different websites. At launch, the leaderboard covers 70+ models from providers including Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM, and Arcee, with more added over time.
The following screenshot shows the leaderboard in SageMaker Studio, with benchmark scores, performance metrics, and estimated cost for each model.
Key concepts
This section defines the terms the leaderboard uses: the quality benchmarks, the use case profiles and optimization goals that shape the performance numbers, and the performance metrics themselves.
Quality benchmarks
A benchmark is a standardized test: a fixed set of questions with known answers. Running every model through the same test gives you a score you can compare. At launch, the leaderboard reports three reasoning benchmarks for LLMs:
| Benchmark | What it measures, in plain terms | 
| BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) | A set of challenging tasks that require multi-step reasoning, such as logical deduction, tracking objects, and multi-step arithmetic. | 
| GPQA Diamond | Graduate-level science questions that are difficult to answer by searching the web. A good signal of deep reasoning. | 
| MMLU-Pro | Broad knowledge and reasoning across many subjects, such as science, law, and engineering, using harder multiple-choice questions. | 
Higher is better for all three. The leaderboard shows each benchmark separately rather than blending them into one number. That keeps the results transparent: You can weigh the benchmarks that matter for your application and check each score against the public definition of the benchmark.
Use case profiles and optimization goals
Speed and cost depend on your workload and on how the model is deployed. Two menus above the leaderboard control which performance and cost numbers you see:
- Use case profile. Select the profile closest to your workload from the View benchmarks for your use case menu. The default is Max Context. The profile changes only the performance and cost metrics. Quality benchmark scores are the same for every profile.
- Optimization goal. For each profile, a model can have several deployment configurations, and the leaderboard shows metrics for one at a time. Choose which one with the Optimized for menu. The default is Balanced.
Each optimization goal picks a different configuration:
| Optimization goal | Configuration shown | 
| Balanced | The configuration with the lowest estimated cost per token. Because cost per token depends on both instance price and throughput, this balances what you pay per hour against how fast the instance generates tokens. | 
| Cost optimized | The configuration with the lowest hourly instance price. Latency can be higher and throughput lower than with other goals. | 
| Latency optimized | The configuration with the lowest time to first token. | 
| Throughput optimized | The configuration with the highest throughput. These configurations can use speculative decoding. | 
Performance metrics
| Metric | What it tells you | 
| Time to first token (TTFT) | How long a user waits before the model starts responding. Lower is better, and it matters most for chat. | 
| Throughput per request (tokens/s) | How many tokens the model generates per second. Higher is better, and it matters for batch and high-volume workloads. | 
| Instance cost ($/hr) | The estimated cost per hour given a specified instance type. | 
A note on cost: Estimated cost reflects SageMaker instance cost only, based on the on-demand hourly rate for the configuration’s default instance type. It does not include data transfer, storage, inference component costs, or discounts such as Reserved Instances or AWS Savings Plans. Your actual bill will vary. Use the AWS Pricing Calculator for billing estimates.
How we benchmark
Published benchmark scores often come from different teams using different prompts, settings, and hardware, which makes them hard to compare. We took a different approach:
- One method for every model. AWS runs each benchmark with the same evaluation harness and settings across all models on the leaderboard.
- Measured on SageMaker. Performance and cost come from sending a standardized test workload to an endpoint deployed with each JumpStart deployment configuration, the same configurations you can launch.
For full details, including prompts, generation settings, and how configurations are measured, see JumpStart leaderboard methodology.
Walkthrough: Finding a model
The following steps show how to go from browsing to a deployed model. You need access to SageMaker Studio and permission to deploy JumpStart models.
Step 1: Open the leaderboard
In SageMaker Studio, open the Models page, then select the Leaderboard view. The leaderboard keeps the same search bar and filters as the other views, and it has its own URL. You can bookmark it or share a direct link with your team.
The following screenshot shows the Models page with the Leaderboard view selected.
Step 2: Narrow the list with filters
Use the same search and filters you already use elsewhere in JumpStart to keep only the models that fit your requirements. Common filters include license, provider, and input and output modality. Start with hard requirements, for example a license that allows commercial use, before you look at scores.
The following screenshot shows the leaderboard filtered by input modality, output modality, and license.
Step 3: Choose a use case profile and optimization goal
Above the leaderboard, select the profile closest to your workload from the View benchmarks for your use case menu (default: Max Context). Then choose a goal from the Optimized for menu (default: Balanced). For a chatbot your customers interact with, Latency optimized is a sensible start. For overnight document processing, Throughput optimized or Cost optimized may fit better. The performance and cost columns update, and quality scores stay the same.
The following screenshots show the View benchmarks for your use case and Optimized for menus above the leaderboard.
Step 4: Read the heatmap and customize columns
Each column has a blue heatmap, so the top-performing models stand out at a glance: the deeper the blue, the stronger the result in that column. Sort any benchmark column to rank models by the metric you care about most. Use the column settings (gear icon) to hide metrics you don’t need, and scroll horizontally to see more. The model name columns stay frozen as you scroll, and a fade at the edge shows when more columns are available.
The following screenshot shows the heatmap and the column settings menu.
Step 5: Deploy or customize the model
Choose a model to open it. From there, you have options to deploy the model or, for models that support serverless customization, to customize it. If you deploy, choose the same use case and optimization goal you compared on the leaderboard. Each metric applies to the configuration it was measured on, and a different configuration can change quality, latency, throughput, and cost.
The following screenshot shows a model page with the Deploy and Customize options.
Example: Picking a model for a chat assistant
Suppose you are building an internal help-desk assistant. Employees ask questions and expect fast, accurate answers that follow a set response format. You need a commercially licensed model and want to keep costs predictable.
After filtering by license and choosing a chat-like use case profile with Latency optimized, your shortlist might look like this:
| Model | BBH | MMLU-Pro | TTFT (s) | Throughput (tokens/s) | Instance cost ($/hr) | 
| Model A (large) | 95.9 | 87.2 | 2.33 | 37 | $37.66 | 
| Model B (medium) | 94.2 | 84.9 | 0.98 | 44 | $5.75 | 
| Model C (small) | 77.4 | 66.1 | 0.27 | 61 | $2.61 | 
Reading the table, Model A has the highest knowledge score but also the highest cost and the slowest first response. Model B scores almost as well, holds up on multi-step reasoning, and runs on a smaller, cheaper instance. For a help desk, where reasoning through a question and responding quickly matter more than the last few points of general knowledge, Model B is the better starting point. A bigger model is not always the better choice, and the leaderboard makes that trade-off visible in seconds.
From there, you would deploy Model B, test it with real questions from your help desk, and keep Model C in mind as a lower-cost option if quality holds up.
Tips and things to know
- Use the leaderboard to build a shortlist, not to make the final call. Benchmarks measure general ability. Always evaluate your top two or three models on your own data and prompts before going to production.
- Filter first, then rank. Requirements like license and input or output modality rule models in or out. Scores only help you order what is left.
- Compare models within a benchmark. Each benchmark has its own difficulty, so a score on one benchmark isn’t directly comparable with a score on another.
- Account for model type. Reasoning and non-reasoning models are evaluated with different generation parameters, and GPQA Diamond scores for reasoning models are averaged over 10 passes. Comparisons between the two types are approximate.
- Check the deployment configuration. Each metric applies to the configuration it was measured on. Compare models on the configuration you plan to deploy.
- Treat close scores as ties. Small differences can fall within normal run-to-run variation and don’t mean one model is meaningfully better. Look for clear gaps.
- Coverage is growing. Not every JumpStart model has benchmark scores yet, and launch benchmarks focus on LLMs. A model without a score is not a weak model. It simply has not been benchmarked yet.
What’s next
We’re continuing to expand the leaderboard. Areas we’re exploring include:
- Private hub support, so organizations that use curated JumpStart private hubs can see a leaderboard for their approved models.
- More task leaderboards beyond LLM text generation, such as object detection, text embeddings, and image understanding.
- More models and benchmarks as new models are added to JumpStart.
Conclusion
The SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard brings quality, speed, and cost together in one place, measured consistently on SageMaker. Instead of comparing numbers from different sources, you can filter to the models that fit your requirements, compare them on the configuration you plan to run, and deploy with a few clicks.

articles.title: Koduri’s Oxmiq Offers IP, Tools for Indian Teams to Design AI Chips - EE Times
articles.text:
In an exclusive interview, Raja Koduri, founder and CEO of Oxmiq Labs, discussed the company’s India initiative, the role of memory hierarchy in AI computing systems, custom silicon economics, and India’s infrastructure requirements.
Oxmiq Labs has developed tools and intellectual property (IP) to help teams in India design their own AI chips. The company is also working on an India initiative that it expects to detail in December, Koduri told EE Times.
“We have built tools to enable teams in India to make their own chips,” he said. “We are working on an initiative in India, and hopefully, when I return to India in December, I will be able to share some of those initiatives publicly.”
The aim, Koduri said, is to develop state-of-the-art chips designed to produce AI tokens as efficiently as possible.
Separately, Oxmiq is an architecture and engineering partner to AM Intelligence Labs, the AI compute division of AM Group, the parent company of Greenko, India’s renewable energy producer with a portfolio target of 50 GW by 2030. The partnership covers site selection, compute design, and partner selection. The initial build will use Nvidia GPUs, with locally developed designs to follow.
“To begin with, we are bringing the best technology available today, which is Nvidia GPUs,” he said. “But as we move toward 2030, we will also leverage designs developed in India.”
Koduri said India must develop its own designs, chips, and infrastructure to bring down the cost of converting electricity into AI output, even if manufacturing remains overseas.
“Chips designed in India can be manufactured in Taiwan or South Korea,” he said. “That is perfectly fine. But the products should be owned by India.”
From megawatts to intelligence
Koduri said the main constraint in AI computing is how efficiently a data center converts power into AI output. At the technical level, he said, the memory hierarchy matters more than floating-point operations and compute.
“It is all a memory hierarchy problem, from NAND flash storage to double data rate [DDR] memory attached to the central processing unit [CPU], high-bandwidth memory [HBM] attached to the GPU, and static random-access memory [SRAM],” he said.
A startup might focus on one type of memory, such as SRAM, and position it as the answer to a particular computing problem. But Koduri said the system-level requirements are broader.
“We look at the problem as a memory hierarchy and exploit each level as efficiently as possible,” he said.
Asked what changes when energy, compute, cooling, networking, and software are designed together, Koduri said the industry has traditionally operated in separate layers. Chipmakers typically design and sell a chip to a systems company, which builds a system. Another company builds the rack, while a data center operator handles installation, thermal management, and cooling.
“There are multiple layers in the ecosystem before everything comes together,” he said.
However, the scale of AI data center expansion is changing how companies approach the design process. Koduri said engineers must consider the entire data center rather than optimize an individual chip in isolation.
“We have to think about the whole system,” he said. “Not just the system, but the entire data center.”
The objective, he explained, is to convert incoming electricity into tokens as efficiently as possible while managing the heat generated by the chips.
Koduri described this as an optimization problem that will continue to evolve as AI models and computing architectures change. Over the past five years, he said, the industry has moved from basic transformers to mixture-of-experts models, DeepSeek optimizations, and decision-making models. GPU optimization is also continuing.
“The real constraint is that we have megawatts coming in and intelligence coming out,” he said. “How efficiently can we transform those megawatts into intelligence?”
Customers, Koduri said, care about the output of the complete system. “They want to plug in electricity, provide cooling, and get tokens they can sell. That is all.”
Oxmiq’s role at AM Intelligence Labs
Oxmiq’s work with AM Intelligence Labs covers data center planning and the selection of technology partners, Koduri said.
The company’s support begins with site selection and data center design. It then works on compute design, rack placement, networking and storage requirements, thermal management, cooling, and software stack operations.
“We provide all that expertise,” he said.
“We do not necessarily solve every problem ourselves,” Koduri said. “For example, we may select a suitable partner to provide the system, such as an original equipment manufacturer. That is the kind of support we are currently providing to [AM Group], because we come from the technology world, while they come from the energy world.”
Koduri pointed to AM Intelligence Lab’s first AI factory in Hyderabad, which he described as probably the first such deployment in Asia. The company has ordered about 9,000 Nvidia Rubin GPUs for the 30-MW facility, with delivery of Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale systems scheduled for the first quarter of 2027. It has since placed an additional order for 20,000 Rubin GPUs for sites in India and Malaysia.
Custom silicon economics and India’s infrastructure needs
Koduri said companies can potentially improve computing efficiency by designing the silicon, systems, and infrastructure for a specific data center rather than relying entirely on components designed for a wide range of customers.
Traditionally, a chipmaker had to sell its product to many data centers to generate revenue. That required designing a flexible product that could accommodate different customer requirements, standards, and features, even if those compromises reduced efficiency.
“If I am designing for one data center and its specific constraints, I can build something that is twice as cost-effective,” he said.
For a 1-GW data center, which Koduri estimated could cost around $55 billion to build, he said custom-designing the system could potentially deliver twice the compute by using power more efficiently.
He said this approach could change both the engineering mindset and the business model. A company developing silicon could now target the data center problem itself, with a single customer potentially generating multibillion-dollar revenue.
Koduri said custom silicon, systems, and software begin to make economic sense for customers planning at least 100 megawatts (MW) of computing capacity.
He put the cost of 100 MW of computing capacity at approximately $5.5 billion using off-the-shelf hardware. By comparison, R&D for a state-of-the-art chip manufactured by TSMC could cost around $100 million to $150 million. Developing a complete custom system could cost up to about $500 million, even with generous spending, he said.
If a custom system roughly halved that cost, a customer could save more than $2 billion even after spending $500 million on development, he said.
However, customers need the IP, tools, and technical know-how to develop custom systems, and Koduri said Oxmiq is building a solution to that problem.
Koduri said Oxmiq’s customers fall into three categories. The first comprises infrastructure companies such as AM Intelligence Labs, which are building computing capacity and need support across the system. The second includes companies designing silicon for applications such as data centers, physical AI, and enterprise AI.
Oxmiq can provide hardware and software IP to startups developing products such as chips for robots, allowing them to focus on their customers’ requirements, Koduri said.
The third category includes companies developing new materials and new physics, such as new forms of memory, silicon, silicon photonics, and photonics-based interconnects. They can license Oxmiq’s IP rather than develop the computing technology alongside their research.
In India, Oxmiq is engaging with customers in the infrastructure and silicon design categories. In the U.S., it works across all three categories, with most customers in infrastructure and new-physics applications, he said.
India’s installed data center power capacity stood at 1.57 GW in August 2026, up from about 375 MW in 2020, and is projected to reach nearly 8 GW by 2030, according to the Indian Press Information Bureau. About $70 billion of investment is underway, with a further $90 billion in announced projects.
Koduri said a 1-GW data center costs approximately $55 billion to build. By comparison, he said capital expenditure per gigawatt in China was moving toward $10 billion. “They can get things done at one-fifth, and perhaps one-tenth, of the cost of the rest of the world,” he said.
He estimated that India would need at least 6 GW of infrastructure to provide intelligence to its entire population, adding that the actual requirement would be much higher. The combined GPU capacity currently available in India, including planned deployments by AM Intelligence Labs, would not reach 100 MW, he said. That suggests India would need to increase that capacity at least 60-fold before the end of the decade.
For Koduri, the opportunity is not limited to building more data centers. It also includes developing the chips, systems, and software that convert electricity into AI output. “The opportunities for design teams, systems teams, and software teams in India are tremendous,” he said. “This is a build-out that India should participate in.”

articles.title: Windows will soon grade your PC's security, and apps like Battle.net get to see the score
articles.text:
The big picture: Plenty of online PC games already refuse to launch unless Secure Boot is enabled. Microsoft now wants to turn checks like that into one standard question that any Windows 11 app can ask your PC. If the answer comes back no, the developer decides what happens next. Some apps may just show a warning; others could refuse to run altogether.
Microsoft calls the feature Windows baseline protection. Insiders can already try it, though a broader release isn't planned until 2027. None of the protections it checks are actually new. The feature simply rolls eight existing ones into a single pass-or-fail result. Those include TPM 2.0, Secure Boot, virtualization-based security, and memory integrity, along with a few rules that stop unsigned or known-flawed drivers from loading.
Ironically, Microsoft's own advice could trip up some gamers. Back in 2022, it suggested turning off memory integrity to claw back a few frames. Windows began switching the feature on automatically in October, but PCs where someone disabled it by hand are left alone, so those machines fail the check.
Secure Boot causes the same problem for anyone who switched it off to dual-boot Linux. Those PCs already can't play Battlefield 6, since its anti-cheat demands Secure Boot too.
Most of this can be fixed from a new Baseline protection page under Settings > Security. A single button there turns on whatever Windows can handle by itself, then restarts the PC. Secure Boot still means a trip into the UEFI menu, but Windows will at least walk users through it with a QR code.
On the developer side, apps can ask for a plain yes or no or for a list of exactly what's missing. For higher-stakes cases, Windows can also hand over a hardware-backed token that the developer verifies on its own servers. As Windows Latest points out, that's much harder to spoof than a check running on the PC itself.
Adobe, Battle.net, 1Password and exam software maker Schoolyear are already testing the feature. Microsoft's own blog post lists launcher app Raycast as an early partner, too. Schoolyear has the clearest use for it so far. The company says it checks a student's PC against the standard before an exam starts. That said, none of these companies has announced plans to actually lock out PCs that fail.
Even so, the check makes that kind of lockout much easier to set up. Until now, any app that wanted to vet a PC's security had to build its own check, like Battlefield's anti-cheat does. Now Windows hands over the answer ready-made, so far more developers could start asking for it.
The bar those apps check against will keep moving, too. Microsoft plans to raise it with each new version of the baseline, so a PC that clears it now could fall short later.

articles.title: Liquid cooling supply chain demands mean building past forecasts - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
AI factories push liquid cooling beyond CPUs and GPUs to nearly every rack component
The liquid cooling supply chain is under mounting pressure as AI factories pack more heat into every rack.
To meet demand, operators have invested heavily in denser racks and liquid cooling, as well as the hoses and couplings that move the fluid must arrive faster and in larger volumes than ever. But for component makers, keeping up takes more than extra shifts. With liquid cooling reaching more of the rack, equipment makers need connections suited to a wider range of components, according to Tyler Glenn (pictured, right), engineer, product applications and data centers, at Danfoss Power Solutions, a division of Danfoss A/S.
“We went from air cooling to hybrid cooling and we’re moving a lot now towards full liquid cooling,” Glenn said. “Traditionally, it was just the CPUs and GPUs that were being liquid cooled. But as more components are starting to have to get integrated, there’s a lot more opportunity for us to have different types of connections to solve specific challenges that this industry faces.”
Glenn and Lauren Witter (left), vice president of sales at Omni Services Inc., spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the liquid cooling supply chain, the universal quick disconnect and designing systems for rising heat density. (* Disclosure below.)
Engineering the liquid cooling supply chain for speed
When a rush order comes in for a large data center build, suppliers need parts on hand to assemble hoses quickly, Glenn explained. Danfoss works with distributors that carry its hoses and couplings to keep a minimum stock available as part of a strategy to stay ahead of projections
“A lot of times our customers will provide us forecasts, but we like to shoot above that and look ahead and make sure that in case that the demand increases beyond that, that we’re prepared for that,” Glenn said. “When it comes to our component suppliers, we’re making sure to order additional materials, but also keeping track of making sure we have enough stock.”
But when a data center builder needs parts for denser AI racks on short notice, having stock on hand gives distributors a head start. Omni’s CoolFlow division works directly with Danfoss’s data center team to handle those requests, according to Witter. Both teams focus on liquid cooling, so Omni can take a rush order straight to the engineers it already works with.
“No one gets frustrated when we’re calling Tyler saying we need these parts yesterday,” Witter said. “They get it. They’re playing the same game we are.”

articles.title: Amidst fears of AI cyberattacks, Satya Nadella says lots of critical infrastructure is 'unpatchable' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
During his appearance at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella lamented the fact that a lot of America’s software systems — including those governing everyday hardware and transportation systems — suffer from unfixable software vulnerabilities that, in the age of AI-aided cyberattacks, are just waiting to be exploited.
“Remember, there is a lot of stuff in our critical infrastructure that’s unpatchable,” Nadella said. “I mean, think about all the firmware and the chillers [a cooling device often used in data centers] and the HVAC systems everywhere else. So all of that, by the way, they’re on the internet.”
In other words: The smartification of the economy, in which much of the world’s “dumb” devices were hooked up to the internet, is now causing tremendous headaches.
The conversation took place against the backdrop of a wave of recent large-scale outages — including one involving Microsoft Outlook. Others have involved the NSA, the FFA, and Apple. Concerns have swirled that these outages are the result of cyberattacks, although officials have denied those claims. Still, the reality of AI-aided cyberattacks is spurring companies to find new strategies for vulnerability discovery and remediation.
Nadella touched briefly on the recent Outlook situation, noting that the global inconvenience was the result of a “latent bug” that led to a “perfect storm.”
“We put out an incident response, and we’re going to obviously take all of the learnings, both upstream architectural, as well as operational, and fix that,” he added.
“Somebody was telling me about sort of even the transportation systems and the amount of stuff that’s discoverable but with unpatchable firmware,” Nadella also added on the topic of vulnerable systems. “So we’ll have to really modernize for sure … and then we will have to assess what the threat vector looks like, what our own ability to both detect and then defend in real time looks like.”
Nadella made a broader point as well, which is that the process of patching software vulnerabilities has escalated to match the speed of potential exploitation, but that this has caused more problems.
“We now have a very powerful tool that finds vulnerabilities,” he said. However, companies used to have more time to test those patches, understand a situation, and deploy them, he said. At the same time, AI has made sophisticated cyberattacks much easier to enact.
“The patch [now] needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production, because it’s being exploited in the wild, right? So that’s going to create instability.”

articles.title: Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI suffers chemical spill at Mississippi AI data center — up to 6,000 gallons of propylene glycol heat transfer fluid lost, environment agency says no threat to residents
articles.text:
Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI suffers chemical spill at Mississippi AI data center — up to 6,000 gallons of propylene glycol heat transfer fluid lost, environment agency says no threat to residents
5,000 to 6,000 gallons of propylene glycol spilled from the facility before reaching a nearby drainage ditch.
A chemical spill at a SpaceXAI facility in Southaven saw the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ) get involved, with between 5,000 and 6,000 gallons of propylene glycol confirmed to have spilled. The chemical is a heat transfer fluid used in a variety of products, such as antifreeze. The chemical ultimately found its way into a drainage ditch, but MDEQ has told residents that there is no immediate threat to their health or safety, according to local news reports.
However, it has also been confirmed that water samples will be collected for further laboratory analysis while workers continue to clean the area and monitor for any further issues. It's also been reported that the chemical was contained to the drainage ditch and did not reach the nearby Horn Lake Creek.
It hasn't been a great November for SpaceXAI in Southaven. Earlier this month, it suffered a setback in a lawsuit over pollution in the area caused by its data center. The April 2026 suit targets the company's gas-powered power plant, which is used to supply power for its facility in the Greater Memphis area. It's argued that 27 gas turbines were installed without obtaining the required permits. It's also alleged that the plant could emit more than 5,000 tons of nitrogen oxides and 47 tons of formaldehyde — a cancer-causing chemical — annually. The company has tried to classify the turbines as mobile units to get around the issue, but a judge rejected that manoeuvre.
Clearly aware of the local sentiment towards its presence, SpaceXAI offered a 50% Starlink discount to anyone living near its two Memphis data centers. It also said that it would waive the hardware cost, saving customers $349. SpaceXAI said that, between late June and early September, around 2,000 residents of the greater Memphis and Southaven area had signed up for Starlink connectivity.
It was also recently announced that the City of Memphis was ready to make its first major investment as part of its new Community Benefits Ordinance, a fund that uses revenue from SpaceXAI's Colossus 1 facility. Almost $3.3 million will be pumped back into the city to help with housing and neighborhood improvements.

articles.title: Windows 11 : Microsoft Defender va surveiller ce que les pirates glissent dans votre presse-papiers
articles.text:
Microsoft commence à déployer une nouvelle protection contre les attaques ClickFix, une technique de piratage qui pousse les internautes à exécuter eux-mêmes des commandes malveillantes. L'antivirus de Windows pourra les intercepter dans le presse-papiers avant leur exécution.
Le presse-papiers de Windows n'a jamais eu vocation à devenir un outil de piratage, et pourtant, les cybercriminels ont trouvé le moyen de s'en servir pour contourner la méfiance des internautes et les amener à infecter eux-mêmes leur ordinateur. Une méthode baptisée ClickFix, qui a pris de l'ampleur ces derniers mois. À l'occasion d'Ignite 2026, Microsoft a dévoilé sa riposte : une nouvelle protection pour son antivirus Defender, conçue pour prendre les pirates de vitesse.
Désamorcer le piège avant le copier-coller fatal
Pour couper court à ces attaques, Microsoft a choisi d'intervenir avant même que la commande malveillante soit exécutée. La nouvelle protection repose sur un processus baptisé DefenderSessionHelper.exe, chargé de repérer les instructions dangereuses copiées depuis une page web et de les supprimer du presse-papiers avant qu'elles ne puissent être lancées.
Une parade qui cible directement le mode opératoire des attaques de type ClickFix. Sur un site compromis ou une page frauduleuse, les pirates affichent un faux CAPTCHA ou un message d'erreur invitant l'internaute à effectuer quelques manipulations pour confirmer son identité ou résoudre un prétendu problème technique. Dans sa forme la plus courante, la page copie une commande malveillante dans le presse-papiers, puis demande à la victime de la coller dans la fenêtre Exécuter de Windows, dans un terminal ou dans la barre d'adresse de l'Explorateur de fichiers.
Si la personne suit ces instructions, elle déclenche elle-même l'exécution de la commande, qui peut alors télécharger un logiciel malveillant, dérober des données ou ouvrir un accès à son ordinateur. Avec sa nouvelle protection, Defender entend donc briser cette chaîne d'infection avant que l'internaute ait eu l'occasion de la lancer.
ClickFix, une menace qui prolifère
Et Microsoft a de bonnes raisons de s'attaquer à cette méthode. D'après les données recueillies par Defender, les attaques ClickFix ont représenté 12,8 % des intrusions observées entre juin 2025 et juin 2026. Après un recul à la fin de l'année dernière, leur volume a été multiplié par 23 entre décembre 2025 et mai 2026, signe que cette technique de manipulation continue de séduire les cybercriminels.
Bonne nouvelle pour les particuliers, la nouvelle protection ne sera pas réservée aux entreprises. Microsoft a confirmé que son déploiement avait déjà commencé sur les appareils utilisant Microsoft Defender Antivirus, avec une généralisation prévue d'ici la fin de l'année 2026. Les équipes de sécurité des organisations équipées des solutions professionnelles de Defender pourront, de leur côté, retrouver les détections dans leur portail d'administration pour examiner les tentatives d'attaque et mener leurs investigations.
- Moteur de détection de dernière génération efficace et discret
- Intégration dans Windows 10 et Windows 11
- Pare-feu

articles.title: Rekord-Börsengang: Anthropic überholt SpaceX und startet mit 1,5 Billionen Dollar Bewertung
articles.text:
Rekord-Börsengang: Anthropic überholt SpaceX und startet mit 1,5 Billionen Dollar Bewertung
Der KI-Firma Anthropic ist mit einem Erlös von insgesamt 107,3 Milliarden Dollar ein Rekord-Börsengang gelungen. Anthropic übertraf damit deutlich die Einnahmen von Elon Musks Weltraumunternehmen SpaceX, das erst im Juni den vorherigen Bestwert aufgestellt hatte. Der schärfste Konkurrent des ChatGPT-Entwicklers OpenAI startet damit heute an der Börse mit einer Bewertung von rund 1,5 Billionen Dollar.
Der Rekord-Börsengang ist ein wichtiger Meilenstein für Anthropic und die gesamte KI-Industrie. Zum einen zeigt er das Vertrauen der Anleger in die Firma, die bisher hohe Verluste schrieb und noch hunderte Milliarden Dollar in Infrastruktur investieren will. Für die Branche bedeutet er auch, dass der Markt sich bislang nicht grundsätzlich durch die Angst vor Risiken Künstlicher Intelligenz und Zweifel an den Gewinnaussichten abschrecken lässt.
Es ist der erste Börsengang einer der großen KI-Firmen, die Vorreiter bei der Entwicklung der Technologie sind. OpenAI will im kommenden Jahr folgen. Eine spannende Frage ist nun, ob es für die Aktie auch nach dem bevorstehenden Handelsstart (15.30 Uhr MEZ) aufwärtsgehen wird. Oder hat Anthropic den Bogen mit seiner stolzen Bewertung womöglich überspannt?
Anthropic: Mehr Aktien zum höheren Preis
Der Ansturm von Interessenten war so groß, dass Anthropic nicht nur den Ausgabepreis über der zunächst vorgegebenen Spanne von 70 bis 78 Dollar festsetzte – sondern auch mehr Aktien als geplant herausrückte.
So sollten im Hauptteil der Platzierung zunächst 825 Millionen Aktien ausgegeben werden – am Ende wurden es 980 Millionen. Zu einem Ausgabepreis von 83 Dollar brachten sie rund 81,3 Milliarden Dollar ein. Darüber hinaus verkaufte Anthropic Aktien im Wert von rund 26 Milliarden Dollar direkt an Investoren wie Google, Microsoft und die Chipfirma AMD. Dadurch entstand ein Gesamterlös von 107,3 Milliarden Dollar (aktuell knapp 98 Milliarden Euro).
Ein Großteil des Geldes geht direkt an Anthropic. Aktien im Wert von knapp zwei Milliarden Dollar wurden von frühen Aktionären verkauft, die damit richtig Kasse machten.
Das Angebot war Medienberichten zufolge stark überzeichnet. Am oberen Ende der Preisspanne wären die ursprünglich in der Platzierung angebotenen Aktien rund 64 Milliarden Dollar wert gewesen. Dem stand nach Informationen des Wirtschaftssenders CNBC eine Nachfrage von rund 500 Milliarden Dollar gegenüber.
Erfolg trotz Sorgen und Skepsis
Anthropic konkurriert mit seinem KI-Assistenten Claude nicht nur mit ChatGPT, sondern auch mit Tech-Schwergewichten wie Google, Microsoft und dem Facebook-Konzern Meta. Einen Großteil seines Umsatzes macht Anthropic mit professionellen Anwendungen, etwa für das Programmieren von Software.
Zuletzt war die schon lange schwelende Sorge von Anlegern, ob die gewaltigen KI-Investitionen zurückverdient werden können, wieder etwas größer geworden. Dem Börsengang von Anthropic schadete dies aber nicht.
Zudem gibt es nach eigenständigen Hacking-Attacken durch KI-Software eine verschärfte Debatte um die Risiken der Technologie. OpenAI verschob seinen Börsengang ins kommende Jahr – unter anderem unter Verweis auf eine aktuell negative Stimmung gegenüber der Technologie. Insbesondere im jüngsten US-Parlamentswahlkampf war deutlich geworden, dass viele Amerikaner den Bau riesiger Rechenzentren für Künstliche Intelligenz ablehnen und der Technologie insgesamt misstrauen.
Anthropic vermarktet sich als das Unternehmen, das die Entwicklung Künstlicher Intelligenz besonders verantwortungsvoll vorantreiben will. Zugleich sorgte ein Manager vor einigen Monaten für Schlagzeilen mit dem Eingeständnis, aus seiner Sicht sei das Risiko real, dass KI die Menschheit auslöschen könnte.

articles.title: Ya es Black Friday en Amazon: estas son las mejores ofertas en Nintendo Switch 2, Kindle, teléfonos, tablets, ordenadores y más
articles.text:
Aunque el Black Friday 2026 llegará oficialmente el viernes de la próxima semana, día 27 de noviembre (tras la festividad norteamericana de Acción de Gracias), muchas tiendas llevan inmersas en sus propias campañas anticipadas desde hace tiempo.
Google Pixel 11
Una de ellas es Amazon, que lanzó un buen puñado de ofertas previas al Black Friday hace unos días. Pero ahora, recién estrenado el jueves 19 de noviembre, acaba de dar el pistoletazo de salida oficial a su Black Friday 2026. El cual está disponible desde ya y lo estará hasta el próximo lunes, 30 de noviembre.
En un año en el que el hardware, los componentes y dispositivos tecnológicos no dejan de subir de precio por la crisis de memorias RAM y el auge de la IA, se hace casi más importante que nunca estar atentos a buenas ofertas si queremos sacarle el máximo partido a nuestra inversión al comprar videoconsolas, teléfonos, tablets, ordenadores, televisiones y toda clase de artículos.
Así que para facilitar la búsqueda de chollos entre tanta oferta activa ya en Amazon, a continuación recopilamos algunos de los mejores que ya podemos aprovechar en esta tienda sin esperar al viernes 27 de noviembre:
- Pack Nintendo Switch 2 por 479,99 euros, con la consola, un juego y suscripción al servicio online
- Ninja Crispi Pro XL por 189,05 euros, modelo de mayor capacidad de la freidora superventas de Ninja
- Pixel 11 por 699 euros, el nuevo gama alta de Google al precio más bajo hasta la fecha en Amazon
- Lenovo Legion Pro 5 por 2.279 euros, un portátil gaming a mínimo histórico con RTX 5070, 32 GB de RAM y mucho más
- Kindle básico por 124,99 euros, lanzamiento reciente de última generación y el Kindle más económico de Amazon
- Fire TV Stick 4K Select por 27,99 euros, un dispositivo ideal para dar una segunda vida a viejas televisiones
- iPad Mini por 619 euros, la tablet Apple más compacta rebajada en la versión de la anterior generación
Nintendo Switch 2 pack
Aunque subió recientemente de PVP, no es extraño ver a Nintendo Switch 2 protagonizando algún chollo en muchas tiendas. El Black Friday de Amazon no iba a ser menos y ha rebajado el nuevo pack que incluye la consola, 'Nintendo Switch Sports Resort' y tres meses gratis de suscripción a Nintendo Switch Online. Todo, por 479,99 euros. Lo que, teniendo en cuenta que sólo la consola cuesta oficialmente 499,99 euros, es una rebaja como para no dejar escapar.
Nintendo Switch 2 HW + Nintendo Switch Sport Resort + 3 meses NSO
Ninja Crispi Pro XL
Una freidora de aire con dos recipientes de cristal de gran capacidad (aptos para lavavajillas), que sirven tanto para cocinar como para servir en la mesa o almacenar en la nevera. Con doble capacidad de 2,3 y 5,7 litros, la Ninja Crispi Pro XL da de sobra para elaboraciones para varios comensales. Cuenta con cinco programas establecidos de serie y alcanza un máximo de 2.050 W. Ahora, a un precio de 189,05 euros.
Ninja CRISPi PRO XL
Google Pixel 11
Disponible desde hace unos meses, el Pixel 11 de Google ya se encuentra habitualmente rebajado. Ahora, Amazon ha tumbado su precio hasta su mínimo histórico en dicha tienda y está disponible por 699 euros en sus cuatro colores y 256 GB de capacidad. Un gama alta con pantalla OLED de 6,3 pulgadas y 120 Hz, el procesador Tensor G6 y 12 GB de memoria RAM. Con un excelente apartado fotográfico, carga rápida de 30 W y siete años de actualizaciones por delante.
Google Pixel 11
Lenovo Legion Pro 5
2026 no está siendo el mejor año para comprar hardware, menos aún si es gaming y entre él se incluye buena cantidad de memoria RAM DDR5. Sin embargo, en el terreno de los portátiles sigue habiendo buenos precios a día de hoy y este Lenovo Legion rebajado a 2.279 euros en Amazon (su mínimo aquí) es buen ejemplo. Un equipo con 32 GB de RAM DDR5, la NVIDIA RTX 5070, 1 TB de SSD, el procesador AMD Ryzen 9 8945HX y una pantalla de 16 pulgadas a 240 Hz.
Lenovo Legion Pro 5
Kindle básico
Lanzado hace pocas semanas, el nuevo Kindle básico ya se puede conseguir rebajado por 124,99 euros. La primera gran oportunidad para comprarlo ahorrando un pellizco, tras la subida de PVP de este y otros dispositivos de Amazon. Ligeramente más fino que en anteriores generaciones, también es más ligero y más rápido. Con pantalla de 6 pulgadas con luz integrada, 16 GB de capacidad y autonomía de sobra para semanas de uso con una sola carga.
Amazon Kindle (última generación)
Fire TV Stick 4K Select
Ahora que está rebajado a sólo 27,99 euros desde sus 69,99 euros originales, el Fire TV Stick 4K Select es posiblemente la opción con mejor relación calidad precio de todo el catálogo de Fire TV Sticks de Amazon. Ideal tanto para convertir viejas televisiones en modelos inteligentes como para disparar el rendimiento de actuales televisores con un hardware modesto. Alcanza el 4K y es compatible con Alexa+.
Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Select con Alexa+
iPad Mini
Aunque recientemente Apple renovó su familia de tablets iPad Mini con un modelo de última generación, el anterior Mini con el procesador A17 Pro se sigue vendiendo y sale por unos 100 euros menos. La mejor opción si buscamos la mejor relación calidad precio ahora que está rebajado a 619 euros en su versión WiFi de 128 GB. Disponible en varios colores, con pantalla de 8,3 pulgadas y iPadOS.
Apple iPad Mini (A17 Pro)

articles.title: Tiene 31 años, dejó Buenos Aires y construyó una casa de 56 m² con barro y 5.000 botellas de vidrio junto a su pareja en las montañas de Córdoba, Argentina
articles.text:
Ailu tiene 31 años y hace unos años que dejó atrás Buenos Aires para irse a vivir con su pareja, Jerónimo, a las montañas de Córdoba, en Argentina. Allí ambos acabaron acabaron construyendo con sus propias manos una casa sostenible de 56 metros cuadrados hecha de barro y materiales reciclados, una historia que contaron en una entrevista para el canal de YouTube Historias de Valientes.
De un terreno a un hogar. Después de unos cuantos años de búsqueda y de viajes, la pareja acabó convirtiendo un terreno de Los Hornillos, en el valle de Traslasierra, en su casa. Allí han puesto en marcha un proyecto de permacultura que combina la bioconstrucción, la producción de alimentos y diferentes prácticas sostenibles con las que quieren reducir su impacto ambiental, según explican en la propia entrevista.
Eso sí, aunque en algunas fases de la obra recibieron ayuda de otras personas, la mayor parte del trabajo la hicieron ellos solos.
Quincha y botellas bajo el suelo. Para las paredes utilizaron la quincha, una técnica de construcción que combina madera y paja para conseguir que la estructura tenga un buen aislamiento térmico.
Pero uno de los detalles que más llaman la atención está debajo del suelo, donde hay más de 5.000 botellas de vidrio colocadas para crear una especie de cámara de aire. Vamos, que pisan sobre miles de botellas recicladas que hacen de colchón de aire. La vivienda también tiene un techo verde y un calentador solar con el que aprovechan la energía del sol para calentar el agua.
Muebles de barro y herencias familiares. Por dentro, la casa tiene muebles de obra hechos de barro y una cocina integrada. Además, hay diversos objetos que la pareja ha reutilizado y que le dan un toque propio a la decoración de cada estancia, y algunos de ellos tienen valor sentimental, como las mesitas de noche que pertenecían a la abuela de Ailu. Otras piezas y materiales les llegaron como regalo y acabaron teniendo una nueva función después de adaptarlos.
La vivienda cuenta también con una habitación extra que funciona a la vez como estudio, zona de descanso y sala de lectura. Y en la planta de arriba está el dormitorio, con un ventanal amplio que da a las montañas.
Frutales y zonas verdes. Fuera, en el terreno, cultivan diferentes árboles frutales, como manzanos, cerezos, mandarinos, melocotoneros y aguacates, y tienen varias zonas verdes que forman parte de su idea de vivir en armonía con el entorno.
Por qué dejaron la ciudad. Antes de instalarse en Córdoba, los dos pasaron por diferentes experiencias que les hicieron replantearse la vida urbana y buscar una forma más cercana y consciente de relacionarse con lo que les rodea. Jerónimo empezó a viajar con 19 años y pasó buena parte de los años siguientes llevando una vida nómada.
Ailu, por su parte, siempre ha tenido curiosidad por otras culturas y por conocer otras formas de vida. Con el tiempo, los dos se dieron cuenta de que compartían las ganas de vivir más en contacto con la naturaleza y de estrechar lazos con la comunidad.
Pero la casa es únicamente una parte de un proyecto más grande, el de crear un espacio de convivencia basado en la sostenibilidad y la vida en comunidad. Por ahora viven allí con sus dos gatos, aunque su intención es seguir levantando otras casas y compartir lo que han aprendido sobre bioconstrucción con quien quiera apostar por este estilo de vida.
Foto | YouTube

articles.title: GTA 6 : test, notes et avis, ce que disent les premiers tests du jeu
articles.text:
L’attente a duré treize ans, et le verdict de la presse est tombé quelques heures avant la sortie du jeu en France, prévue cette nuit à minuit. À l’heure de ces lignes, Grand Theft Auto VI affiche une moyenne de 99 sur 100 sur Metacritic, sur la base de 141 tests, ce qui le place au niveau des jeux les mieux notés de l’histoire. En France, Gamekult lui attribue même un 10/10, une première pour le site, qui explique avoir longuement débattu avant de « faire sauter un verrou ». Jeuxvideo.com lui donne 19/20, le Journal du Geek 9/10. À l’étranger, Eurogamer lui accorde la note maximale de cinq étoiles, IGN lui donne 10/10 et parle du « jeu vidéo le plus impressionnant » que son testeur ait jamais pratiqué, et Jason Schreier, journaliste de Bloomberg et l’un des meilleurs connaisseurs de l’industrie, n’hésite pas à qualifier le jeu de « chef-d’œuvre ».
Un monde ouvert qui met tout le monde d’accord
S’il y a un point sur lequel tous les tests s’accordent, c’est la richesse du monde ouvert. « Peu de jeux vidéo ont des villes aussi vastes, aussi denses, aussi pleines de secrets et de systèmes qui s’imbriquent », écrit Jason Schreier, qui raconte avoir été incapable de terminer l’histoire à temps, sans cesse distrait par les rencontres improbables de Vice City. Jeuxvideo.com parle du « plus bel open world urbain jamais conçu », Gamekult du « monde ouvert le plus vivant et palpable » qu’il ait connu. Tous citent les personnages non-joueurs, qui réagissent de manière crédible à vos actes, du conducteur qui sort de sa voiture pour en découdre après un coup de klaxon au mendiant qui sort une arme quand on ne lui donne que dix dollars.
L’ambiance sonore fait elle aussi l’unanimité, avec une sélection de radios jugée quasi parfaite et une bande originale signée notamment par le duo français Justice. La conduite est également saluée, IGN la jugeant la meilleure de la série. Plusieurs tests soulignent au passage l’intérêt des gâchettes adaptatives de la manette DualSense sur PS5, qui permettent de mieux doser l’accélération.
L’histoire et le réalisme divisent davantage
Les avis sont plus partagés sur le scénario et Jeuxvideo.com, IGN ou encore Gamekult saluent un duo Jason-Lucia attachant et une écriture qui a gagné en maturité, à la manière de Red Dead Redemption 2. Le Journal du Geek se montre beaucoup plus critique, dénonçant une narration « décousue » et un côté satirique en retrait, qu’il attribue au départ de Dan Houser, cofondateur et scénariste historique de Rockstar. Jason Schreier se situe entre les deux et estime que l’histoire est meilleure que celle de GTA V, mais n’atteint pas les sommets émotionnels de Red Dead Redemption 2.
Le virage vers le réalisme ne convainc pas non plus tout le monde. Il faut désormais nourrir ses personnages, les faire dormir et aller à la salle de sport, faire le plein d’essence ou laisser ses armes dans le coffre de sa voiture. Le Journal du Geek y voit une « charge mentale » inutile, quand Gamekult, d’abord sceptique, a fini par se prendre au jeu de ce qu’il appelle « le Tamagotchi le plus cher de l’histoire » du jeu vidéo. GTA 6 introduit aussi un profil moral, de « Professionnel » à « Irrécupérable » selon Jeuxvideo.com, qui évolue selon votre façon de jouer et influence la réaction de la police, mais aussi la fin de l’histoire, qui en compte plusieurs. Ceux qui espéraient un défouloir sans conséquence risquent d’être déçus, prévient le site spécialisé. Quelques reproches reviennent enfin, comme une interface parfois confuse, des repaires de gangs peu inspirés ou un premier chapitre très lent.
30 images par seconde, mais une claque technique
Côté technique, le jeu tourne à 30 images par seconde sur toutes les consoles, y compris sur PS5 Pro, et les testeurs disent pour la plupart s’en être accommodés. L’analyse la plus poussée vient de Digital Foundry, référence en la matière, titre sur « une réussite marquante qui redéfinit une génération de consoles ». Sur PS5 comme sur PS5 Pro, le jeu est calculé en 1440p. La PS5 Pro s’appuie ensuite sur son upscaler PSSR pour obtenir une image proche de la 4K, là où la PS5 classique affiche une image plus douce. La PS5 Pro tient ses 30 images par seconde sans faiblir, tandis que la PS5 standard peut descendre autour de 25 images par seconde lors des scènes les plus chargées en explosions. Le Journal du Geek et Jeuxvideo.com disent pourtant avoir constaté quelques chutes, même sur PS5 Pro, lors de grosses fusillades.
Digital Foundry salue surtout l’usage massif du ray tracing, pour l’éclairage global et les reflets sur toutes les consoles, et pour les ombres sur la PS5 Pro, qu’il juge peut-être « la meilleure implémentation du ray tracing » vue à ce jour. Selon lui, la densité de la simulation, jusqu’aux cheveux de chaque passant animés mèche par mèche, explique pourquoi un mode 60 images par seconde n’était pas envisageable sur les consoles actuelles. Gamekult précise enfin que Rockstar a déjà publié deux correctifs durant sa période de test.

articles.title: Ce trépied Neewer noté 4,5/5 perd 52,34 € et tombe à 132,99 € pour le Black Friday 2026
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 – Le trépied Neewer LT32 à 132,99 € (-30%)
Le trépied Neewer LT32 passe sous les 150 € chez Amazon soit une baisse d'environ 30% sur le prix habituellement constaté.
Un trépied de voyage est un accessoire indispensable pour de nombreux photographes. Idéalement, il doit être compact et léger pour le transport, rapide à mettre en place, et enfin stable pour sécuriser son matériel et affiner le cadrage. Le Neewer LT32 semble cocher toutes les cases.

Points faibles
