articles.title: US closes the AI chip loophole that let China rent Nvidia hardware abroad
articles.text:
Why it matters: US export controls on advanced AI chips have mostly focused on where the hardware ends up. Now, a new Commerce Department rule dictates who gets to use it. Under the rule, companies must get a license to ship chips from Nvidia and other US suppliers to Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore and Brazil, a move meant to stop Chinese customers from tapping data-center capacity in those countries over the network.
The gap the rule addresses is simple. A Chinese company that can't legally buy a cutting-edge Nvidia processor can still rent time on one, as long as the chip sits in a server rack outside China. The silicon never crosses the Chinese border, but the computing power does.
Firms such as Megaspeed International have built a business on that arrangement. They used billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips to build data centers across Southeast Asia, then sold the computing capacity to Chinese tech giants trying to catch up in artificial intelligence. Shutting down that channel is the main goal of the new rule.
"The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security said in a release.
The rule reaches beyond the five named countries, making it harder for data-center operators anywhere in the world to give Chinese companies remote access to AI chips. It also tightens a separate point in the supply chain by making it more difficult for Chinese chip designers to work with TSMC.
US tech companies could get exceptions to the licensing requirement. The rule took effect immediately, and companies have 60 days to submit comments.
Megaspeed's role has put the rule at the center of a scandal involving Nvidia's top ranks. Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Megaspeed and a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, was having an affair with Jensen Huang, who has stepped down as Nvidia's chief executive. Before he left, Jensen Huang had lobbied President Trump to let Nvidia ship some chips directly to China and to keep export controls loose. His argument was that US companies competing abroad would help push back against Chinese rivals.
How the rule was written has drawn nearly as much attention as what it says. Normally, the Bureau of Industry and Security drafts chip-export rules and then sends them to the State and Treasury departments and the National Security Council for feedback. This time, the order was reversed. The release said the rule was "written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council."
Export-control analysts called that an unusual step. Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations who previously worked on tech and security issues at the State Department, said it signaled a fight inside the administration.
"It is unprecedented for a Commerce Department rule to be written by the National Security Council and the Treasury Department," McGuire told The Wall Street Journal. "The fact that the Commerce Department press release says this shows that Commerce resisted publishing this rule to the bitter end, and was forced to do so by the White House."
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other officials had accused Commerce of moving too slowly to close export-control loopholes. Bessent said last week that Treasury and other agencies had pushed for months for action on Megaspeed and chip exports, and that Commerce stood in the way. National security adviser Marco Rubio, who is also secretary of state, has joined Bessent in pushing for tighter controls.
Both men were among the officials frustrated when Megaspeed and other companies suspected of chip diversion were considered for the Entity List, a trade blacklist, and Commerce didn't move forward. Administration officials have said the agency is wary of upsetting China during trade talks. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has taken much of the blame inside the administration. The Commerce Department didn't respond to a request for comment on the dynamics between agencies.
Trump defended Lutnick this week. He said the commerce secretary has done a good job and that delaying action on Megaspeed made sense, even though hawkish advisers objected.
"He was doing it because if you didn't delay it, you could have a blowup with China," Trump said. "We're having a very good relationship with China right now."

articles.title: “Me contactó con médicos de Stanford”, empleado de Nvidia reveló que Jensen Huang lo ayudó cuando tuvo cáncer
articles.text:
Jensen Huang, cofundador y exdirector ejecutivo de Nvidia, recibió el reconocimiento público de uno de sus empleados después de que este revelara cómo lo ayudó durante su lucha contra el cáncer. Se trata de John Zedlewski, un alto ejecutivo de la compañía que explicó que Huang utilizó sus contactos en la Universidad de Stanford para facilitarle el ingreso a un ensayo clínico cuando su estado de salud se había complicado.
El testimonio fue publicado en la red social X el 13 de noviembre dfe 2026 y apareció en medio de las críticas y discusiones sobre la personalidad del empresario, quien dejó la dirección de Nvidia después de más de tres décadas al frente de la compañía.
“Tengo un caso de cáncer particularmente grave. Cuando volví a ser hospitalizado en mi peor momento el año pasado, se lo conté a Jensen. Inmediatamente se puso en contacto con sus contactos en Stanford, quienes lograron superar los obstáculos burocráticos y conseguir que me admitieran en un ensayo clínico para el que he resultado ser un candidato perfecto”, escribió Zedlewski.
El ejecutivo también expresó su agradecimiento por la intervención del empresario y cuestionó las versiones que lo describen como alguien indiferente a sus trabajadores.
“Creo que cada uno puede tener su propia opinión sobre los acontecimientos recientes. Pero cualquier afirmación de que a Jensen realmente no le importaban sus empleados es simplemente inexacta. Personalmente, le debo más de lo que puedo expresar”, añadió.
Quién es el empleado de Nvidia que contó su experiencia con Jensen Huang
John Zedlewski ocupa el cargo de vicepresidente de Ciencia de Datos Acelerada en Nvidia y lleva más de una década vinculado a la compañía. Su trayectoria incluye trabajos relacionados con RAPIDS, aprendizaje profundo para vehículos autónomos, imágenes médicas y análisis de datos.
Su publicación no se limitó a contar el episodio relacionado con su enfermedad. También aprovechó para explicar qué aspectos del liderazgo de Huang considera importantes para mantener la cultura de innovación de Nvidia.
Zedlewski sostuvo que la mejor manera de reconocer el legado del empresario es continuar desarrollando tecnología y mantener los principios de trabajo que aprendieron durante años dentro de la organización.
Entre ellos mencionó la importancia de trabajar con rapidez, asumir riesgos calculados y reconocer los errores sin ocultar información. También destacó una filosofía interna conocida como Speed of Light, que busca que los equipos técnicos alcancen el máximo rendimiento posible de sus sistemas.
El estilo de liderazgo de Jensen Huang genera opiniones divididas
El testimonio del vicepresidente de Nvidia contrasta con otras experiencias recogidas por The Wall Street Journal en un reportaje sobre la cultura laboral de la compañía.
El periódico describió un ambiente de trabajo exigente, con reuniones en las que Huang cuestionaba duramente a sus colaboradores cuando consideraba que no tenían suficiente conocimiento sobre sus proyectos o no conseguían los resultados esperados.
Algunos trabajadores señalaron que el empresario podía reprender públicamente a sus subordinados y generar situaciones de mucha presión. Sin embargo, otros destacaron su participación directa en los problemas técnicos y su capacidad para involucrarse en las decisiones de diferentes equipos.
Zedlewski también recordó una reunión relacionada con el desarrollo de vehículos autónomos. Durante ese encuentro, Huang pidió a un ejecutivo que explicara en una pizarra cómo funcionaba un sistema informático para identificar operaciones innecesarias que reducían su velocidad.
Para el trabajador, esa experiencia demuestra que los directivos deben conocer los detalles técnicos de sus proyectos y no limitarse a recibir informes de sus subordinados.

articles.title: Windows Server 2028 trades compatibility for out-of-the-box security
articles.text:
Microsoft’s Ignite announcements this week went beyond the Office-in-Copilot overhaul with the reveal of the Windows Server 2028 Public Preview and its new security-by-default stance and what Microsoft calls Hardened Server Core. Windows Server 2028 will implement a default security framework that Microsoft says is aligned with hardened DoD benchmarks, such as the Defense Information Systems Agency’s (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG).
STIGs work by providing a standard security framework for system administrators to follow recommended guidance. In the past, Windows Server admins were left to start from a blank canvas and then implement hardening configurations for operations. Secure baselines were available but not the default. Microsoft says that concern is now managed: “The secure configuration is the starting state, not a project you run after setup. That closes the window where a newly deployed server sits exposed while it waits to be hardened.”
The new Windows Server 2028 hardened-by-default state will only be available for the Server Core installs. Windows Server Desktop Experience installs do not include the changed stance.
This isn’t to say that system administrators won’t still have the final say on which security protocols are activated, just that the default package now ships in a pre-hardened state. Kerberos is now the default over NTLM, with protections added to LSASS; TLS is automatically restricted to modern cipher suites; key exchange uses “hybrid post-quantum key exchange” based on the quantum-safe ML-KEM; and remote desktop authentication and PowerShell script block logging get stricter as well.

articles.title: Nvidia não venderá mais chips de IA para a China • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Nvidia não venderá mais chips de IA para a China
Empresa vendeu US$ 2,4 bilhões em chips Hopper licenciados no último trimestre, mas não prevê novas remessa.
Resumo IA
- A Nvidia não venderá mais chips de IA da geração Hopper para a China, que dependem de licença dos EUA.
- A empresa vendeu US$ 2,4 bilhões em chips Hopper licenciados no último trimestre, mas não prevê novas remessas.
- A Nvidia desenvolveu produtos compatíveis com as regras americanas de exportação, como o chip H20, mas retirou novas vendas dos produtos das projeções financeiras.
A Nvidia não enviará mais à China chips de IA da geração Hopper que dependem de licença dos Estados Unidos, como o H200. A mudança foi confirmada pela CEO interina Colette Kress durante a divulgação dos resultados trimestrais nesta terça-feira (17/11).
A executiva não explicou o motivo para interromper os embarques dos chips para a China, que representaram US$ 2,4 bilhões (R$ 13,9 bilhões) das vendas, nem se a decisão é permanente. Ainda assim, a empresa retirou novas vendas dos produtos das projeções financeiras.
Huang, que costumava afirmar que a saída da companhia favorecia o desenvolvimento de tecnologias avançadas pela própria China, deixou o cargo na semana passada em meio a crises de relacionamentos extraconjugais. Um deles envolve Alice Huang, uma executiva investigada por autoridades americanas por suposta espionagem.
Ex-CEO intermediava assunto com o governo
O recuo coloca um freio em um dos principais legados do ex-CEO Jensen Huang para a companhia. O executivo tinha contato direto com o governo para preservar o acesso da Nvidia ao mercado chinês apesar das restrições impostas pelos Estados Unidos, que começaram em 2022.
A companhia desenvolveu ao longo dos últimos anos diferentes produtos compatíveis com as regras americanas de exportação. Um deles é o chip H20, desenvolvido para permanecer abaixo dos limites de desempenho definidos por Washington.
Indo mais além, em agosto do ano passado, fabricantes como Nvidia e AMD concordaram em repassar 15% da receita obtida com determinados chips vendidos à China. Depois de meses de pressão da Nvidia e de negociações entre Washington e Pequim, Trump anunciou no fim de 2025 que permitiria a venda do H200 a clientes chineses aprovados.
Em janeiro deste ano, o governo passou a analisar os pedidos de exportação individualmente e sob condições de segurança. Dez empresas chinesas, entre elas Alibaba, Tencent e ByteDance, receberam autorização para comprar os chips. A China, por outro lado, passou a limitar a entrada dos chips para reduzir a dependência do país de tecnologia estadunidense.
Nvidia enfrenta investigações
Após os casos que levaram à saída de Huang, o conselho da empresa iniciou uma investigação independente sobre o episódio e criou um comitê voltado a segurança nacional e controles de exportação. No Congresso, parlamentares investigam possíveis falhas nos controles sobre o acesso chinês aos chips avançados e querem esclarecimentos sobre a relação com uma pessoa suspeita de atuar para a inteligência de Pequim.
A crise também atingiu o valor da companhia. Na semana da renúncia, as ações haviam recuado mais de US$ 1,8 trilhão (cerca de R$ 10 trilhões), segundo a Reuters. O movimento ocorreu em meio não apenas ao escândalo envolvendo Huang, mas também a dúvidas mais amplas sobre investimentos em IA e à possibilidade de novas restrições às exportações.
Apesar da turbulência, os negócios da Nvidia continuam crescendo. A companhia superou as expectativas de receita no último trimestre e projetou US$ 130 bilhões (R$ 754 bilhões) em vendas para o período seguinte — sem contabilizar novas vendas de chips de data center para a China.

articles.title: The Downfall of Jensen Huang — a timeline of allegations and scandals that brought down the king of AI infrastructure
articles.text:
The Downfall of Jensen Huang — a timeline of allegations and scandals that brought down the king of AI infrastructure
Affairs, geopolitics, and the global AI race. Plus a whole lot of money.
Nvidia rose from a niche gaming hardware company with an unofficial motto of "Our company is thirty days from going out of business” to becoming the world’s most valuable company by market capitalization in 2024, and co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang was the man behind its meteoric rise.
He planned and founded the company in 1993 alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem while sitting inside a Denny’s diner in the Silicon Valley area. After more than 30 years, Nvidia had thousands of employees, a global footprint, and a name that people equated to AI chips.
All this came crumbling down for the billionaire founder in a matter of weeks, but the cracks started long before the first accusation. Let’s go back and see how it all began. This is an ongoing saga, so we have listed stories related to the scandal below, which we will update as events unfold.
The end of an era
Jensen resigned from Nvidia on November 12, after two weeks of news reports accusing him of multiple affairs, one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with his own subordinate. This is significant for Nvidia, which has had a single CEO since its inception. Huang was the face of the company, and many of its employees, shareholders, partners, and fans still support him despite the circumstances of his departure. He steered Nvidia into the giant that it is today by having the vision to develop CUDA nearly 20 years before ChatGPT made AI accessible to the average user and buying companies that helped it scale deployments to hundreds of thousands of AI GPUs.
Jensanity
By 2022, ChatGPT’s arrival and subsequent boom set the AI race in motion, with tech giants and AI startups buying up as many GPUs as they could get their hands on. The increased demand for Nvidia’s products caused it to break the trillion-dollar mark in less than a year after the release of OpenAI’s LLM. As the largest individual shareholders of the company, Huang and his wife, Lori, became some of the wealthiest people in the world.
The billionaire founder hasn't always gloated about his position. He once said in a podcast that if he could turn back time, he wouldn’t have founded Nvidia at all, and also cringed at the praises that the Caltech Board of Trustees chairperson heaped on him before he gave the 2024 keynote speech at the institute’s commencement exercises. He has frequently cited his history working as a “Dishwasher, Busboy, Waiter” at Denny’s, noting it under his experience on his LinkedIn page. More than that, people have seen Jensen go where other celebrity CEOs are rarely seen — enjoying street food in Vietnam, dining at a local fried chicken joint in Korea, and even dragging along 35 of Taiwan’s semiconductor CEOs to a restaurant in Taipei.
But even as he’s building his “Man of the People” persona, his position as the head of arguably the most important chipmaker in the AI industry meant that he was also gaining influence in business and governance. Industry leaders noticed the power that Nvidia held over those who want GPUs to train their AI models, with some of his fellow billionaires begging him over dinner to sell them GPUs. Just weeks into President Donald Trump’s second term, Jensen Huang was meeting with him at the White House, discussing AI policy and hardware export controls — something the Biden administration started in 2022 in an attempt to hold back China’s ambition'sin AI.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The China problem
The rivalry between the U.S. and China has been simmering for years, with Chinese companies like Huawei getting blacklisted because of their work with the People’s Liberation Army. In August 2022, about three months before ChatGPT made AI a household term, Washington expanded its trade bans on Beijing and imposed export controls on Nvidia’s H100 and A100 GPUs. The company responded to this by building a new data center GPU that conformed to U.S. standards specifically for the Chinese market, called the A800, by November of that year. Despite delivering only 70% of the performance of the A100 it was based on, the GPU reportedly still saw great demand from Chinese customers.
However, the A800 only had a relatively short run as the Biden administration once again increased the performance threshold in October 2023, which resulted in the export prohibition of A800 and H800 GPUs to China. This move forced the company to iterate once again, creating new models that it could sell to Chinese companies, like the Nvidia H20. These chips arrived on the market in early 2024, but before the Biden administration ended in January 2025, it proposed even stricter rules called the AI Diffusion Policy. This sorted nations into different tiers based on trust and risk levels — countries in tier 1, which includes the U.S. and its closest allies, have minimal restrictions, while those in tier 3 are effectively barred from receiving advanced AI GPUs containing U.S. technology.
This is problematic for Nvidia, as China is the second-largest computer market in the world t and represented between 20% and 25% of Nvidia's data center sales. The company lobbied the U.S. government to ease AI GPU export restrictions, with Trump reportedly suspending the proposed Nvidia H20 ban after Jensen spent $1 million to have dinner with the president in early April 2025. The White House went ahead anyway and banned the sale of the AI GPU less than a week after that, resulting in a $5.5 billion write-off for the company.
Jensen Huang himself had harsh comments about Washington’s trade ban, saying that “export control was a failure,” and that it had caused the company’s AI GPU market share in China to go from 95% to zero. He even argued that “conceding an entire market the size of China probably does not make a lot of strategic sense, so I think that has already largely backfired.”
But even as Huang was fighting to have the trade ban on the Nvidia H20 chip lifted, he continued praising Trump’s tariff plan, calling it “utterly visionary.” The president eventually reversed the ban three months later, and by December 2025, he had approved Nvidia H200 exports to China, but only if Nvidia pays a 25% fee. The newer Blackwell and Vera Rubin chips remain out of reach for Chinese companies, though — at least on paper.
“There’s no evidence of any AI chip diversion”
Allegations that Chinese companies have been breaking Washington’s trade ban and smuggling Nvidia AI GPUs into China have been circulating since June 2023, after Reuters revealed that vendors in Shenzhen could secure A100 chips when asked discreetly. They reportedly bought these chips from the excess stocks sold in the open market or through intermediaries in India, Taiwan, and Singapore. Another story published in January 2024 asserted that the Chinese military and related institutions, state-run data centers, and even universities continue buying banned A100 and H100 chips. Six months after that, accounts of underground networks dedicated to smuggling AI GPUs — even entire servers — through other countries started emerging.
In 2025, an investigative report showed that at least a billion dollars’ worth of Nvidia AI chips were allegedly funneled into China. Some sellers likened the illicit AI GPU trade to a seafood market, with brokers and retailers openly advertising the most advanced Nvidia AI chips online, from RTX 5090 GPUs to complete B200 servers.
Even with all these reports, Huang continued denying that Nvidia’s chips were being smuggled into China. “There’s no evidence of any AI chip diversion,” the then-CEO told reporters at Computex 2025. He also added, “The Grace Blackwell system is nearly two tons, and so you’re not going to be shipping — you’re not going to be putting that in your pocket or your backpack anytime soon. And so, these systems are fairly easy to keep track of... but the important thing is that the countries and the companies that we sell to recognize that diversion is not allowed, and everybody would like to continue to buy Nvidia technology, and so they very well monitor themselves very carefully and they’re quite careful about that.”
In the midst of all these AI chip smuggling rumors, the Bureau of Industry and Security, the agency in charge of enforcing U.S. trade sanctions, was found to be “inadequate” and underfunded, and it has been relying on outdated manual processes to enforce restrictions on Chinese tech companies. Despite that, companies and individuals across the world are being investigated and arrested for bypassing Washington’s export controls.
Singaporean authorities broke up a smuggling ring in early 2025 that smuggled Nvidia GPUs for Chinese AI lab DeepSeek, resulting in a raid of 22 different locations and the arrest of nine people. In October of the same year, a Singapore company called Megaspeed, which was led by Alice Huang, allegedly diverted $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips. Four Americans were then arrested the following month for shipping 400 Nvidia A100s and attempting to send 50 more Nvidia H200 GPUs to China.
An even bigger smuggling scandal unfolded some four months after the arrests, after three Super Micro employees were arrested for smuggling $2.5 billion of Nvidia hardware into China. The suspects included company co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, although Super Micro itself was not implicated. The Super Micro case spanned the globe, with Taiwanese authorities raiding 12 locations related to the case in May 2026, with another nine sites and six people investigated in June. Jensen Huang urged the company to fix its export control compliance after the arrests and raids, telling the media, “We insist our partners are compliant. We hope that they will enhance and improve their regulatory compliance and prevent that from happening in the future.”
But just five months after he made this statement, one stunning accusation unraveled it all.
Scandal erupts
On October 29, 2026, The New York Times published a report that Jensen Huang may have been the target of a Chinese spy plot through the executive of a firm who was “close” to him — that executive is Alice Huang. Nvidia denied the accusation. “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” a company spokesperson told Tom's Hardware. “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security."
But a little over a week later, U.S. intelligence sources claimed that the former Nvidia chief had an affair with the Megaspeed executive. This is the same Megaspeed that has been accused of smuggling Nvidia chips to the tune of $2 billion. By the evening of Sunday, November 8, Jensen admitted to the affair, although he did not name the third party in his statement.
Many government officials would usually turn a blind eye towards a tech executive’s personal life, but the fact that he is the leader of the U.S.’s premier AI chip maker and that he is also close to the president has caught the attention of authorities. This has led to the U.S. Congress asking him to a closed-door meeting to discuss Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and the FBI investigating his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy.
The admission and allegations led to people digging deeper into Alice Huang. An investigation by The Information revealed that she was connected to a “labyrinth” of companies spanning Singapore, China, and the British Virgin Islands, and that she allegedly helped move around $7.5 billion worth of AI GPU imports. $2 billion was routed from Megaspeed to Speedmatrix, its Malaysia subsidiary, while another $4.6 billion moved directly from the Singaporean company into Shanghai Century Litong, a China-based cloud services company. It has also reportedly bought Nvidia GPUs from other sources, resulting in the estimated total value of its imports.
People close to her also said that she would leverage her relationship with Jensen to customers, often posting pictures with him on her WeChat account, showing potential clients unpublished photos with the Nvidia chief, and even boasting that he would take her to dinner and give her gifts on her birthday. It also seems that Alice Huang was not acting alone. 
Multiple sources say that Kang Wei, Alice Huang’s husband, was central to the operation to acquire AI GPUs. He even seemingly acknowledged her relationship with Jensen Huang and has jokingly said that she was a personal assistant to the billionaire.
However, it seems that the straw that broke the camel’s back was another allegation that Jensen had an affair with another woman — this time, with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care who directly reported to him. Hours after this revelation, the company board announced that Jensen had resigned from all his leadership positions at Nvidia, with employees saying he looked “broken and shattered” as he left the company he spent over three decades building in disgrace. 
Nvidia is looking for internal and external CEO candidates. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim chief executive.
Huang resurfaces
It may be the end of an era, but this does not necessarily spell the end for Jensen Huang. Despite his sudden downfall and quick removal from Nvidia, his status as the king of AI infrastructure remains valuable to the AI industry. Elon Musk even said on X that it “would be an honor” to hire him, and this could ring true for any business that wants to break into the semiconductor space. But does he even want to return?
Huang's first public statement after his resignation came on X on Nov. 17, in which the former CEO said he has "outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," and that if asked by the company's board, he would be "honored" to take the job."
Over 190,000 shareholders, partners, current and former employees, and fans, including Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, have signed an online petition to bring him back as the leader of the company. President Donald Trump called for his reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.
The board, however, may not see things the same way. Multiple reports suggest that the board isn't considering bringing Huang back, and instead is focusing on a new candidate, the ongoing investigation into Huang, and preparing for national security investigations.

The best Black Friday deals at Amazon UK — 28 top offers on Kindles, Ninja, PlayStation 5, De'Longhi, Oral-B, and more
All the best early deals ahead of the full sale on November 19
The Amazon Black Friday sale is about to start. The retailer has confirmed that its mega end-of-year deals event will officially kick off on November 19, but it's also building up to the big day by teasing some early Black Friday offers. I'm finding all of the best ones right here, including discounts on smart home tech, TVs, Kindles, appliances, headphones, and more.
Unsurprisingly, Amazon devices feature heavily in the retailer's early deals, with offers on Ring doorbells, Blink cameras, and even a first-ever price cut on the brand-new Kindle.
Outside of those, though, you can also find a record-low price for our TV of the year, some great savings on PS5 games and accessories, and lots of discounts on top-rated appliances from the likes of Shark, Ninja, KitchenAid, Sage, and more.
With hundreds of more offers on the way tomorrow, I'm going to be busily scouring the digital shelves to bring you the top deals, alongside the standout savings that are already live.
Do stick around for regular updates, including price cuts on top-rated products we've tested, cheap essentials for the home, and cheap tech that work great as gift ideas.

I'm here to help you save money, bring you the best products for the lowest prices that we've tested and love here at TechRadar, and uncover those hidden bargains you don't want to miss.
My top 28 Black Friday deals at Amazon UK
This excellent value bundle includes the latest version of the Ring Video Doorbell and a Ring Indoor Camera for a cheap and easy way to get started with home security. We've tested these and have been impressed with the video quality, high zoom, and night vision colour, but it's a shame that some of this device's value is only usable with a Ring Protect subscription. However, if you're fine with paying for a subscription or already using a Ring-based home security system, it's worth the cost.

This entry-level electric toothbrush is a solid pickup while it's less than half price in Amazon's latest sale. It doesn't boast many impressive high-end features but it has the basic ones you really need to brush your teeth effectively and efficiently, including a two-minute timer and a visible pressure sensor. Plus, you get a handy carry case and a spare brush head included for free.

Amazon's brand-new Kindle has only been available for a few weeks, but it's already discounted to a record-low price for Black Friday. This "thinner, lighter, and faster" Kindle scored four stars in our review, making it a solid choice for most readers — even if older models might offer better value, upgrading to the slightly more expensive Paperwhite could be worth it for the extra features.

The Ninja AF300UK remains an extremely popular and number one best-selling air fryer all these years after its release — and it's now back to the lowest price we've seen all year at Amazon. It's an excellent offer for a large dual-basket air fryer that can prepare multiple foods at once, while being faster and arguably healthier than other conventional cooking methods.

Amazon's newest 4K streaming stick is already down to its lowest-ever price — less than two months after launch. Considering it's only slightly more expensive than the basic HD version, you might as well pay for the upgrade to get a fancy new remote and access to higher-resolution streaming — as long as you have a 4K TV. It lacks a few premium features found in the more expensive Plus and Max models, such as improved Wi-Fi and Dolby Atmos, but this is more than enough to cover general everyday use.

The original Sony WH-1000XM4 were our pick for the best over-ear headphones ever for a long time. This refreshed model of the classics offers top-notch audio, excellent comfort, and effective noise cancellation all at a reasonable price point that's over £100 cheaper than the newer Sony XM6. We still rate these as the best headphones for most people, exactly because you can find them at a price like this when they are on sale.

No matter if you're watching films, streaming TV shows, playing games, or watching sports, it's up to the job.

For starters, it's small and super-slim, making it easy to carry around in a pocket or slip into your bag, while still offering enough juice to charge some of the latest phones and tablets to above 50%. You still get a bright and easy-to-read seven-inch glare-free display, an auto-adjusting front light, space for thousands of books, handy wireless charging support, and a thin, waterproof design. articles.title: GTA VI décroche 99/100 sur Metacritic et rejoint enfin le seul jeu qui régnait depuis 28 ans
articles.text:
Il aura fallu attendre vingt-huit ans pour voir un jeu se hisser aux côtés de Zelda: Ocarina of Time. À la veille de sa sortie, GTA VI compte déjà 145 critiques positives sur Metacritic. Qu’a donc trouvé la presse à Vice City pour lui faire un tel accueil ?
Treize ans qu’on attend de pouvoir écrire ces mots : demain, on retourne à Vice City. Ceux qui ont connu la ville sur PS2 y ont encore une station de radio préférée. D’autres ont grandi à Los Santos et s’apprêtent à la découvrir pour la première fois. On se demande tous un peu la même chose : une fois la manette en main, où est-ce qu’on file en premier ? Les journalistes qui ont déjà passé des dizaines d’heures sur GTA VI avaient un sacré avantage sur nous. À lire leurs tests, certains ont pourtant eu un mal fou à se décider à finir le jeu. Et les raisons qu’ils donnent sont encore plus réjouissantes que ce fameux 99/100.
BenQ iScreenBar : la barre lumineuse qui s’accorde avec l’iMac
Des lignes en harmonie avec celles de l’ordinateur d’Apple, une conception rigoureuse, des matériaux sélectionnés, rien n’a été laissé au hasard, tout comme le service qu’elle rend une fois allumée !
GTA VI en tête de Metacritic, à égalité avec Ocarina of Time
Il faut remonter à 1998, à la Nintendo 64 et au jour où Link est sorti de la forêt pour découvrir la plaine d’Hyrule. Depuis, combien de jeux a-t-on vu passer sans que personne vienne déloger Ocarina of Time ? Ce 18 novembre, Metacritic attribue 99/100 à GTA VI sur PS5. Le site le place en tête de son classement général, juste devant Zelda, qui affiche exactement la même note. Sur la fiche de GTA VI, les 145 critiques recensées à l’heure où nous écrivons sont toutes positives.
Côté français, Gamekult, Gameblog et IGN France accordent tous trois à GTA VI la note maximale sur le barème de Metacritic. Mais ce qui retient Gamekult, c’est la patience nouvelle de Rockstar : à laisser souffler Jason et Lucia entre deux coups, le studio prend le risque de perdre les plus pressés et gagne le temps de nous attacher à eux. Gameblog en raconte l’autre bout, ce petit vide qui s’installe quand le générique défile et qu’on aimerait bien passer encore un moment avec le couple.
Le plus beau braquage de Rockstar, c’est Jason et Lucia
Trevor, Michael et Franklin avaient chacun leurs raisons de courir après l’argent. Jason et Lucia, eux, aimeraient en mettre assez de côté pour pouvoir un jour raccrocher ensemble. La nuance change jusqu’à la façon de jouer. The Verge raconte qu’entre deux grands braquages, on peut alimenter la cagnotte du couple en revendant une voiture volée ou en allant chercher un trésor au fond de la mer, le prochain gros coup peut attendre.
Dans le Guardian, Keza MacDonald, qui a souvent levé les yeux au ciel devant la façon dont GTA traitait les femmes, raconte combien elle s’est attachée à Lucia et Jason. Le journaliste du Washington Post en donne peut-être la plus belle illustration : après 120 heures, il ne s’était toujours pas résolu à leur faire tuer des innocents, même par curiosité. Si vous avez déjà semé une pagaille monstre dans un GTA juste pour voir combien de temps vous tiendriez, vous mesurez le tour de force. Cette fois, on se soucie de ce qu’ils vont devenir.
Vice City se découvre aussi entre deux feux rouges
The Verge raconte une anecdote qui va vous faire sourire : un SMS arrive alors qu’on conduit, on sort le portable pour le lire et, pendant ce temps, la voiture continue de rouler… On finit donc par faire dans GTA ce qu’on aurait dû faire depuis longtemps dans la vraie vie : se garer ! Ars Technica s’attarde de son côté sur les intérieurs et sur ces moments de calme que Rockstar glisse entre deux courses-poursuites. On peut aider un voisin à bricoler sa voiture ou faire griller des burgers au bord de l’eau…voilà qui explique peut-être pourquoi des journalistes pressés par une embargo, ont tout de même trouvé le temps de jouer au minigolf.
En France, Julien Chièze dit avoir bouclé l’histoire en une cinquantaine d’heures et passé près du double dans le Leonida. Il retient notamment le comportement des véhicules, assez différent d’un modèle à l’autre pour donner envie d’en essayer un de plus. Son enthousiasme a pourtant une limite : à force de soigner la mise en scène et de vouloir que tout s’enchaîne sans accroc, Rockstar laisse parfois les amateurs de défi sur leur faim. Et si votre plaisir, dans GTA V, était de sillonner la ville derrière le pare-brise, il relève que la conduite en vue intérieure manque à l’appel.
Sur PS5 Pro, Rob Dwiar, qui approche la centaine d’heures de jeu pour TechRadar, aurait volontiers échangé un peu de cette splendeur contre une animation plus fluide que les 30 images par seconde visées. Le débat risque de nous occuper un moment, tout comme les huit nominations de GTA VI aux Game Awards. Mais demain, quand le jeu sera lancé sur PS5 et Xbox Series X|S, on doute que les notes nous occupent bien longtemps. On aura enfin les clés de Vice City.

articles.title: La reflexión del actor Maxi Iglesias sobre el trabajo: “Trabajamos para pagar cosas que no necesitamos”
articles.text:
Durante la promoción de una de sus películas ha habido una reflexión que me ha llamado la atención. Se trata de cuánto tiempo invertimos en nuestro trabajo y qué hacemos con el dinero obtenido. “Trabajamos para pagar cosas que no necesitamos”, dice Maxi Iglesias. Porque en este modo de gestionar nuestra vida siempre parece haber algo más que conseguir.
En la conversación, él mismo lo asocia a un problema de consumismo. Y para explicarlo utiliza la película “El club de la lucha” (David Fincher, 1999), protagonizada por Brad Pitt y Edward Norton.
Y en ella se asocia el hecho de ganar dinero con el de comprar cosas. De tal forma que si nuestras ambiciones materiales van en aumento, también tenemos que trabajar para ello. Es importante pararse a pensar en estas metas.
La obligación de sentirse productivo
Por otro lado, es relevante dejar claro que no hablamos de la vivienda. “Dejando el tema de la vivienda a un lado, somos muy autómatas en ese sentido, seguimos lo que el sistema nos ha dicho que hay que hacer: generar, producir, sentir que somos productivos, que hacemos y generamos”.
Hay que destacar esta idea de que tenemos que estar haciendo algo. Además de añadir metas a las anteriores. También es importante destacar que el problema está en que esperamos seguir creciendo sin saber dónde está el límite. “¿Hasta dónde se va a engordar la lista? ¿Hasta dónde se va a crecer?”, plantea.
Por otro lado, se puede reflexionar sobre el papel que tiene el trabajo en nuestra vida personal. Es importante repensar nuestras prioridades e incluso el tiempo que dedicamos a otras actividades sin recompensa económica inmediata.
Con el trabajo podemos satisfacer nuestras necesidades. Además, nuestro objetivo puede ser avanzar en nuestro ámbito profesional. Sin embargo, hay que tener cuidado con caer en el problema de ir añadiendo requisitos de manera inercial sin pararnos a pensar para qué sirven. “Lo llevo diciendo muchos años: esto en algún momento va a explotar”.

articles.title: How VedaCorp Sealed the Rs 1,600 Crore A2B–Bodhi Tree Deal After 8 Years
articles.text:
How VedaCorp Sealed the Rs 1,600 Crore A2B–Bodhi Tree Deal After 8 Years
From a single sweet shop in Rajapalayam to 190+ outlets worldwide, A2B is betting on Bodhi Tree to grow its restaurants, snacks and overseas business. The dealmaker behind the Rs 1,600 crore deal shares the inside story.
Adyar Ananda Bhavan (A2B) is one of India’s most trusted food brands. Bodhi Tree Systems, the platform of James Murdoch’s Lupa Systems and Uday Shankar, recently bought a majority stake in the company for about Rs 1,600 crore ($180 million). After the deal, A2B’s total value is estimated at about $350 million (around Rs 2,800 crore to Rs 3,400 crore).
A2B was started about 60 years ago. It took this investment to expand across India and around the world, and to become a global leader in the Indian food business. Under the deal, the majority stake in A2B has now passed to Bodhi Tree Systems.
A2B co-founder K.T. Srinivasa Raja said the company is delighted to begin this next chapter with Bodhi Tree. He said the goal of the partnership is to make A2B a company ready to list on the stock market.
A2B is a leading brand for South Indian restaurants, sweets and savouries. It has a strong base in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka and a growing number of outlets across India. Today it runs 160 outlets in India and more than 30 abroad, with over 15,000 employees.
Few brands in South India’s food business have earned the trust, wide affection and lasting reputation that A2B has built over generations. Adyar Ananda Bhavan has long been known as a family business, and it has now passed into the hands of a Mumbai-based investment firm. Even so, the deal is widely seen as a boost to A2B’s growth. Bodhi Tree’s strategy is to take strong consumer brands towards modern technology and global expansion, and its investment is expected to strengthen that path.
A2B began as a single sweet shop in Rajapalayam. Today it is a strong brand in India and overseas, with operations in Singapore, the US, Australia, Malaysia and the UK. James Murdoch and Uday Shankar, co-founders of Bodhi Tree Systems, said they are eager to take the brand’s authentic traditional food to many more customers around the world.
The deal is also seen as the start of A2B’s next chapter with Bodhi Tree. The plan is to make the company ready for the stock market, and in doing so build a better future for its customers, employees and investors alike.
So how did a traditionally run company like A2B decide to take outside investment on this scale and give up its majority stake? And who was the key link behind the deal?
How the A2B–Bodhi Tree deal came together
The groundwork for A2B’s landmark deal was laid by VedaCorp, a leading investment bank and corporate finance advisory firm founded in Chennai in 2003.
VedaCorp has more than 23 years of experience helping growing companies raise private equity and handle mergers and acquisitions (M&A). It works across sectors such as IT, healthcare, consumer goods, retail, fintech and manufacturing.
The firm has closed more than a hundred major transactions so far and has played a key role in several notable Indian business deals. These include Titan’s acquisition of a majority stake in online jewellery retailer CaratLane and ChrysCapital’s investment in CavinKare, among others. It also closed a major deal for Kovai Pazhamudhir Nilayam (KPN), a leading Tamil Nadu retail company. In that all-cash deal, private equity firm WestBridge Capital bought about 70% of KPN for Rs 550 crore to Rs 600 crore, valuing the company at Rs 800 crore.
Sivaraj Sekar, Managing Director of VedaCorp, played a central role in the A2B deal. He spoke to YourStory Tamil in detail about it. Here are edited excerpts from the conversation.
Induja: You played a key role in this deal. How did you bring a traditional family business to the negotiating table? How did you begin as the middleman?
Sivaraj Sekar: We were the exclusive advisors for this transaction. I led it together with my co-partner Atul. A2B is a famous brand with a legacy of about 50 years. We have known the company for the past 7–8 years and have met and spoken with them from time to time.
There are many hotel brands, but names like Sangeetha or Geetham usually stay within one city or one state. That is because food habits and tastes change from state to state. For example, Tamil Nadu sambar is very different from Karnataka sambar. Travel just 200 to 300 km and the food changes. I noticed eight years ago that A2B had overcome this challenge.
In 2016–17, we met A2B’s founders, Srinivasa Raja and Venkatesan. We asked them:
“What is your next plan? A2B is a very strong brand. If you bring in institutional capital like private equity, you could take the company to the next level much faster.” Back then they said, “No, we have enough internal funds. We are growing in our own way, and we don’t need outside capital right now.”
People who have run a business successfully for 50 years have that self-belief and fighting spirit, and that is what brought them this far. But we kept talking to them.
We explained, “Borrowing from a bank is very different from bringing in outside investors. Investors bring not just capital but also fresh thinking and best business practices. They will widen your vision.”
Induja: So the deal became possible only after talking for nearly 7 to 8 years?
Sivaraj: We have known them for 7–8 years, but things really picked up only in the last two years. Beyond Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, they have 170 outlets across India, including Andhra Pradesh and Delhi. They also have 30 outlets abroad in the US, Australia, Sri Lanka, Singapore and Malaysia, and they are about to enter Europe. When we met them again two years ago, we told them:
“If you want to do justice to the original vision you had when you started this company with your father and brothers, this brand has to travel the world.” They really liked that.
We had earlier advised Kovai Pazhamudhir Nilayam. Their family business had been split among several partners, and we brought it together as one company and helped it raise investment. We also brought Temasek’s investment into Milky Mist. We shared those experiences with A2B too.
Induja: Traditional family businesses usually have a deep emotional bond with their brand. How did you handle that as an advisor?
Sivaraj: Yes, that’s true. But what sets us apart is that we don’t look only at the numbers, like the valuation or how much money will come in. We also look at the chemistry between the two sides. So we encouraged Srinivasa Raja to speak with Senthil, the founder of Kovai Pazhamudhir Nilayam (KPN). Senthil shared his experience of working with investors.
He explained that bringing in a professional team cut the capital cost of opening an outlet from Rs 100 to Rs 70–80, which let them open more outlets. He also talked about best practices in areas like people development and cutting food waste. Because KPN is also a Tamil Nadu company, this gave A2B a lot of confidence.
They will also judge whether we are talking just to close a deal or truly for their growth. So we earned their trust and clearly defined what their role in the transaction would be.
Induja: When you were convincing them, did you have Bodhi Tree Systems in mind? Or did you look for investors after they agreed? What was it like bringing the two sides together?
Sivaraj: When we first meet any company, we never have a particular investor in mind. First, we build their belief that they have a big growth opportunity and can raise outside capital. Only after they agreed did we start approaching investors.
“Several investors came forward, and we assessed them on many criteria, including valuation, cultural fit, and rights and obligations. We chose Bodhi Tree because they are excellent operators. We have seen how they scaled the Allen education business in a big way, and how they performed at JioStar. They are very good at spotting the right talent and bringing it into a company.”
Indian food is hugely popular around the world. But unlike pizza or cookies, we can’t mass-produce and sell dosas or puris. Each one takes time to make. So scaling up without losing quality needs the right team and the right mindset.
“I hear that people wait 40 minutes for a table at the A2B restaurant in New Jersey, US. It isn’t just the restaurants. Their sweets and savouries are loved by everyone from 6 to 60. We chose Bodhi Tree because this brand needs the right team to take it to the next level.”
Induja: When did Bodhi Tree join the talks? How did the final stages play out?
Sivaraj: Bodhi Tree came into the talks about a year ago. They were very keen and moved very fast. But A2B had never raised outside capital before, so we needed a year to get the company ready. Of the last two years, we spent one full year just preparing the company for this. Only after that was the deal closed.
Induja: A2B is a family business. How did the second and third generations respond to this investment decision?
Sivaraj: They were very welcoming. Many of them studied abroad in places like Australia and Singapore and have worked at large companies. They understand the global market, so they were very open-minded.
Once the founders agreed, they told us that this was a 50-year legacy and the family had to be consulted. We held several rounds of meetings with the family. They asked very sharp, direct questions. We gave clear answers and helped them understand.
Induja: Now that the majority stake has gone to Bodhi Tree, what is next for A2B?
Sivaraj: They plan to grow the company in three key areas:
- More outlets: Opening many more outlets in India and abroad. There are still many places in India they have yet to reach.
- Snacks business: Haldiram has grown into a company earning Rs 12,000 crore in revenue and now plans to go public at a market value of Rs 1 lakh crore. That shows how big the Indian snacks market is. A2B also plans to expand its snacks business in a big way.
- International expansion: They will focus strongly on adding more outlets overseas.
Induja: With the majority stake now with an investment firm, will A2B’s distinctive quality and people’s bond with the brand stay the same? What will the family’s role be from now on?
Sivaraj: Their next goal is to list the company on the stock market (IPO/listing) in the next 2 to 4 years. A heritage brand from South India going public would be a huge milestone. Milky Mist has grown well since going public, and we believe A2B will do very well too. That belief is why we have taken steps like professionalising the company and bringing in outside investment.
“As for the founders, they will stay on the board, and the second generation will continue in their roles. The company’s core DNA and its distinctive quality will not change. The deal has been designed so that this quality continues.”
Induja: Will your journey with A2B continue from here?
Sivaraj: Our job is to raise capital for companies, but we always stay in touch with them. A company needs several rounds of funding as it grows, so our advisory journey with them will carry on.
Induja: Today, startups are usually the ones most eager to raise investment. What message do you have for those running traditional family businesses?
Sivaraj: I have seen companies that once saw selling a stake as being like pawning the family jewels. But today I am also seeing a shift, with founders keeping just 5–6% of their company and growing it to a very large scale.
I have just one thing to say to heritage brands:
“If you have a strong brand and have grown it as far as you can, the only thing holding back the next phase of growth is the mindset of the people at the top. If you want to truly do justice to your brand and want it to travel beyond borders, you have to think big. It could be private equity or a partnership. You have to be open to talking about it.”

articles.title: How Airbnb uses cost per task to operate coding agents on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Airbnb uses cost per task to operate coding agents on Amazon Bedrock
Amazon Bedrock provides access to foundation models from multiple providers through a common API, with AWS managing the model infrastructure. It integrates with AWS access controls and monitoring, and processes prompts, code, and model responses within AWS.
As coding agents move into production, changes in models and usage can affect latency, capacity, and cost. Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics in Amazon CloudWatch help teams investigate latency increases, throttling, and changes in token consumption. Evaluations, or evals, complement these operational metrics by assessing the quality of an agent’s work on a fixed set of representative tasks.
In this post, we show how Airbnb evaluates models for coding agents and monitors their use on Amazon Bedrock. We explain how cost per task guides model selection and how production data helps us revisit those choices as usage changes. We also describe the runtime signals used to investigate latency, throttling, and spend.
At Airbnb, thousands of engineers and engineering-adjacent people use AirChat, our internal tool for running coding agents, every week. The agents send their model requests through our large language model (LLM) gateway, which runs on Amazon Bedrock. Bedrock processes Airbnb’s code, prompts, and model responses within AWS. Eight new models came out in about five weeks. By mid-October, about two thirds of the requests our engineers sent through coding agents went to those new models.
Each release can change output tokens, cost, latency and capacity at once, and the benchmark charts published with a launch don’t show how a model handles our engineers’ work. So we run two systems side by side. Before a rollout, we run evals on our own tasks to measure each model’s score and cost per task. Cost per task is the list-price cost of all the tokens an agent uses to finish one task.
After a rollout, observability shows us what changed in production. When production usage doesn’t match the eval results, we find out why.
Solution overview
You can diagnose most production problems with a few signals in the AWS/Bedrock namespace in CloudWatch:
- Latency: InvocationLatency, TimeToFirstToken, OutputTokenCount, and output tokens per second (OTPS), which you derive.
- Throttling: InvocationThrottles, plus the tokens each request reserves against your quota, which you publish yourself. Bedrock also publishes EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage, which measures your estimated tokens per minute (TPM) quota consumption, including cache write tokens and output burndown multipliers, across all inference APIs (Converse, InvokeModel, ConverseStream, and InvokeModelWithResponseStream). You can use this metric to set proactive alarms before reaching your quota limit, track your quota consumption across your models, and request further quota increases before usage is rate limited.
- Cost: InputTokenCount (uncached input), CacheReadInputTokenCount, CacheWriteInputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount, each priced at its own rate. Cache reads cost less than uncached input, and cache writes can cost more depending on the model. A lower cache hit rate can increase cost per request.
On top of these metrics, we add cost per task. Our evals measure a score and a cost per task for every model and every reasoning effort we allow. Reasoning effort is a setting that controls how much a model reasons before it responds. We use the results to choose each default, which is the model and effort that our coding tools use unless an engineer picks another, and each effort ceiling, which is the highest effort we allow for a model.
Architecture
Engineers run AirChat on their AirDev workspaces, which are personal development machines in the cloud. They can also hand a task to AirChat Remote, which runs cloud agents in separate cloud workspaces while the engineer does something else. Both paths go through our LLM gateway to Amazon Bedrock.
Figure 1 shows how AirChat and AirChat Remote reach Amazon Bedrock through our gateway. It also shows how evals and production monitoring guide model defaults and effort ceilings.
The gateway records the model, client, team, and user for each request. We use these records only in aggregate, for cost and capacity planning. CloudWatch supplies token counts, latency, errors, and throttles. We compare those production signals with our eval scores and cost per task to decide when defaults or effort ceilings need to change.
Prerequisites
On the AWS side, you need:
- Access to the models in Amazon Bedrock you plan to run and evaluate. For model availability by AWS Region, see Regional availability by models in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.
- Streaming calls through ConverseStream or InvokeModelWithResponseStream. Bedrock publishes TimeToFirstToken only for the streaming APIs.
- Model invocation logging, turned on in every AWS Region you call. It’s off by default. The logs can hold full prompts and responses along with the caller’s identity, so restrict who can read them and set a retention period.
Tagged IAM roles for your callers, with cost allocation tags activated. Activate them before you start collecting, because activation doesn’t backfill earlier costs.
You also need three things of your own:
- A set of tasks from your own engineering work. Give each one a starting repository state, the prompt an engineer would write and a grader you trust. A grader is the program or model that scores the agent’s work. We build our tasks from real code changes, the review comments on those changes and the decisions that the original ticket didn’t spell out. Step 2 shows one.
- A gateway or proxy in front of Bedrock that records the model, the client, the team, the user and the token counts for each request.
- A table of public list prices for every model you run, with a date on each entry, so you can price eval tokens and production tokens on the same basis.
Before rollout, define what the agents can access and which actions need human review. Run code in isolated workspaces and test generated changes before merging. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can help filter harmful content and sensitive information in prompts and responses. For responses based on supplied reference material, contextual grounding checks can flag unsupported claims. Test these controls on your own tasks and include their latency and cost in your measurements.
Walkthrough
Start by measuring what a complete task costs. Then use those results to choose model defaults, check production behavior, manage capacity, and attribute spend.
Step 1: What does one finished task cost you?
A coding agent takes many requests to finish one task, and on each request the model re-reads the context so far. So we price the whole task.
Bedrock reports four kinds of tokens for each request: uncached input, cache reads, cache writes and output. In an eval run we price all four for every request and add up the requests in the task. Every cost in this post uses the public list prices dated for that run. We record the average cost next to the score for every model, reasoning effort and agent client we test, and the average includes low-scoring attempts.
Reasoning effort changes both score and cost. On one model we tested, moving from low to high effort raised the score by 0.8 points. Cost per task was 2.5 times as high. We use these results to set effort ceilings, which the gateway enforces.
Step 2: How fast can you evaluate a new model?
On the afternoon a new model came out, a single request to our agents started an eval campaign, which runs the new model through all our task suites. A suite is a fixed set of tasks of one type, and we have seven. Agents spread hundreds of tasks across the suites and several cloud workspaces, and each result appeared as soon as a grader scored it. First results arrived within hours. By the next morning, every suite had a score and a cost per task, and we had what we needed for a deployment decision for the entire org.
That speed depends on tasks that are already written down. Each task is a folder that holds everything one run needs. Here is a trimmed task from our machine learning work:
The grader recomputes the right answer from frozen data on every run, and the agent earns a reward of 1 only if every check passes. To test one model at every effort, list each effort as its own agent in a job config:
Both examples use the formats of Harbor, an open-source framework for running agent evals in sandboxes. It’s one option if you’re starting out.
Running the evals can be optimized. Writing the rubric, the scoring guide that a grader follows, is the hardest part. Our long tasks run over several rounds, with a simulated reviewer pushing back between rounds. A model grader scores each run on eight weighted dimensions. Each dimension gets a score from 0 to 3.
Because of ceilings like this one, an agent that needed rescuing can’t score well on polish alone.
Step 3: What do you watch after a rollout?
When latency rises, chart three signals before you open a support case: TimeToFirstToken for the wait before generation starts, OutputTokenCount for response length, and OTPS for generation speed. Bedrock has no native OTPS metric. You derive it with metric math, as the Amazon Bedrock User Guide describes:
In the example from our session, latency rose 40 percent while time to first token and OTPS stayed flat. Someone had changed the system prompt to ask for more thorough answers, and output tokens per request rose 50 percent. The model generated at the same speed and wrote longer responses. Treat prompt changes and model upgrades as deploys, and mark them on your dashboard.
Each week we put the CloudWatch runtime metrics next to the usage records from our gateway for each model. For cost and capacity planning, we also look at usage in aggregate: cost per request and the average number of requests per user each week. A new model can move both. After every rollout, we compare them with what we expected from the eval’s cost per task.
Step 4: The evals looked good. What did production show?
One model, which we call model A, looked good in our evals. On our coding tasks, it scored more than three points above our previous best model. Cost per task was about the same, and the same grader scored every model. We rolled it out, capped effort at high, and asked people to use low or medium for most work.
A few weeks after launch, we priced model A’s production usage at list price and looked at it in aggregate. Average weekly spend per user was several times higher on model A than on the model before it. Each model A request cost about three times as much, and the average model A user sent about three times as many requests.
Output tokens made up only a tenth of a request’s cost. Most of the cost went to cached context, which the model re-read on every request. Model A could work on its own for a long time, so people started long, self-directed sessions with it.
The eval measured the model on a task. Production measured how people chose to work with it.
Later, a newer model scored higher than model A on the same tasks and grader, at about a sixth of its cost per task. We moved model A’s users to it with a configuration change.
We then checked the change in aggregate on the same user group, the heavy users of model A. In their first full week on the newer model, the group sent about the same number of requests to their main model, and the group’s spend on that model fell to about a seventh.
Step 5: Why you get throttled, and where traffic goes next
On the bedrock-runtime endpoint, Bedrock checks your tokens-per-minute quota when a request arrives, before the model writes anything. It reserves your uncached input tokens and your cache writes, plus max_tokens, the most output the request is allowed. It adjusts that reservation as the model generates and returns the unused part when the request settles. Cache reads never count against the quota, so a request can be cheap against your quota and expensive on your bill. Output tokens settle at a burndown rate that is 1:1 on most models and several times that on some current models, so check your model’s rate.
A dashboard of billed tokens can show room while requests are being throttled. In our session’s example, the quota was 1 million tokens per minute and traffic was 300 requests per minute. The dashboard showed about 30 percent of quota. After applying a 5:1 output-token burndown rate, completed requests consumed about 77 percent.
Admission uses a different calculation. Each request initially reserved 600 uncached input tokens plus a max_tokens of 4,096, for a total of 4,696 tokens. Responses were about 800 tokens at p99.
Lowering max_tokens to 1,024 cut the initial reservation to 1,624 tokens, about 65 percent smaller. The limit was still above p99. For unchanged input and output, final quota consumption stays the same. The smaller reservation leaves more room to admit requests. Monitor stopReason to catch truncated responses. Use backoff and jitter, and cap retries.
Demand can also outrun the headroom you have on any one model. You want to know where work can go before you need it, and our evals answer that. The answer can be a model from another model family. For every major model we use, we keep at least one equivalent that performs as well on our evals and that we can load-balance to. Without those evals, choosing where the work goes would be guesswork.
If headroom on a model stays tight, we can rebalance by changing a default in our configuration. First check that the equivalent model has capacity for the extra load and that your quota covers it. Keep enough traffic on it to hold your access, too: after a model enters its Legacy period, existing customers can lose access after 15 days of inactivity. A Legacy model works until end-of-life, and after that Bedrock removes it from every Region, requests to it fail, and Bedrock doesn’t move your traffic automatically. Alarm when LegacyModelInvocations rises above zero.
Step 6: Whose spend is it?
Bedrock runtime metrics are dimensioned by ModelId, so you can see which model served a request but not which team sent it. Bedrock publishes these metrics both with and without the ModelId dimension, and a request that fails before Bedrock resolves the model appears only in the series without it, so filtering by ModelId undercounts errors. Bedrock offers three ways to attribute spend:
- Which team or user? Bedrock records the caller’s IAM identity on every request. Tag your roles, or pass session tags, to see cost by tag in AWS Cost Explorer and the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR 2.0).
- Which application? Application inference profiles are model-specific, so create one tagged profile per application and model, and call the matching profile’s ARN.
- Which feature or prompt? Pass key-value pairs in requestMetadata on Converse. Bedrock writes them to the model invocation logs and leaves them off the bill. To price them, multiply the token counts in the logs by the published rates. Neither classic CUR nor CUR 2.0 carries a per-request ID, so reconcile the two by comparing totals by model, usage type and time period.
Behind a gateway, Bedrock sees the gateway’s role, so have the gateway assume a role for each user with its own RoleSessionName or session tags. Cache those credentials for the session, because assuming a role on every request can exceed your AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) rate quotas. Requests keep succeeding when attribution breaks, so set an alarm for when Bedrock fails to deliver invocation logs.
Our usage records let us attribute usage by model, client, team and user, which we use only in aggregate for cost and capacity planning. We compute cost per task from the same four token counts, so we can compare token mix and cost between our evals and production.
Results
We can go from a model release to a deployment decision overnight. After one rollout, average weekly spend per user on model A was several times that on the previous model. We moved its heavy users to a newer model. In their first full week, the group’s spend on its main model fell to about a seventh, with roughly the same number of requests. For every major model we use, our evals identify an equivalent we can rebalance to.
Clean up
After testing, stop the eval jobs and agent processes you started. If you enabled model invocation logging only for this walkthrough, disable it in each Region using DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration.
After callers no longer use them, delete the application inference profiles you created using DeleteInferenceProfile. Remove IAM roles, policies, and resource tags created only for this walkthrough. Deactivate cost allocation tags used only for these tests. Delete test CloudWatch log groups and S3 log objects you no longer need.
Conclusion
We run four checks every time a model ships:
- Release day: run the new model on your own tasks at every effort, and record a score and a cost per task together.
- Before rollout: choose the default and cap effort from those numbers. Block any effort that costs more and scores less than a lower effort.
- First weeks: compare cost per request and average requests per user with the eval’s cost per task, pricing both from the same four token counts.
- Before you need it: know which models score the same on your evals, from any model family, and check their capacity and your quota before you rebalance.
We chose Amazon Bedrock for access to multiple model families through one API. It lets us use our existing AWS access controls and logging while AWS manages the model infrastructure. We use evals to choose models for our work and observability to know when those choices need another look.
To go further, see these pages in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide:

articles.title: Semantic caching helps enforce AI agent governance inline - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Agents want the crown jewels: HPE and Daxa push governance down to the data layer
Enterprises are handing AI agents their most sensitive data, and governance is struggling to keep pace. Techniques such as semantic caching are emerging as a way to enforce controls inline without slowing agents down.
Moving agents from pilot to production means letting them read, change and even delete the records that matter most. That shift makes data access the central security question for agentic AI, according to Huseni Saboowala (pictured, right), co-founder and chief executive officer at Daxa Inc.
“For agents to really get to value, they need to be able to interact with your real enterprise data, and that includes your crown jewels, your intellectual property, your customer data in your [customer relationship management] and your proprietary trading algorithms,” he said. “That creates an unprecedented level of risk for enterprises because the agents are not just reading data; they’re also able to now go manipulate data at scale.”
Saboowala and Robin Braun (left), vice president of AI business development at Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., spoke with theCUBE’s Enterprise Editor, Paul Gillin, during coverage of SC26 on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. Daxa is a partner in HPE’s Unleash AI program, which offers pre-validated software on HPE Private Cloud AI. (* Disclosure below.)
Semantic caching brings governance into agent workflows
Firewalls, data loss prevention and identity management still have a job to do. But they were built for users and applications, not software that reasons over data, Saboowala explained.
“Those agents are operating, though, at layer 8, what we call the cognitive layer,” he said. “This is where you have the prompts, the responses, the retrievals and the tool calls happening. Traditional tools really are not operating at this layer.”
Saboowala’s answer is reasoning-based access controls, backed by agents that flag abnormal behavior. HPE builds governance into its Private Cloud AI stack from the start, according to Braun.
“Being able to build in that governance from day one allows you to understand what is it going to look like so that … you’re not bolting it on later,” she said. “Instead, it’s a part of the workflow.”
Timing matters as much as policy. Offline governance arrives too late for agents working at machine speed, so enforcement must happen inline through semantic caching, specialized small language models and a distributed data plane, Saboowala explained. A regional bank that deployed Daxa with HPE has since connected its agents to source code and regulated customer data.
“I believe that the winners in this agent era are not just the ones who have the most [graphics processing units],” Saboowala said. “But they will be enterprises who have agents they can trust with their data.”
