articles.title: Private certificate authority support in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Private certificate authority support in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity
Many teams that build applications self-host their identity provider (IdP), such as Keycloak or PingFederate, inside a private network. These IdPs usually present a TLS server certificate from a private certificate authority (CA). With private CA support in AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, your agents can now connect to these IdPs while trusting the private CA that your organization already uses.
AgentCore Identity now supports private CA certificates for private identity providers. You store the PEM-encoded CA certificate in AWS Secrets Manager or Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and reference it from your credential provider. The CA certificate contains only the public certificate, not its private key. AgentCore Identity uses it to validate the server certificate presented by your IdP’s discovery, JSON Web Key Set (JWKS), and token endpoints. The CA certificate must be a root or intermediate CA certificate.
In this post, we show you how to issue an IdP certificate with AWS Private Certificate Authority. We then configure an AgentCore Identity credential provider to trust it and rotate the CA while minimizing downtime. We also show how to protect the CA certificate so that only your IdP team can change it. Although AgentCore Identity supports any private CA, including enterprise, third-party, and self-signed root CAs, the walkthrough in this post uses AWS Private CA and Keycloak as the IdP.
Solution overview
Consider an agent that needs to call an internal wiki API protected by your Keycloak IdP. The agent runs on AgentCore Runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which hosts your agent code. To get an OAuth 2.0 access token from Keycloak, the agent uses an AgentCore Identity credential provider, which holds the IdP connection details and client credentials.
The following diagram shows this setup. Keycloak runs in your virtual private cloud (VPC) behind an internal Application Load Balancer. The load balancer presents an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) private certificate signed by AWS Private CA. The CA certificate that AgentCore Identity trusts is stored in Secrets Manager or Amazon S3.
AgentCore Identity reaches the IdP privately through Amazon VPC Lattice, which connects to your VPC through a resource gateway, an entry point for VPC Lattice traffic into your VPC. VPC Lattice is required for private CA support. If you choose the managed option, AgentCore Identity creates and manages the VPC Lattice resources for you.
The flow works as follows:
- You store the CA certificate in Secrets Manager or Amazon S3.
- You create a credential provider that points to your IdP and to the CA certificate.
- AgentCore Identity reads the CA certificate and checks that it’s a valid CA certificate.
- Your agent requests an access token from AgentCore Identity.
- AgentCore Identity connects to the IdP through VPC Lattice and checks the load balancer certificate against your CA.
- The IdP issues the token and AgentCore Identity returns it to your agent.
Agents that use machine-to-machine, on-behalf-of, and user-delegated flows can also use the private CA without changing their code.
Prerequisites
To follow this walkthrough, you need:
- An AWS account with access to the AgentCore console, in a supported AWS Region where AgentCore Identity supports private IdPs.
- A self-hosted, OpenID Connect (OIDC) compliant IdP that runs in your VPC, with an OAuth client registered for your agent. The networking requirements, including subnets, security groups, and a private hosted zone for the IdP hostname, are described in Connect to private identity providers.
- The latest version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and OpenSSL.
- Permission to create credential providers, plus read access to the CA certificate. AgentCore Identity reads the certificate with the credentials of the principal that calls CreateOauth2CredentialProvider, so that principal needs secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on the secret or s3:GetObject on the object. If the secret or object is encrypted with a customer managed AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key, the principal also needs kms:Decrypt on that key.
Considerations
Keep the following in mind when you plan your deployment:
- Private IdPs only: A credential provider or authorizer must have a privateEndpoint to use a private CA. Otherwise, the request fails with the message The private certificate authority feature can only be used with private IdP.
- CA certificates in PEM format: The file must be PEM-encoded and no larger than 16 KB. It must contain only root or intermediate CA certificates that are within their validity period.
- One certificate source per provider: Each credential provider references one secret or one S3 object. To trust more than one CA, put the certificates in the same PEM file.
- Storage location: The secret or S3 object must be in the same AWS Region as the credential provider. Secrets Manager secrets must also be in the same account as the credential provider. S3 objects can be in another account when you provide bucketOwnerAccountId and the bucket policy grants access.
- Regions: Private CA support depends on VPC Lattice and is available in the AWS Regions where AgentCore Identity supports private IdPs.
Walkthrough
The walkthrough has four steps. If your IdP already presents a certificate from your enterprise CA, skip to Step 2.
Step 1: Issue a server certificate for your IdP
Start by creating a root CA in AWS Private CA. For instructions, see Create a private CA and Install the CA certificate. Choose general-purpose mode, because short-lived certificate mode issues certificates that are valid for 7 days or less. When you create the CA, authorize ACM to renew certificates, so that ACM can renew the IdP’s server certificate before it expires.
Next, request the server certificate. AgentCore Identity checks that the certificate matches the IdP hostname, so include each hostname that appears in your IdP’s discovery document as a subject alternative name (SAN). In most Keycloak deployments, the discovery, JWKS, and token endpoints share one hostname. For example, if your discovery URL is https://keycloak.example.local/realms/agents/.well-known/openid-configuration, add keycloak.example.local as a SAN.
To request a private certificate for the IdP (console)
- Open the ACM console and choose Request.
- Choose Request a private certificate and then choose Next.
- For Certificate authority, choose the CA that you created.
- For Fully qualified domain name, enter the IdP hostname, for example keycloak.example.local.
- Choose Request.
- Attach the certificate to the HTTPS listener of the internal load balancer in front of your IdP. For instructions, see Update an HTTPS listener.
Step 2: Store the CA certificate
AgentCore Identity needs to trust the CA certificate to validate the IdP’s server certificate. Because it trusts the CA rather than the server certificate itself, you don’t need to update the credential provider each time the server certificate renews.
Export the CA certificate from AWS Private CA in PEM format:
Before you upload the file, check it against the requirements. The file must be PEM-encoded and meet size requirements, containing only CA certificates that are within their validity period. The following commands show the CA flag, expiry date, and file size. The last command confirms that the IdP’s certificate chains to this CA. Run it from a host that can reach the IdP. It returns Verify return code: 0 (ok) when the chain is valid.
The output looks similar to the following:
Store the file in Secrets Manager or Amazon S3. A Secrets Manager secret must be a string secret in the same account as the credential provider. An S3 object can be in another account, which suits organizations that run the IdP in a central account.
Give write access to the secret or object only to the team that operates your IdP. For an example policy, see Protect the CA certificate later in this post.
Step 3: Create the credential provider
You can create the credential provider in the AgentCore console or with the AWS CLI. The private CA settings appear on the console only after you connect the OAuth client to a VPC, because private CA support applies only to private IdPs.
To create a credential provider that trusts your private CA (console)
- Open the AgentCore console and in the navigation pane under Connections, choose Outbound Auth. Then choose Add OAuth client.
- For Provider, choose Customized provider. For Configuration type, choose Discovery URL and enter your IdP’s discovery URL, for example https://keycloak.example.local/realms/agents/.well-known/openid-configuration. Then enter the client ID and client secret.
- Expand Additional configurations. Under VPC security, choose Managed and select the VPC, subnets, and security groups that can reach the IdP. If you manage your own VPC Lattice resources, choose Self-managed and select the resource configuration instead.
- Under Root certificate authority, choose Add root certificate.
- In the Add root certificate panel, for Certificate source, choose AWS Secrets Manager and select the secret that you created in Step 2. To use Amazon S3, choose Amazon S3 and enter the S3 URI. For an object in another account, also enter the Bucket owner account ID.
- Choose Apply.
- Choose Add OAuth client.
The Root certificate authority field accepts either a root or an intermediate CA certificate.
To create the same credential provider with the AWS CLI, add certificateConfigurations to the custom OAuth 2.0 provider configuration:
To use Amazon S3 instead, replace the certificateConfigurations entry with {"s3": {"uri": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/trust-anchors/keycloak-root-ca.pem", "bucketOwnerAccountId": "444455556666"}}. If you leave out bucketOwnerAccountId, AgentCore Identity expects the bucket to be in your own account. To keep the client secret out of your shell history, you can reference a client secret that you store in Secrets Manager.
Step 4: Verify the credential provider
AgentCore Identity validates the certificate and sets up private connectivity in the background, so a new credential provider starts in the CREATING status. Check the status after a few minutes:
On the console, the credential provider’s details page shows the configured certificate under Root certificates. When the status is READY, your agents can request tokens from the IdP. If the status is CREATE_FAILED, the failureReason field explains why. For example, Leaf certificates are not allowed, must provide CA certificates only means that you uploaded the server certificate instead of the CA certificate. If you see Unable to access S3 object or Secrets Manager can't find the specified secret, check that the URI or Amazon Resource Name (ARN) is correct. Also confirm that your identity can read the object or secret. If the provider is READY but token requests fail, confirm that the IdP’s server certificate was issued by the configured CA and has a SAN that matches the IdP hostname.
Monitor and rotate the CA certificate
After you verify that the credential provider trusts the private CA, monitor the CA certificate’s expiration and rotate it before it expires to prevent token request failures. AgentCore Identity publishes the EarliestCertificateDaysToExpiry metric to Amazon CloudWatch in the AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore namespace when your agents request tokens through a credential provider that uses a private CA. The metric reports the days remaining until the earliest certificate in your PEM file expires. It has ProviderName, ProviderArn, and TokenVault dimensions. When you create an alarm, specify all three. We recommend a CloudWatch alarm that notifies you well before the value reaches zero, because token requests to the IdP stop working when the CA certificate expires.
        NOTE: AgentCore Identity reads the certificate only when you create or update the credential provider. If you change the secret or S3 object, call UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider afterward so that AgentCore Identity reads the new content. Include certificateConfigurations in the update request. If you leave it out, the credential provider stops trusting your private CA.
A PEM file can contain more than one CA certificate and AgentCore Identity trusts each of them. You can use this to rotate to a new CA while minimizing downtime:
- Combine the current and new CA certificates in one file, for example with cat current-ca.pem new-ca.pem > rotation.pem. Upload the file to your secret or S3 object.
- Call UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider and wait for the status to return to READY.
- Replace the IdP’s server certificate with one issued by the new CA.
- After token requests succeed, upload a file that contains only the new CA certificate and call UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider again.
AgentCore Identity doesn’t check certificate revocation lists (CRLs) or use the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP). This means that if an unauthorized party obtains the private key for an IdP server certificate, AgentCore Identity continues to trust that certificate. This trust lasts until the certificate expires or until you stop trusting the CA that issued it. To stop trusting a CA, remove it from the PEM file and update the credential provider.
Protect the CA certificate
A CA certificate contains no private key and is public by design, because you hand it to every client that has to trust your IdP. What you need to protect is the data integrity of the trust store, meaning the secret or S3 object that holds the certificate. If someone replaces the certificate or adds another CA certificate to the trust store, the next update could let an unauthorized party who can redirect traffic impersonate your IdP.
We recommend that you scope permissions around writes rather than reads. Give write access, such as s3:PutObject or secretsmanager:PutSecretValue, only to the team or pipeline that operates the IdP. Give read access to the principals that call CreateOauth2CredentialProvider or UpdateOauth2CredentialProvider. During these operations, AgentCore Identity reads the CA certificate using the caller’s IAM permissions. The following bucket policy for a central identity account (444455556666) lets only the role that manages credential providers in a workload account (111122223333) read the CA certificates. It also requires that role to belong to your organization in AWS Organizations, and it denies writes from principals other than the IdP administrator role:
The principal in the workload account also needs s3:GetObject in its own IAM policy. For Secrets Manager, which must be in the same account, use a resource-based policy on the secret to restrict writes to the IdP administrator role.
Because the secret is in the same account, IAM policies can grant read access, so the resource policy only needs to deny changes:
Turn on S3 Versioning to recover an overwritten file and AWS CloudTrail data events to record each change. Because the CA certificate isn’t confidential, SSE-S3 encryption is sufficient and avoids the cross-account AWS KMS permissions that a customer managed key requires.
Keep the trust scope of each credential provider narrow. Upload only the CA that issues your IdP’s server certificate, rather than your organization’s full trust bundle. If your IdPs use different CAs, store each CA certificate in its own secret or S3 object so that each credential provider trusts only the CA that it needs.
Use a private CA for inbound authorization
You can also use a private CA for inbound authorization. When AgentCore Runtime or AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, validates JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) issued by a private IdP, it fetches the IdP’s discovery document and its signing keys from the JWKS endpoint. AgentCore Gateway validates the discovery URL when you create the gateway. If the CA certificate is missing or doesn’t match the IdP’s certificate chain, the gateway status changes to FAILED with the reason Failed to validate discovery url. To trust a private CA for that connection, add certificateConfigurations to the customJWTAuthorizer configuration, next to the existing privateEndpoint:
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources that you created:
- Delete the credential provider in the AgentCore console, or run aws bedrock-agentcore-control delete-oauth2-credential-provider --name keycloak-private-ca.
- Delete the secret in Secrets Manager or the object in Amazon S3.
- Remove the certificate from the load balancer listener and then delete it in ACM.
- Disable and then delete the private CA in the AWS Private CA console. AWS Private CA charges a monthly fee for each CA until you delete it. For details, see AWS Private CA pricing.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how to connect AgentCore Identity to a self-hosted IdP that uses a certificate from your own CA. You issued a server certificate with AWS Private CA, stored the CA certificate in Secrets Manager or Amazon S3 and referenced it from a credential provider. You also saw how to rotate the CA with a combined PEM file and how to limit who can change the certificate that your agents trust.
To learn more, see Connect to private identity providers in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide. For examples using Keycloak, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore samples repository on GitHub. If you have questions or feedback, leave a comment on this post.

articles.title: LinkedIn Cuts Daily Spark Shuffle Fetch Failures from 750 to 20 with Apache Celeborn
articles.text:
LinkedIn has deployed Apache Celeborn as a shared remote shuffle platform across the majority of its Apache Spark and Apache Flink workloads, separating intermediate data storage from compute infrastructure. The deployment reduces daily shuffle fetch failures from approximately 750 to 20, lowers compute costs by 10%, and improves application runtimes by 14%, compared with its previous Magnet implementation.
Daily shuffle fetch failures decreased from approximately 750 to 20 (Source: LinkedIn Blog Post)
LinkedIn's offline data platform executes more than 300,000 Spark jobs daily across thousands of production nodes, consuming approximately 200 petabyte-hours of compute. As the company moves toward a unified Flink architecture for real-time and historical processing, large-scale backfills introduce additional shuffle workloads. Shuffle moves intermediate data between processing stages, potentially stressing networks, disks, and application runtimes.
LinkedIn previously addressed shuffle read inefficiencies with Magnet, its push-based shuffle implementation contributed to Apache Spark 3.2. Magnet aggregates shuffle blocks by reducer partition into larger files, reducing random disk reads. However, shuffle storage remained within the compute cluster, where External Shuffle Services shared CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network resources with compute workloads.
With Apache Celeborn, map tasks push intermediate data to dedicated workers, which aggregate and store partitions independently of compute executors. Reducers fetch the data directly from these workers, allowing shuffle storage to scale independently of compute and reducing dependence on executor lifecycles. Unlike Magnet, which uses merger External Shuffle Services within the Spark compute cluster, Celeborn runs as a separate shuffle service with dedicated workers and a replicated control plane. This separation reduces resource contention between compute and shuffle workloads.
Celeborn architecture at LinkedIn (Source: LinkedIn Blog Post)
Aravind Patnam, a staff software engineer at LinkedIn, explained,
Operating it reliably across thousands of nodes and hundreds of thousands of daily applications required substantial engineering beyond the upstream project.
The deployment uses a five-node Raft-based control plane distributed across availability zones, with Apache Ratis providing metadata replication, leader election, and failover. LinkedIn also introduced network-aware replication and integrated Celeborn with its host health platform to deprioritize workers approaching maintenance and exclude degraded workers. These changes contributed to a 20-fold reduction in task failures during infrastructure disruptions compared with Magnet.
LinkedIn further optimized the data plane by moving shuffle storage to NVMe SSDs, reducing overall shuffle duration by 40%. Using Zstandard compression instead of LZ4 reduced the required shuffle worker fleet by approximately 35%. The company also provisioned workers with 100 Gbps network interfaces and improved slot selection time sixfold through JVM and data-plane optimizations. Across the fleet, shuffle cost decreased by nearly 90% per task, while the proportion of executor runtime spent waiting on shuffle operations fell by approximately 10–15% from its peak.
The converged Flink platform processes hundreds of millions of events per hour in historical backfills, completing multi-day workloads in single-digit hours. Thousands of pipelines now use unified Flink computations for nearline processing and historical corrections, replacing parallel Spark implementations. LinkedIn is exploring caching and faster upstream upgrades while continuing to contribute to Celeborn.

articles.title: L'armée de Terre teste un génial robot terrestre conçu en un an pour porter le barda des soldats
articles.text:
En plein exercice DOUMENC, l'armée de Terre vient de mettre à l'épreuve un robot terrestre conçu en un an seulement. Il a pour mission de transporter du matériel, épauler la maintenance et limiter l'exposition des soldats au danger.
Le robot terrestre testé par l'armée de Terre lors de l'exercice DOUMENC, qui avait lieu du 7 au 11 novembre 2026, a été confié à la Brigade de maintenance, pour une première expérimentation présentée par la Section technique de l'armée de Terre (STAT). Conçu pour porter du matériel et appuyer la maintenance, l'engin sera prochainement rejoint par deux autres robots. Son emploi progressera par étapes, du pilotage à la manette jusqu'à l'autonomie, selon les capacités prévues par l'offre de KNDS FORVIA, son fabricant.
Un robot terrestre pour délester les combattants de l'armée de Terre
Toute la logique du projet consiste à charger la machine plutôt que le soldat. Selon la Section technique de l'armée de Terre (STAT), qui a présenté l'expérimentation, le robot doit transporter du matériel et faciliter les opérations de maintenance. Les mécaniciens ne seront pas les seuls servis d'ailleurs, car ces engins ont vocation à appuyer l'ensemble des combattants et des unités. Les photos, créditées au CALT, montrent un châssis à quatre roues frappé du logo KNDS, un plateau grillagé pour le chargement et un petit mât surmonté de capteurs.
Les militaires en attendent trois bénéfices de ce robot. Le plus vital, réduire l'exposition des soldats aux risques et aux tirs adverses, car mieux vaut exposer une machine qu'un homme. Le deuxième parlera à quiconque a déjà crapahuté avec un sac trop lourd, à l'école, en rando ou au boulot, c'est alléger le paquetage individuel. Et le troisième consiste à faire entrer la robotique dans les mœurs des unités, y compris dans ses usages les plus élémentaires.
Encore une fois, l'armée a su faire preuve de rapidité. L'armement est d'ordinaire le royaume des programmes au long cours, et pourtant ces robots ont émergé en un an. La STAT salue ici la patte de la démarche « Division de combat », qui fait écho à l'objectif fixé à l'armée de Terre, qui est de pouvoir projeter dès 2027, en trente jours, une division de 27 000 hommes et 10 000 engins. Pour tenir ce rythme, la méthode mise sur une boucle courte, où le besoin exprimé passe vite au développement, puis à l'expérimentation. L'armée de Terre revendique cette agilité, en partenariat avec la Direction générale de l'armement, et la Brigade logistique.
De la manette à l'autonomie, un robot qui fait ses classes
L'utilisation de ce robot montera en puissance progressivement. D'abord, il servira à la téléopération directe. En gros, ici, un opérateur le suit et le pilote à vue, manette en main, à la manière d'une voiture radiocommandée. Ensuite, arrivera la téléopération déportée, avec un kit de robotisation qui permet de le guider à distance, grâce au retour vidéo d'une caméra. Le troisième et dernier niveau de développement, c'est l'autonomie, dont l'étendue dépendra des capacités définies dans l'offre de KNDS FORVIA.
Le robot terrestre a en tout cas pu se faire les roues lors de DOUMENC26, mené par le Commandement de l'appui et de la logistique de théâtre (CALT). Créée en 2024 pour soutenir cette fameuse division, cette structure chapeaute trois brigades, consacrées à la logistique, à la maintenance et au génie. Concrètement, l'exercice déploie de vraies troupes pour vérifier, selon des documents de l'Assemblée nationale, que l'armée de Terre sait soutenir ses forces dans un conflit de haute intensité, autrement dit les ravitailler, réparer leurs matériels et leur ouvrir la route au cœur d'une guerre majeure. Et ce soutien doit tenir même sous la menace adverse. Le CALT a donc profité de DOUMENC26 pour mettre à l'épreuve ses innovations, qu'elles touchent à l'organisation, comme la dispersion des unités, ou à la technique, avec les robots et l'impression 3D polymère et métal. Les industriels sont associés à la démarche, afin d'adapter plus vite leurs produits aux réalités du terrain.
Mais pour l'heure, il s'agit d'évaluer. Les unités doivent logiquement apprivoiser ces engins, mesurer leur apport réel et préparer leur intégration dans leurs habitudes de travail. Le cap est mis sur une robotique terrestre accessible à tous les combattants, au service de leur protection, de leur mobilité et de leur efficacité. Le nom de l'exercice faisait à Verdun où, en 1916, le capitaine Doumenc lançait les premiers transports motorisés sur la Voie sacrée. Cent dix ans plus tard, la logistique militaire commence à envisager de lâcher, peu à peu, le volant.

articles.title: Trump admin orders Kalshi to halt wagers on what words Trump will say
articles.text:
The Trump administration ordered prediction market Kalshi to stop offering event contracts that pay out based on whether President Trump will say a specific word before a particular date. Kalshi halted trading in the contracts while the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) conducts a review into whether the Trump mention contracts violate federal law.
CNBC reported yesterday that “Kalshi quietly paused trading in a handful of ‘mention’ contracts tied to President Donald Trump at the end of last week at the request of the CFTC.” Kalshi told media outlets that it is complying with the CFTC order.
The markets taken down by Kalshi allowed users to wager on whether Trump would say certain words, including nicknames and the names of countries and companies. A similar expired event contract that can still be viewed on Kalshi’s website asked whether Trump would use the nicknames “Marjorie Traitor Greene,” “Sleepy Joe,” and “Whack Job” or “Wack Job” before April 2026.
The CFTC order issued to Kalshi last week applies broadly to “the TRUMPSAY contract series.” The event contracts in this series include trades in the format, “Will [word] be said by Donald Trump after Issuance and before [date]?” The CFTC order also applied to a specific event contract that asks, “What nicknames will Trump say before 2027?”
Trump teleprompter aide bet on what Trump would say
The CFTC order came several months after the federal agency settled charges against a Trump teleprompter aide who made over $100,000 in Kalshi wagers on what Trump would say in prepared remarks. On August 28, the CFTC required the man, Gabriel Perez, to disgorge profits of $107,539.02 and pay a civil penalty of $65,000.
“In his position, Perez had access to presidential speeches prior to those speeches being delivered and Perez misappropriated that information—in breach of his duty of trust and confidence—to trade presidential mention market contracts, generating over $107,500 in profits,” the CFTC said at the time.

articles.title: Quantum error correction ushers quantum into the data center - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Quantum computing drops its decade-away tag as error rates fall 200-fold in two years
Quantum computing is shedding its reputation as speculative as gains in quantum error correction turn fragile machines into reliable ones. For the supercomputing community, which now measures data centers in gigawatts of power, the more pressing question is how quantum fits beside the processors already on the floor.
For years, the field faced a trade-off between speed and reliability, because correcting errors inside a quantum computer slowed it down. That trade-off is fading fast, according to Rajeeb Hazra (pictured), chief executive officer of Quantinuum Inc., which listed on the Nasdaq in June.
“We are now at a stage in 2026 where we have the ability to have tremendous amounts of computation at a very high reliability rate,” Hazra said. “Just two weeks ago, we announced we were doing up to a million operations with five errors. To put it in contrast, just two years ago, we were trying to do 1,000 operations with one error. That’s how fast it is.”
Hazra spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed advances in quantum error correction and how AI and quantum computing work in tandem. (* Disclosure below.)
Quantum error correction opens a path for AI
Quantinuum’s 100-qubit Helios system recently set an error-correction record, reaching logical fidelity equivalent to five errors per million operations. The company builds the full stack, from hardware to developer tools, so customers can model problems such as how a drug ages and loses potency, Hazra explained. That positions quantum less as a rival to AI than as a tool AI will lean on for accurate simulation.
“We see AI and quantum working in tandem, or rather AI using quantum computers,” Hazra said. “I don’t think it’s people using quantum computers; it’s AI programming quantum computers to get the data they need to do what AI does best, which is reasoning and prediction.”
Two cloud service providers have already struck deals with Quantinuum, and most of its use-case customers are commercial companies in pharma, energy, chemicals and financial services, Hazra explained. With quantum error correction maturing, the payoff lies in designing materials that release medicine only where the body needs it.
“My view is in five to seven years max, you’re not going to get a prescription for amoxicillin,” Hazra said. “You’re going to get a sheet of paper that basically says this is your pathology. It’ll get matched up at CVS Pharmacy with the available proteins, if you will, and you will get your personalized medicine.”
Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of SC26:

articles.title: Qwen4-Max vs. Claude Opus 5.5: The cheaper model costs you somewhere else.
articles.text:
Qwen4-Max vs. Claude Opus 5.5: The cheaper model costs you somewhere else.
Qwen4-Max, made available in preview to Token Plan subscribers on November 11 and generally released on November 16, is quite the talker.
When the independent testing firm Artificial Analysis ran its standard test suite on Alibaba’s new model, Qwen4-Max generated 127 million output tokens. That’s roughly twice the median for comparable models. Artificial Analysis reports 218 million output tokens for Claude Opus 5.5 at max effort with default fallback enabled. That is more than Qwen4-Max uses, but Opus’s default effort setting is medium.
Writing a lot of tokens doesn’t automatically mean a higher bill, especially with Qwen4-Max, because Alibaba charges very little for those tokens. Qwen4-Max costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens. Claude Opus 5.5 costs more, billing at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. Cached input has separate pricing: Qwen4-Max lists $0.075 per million cached input tokens, while Opus 5.5 cache reads cost $0.20 per million tokens. Cache writes also have separate rates.
Cheaper only wins if you don’t give up accuracy to get it.
Costs and tokens are only part of the picture, though. Cheaper only wins if you don’t give up accuracy to get it. Alibaba’s launch post calls Qwen4-Max “your new teammate,” which I take to mean it’s positioned as an everyday workhorse. Alibaba’s launch chart shows wins and losses against Opus on agent benchmarks, where a model works through a job step by step using tools. Its coding results are mixed too: Qwen4-Max trails Opus 48.5% to 59.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, but leads on DeepSWE v1.1. These published results use different benchmarks and evaluation setups; they are not a single controlled comparison.
I’ve seen fact and fiction in launch marketing materials (including benchmarks), so I wanted to get to the bottom of this. Is Qwen4-Max a better alternative to Opus 5.5 for some day-to-day work? I ran a few tests to answer that question for everyday users.
The tests
I ran each model once per test at default settings, with no turn cap. Opus 5.5 ran through Anthropic’s API, and Qwen4-Max ran through OpenRouter on Alibaba’s own servers. Opus’s dollar figures are estimates based on reported token usage and Anthropic’s list prices. Qwen4-Max’s are what OpenRouter billed. The aggregate token totals below don’t separate uncached input, cache writes, and cache reads, so they aren’t sufficient to independently reproduce the cost estimates. I wrote a script that graded each model’s answers against an answer key I built along with the tests.
I wanted to make sure the tests were hard for each model, so I used GPT-5 as a baseline and ran each test through it first. When GPT-5’s score was low enough to count as a failure, I considered the test “hard enough.”
Here are the three tests I used:
- Multi-app workflow (76 points) – I set up a fake company with a ticket tracker, code repo, chat, and calendar, and each model worked across all four as an agent. It had to triage a customer bug, find the code change that caused it, assign the right owner, calculate deadlines, count tickets, and refuse two requests that company policy forbids.
- Incident investigation (60 points) – The models had to dig through logs, metrics, and change history to explain three overlapping outages that happened at the same time. The data included decoy deploys, two servers with wrong clocks, and a misleading alert.
- Agent bug fix (47 points) – Each model fixed an accounting library with 11 planted bugs. Six of those bugs don’t fail any test the model can see, so it had to find them by comparing the code with the documentation. Three of the library’s own tests are wrong, and the model should report them without editing them.
Multi-app workflow
Opus 5.5 scored all 76 points. Qwen4-Max scored 71.
All five of Qwen4-Max’s missed points came from the same mistake. Three questions asked which team owns a piece of code. The repo’s ownership file says that when several rules match, the last one in the file wins. Qwen4-Max picked the most specific rule each time. Everything else it did was correct, including the deadline math across time zones and both refusals.
…Qwen4-Max can handle a long, messy office job, but one misread rule followed it through the whole task.
That tells me Qwen4-Max can handle a long, messy office job, but one misread rule followed it through the whole task. In a real company, that mistake sends tickets to the wrong team, creating more confusion.
Qwen4-Max wrote almost twice as many output tokens as Opus but cost less than a third. It also took more than three times as long for a little more than half as many turns.
The numbers:
- Opus 5.5: 44 turns, 2,451,342 in, 26,617 out, $2.13, 248 s.
- Qwen4-Max: 25 turns, 1,746,170 in, 51,264 out (41,644 reasoning), $0.62, 791 s.
Incident investigation
Qwen4-Max narrowly pulled ahead on accuracy here. It scored 59 of 60, and Opus 5.5 scored 58.
Both models untangled the three outages, named the two-step cause of the main one, ruled out every decoy, and caught both bad clocks. Both also made the same kind of slip. They credited a customer-facing error code to the wrong service, Opus twice and Qwen4-Max once.
This was Qwen4-Max’s strongest result in my tests. On this investigation task, it scored one point higher than Opus for about 31% of the reported cost. One run does not establish a general advantage in agent work. Opus 5.5 pulled ahead on time, though. Qwen4-Max took about 9.5 minutes, and Opus took under 4.
The numbers:
- Opus 5.5: 22 turns, 1,216,769 in, 23,642 out, $1.41, 221 s.
- Qwen4-Max: 18 turns, 1,104,031 in, 33,036 out (23,153 reasoning), $0.44, 570 s.
Agent bug fix
Just like the last test, neither model scored perfectly on accuracy. Opus 5.5 scored 45 of 47, and Qwen4-Max scored 40. This was the coding test, and its result was consistent with Opus’s lead on Terminal-Bench 4.0, though Alibaba’s coding results were mixed.
Opus fixed all 11 bugs. Its only miss was the third wrong test, which it didn’t report, costing it two points. Qwen4-Max missed that same test and lost five more points. It fixed 10 of the 11 bugs and missed one where splitting a payment across invoices loses a cent. It also left a scratch file in the tests folder, which my rules count as changing the tests.
The tool logs show how differently they worked. Opus made its first fix on turn 4 and finished in 12 turns. Qwen4-Max read files for 15 turns before its first edit and took 30 turns in all. More reading didn’t translate to a better score in this case, though.
The cost gap was smallest on this test. Qwen4-Max used more than three times the input tokens, so its bill came to about two-thirds of Opus’s.
The numbers:
- Opus 5.5: 12 turns, 228,824 in, 6,433 out, $0.38, 64 s.
- Qwen4-Max: 30 turns, 827,545 in, 15,813 out (6,701 reasoning), $0.25, 310 s.
Results
| Test | Claude Opus 5.5 | Qwen4-Max | 
| Multi-app workflow (of 76) | 76 | 71 | 
| Incident investigation (of 60) | 58 | 59 | 
| Agent bug fix (of 47) | 45 | 40 | 
| Total tokens in / out | 3,896,935 / 56,692 | 3,677,746 / 100,113 | 
| Total cost | $3.91 (estimated) | $1.31 | 
| Total time | 533 s | 1,671 s | 
The talker reputation checked out. Qwen4-Max generated 77% more output tokens than Opus across the three tests. Those totals include reasoning tokens, so they do not measure just the length of the visible answers; the models also use different tokenizers.
What Qwen4-Max really costs is time and accuracy.
Its prices are low enough that it didn’t matter, and the total bill still came to about a third of Opus’s. What Qwen4-Max really costs is time and accuracy. It took about 3.14 times as long in total and scored 170 of 183 points, nine fewer than Opus’s 179.
What do I think?
Each model ran once, so a gap of a point or two could shift on another run. I’d try Qwen4-Max on your own long-running agent jobs before trusting it with code. I recommend checking its answers against source material and verifying code with tests and human review; a second model’s agreement alone does not establish accuracy.
I’d keep Opus 5.5 for coding and for any job where a wrong answer could cause problems down the line. It was more accurate on two of the three tests, and it finished the three tasks in about a third of the total time.
Qwen4-Max earned a place, though. For investigation work, where the model digs through a lot of data and can wait a few extra minutes, it matched Opus for a fraction of the price. Qwen4-Max’s one-point lead on this investigation task is encouraging, but these single-run tests cannot validate Alibaba’s broader agent claims or establish a general coding ranking.

articles.title: The latest Google Home updates cover Nest Thermostats, video doorbells, Google Wallet, and Gemini AI
articles.text:
Another batch of Google Home updates are arriving — and Nest Thermostat owners get the biggest new features
Here's what's coming
- Another substantial Google Home update is rolling out
- Nest Thermostats are getting several new features
- There are upgrades for Gemini and video doorbells too
It hasn't been the easiest few months for Google Home users, but the updates keep on arriving, and it looks like Google is gradually getting its smart home devices and software back on an even keel. The latest batch of upgrades are now rolling out to users — including some notable new features for Nest Thermostat owners.
Google has put up a couple of posts (via 9to5Google) on what's new, and you'll see that Nest Thermostats in the US and Canada will soon start showing estimated cumulative savings on your heating bills. That's due to go live in December.
Nest Thermostats will also now be able to proactively warn you about issues with compatible heat pumps or air-conditioning compressors, via email, in the Google Home app, and on the face of the thermostat itself. The thermostat controller is getting a little redesign too, so the Eco mode settings are easier to access.
Owners of a 4th-gen Nest Learning Thermostat get a couple of extra features. First, there's the ability to balance hot and cold spots around the home, with the help of third-party room sensors, in addition to Google's own sensor.
Second, the 4th-gen and latest model is also getting some new Dynamic Farsight faces (like watch faces for your thermostat). These new designs will "match your aesthetics", whatever they may be, and it sounds like we're going to get seasonal options, as well as a lunar face that tracks the phases of the Moon.
Video devices and Gemini
Besides the thermostat updates, video doorbell themes (including seasonal themes) can now be previewed right inside the Google Home app, saving you a trip to the front door to see how they sound. On video cameras more generally, activity zones can now be more precisely set, cutting down on false positives.
With Gemini for Home, the digital AI assistant will handle requests up to 20% faster, and is expanding to six new countries: India, Taiwan, Singapore, Colombia, South Korea, and Brazil. Background chatter will now be less of a problem for voice commands too.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
For those of you who use Google Home on the web, you should find that reviewing recorded footage from your connected cameras is more straightforward, with faster scrubbing and support for arrow key control.
If you're a Google Home Premium Advanced subscriber, there's something else too: motion-triggered camera and doorbell event descriptions will now include audio descriptions too, so you'll know about breaking glass or barking dogs.
Rounding out this substantial update, we've got support for digital home keys in Google Wallet. This was actually announced last week, and means that controls for compatible smart locks can be added to Google Wallet, via the Google Home app. All you'll need to do is tap your phone on the lock when you get home.

articles.title: Quebecor CEO says Starlink motivated push to buy Telus
articles.text:
Quebecor CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau said that his pursuit of purchasing Telus is driven by the rise of Elon Musk’s Starlink.
According to the Financial Post, Péladeau’s pitch essentially was that, with the rapid growth of satellite companies like Starlink, these companies threatened traditional mobile communications, pointing to what happened when streaming services upset the cable television industry.
The Financial Post report also said that Péladeau flew to London, England, to pitch the idea to former Telus CEO Darren Entwistle, who, surprise, surprise, didn’t jump at it. Shareholders also didn’t show any interest when they submitted more formal (though non-binding) offers to the board of directors on June 26, and again just recently.
To add some context, this offer would see Quebecor purchase Telus for a cash-and-stock offer of $19.45 per share — a total of about $31 billion — and also promised nearly $400 million in operational savings.
Péladeau said that this near-$400 million could go toward deleveraging and investing in what he described as the “network of the future,” and it could better allow the combined companies to compete with the likes of Starlink, Amazon’s Leo constellation, and possibly others who will follow suit.
He expressed hope that members of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government will give his team a fair hearing on the proposal when he takes it before them, noting that Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has a history with Quebecor through earlier work as minister of innovation, science, and industry.
Péladeau also confirmed that he is still working on purchasing Telus, as he and current Telus CEO Victor Dodig are expected to meet again with the chief financial officers of both companies on Nov. 23.
Honestly, saying that the two companies need to join forces to compete against Starlink doesn’t seem like a compelling reason to merge. Even though Starlink is trying to spin up a mobile network, the reality is that satellite-to-mobile services are better suited to supplementing existing terrestrial networks.
Rogers already offers satellite-to-mobile service (in partnership with Starlink). Bell and Telus are working on their offerings —and even though they use American operators like AST SpaceMobile, there are Canadian companies like Ottawa-based Terrestar Solutions and Toronto-based MDA Space that companies can switch to (Telus has already partnered with TerreStar) if they want to abide by Carney’s Canada-first desires.
Source: Financial Post

articles.title: Nvidia's revenue hits $115.8 billion as Vera Rubin generates $20 billion in another record-setting quarter — commitments increase to $390 billion, FY28 forecast raised
articles.text:
Nvidia's revenue hits $115.8 billion as Vera Rubin generates $20 billion in another record-setting quarter — commitments increase to $390 billion, FY28 forecast raised
Another record quarter and strong guidance.
For the first time in its 33-year history, Nvidia on Tuesday reported quarterly financial results without Jensen Huang at its helm or on the call, after its cofounder and longtime chief executive departed five days ago. To no one's surprise, Nvidia continues to set new financial records as demand for its AI accelerators shows no signs of slowing down. The company reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the third quarter of its fiscal 2027, with its latest Vera Rubin platform generating $20 billion. Meanwhile, its supply commitments surged to $390 billion.
'Momentum is real'
"Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," said Colette Kress, interim chief executive and chief financial officer of Nvidia. "Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track, and our ambition has never been greater."
For the third quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended on October 25, 2026, Nvidia posted revenue of $115.844 billion, an increase of 20% sequentially and 103% year-over-year. The company's net income reached $65.287 billion, up 105% from the same quarter last year, while gross margin hit 74.8%. Revenue from the Compute & Networking segment totaled $106 billion, up 20% quarter-over-quarter and 108% year-over-year. Meanwhile, the Graphics segment generated $9.8 billion, a sequential increase of 25% and 62% compared with the same period a year ago.
As expected, Nvidia's results during the quarter were primarily driven by its Data Center business, which generated $107.6 billion in revenue (and accounted for approximately 93% of the company's sales), up 21% sequentially and 110% YoY. Hyperscale customers accounted for $60.1 billion, an increase of 23% QoQ and 71% YoY, while sales to AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise customers reached $47.5 billion, up 18% sequentially and 195% compared to the same period last year. Although hyperscalers remain Nvidia's largest customer category, demand from AI cloud providers, industrial companies, and enterprises continues to grow considerably faster on an annual basis. Meanwhile, Edge Computing revenue reached $8.2 billion, up 14% sequentially and 42% year-over-year.
One of the main contributors to Nvidia's growth was its Vera Rubin platform, which generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments, which Nvidia described as the fastest product ramp in its history. The company also reported strong demand for standalone Vera CPUs and continued sales growth for Blackwell Ultra. According to Nvidia, its hyperscale partners brought Vera Rubin systems into production in approximately one month, which is two times faster than the previous-generation Grace Blackwell platform.
"Vera Rubin is off to an extraordinary start: in its first quarter of production shipments, the Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in revenue, making it the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history," Kress said. "We continue to see very strong demand for Vera and expect total CPU revenue to more than double in FY2028."
Supply commitments reach $390 billion
To support the expected growth of its AI infrastructure business, Nvidia has substantially increased its long-term procurement obligations. The company's supply and capacity commitments reached $390 billion at the end of Q3 FY2027, compared with $279 billion three months earlier and $119 billion at the end of Q1. Nvidia attributed the latest increase primarily to multiyear memory procurement agreements.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The company expects to fulfill $69 billion of these commitments during the remainder of FY2027 (which ends in late January), followed by $203 billion in FY2028 and $92 billion in FY2029. Another $26 billion is scheduled for FY2030 and beyond. In other words, Nvidia has already committed to purchasing $390 billion worth of components and manufacturing capacity through the end of FY2030, though given the fact that its purchases in FY2028 are set to exceed $200 billion, expect its procurements in FY2030 to be higher.
The commitments reflect Nvidia's efforts to ensure that its suppliers can manufacture sufficient quantities of advanced processors, memory, substrates, and packaging components. In addition to its existing agreements with partners like TSMC, Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, Nvidia on Wednesday announced new partnerships with Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Kinsus for substrates, as well as SPIL for advanced packaging. In addition, the company disclosed agreements with Amkor, Ibiden, KYEC, and Unimicron.
During the earnings call, Kress said that demand for Nvidia's products continues to exceed available supply, prompting the company to work with manufacturing partners to expand production capacity. She also indicated that Nvidia could provide suppliers with prepayments or other financial assistance to accelerate capacity expansion.
Although these procurement commitments are gargantuan, Nvidia expects demand for its AI infrastructure to remain strong, which will justify the expenditures. The company raised its revenue growth forecast for FY2028 from approximately 70% to 75% due to stronger demand and additional manufacturing capacity that it expects to secure.
In addition to its supply commitments, Nvidia disclosed $32 billion in agreements with neocloud providers that allow it to earn revenue from hardware sales and participate in cloud rental revenue above a guaranteed minimum. Meanwhile, the company's maximum financial exposure under various guarantees reached $118 billion, including $105 billion in credit support for the PORTS-Pike AI data center campus in Ohio, which will serve OpenAI under 20-year leases.
In total, Nvidia's commitments reached $540 billion as of early Q4 FY2024.
2028 pricing strategy and beyond
Nvidia currently absorbs higher component and manufacturing costs to honor existing purchase orders and maintain previously agreed prices for its customers. As a result, the company expects its GAAP gross margin to decline from 74.8% in Q3 FY2027 to 71% – 72% in Q4, which it considers the bottom of the current margin cycle.
Going forward, Nvidia plans to introduce revised pricing in FY2028 to help offset higher supply costs and restore profitability, which is when the company expects gross margins to recover to 72% – 73% next fiscal year, although it has not disclosed the magnitude of its planned price adjustments or the products they will affect.
"We thought about in terms of our prices and pieces of that, and a lot of the costs were some of the things that we absorbed in those numbers that we included," Kress said. "What we provided here in Q4 is our bottom. If you recall, that was our bottom as we honored many of the different POs that we had already received from our customers, and we just wanted to make sure that was held solid as we moved to a new pricing, as we moved into the new year."
Perhaps more importantly is that Colette Kress largely sidestepped the question about custom AI accelerators and their potential impact on Nvidia's pricing power. During the conference call, an analyst asked whether Nvidia would accept lower margins to protect its market share against custom AI accelerators developed by hyperscalers. The interim CEO avoided directly addressing whether competition from custom silicon could undermine Nvidia’s competitive position, leaving considerable room for speculation.
Nvidia expects $130 billion in Q4
For the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, Nvidia projects revenue of approximately $130 billion ±3%, which would represent an increase of about 12% sequentially. The company expects GAAP gross margin of 71% to 72% and GAAP operating expenses of approximately $11 billion during the quarter. Nvidia’s forecast excludes Data Center compute revenue from China and accounts for an additional week in the quarter. While Nvidia expects its gross margin to decline during the Vera Rubin transition, Kress said that the company anticipates a recovery to 72% – 73% in FY2028.

Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

articles.title: Sul-coreano confessa ter usado IA para colar em prova de concurso • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Sul-coreano confessa ter usado IA para colar em prova de concurso
Han Won-seok, de 34 anos, quase gabaritou uma prova para certificação de contador tributário na Coreia do Sul ao usar uma minicâmera e inteligência artificial para colar.
Han Won-seok, de 34 anos, quase gabaritou um dos exames profissionais mais importantes da Coreia do Sul. Ele errou apenas uma das 160 questões aplicadas, obtendo 397,5 pontos de um total de 400. Teria sido um desempenho notável se não fosse por um detalhe: o candidato usou uma minicâmera e IA para “colar” na prova.
O exame em questão consiste em um disputado concurso para obtenção de certificado de contador tributário. Trata-se de uma prova tão complicada que os 397,5 pontos registrados por Han Won-seok, que o colocaram na primeira colocação da lista de aprovados, logo fizeram outros candidatos e profissionais que já atuam no segmento tributário suspeitarem de fraude.
Inicialmente, Won-seok negou as indagações. Mas, sentindo-se pressionado e sugerindo estar arrependido, o homem admitiu ter fraudado a prova. A confissão foi feita por meio de um vídeo publicado no canal de seu advogado, Lee Don-Ho, no YouTube.
No vídeo, Won-seok explica que recorreu a uma câmera em miniatura para fotografar as questões, que eram enviadas automaticamente ao seu smartphone. Ele programou o celular para enviar as imagens a uma ferramenta de IA generativa, que gerou as respostas.
As respostas, por sua vez, eram consultadas por meio de uma tela auxiliar ligada ao smartphone. Inicialmente, havia a suspeita de que ele usasse fones de ouvido para obter as respostas da IA, mas não foi o caso.
O esquema deu tão certo que Won-seok o repetiu na segunda etapa do exame, realizado três meses depois, quando então ele obteve 663 de 800 pontos, novamente terminando em primeiro lugar.
É possível que a trapaça tivesse sido impedida se os candidatos houvessem sido proibidos de entrar no local da prova portando o celular. No entanto, eles foram apenas orientados a desligar e guardar o aparelho. Havia dois fiscais na sala onde a prova foi aplicada, nas duas ocasiões, mas nenhum deles notou comportamentos suspeitos por parte de Han Won-seok.
Além de ter confessado a fraude em um vídeo, Han Won-seok afirma ter se entregado à Polícia Metropolitana de Seul, que segue investigando o caso. Ainda não está claro quais punições serão aplicadas ao homem, mas, muito provavelmente, ele perderá a certificação e poderá ficar impedido de prestar um novo exame por cinco anos.
Como o caso foi parar na esfera criminal, existe também chances de Han Won-seok receber uma pena de prisão, embora as investigações sigam com ele em liberdade.
Independentemente do desfecho desta história, o episódio deve servir de base para que as autoridades da Coreia do Sul revisem normas e procedimentos para aplicação de exames públicos. Isso porque casos de fraude em provas envolvendo inteligência artificial não são inéditos no país. Quatro exemplos recentes envolveram o uso de óculos com IA em exames escolares.
Com informações de BBC e The Korea Herald

articles.title: Satya Nadella predicts AI agents will reshuffle the economics of the web | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella predicts that the rise of AI agents is going to reshape the economics of the internet, impacting the business models of the companies that rely on advertising and what he referred to as “human web” traffic.
Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the tech executive argued that the shift to an agentic web could change which companies pay others for traffic and for transactions, similar to how the transition from web portals like Yahoo to search engines like Google did years ago.
“The current aggregators who have a business model which was for the human web will get, in some sense, reshuffled,” said Nadella. “And if you were monetizing ads because of the eyeballs, you now have to probably get down to essentially maybe CPC [cost-per-click] wins; maybe it’s more transactional,” he continued. “And so if you don’t accept the agent, somebody else will.”
The discussion turned to Amazon and its decision to block AI agents from accessing its retail website, preventing them from browsing its catalog and making purchases on behalf of their users. Nadella suggested that companies trying to protect their existing business models could lose out to others that are more willing to embrace the AI agents. For instance, if Amazon continues blocking agents, another shopping platform such as Shopify, could allow them, and gain an advantage.
“I think this is going to be interesting,” he said, speaking to the changing models. “It’s the same thing that’s happening in other categories, right? Which is, if you’re in love with a particular business model, you have to kind of scramble,” he said.

articles.title: Amazon lance une tonne de nouvelles offres pour la Black Friday Week : le TOP en DIRECT — Frandroid

Bref, si vous recherchez un nouveau smartphone, une tablette, une TV, un PC portable, un casque ou des écouteurs sans fil, des objets connectés ou tout autre produit tech à prix bas, vous êtes au bon endroit.
Black Friday Amazon : les meilleures offres en DIRECT

articles.title: Conduite autonome Tesla (FSD) : la France accusée de mener une fronde secrète pour bloquer son homologation
articles.text:
Tesla n’a plus qu’un obstacle (de taille) avant de proposer sa conduite supervisée dans toute l’Europe. Son FSD, rebaptisé Tesla Assisted Driving sur le continent, est déjà autorisé dans 11 pays de l’Union. La Finlande a été la dernière à donner son accord, le 10 novembre. Pour être valable dans les 27 pays, l’autorisation doit encore passer par un vote du TCMV, le comité technique où siègent les États membres, à la majorité qualifiée : au moins 15 pays représentant 65 % de la population.
Or, ce mercredi 18 novembre 2026, le compte X FSD in Denmark (@FSDEurope) a accusé la France de manœuvrer en coulisses pour faire échouer ce vote. Le poids de Paris compte, parce que sans la France et l’Allemagne, qui pèsent à elles deux environ un tiers de la population de l’UE, le seuil de 65 % deviendrait presque impossible à atteindre.
Une rumeur au fondement crédible
D’après le compte @FSDEurope, une source travaillant dans l’administration d’un État membre lui aurait révélé que Paris a envoyé un courriel à tous les pays de l’UE. La France y affirmerait que le FSD ne respecte pas certaines exigences réglementaires, notamment sur la vitesse, et pousserait ses partenaires à voter non.
Pour obtenir ces messages, l’auteur du compte a déposé des demandes d’accès aux documents administratifs dans plusieurs pays européens. En Bulgarie, le ministère des Transports lui a répondu n’avoir eu aucun échange avec Paris sur le sujet. Pourtant, le régulateur automobile bulgare a refusé de lui transmettre la correspondance, car les autorités françaises ont demandé que « toute correspondance concernant le FSD » reste confidentielle. Une réponse qui a tendance à confirmer la rumeur.
Un compte militant, à prendre avec des pincettes
Le compte a déjà publié de véritables documents administratifs, comme une note bulgare du 11 août qui s’inquiétait d’un FSD capable de rouler à 70 km/h sur une route limitée à 50 km/h. En revanche, le refus bulgare prouve seulement que la France a demandé le secret sur ses échanges. Personne n’a vu les fameux courriels, et FSDEurope reconnaît lui-même que la consigne de voter non n’a pas été vérifiée de manière indépendante.
Il faut aussi garder en tête que le compte a un avis très tranché sur les éventuels opposants au FSD. En réponse à un message de Philippe Tabarot, ministre des Transports, il avait traité ce dernier de « menteur » et l’avait accusé d’être « contre le FSD ». Quant au secret, les discussions préparatoires à une décision réglementaire ne sont de toute façon pas forcément publiques.
Paris jouerait un double jeu sur le FSD
Si l’accusation se vérifiait, elle irait contre les évolutions récentes du discours du gouvernement. Le 22 juillet, Philippe Tabarot jugeait en effet les garanties de sécurité « encore suffisantes pour une autorisation en l’état ». Puis le 2 septembre, après une visioconférence avec Elon Musk, il expliquait sur X que les autorités françaises travaillaient « étroitement avec Tesla sur les adaptations techniques qui permettront à la France de soutenir son homologation ».
Deux voitures équipées devaient être testées sur les routes françaises. Pour autant, les reproches prêtés à Paris ne sortent pas de nulle part : la marge de dépassement de vitesse du FSD a été ramenée de 50 % à 10 % au-dessus de la limite, une modification validée le 3 novembre par le RDW, le régulateur néerlandais à l’origine de la première autorisation.
Plutôt que d’un sabotage, ce pourrait donc surtout être un moyen de pression pour la France, afin d’obtenir les corrections qu’elle demande avant la tenue du vote. Surtout quand ces corrections finissent par arriver aussi rapidement dans les véhicules Tesla utilisant déjà le FSD.
Le vote à l’échelle de l’Union européenne ne devrait pas intervenir avant la réunion du TCMV de décembre, après deux rendez-vous manqués, le 30 juin puis le 6 octobre. L’Allemagne s’est dite prête à plaider pour une homologation rapide, alors que la France n’a toujours pas autorisé le système sur ses routes. Rappelons aussi que si l’Union européenne s’oppose à l’homologation du système, les pays qui l’ont autorisé à titre dérogatoire perdraient la possibilité de l’utiliser. Le sort du FSD reste donc pour l’heure complètement dans le flou.
