articles.title: How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI
Thanks to Amit Gupta, Senior Director- AI/ML and Mark Wang, Software Engineering PMTS from Salesforce for your contributions in the vision and partnership of cross-Region inference routing on SageMaker AI.
Salesforce’s Agentforce Foundation team serves a wide variety of models for products across Salesforce, including Agentforce and the Salesforce Trust Layer, in 30+ global Regions. These include both models trained in house and open source models. Hosting models separately in each Region splits capacity and makes traffic spikes harder to absorb, which turns a capacity shortfall into an availability problem.
This post shows how Salesforce set up the cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI and how it lets the team add capacity securely while keeping its data residency commitments. It also walks through how Salesforce sees where each request was served and why. The cross-Region inference routing gives an application one invocation path across SageMaker AI endpoints in several Regions and accounts, and sends each request to an endpoint that can serve it. Those endpoints are Salesforce’s own, already deployed. The post starts with the capacity problem Salesforce faced, explains how the router works and how Salesforce integrated it into its Internal Gateway, walks through an example setup, and then describes what the team observed.
Why serving these models makes capacity a reliability problem
Salesforce’s Agentforce Foundation team serves customers from the Region their requests come from, across 30+ global Regions and hundreds of AWS accounts, and they provision capacity based on each customer’s traffic. Every customer has its own peak window, and those windows often overlap. Provisioning for the overlapping peak would be the safe choice, but it costs too much. Customers also onboard new business units at short notice, so they must grow the fleet quickly. Adding capacity quickly, Region by Region, leaves Salesforce with capacity fragmentation: some Regions have idle instances while others run out.
Before the cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI, Salesforce used its Internal Gateway to send traffic that the local endpoints couldn’t handle to other Regions. The team built and operated this path, supported by basic health checks, retries, and Region-switching logic. That approach had two gaps. First, the gateway had no capacity signals from either the local or the remote endpoint, so it couldn’t tell when to shift traffic or whether the destination had room. Second, cross-Region traffic had to leave the virtual private cloud (VPC) through a NAT gateway and an internet gateway and travel over public AWS networking. In design reviews, the team also raised the risk of cascading failures: moving traffic during an incident can overload the next Region, so Salesforce needed a cap on cross-Region traffic.
Building this logic separately in every application doesn’t scale across Salesforce. The team needed a managed, capacity-aware routing path.
What the inference router does
The inference router is a Regional SageMaker AI resource in your account. Your application invokes the router instead of an endpoint, passing a routing target name with the same request body and content type it sends to InvokeEndpoint today. A routing target is a name you choose for one logical model, such as a toxicity classifier, and it lists the endpoints and inference components that may serve that model by their full Amazon Resource Names (ARNs). A router holds one routing target per model, and a problem with one model’s endpoints does not move traffic for the others. A routing target can mix single-model endpoints and inference components.
Because each destination is named by its ARN, it can be in another Region or another AWS account. The account that owns an endpoint grants access through a resource-based endpoint policy that allows one named router to invoke it, which is how Salesforce runs it.
The router prefers its own Region, and while the local destination serves successfully, requests stay there. The router judges each destination by the outcomes of recent requests. Platform faults, 5xx errors from the model container, throttles, and timeouts lower a destination’s health. As they persist, the router moves a growing share of new requests to healthy destinations, typically starting within about a minute. It can take several minutes for a destination with little traffic. Signals such as scaling progress and failed instance launches affect how quickly the router responds once errors appear, but they do not move traffic by themselves. After recovery, traffic returns over several minutes, more slowly than it left, so it does not swing back and forth. When a destination fails a request without running the model, for example by throttling it, the router retries that request once on another destination.
Client errors such as invalid input do not move traffic, because they would fail the same way in any Region. Model latency does not move traffic either, because a slow response often reflects a long prompt or output and does not by itself mean the endpoint is unhealthy. The router also does not deploy models, copy artifacts, or add instances. It uses the capacity you have deployed, and each endpoint’s own autoscaling keeps adding instances as its traffic grows.
How Salesforce integrated the router into its Internal Gateway
In Salesforce’s Internal Gateway, the router call sits exactly where the direct InvokeEndpoint call used to be: in the per-request egress path, after the data residency check and before response handling. That check is the one routing decision the gateway keeps. A request tagged with a residency requirement is pinned to its in-Region routing target, whose only destination is the local endpoint, so it can never fail over across a boundary. Everything else goes to the router with the same body, content type, and accept type the gateway already sent. Capacity awareness, health assessment, and failover now live in the routing layer instead of in Salesforce’s code.
Salesforce treats the two routing fields on every response as first-class telemetry. The gateway logs InvokedRoutedResourceArn and RoutingReason on the same structured line as the existing request ID and trace ID, and emits them as application performance monitoring (APM) tags. Because the ARN carries the Region and account, a single log line shows whether a request ran locally or crossed a boundary, and why: local-preferred, failover, capacity-available, or only-healthy. The team joins these fields against the router’s Amazon CloudWatch metrics when investigating a traffic shift.
The gateway’s timeout accounts for cross-Region round-trip latency, so a request that fails over has time to complete in the remote Region. Because the router already retries once on another destination, the gateway adds no retries of its own, which keeps attempts from multiplying during an incident.
Example setup
The following walkthrough shows the configuration Salesforce tested, using example IDs and names. Salesforce first created a router in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2) with a local destination and confirmed that requests were routed to it. The team then registered an endpoint in the US East (Ohio) Region (us-east-2) owned by a different account, removed the local destination, and confirmed that requests reached the remote endpoint across the account and Region boundary. In the examples, the router account is 111122223333, and the account that owns the us-east-2 endpoint is 444455556666.
Authorize the router on the destination endpoint
In the account that owns the us-east-2 endpoint, the owner attaches a resource-based policy that allows the router account to invoke the endpoint, with a condition that limits access to one named router. The router does not need to exist yet, so you can use the ARN of the router you plan to create.
The sagemaker:SourceInferenceRouterArn condition means the router account can reach the endpoint only through that router. The endpoint owner can revoke access at any time with delete-endpoint-policy.
Create the router
In the router account, create the router in us-west-2 with one routing target that lists both destinations by ARN.
Each additional model becomes another entry in RoutingTargets.
Confirm that each destination is routable
Before sending traffic, call DescribeInferenceRouter and check each destination’s RoutingStatus. Routable means SageMaker AI could read the destination and it can serve traffic. Unroutable means the destination was read but can’t serve right now, for example because the endpoint is not InService. Unknown means SageMaker AI couldn’t read the destination with your credentials, for example because you lack sagemaker:DescribeEndpoint (or sagemaker:DescribeInferenceComponent for an inference component), or, for a destination in another account, because its endpoint policy doesn’t grant Describe.
Invoke the router instead of the endpoint
The change in the calling code is small. The request body, content type, and accept type stay exactly as they were. The client and operation change, and the endpoint name is replaced by the router name and the routing target name.
An InferenceId and CustomAttributes are passed through to the destination as with InvokeEndpoint, so identifiers such as a trace ID travel with the request. Members such as TargetVariant and InferenceComponentName are not used, because the routing target replaces them.
Seeing where requests went
Most teams evaluating a routing layer first ask how to tell what it did. The inference router answers on every response and in Amazon CloudWatch. Each response carries the ARN of the destination that served it and a routing reason, in the InvokedRoutedResourceArn and RoutingReason fields and in the matching X-Amzn-SageMaker-Invoked-Routed-Resource-Arn and X-Amzn-SageMaker-Invoked-Routing-Reason headers. Because the ARN includes the Region and account, logging both values with your own request logs gives you a per-request record of whether each call ran locally or crossed a boundary.
The routing reason takes one of four values. local-preferred means a healthy destination in the router’s Region served the request. failover means a destination in the router’s Region exists but isn’t serving reliably, so the router sent the request elsewhere. capacity-available means no destination in the router’s Region could take the request, and it went to one of several healthy destinations in other Regions. only-healthy means it was served by the only eligible destination that was healthy.
In aggregate, the router publishes OpenTelemetry metrics to CloudWatch in its own account and Region, each carrying the router name and destination ARN, so the cross-Region picture is visible from one place. aws.sagemaker.inference_router.invocations counts requests per destination, and its error.type attribute splits failures into invocation_4xx, invocation_5xx (including timeouts), and invocation_model_error for errors returned by the model.
aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.duration measures the time each destination took, and aws.sagemaker.inference_router.overhead.duration measures the time the router added, including the network to and from a remote Region. aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.status reports each destination’s health state as healthy, overloaded, or degraded. You query these metrics with PromQL in CloudWatch Query Studio, and you can place them next to each endpoint’s existing SageMaker AI metrics on a cross-account, cross-Region dashboard.
Testing failover across accounts and Regions
Salesforce tested the router in two configurations. First, same-Region routing in us-west-2, where the Internal Gateway called the local inference router and the router sent requests to the local Endpoint A. Second, cross-account, cross-Region routing, where the router in us-west-2 also listed an endpoint in us-east-2 owned by a separate infrastructure account. Before sending traffic, the team called DescribeInferenceRouter and confirmed that the routing target listed both destinations and that both reported a RoutingStatus of Routable. Requests sent to the router were then served by the local endpoint, with a routing reason of local-preferred. Setup took little effort: the endpoint owner added an endpoint policy for the router’s account, and the router call replaced the direct InvokeEndpoint call in the gateway’s egress path, with the same request body, content type, and accept type.
To test failover, the team flooded the local endpoint in us-west-2 until it was saturated, while a separate probe kept invoking the router and recorded where each request was served and how long it took. For about five minutes of saturation, probe latency at p50 rose from 0.2 seconds to 45 to 58 seconds, and traffic stayed in us-west-2. This is the intended behavior, because latency alone does not move traffic. When requests began to exceed the model container’s 60-second handler timeout and return errors, the router started to shift traffic. The first requests reached us-east-2 about two minutes after the first errors, and within another minute about 78 percent of probe traffic was served in us-east-2. The remaining 20 to 25 percent stayed local so the router could detect recovery.
Once traffic had moved, p50 latency returned to 0.2 seconds, and the cross-Region path added under 100 milliseconds at p50. After the local endpoint recovered, traffic returned to us-west-2 gradually over about 10 minutes, and the probe recorded no errors during failover or failback. The InvokedRoutedResourceArn and RoutingReason fields on each response, together with the router’s per-destination invocation metrics in CloudWatch, showed the whole sequence without any extra instrumentation.
The router lets Salesforce replace operational logic the team used to build and run itself: the health checks, retries, and Region-switching logic in the Internal Gateway. Capacity signals and failover now live in the routing layer, not in each application.
Before broader adoption, Salesforce plans to repeat the failover test with the local endpoint held at saturation for longer, measure cross-Region latency at millisecond precision, evaluate cascading-Region behavior at the cross-Region cap, and roll out the router across more Regions.
        “With the new cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI, we can add capacity securely and keep our data residency commitments. Workloads that must stay in a region stay there, and only eligible traffic can be served from another Region. A single managed call works alongside our existing failover logic, so we didn’t have to re-architect our application or change our payloads. SageMaker AI handles routing, health detection, and fallback, and customer data always stays within the Salesforce trust boundary. We decide which Regions are eligible and control access through endpoint policies that we own. Because inference router works with Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail, we also get a complete observability, cost-tracking, and governance architecture for our workloads.”
— Richard Chang, Software Engineering Architect, Salesforce
Best practices and what to watch
Keep the same model, container image, and artifacts available in every Region you register, because the router does not copy them, and a destination that runs a different model version will return different answers to the same request.
Size each destination Region for its own traffic plus the overflow you expect to send it. The router does not create capacity, and if every eligible destination is busy, your application receives the destinations’ own errors. Configure autoscaling on each destination the way you do today, with enough headroom that a receiving endpoint can scale out under its own policy when traffic arrives from another Region.
Customers can set the cap in the receiving endpoint’s configuration (CrossRegionTrafficConfig), as a per-instance request rate and the largest share of the endpoint’s capacity that remote traffic may use. Local traffic never counts against the cap. When remote traffic reaches it, the endpoint stops accepting additional requests from other Regions and the router sends them to other destinations, so local callers keep their capacity. The cap applies to real-time endpoints.
Conclusion
Salesforce serves a wide variety of models for products across the company in 30+ global Regions, and hosting them separately in each Region had turned capacity shortfalls into availability problems. With the inference router, Salesforce registers the endpoints it already runs in different Regions and accounts behind one call, so traffic that a local endpoint cannot serve reaches capacity elsewhere instead of failing. Requests that must stay in a Region stay there, endpoint owners authorize cross-account access through policies they control, and every response shows where a request ran and why. SageMaker AI handles the routing, health assessment, and gradual return of traffic after recovery, instead of each calling application building that logic itself. This lets Salesforce add capacity securely while keeping its data residency commitments.
The cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI is generally available starting November 18, 2026, in all commercial Regions where inference is supported for real-time endpoints. To get started, see the Inference router documentation in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide and the CreateInferenceRouter API reference.

articles.title: Huawei prépare un drôle d’engin : un « iPhone Duo » qui ne se plie pas
articles.text:
Avec l’Osta O1 Pro, Huawei lance une toute nouvelle sous-marque et un pari ergonomique culotté : reprendre le format passeport ultra-large des récents iPhone Duo et Galaxy Z Fold 8, smartphone pliable d’Apple, mais dans un châssis rigide.
Après s’être arrogé le droit d’être la première marque à sortir un trifold, Huawei montre une fois encore que, malgré l’embargo qui pèse sur ses épaules, l’entreprise en a encore sous le pied niveau qualité d’ingénierie. Alors qu’Apple a popularisé le format « passeport » cet automne avec son iPhone Duo pliable, Huawei s’engouffre dans la brèche avec une idée pour le moins inattendue : garder cette silhouette trapue et généreuse en largeur, mais supprimer purement et simplement la charnière, la structure en deux parties et les complications qui vont avec.
De quoi propulser la nouvelle marque de Huawei
Officiellement dévoilé en images sur la boutique chinoise Vmall à l’approche de sa présentation le 20 novembre, l’Osta O1 Pro inaugure la nouvelle sous-marque Osta. Une stratégie déjà éprouvée chez Huawei avec la marque Honor, qui vole désormais de ses propres ailes. L’appareil mise sur une dalle plate au ratio inhabituel de 16 : 9,5, de 6,39 pouces en OLED, donnant l’impression de tenir un écran externe d’iPhone Duo dopé aux stéroïdes. Fini les téléphones tout en longueur qui dépassent des poches : place à une surface pensée pour le confort de lecture et le multimédia.
Côté design, le constructeur opte pour un dos épuré intégrant un double module photo horizontal, décliné en trois coloris : blanc, noir et un très réussi violet. Les précommandes sont d’ores et déjà ouvertes en Chine avec des configurations démarrant à 12 Go de RAM et 256 ou 512 Go de stockage.
Propulsé par une puce maison Kirin 9030S, cet OVNI technologique, dont le prix et la fiche technique complète seront révélés ce vendredi 20 novembre, reste pour l’heure réservé au marché chinois. Reste à savoir si ce format « passeport rigide » a une chance de s’imposer hors d’Asie, ou s’il restera une simple curiosité.

articles.title: Coinbase blocks $4.7 million in transfers to Elon Musk deepfake scam
articles.text:
Coinbase says it blocked $4.7 million in cryptocurrency transfers to scammers promoting a fake giveaway using an AI-generated deepfake of Elon Musk during a Tesla livestream that attracted more than 500,000 viewers.
The deepfake took place during Tesla's "flying car" demonstration, when scammers created a fake YouTube livestream that appeared to broadcast the event.
The fraudulent stream featured an AI-generated video of Musk, cryptocurrency wallet addresses, and a QR code, promising viewers that any cryptocurrency they sent would be doubled.
According to Coinbase, hundreds of its customers attempted to send millions of dollars to the scammers over about two hours, including many longtime users of the exchange.
However, the company says its AI-powered fraud-prevention systems detected the scam and blocked about 91% of the attempted transfers, totaling $4.7 million.
Unlike traditional cryptocurrency theft involving compromised accounts or stolen credentials, victims in this campaign voluntarily made the crypto transfer after believing the livestream was real.
Coinbase explained that this makes scams like these difficult to detect because the transactions are created and approved by legitimate account holders.
"Most fraud defenses are built to spot activity the customer didn't authorize," Coinbase explained.
"That's not what happened here. The customer was logged in, the customer pressed confirm, and the customer believed it was the opportunity of a lifetime."
AI agents intervene to stop transfers
Coinbase says its scam prevention system uses machine learning models to analyze outgoing cryptocurrency transfers in real time, identifying suspicious activity associated with giveaway scams, brand impersonation, and newly created wallet addresses.
When a suspicious transfer is detected, an AI agent engages the customer in a short conversation, explaining the characteristics of the suspected scam and asking questions intended to help them recognize the fraud.
The system also assigns confidence scores to the agent's responses before presenting them to customers, allowing it to determine when additional safeguards may be necessary.
Coinbase says its AI agent had never encountered this particular campaign before but recognized the underlying scam techniques, including promises to multiply cryptocurrency, time pressure tied to a live event, and irreversible transfers.
The company claims the entire detection and intervention process operated automatically, without human involvement.
"What's notable is that the agent had never seen this scam. Deepfake giveaways tied to a live product launch weren't in its training," Coinbase said.
BleepingComputer contacted Coinbase to ask how many transfers reached the scammers and how much cryptocurrency was stolen, but has not yet received a response.
Elon Musk and his companies have long been popular lures for cryptocurrency scams, with fraudsters hijacking verified Twitter accounts, sending fake giveaway invitations via email, and flooding TikTok with fraudulent promotions.
Scammers have also used deepfake videos of Musk to promote fraudulent cryptocurrency investment platforms, while a separate campaign involving compromised verified Twitter accounts stole more than $580,000 in cryptocurrency in just one week.
To avoid falling victim to these types of scam campaigns, users should independently verify cryptocurrency promotions through official websites and social media accounts rather than trusting livestreams or QR codes displayed in videos.

articles.title: Style Union raises Rs 485 Cr to expand beyond southern India
articles.text:
Style Union raises Rs 485 Cr to expand beyond southern India
Style Union’s parent has raised Rs 485 crore from Venturi Partners and Elev8 Venture Partners to expand nationally, targeting 450 stores by March 2030.
Nexon Omniverse Limited, the parent company of value-fashion retailer Style Union, has raised Rs 485 crore in a Series E round led by Venturi Partners, a consumer-focused investment firm, and co-led by Elev8 Venture Partners, a growth-stage investor.
The funding comprises primary and secondary capital, but the company has not disclosed the split.
The money will support expansion beyond Style Union’s southern base into western and northern India, the company said. The company also plans to grow from 200 stores to 220 by March 2027 and 450 by March 2030.
Whole-time director Rajesh Seth called the investment an endorsement of its effort to make “quality fashion at fair prices” a profitable business. He said the next phase would take the brand into new cities and households.
Launched in 2022, Style Union sells affordable family fashion across eight states and Delhi-NCR. The company said it expanded from 41 stores and Rs 123 crore in net revenue in FY23 to 158 stores and more than Rs 1,150 crore in revenue in FY26.
Venturi founder Nicholas Cator said the company treats value as “a promise, not a price point”. Elev8’s Navin Honagudi cited its focus on “unit economics” and disciplined inventory management.
The fundraise comes as value fashion gains ground. Crisil Ratings expects organised apparel retailers to grow revenue by 12-13% in FY27. It found value fashion’s share of organised apparel revenue rose from 39% to 46% in three years, with the segment growing more than twice as fast as others.
However, higher cotton and operating costs, alongside intense competition, could squeeze margins. CareEdge estimates India’s apparel retail market will reach Rs 16 lakh crore by FY30. Organised retail accounts for about 41% of the market and is projected to grow by 10-13%.
Other fashion businesses have attracted capital too. The Pant Project raised Rs 109 crore in a Series B round led by Mirae Asset in October 2026 to expand stores and product categories. Design-led brand Theater secured Rs 75 crore in September for offline expansion.
Meanwhile, policy changes may support affordable apparel. Since September 2025, readymade garments priced up to Rs 2,500 per piece have attracted 5% GST, extending the earlier threshold of Rs 1,000.
The textile production-linked incentive scheme was also revised to halve the minimum investment requirement, lower the incremental turnover criterion from 25% to 10%, and add 17 man-made-fibre apparel and fabric products. The scheme targets manufacturers rather than retailers directly.

articles.title: Casi 64 millones de visualizaciones en Netflix con sus 6 episodios: la miniserie de Netflix que estrena segunda temporada en noviembre
articles.text:
Si te gustan las historias de espías y conspiraciones, quizás te acuerdes de una serie de Netflix que llegó en diciembre de 2024 y consiguió hacerse un hueco entre los títulos más vistos de la plataforma. Hablamos de Palomas negras (Black Doves), una ficción protagonizada por Keira Knightley que vuelve casi dos años después con una segunda temporada. Y lo mejor es que no tendrás que esperar para descubrir qué ocurre, porque sus seis nuevos episodios ya están disponibles desde el 5 de noviembre.
La primera temporada llegó el 5 de diciembre de 2024 con solo seis capítulos y un reparto encabezado por Keira Knightley, Ben Whishaw y Sarah Lancashire. La serie, creada por Joe Barton, mezcla espionaje, conspiraciones y acción en una Londres ambientada durante las Navidades. ¿Su protagonista? Helen Webb, una mujer que parece llevar una vida familiar normal, aunque esconde un secreto bastante importante: trabaja como espía.
De qué trata Palomas negras y qué puedes esperar de su segunda temporada
Durante diez años, Helen ha estado filtrando información de su marido, un político, a una organización secreta conocida como las Palomas Negras. Todo cambia cuando asesinan a Jason, su amante, y su jefa Reed decide recurrir a Sam Young (un viejo amigo de Helen) para protegerla. A partir de ahí, ambos investigan el asesinato y terminan descubriendo una conspiración que amenaza con provocar una crisis internacional.
Y si te quedaste con ganas de más, la segunda temporada recupera a los protagonistas con nuevos problemas. Según explica Netflix, Helen continúa compartiendo secretos con la organización mientras su marido se prepara para convertirse en primer ministro. Reed también se ve envuelta en una conspiración que amenaza su posición, así que la tranquilidad no parece estar entre los planes de ninguno.
La serie vuelve a contar con Knightley, Whishaw y Lancashire, además de incorporar nuevos nombres al reparto. Entre ellos están Ambika Mod y Neve Campbell, que se suman a esta historia de secretos y traiciones. Todo ello bajo la dirección creativa de Joe Barton, que vuelve como creador y guionista de la ficción.
Y hay otro detalle que caracteriza a Palomas negras: su ambientación navideña. Knightley explicó que la serie funciona como una alternativa a las películas familiares habituales de esas fechas, con una historia donde la acción y el peligro ocupan buena parte de la trama. Si quieres verla, las dos temporadas están disponibles en Netflix, con seis episodios cada una.
Foto | Netflix
En Xataka | Solo cinco episodios ha necesitado esta miniserie de suspense para encaramarse a lo más visto de Netflix

articles.title: Palmer Luckey plant schwimmende Siedlung für US-Industrie
articles.text:
Gesetze umgehen: Oculus-Gründer Palmer Luckey plant schwimmende Siedlung für US-Industrie
Im Jahr 2014 hatte Palmer Luckey seine VR-Firma Oculus für zwei Milliarden US-Dollar an Facebook verkauft. Seitdem trat der Tech-Milliardär unter anderem als Mitgründer der Waffenschmiede Anduril und der Retro-Gaming-Firma Modretro in Erscheinung. Jetzt sorgt Luckey mit einer neuen Geschäftsidee für Aufmerksamkeit.
Schwimmende Siedlung auf hoher See
Wie er in einem X-Posting darlegt, will Luckey eine schwimmende Siedlung im Meer errichten. Auf der SLAB genannten Plattform soll die US-Industrie ihrer Fertigungs- und Forschungsarbeit nachgehen können, ohne sich an geltende Gesetze oder Auflagen halten zu müssen. Luckey nennt diese Gesetze „undurchdacht“.
Die Idee dahinter ist das sogenannte Seasteading, das eine dauerhafte „Landnahme“ auf hoher See beschreibt. Außerhalb der von Küstenanrainern beanspruchbaren Wirtschaftszone von 200 Meilen (370 Kilometern) unterliegt das Meer keinen Gesetzen. Auf einer Plattform, wie sie sich Luckey vorstellt, könnten entsprechend die Regeln und Gesetze gelten, die der Oculus-Gründer ihr gibt.
Zu den Industriebereichen, die Luckey dort ansiedeln will, gehören Metallverarbeitung, chemische Industrie, Ölraffinerien und medizinische Forschung sowie Meerwasserentsalzung. Welche Gesetze ihm konkret ein Dorn im Auge sind, sagte er aber nicht.
Plattform günstiger als Grundstück
Luckey zufolge sei das Errichten einer schwimmenden Siedlung auf hoher See günstiger als der Kauf entsprechender Grundstücke an Land. Geht es nach dem Tech-Milliardär soll seine SLAB-Plattform so designt sein, dass sie 1.000 Jahre lang bestehen kann. Luckey erklärte, dass weitere Investor:innen an Bord seien. Insgesamt soll das in das Projekt gepumpte Kapital bisher schon zu einer Bewertung von einer Milliarde Dollar geführt haben.
Die Pläne, an deren Umsetzung er offenbar seit mehreren Jahren arbeitet, will Luckey jetzt nur preisgegeben haben, weil Medienvertreter:innen davon Wind bekommen hätten. Allerdings sollen diese davon ausgegangen sein, dass er ein schwimmendes KI-Rechenzentrum errichten wolle – was nicht stimme.
Luckey will nicht als Loser dastehen
„Es ist viel cooler, es ist viel älter, und ich hasse es, wie ein Loser dazustehen, der jedem Hype hinterherläuft und mit der Masse schwimmt“, so Luckey. Ziel sei es, die USA wieder stärker zu machen und ein Ventil für „veraltete“ Regeln und Vorschriften zu bieten.
Eine ähnliche Idee hat vor Luckey übrigens schon ein anderer Tech-Milliardär verfolgt: Peter Thiel. Der hatte im Jahr 2008 rund 1,7 Millionen Dollar in das sogenannte Seasteading Institute investiert. Das Projekt wollte politisch autonome Communitys auf dem Wasser errichten, wie Business Insider schreibt. Thiel ließ allerdings später die Finger von dem Projekt und erklärte, dass der Plan nicht umsetzbar sei.
Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: LeBron James demandó a una app de apuestas por un anuncio con su imagen y voz creados con IA
articles.text:
LeBron James demandó a los fundadores de Bron, una aplicación de apuestas deportivas con inteligencia artificial (IA), ante un tribunal federal de Nueva York, Estados Unidos. Los acusa de usar sin permiso su apodo, su imagen y una voz sintética en un anuncio con el que buscaron fama para su producto.
La demanda, de 44 páginas, tiene como acusados a la empresa PlayVision, que opera la app, y a sus cofundadores Anish Gupta y Marc Zoghby. James pide una orden judicial que les prohíba usar su identidad y el nombre “Bron”, además de una indemnización por daños.
El anuncio que mostró a un James creado con IA
El video apareció el 4 de noviembre de 2026 en la cuenta de X de Gupta. Según el escrito, muestra a una versión de James generada con IA en un vestuario, con una camiseta que dice “Bron” sobre el número 23 y sus tatuajes. Habla con una voz que, según la demanda, imita la suya.
En el anuncio, esa figura recorre apuestas sobre otros jugadores de la NBA desde un teléfono y menciona a Kalshi, una plataforma de mercados de predicción. Según la demanda, James tiene un acuerdo de patrocinio con Polymarket, competidora directa de Kalshi, y el anuncio podría perjudicar esa relación.
El escrito sostiene que el video no aclaraba que James no tenía relación con la app, ni que la figura había sido generada con IA, ni incluía un mensaje de juego responsable. Agrega que reunió cerca de un millón de vistas en X en un día.
James afirma que su aval “es único” y que recibe decenas de millones de dólares por asociar su nombre con un producto. Dice que nunca prestó su nombre ni su voz a los acusados.
La carta de advertencia y la respuesta de los fundadores
Los abogados de James enviaron el 5 de noviembre de 2026 una carta para exigir que cesara el uso de su identidad y del nombre “Bron”. Pidieron avisar por escrito a todos los usuarios que apostaron que James no tiene relación con la app. Gupta respondió esa noche que habían retirado el material y que cambiarían el nombre.
Según la demanda, solo se cumplió la retirada del anuncio de las cuentas de la empresa. El 6 de noviembre, Gupta publicó un video que decía que era hora de un nombre nuevo, pero sin revelarlo. El 16 de noviembre, en LinkedIn, volvió a bromear con una posible demanda.
Gupta escribió en redes sociales que el nuevo nombre se anunciaría el miércoles 18 de noviembre, según informó la agencia AP. Hasta el momento de la demanda, la app seguía en la tienda de Apple como “Bron - AI Sports Analysis” y cobraba suscripciones de “Bron Pro”.
La ficha de la tienda describe la app como una herramienta de análisis e información sobre apuestas que no acepta apuestas. En su correo del 5 de noviembre, Gupta dijo que la plataforma “no permite apostar, solo recomendaciones”.
Otro deportista también reclamó
El escrito indica que el anuncio muestra los nombres y fotos de otros jugadores, entre ellos Luka Dončić, Devin Booker y Giannis Antetokounmpo. Según la demanda, ninguno dio su consentimiento. Dončić envió a los acusados un reclamo para que dejaran de usar su imagen.
PlayVision participó en el programa de la aceleradora Y Combinator de otoño de 2025, según CNBC. La app y sus fundadores no habían respondido públicamente a la demanda al cierre de las notas consultadas, según Courthouse News y CNBC.
Los medios señalan que la demanda llega cuando varios jugadores de la NBA enfrentan escrutinio por sus apuestas, entre ellos Damon Jones, excompañero de James, acusado de apostar con información privilegiada. James sostiene que insinuar que un jugador activo apuesta en partidos de la NBA “no es un asunto trivial”.
El caso quedó registrado con el número 1:26-cv-10078 y está en su etapa inicial: no hay sentencia ni acuerdo, y la empresa no había presentado su respuesta al 18 de noviembre.

articles.title: Behind Booking.com's AI Evolution: The Unpolished Story
articles.text:
Transcript
Jabez Eliezer Manuel: Today, Booking.com impacts billions of travel decisions, and behind each of those travel decisions is actually a bunch of ML platforms working behind the scenes. I'm here to talk about them. In the spirit of QCon's 20th anniversary, we are going to go back in time by two decades and take on a journey and then see how these platforms evolve.
To make it easier for you to follow along, I've structured my talk into three layers, the data management layer, the ML engineering, and domain intelligence. In the data management layer, we will see the evolution of our databases, and some of the scale challenges that we had, and the cloud migration that we undertook to actually better our data. In the ML engineering layer, it'll be model serving at scale, and our feature engineering atoms there. In the domain intelligence layer, it'll be a high-level tour of all the machine learning platforms that we have. I'll pick one of them and then do a deep dive, so you get a full evolution of that specific platform, and you'll also have something tangible to take.
The World in 2005
Let's go back to 2005. This was how the world looked like in 2005, if you remember these camera phones. Web 2.0 was taking off as a platform, and Booking.com was just like 9 years old. It had still not joined the Priceline group. Inside Booking, something fascinating was happening. We had run our first A/B experiment. Today everything goes through experimentation. It doesn't matter if it's a simple CSS change or an infrastructure change, everything goes through experimentation. At any point in time, if you're visiting Booking.com, you are subjected to 1,000-plus experiments, literally. Over the period of time, we have run 150,000 experiments or more until now. One thing that's certain is that most of our experiments fail, our success rate is just less than 25%. The goal isn't to get it right, but it is to learn fast. If you see that golden star on the top right, it's my little takeaway marker.
It's my way of hinting to you that there might be a lesson in this slide that is reusable for you. Continuing on experimentation. Experimentation built our data-driven DNA. It gave us a lot of technical benefits, which is sure. The ones that I like are that it eliminated HIPPOs. There were no endless debates internally. You just say, ok, let's go and build, test it, and done. The last is like, no, it created a culture of humility. There were no experts in the room, meaning that nobody could pinpoint and say, yes, let's experiment and then figure it out.
Data Management Layer
Experiments needed data, and that's where we are going to begin our journey in data management. In this part, I want to talk about our MySQL, our Hadoop, and our move to cloud. These are the three topics that I want to cover. This was our original tech stack when Booking.com started. It was just Perl and Postgres. Quickly, we replaced Postgres with MySQL, primarily because of its asynchronous replication capabilities and for other reasons as well. In 2005, our setup was just a single master and four slaves. Fast forward 15 years, we were operating one of the largest clusters in the world. You might be wondering, how do you manage so many instances? Three things. We have a single writer setup, and we have replication chains, which I'll show you. Then we have a lot of automation. Let's make it real with an example, with an image. What you're seeing is a single master topology.
On the left, orange is the master, and then there are replicas or slaves. The colors indicate different data centers out there. As you can see, we minimize the replication across DCs by having intermediate masters. This whole topology is managed by a replication management tool called Orchestrator. If anybody is using MySQL, you might be aware of it. Automation was a necessity. For example, every 60 days, we take these 7,000 instances or so out, deprovision them, and reprovision them again. That meant that for every three minutes, there is some action that is going on. It is not humanely possible for some engineer to sit and do it. We have plenty of automation to do that.
There are a few things that makes our MySQL setup a little bit different. One is we don't use any specialized hardware. It's like simple frontend blades that are used for MySQL. No stored procedures, no UDFs, no views, not even a cache layer. Yes, no cache layers. The secret sauce, what we do is we actually create smaller DBs. The soft limit is 2 terabytes. The hard limit is 10 terabytes. We try to keep everything small. The reason is we want this database to fit into the fast storage of that server blade that we are using. In this example, we were normally using server blade 7 or 9, if you are aware of its configuration. What that meant is our point queries were less than 350 microseconds, which was roughly in the order of some of the memory engines out there. We were effectively using MySQL as a cache.
It also provided several side benefits. It was faster backups, quicker failovers, and primarily also lower cost, because if you're moving away from fast storage to iSCSI, it's expensive. We didn't just use MySQL. We actually helped shape it. What do I mean by that? In the early days of Booking, we had expertise in-house to fork MySQL, but we made a conscious decision to say that we're not going to fork, we're going to contribute upstream. Many of the features that you see today exist because we wanted it. Like, for example, GTID-based replication is because we actually proposed it. We made the case. We shaped the design of MySQL.
I want to sidestep a bit and then give you a picture of how machine learning looked in that era. It was Perl scripts and statistical and scientific computing libraries from CPAN and just cron jobs. The deployment strategy was simple. Copy the script and pray. It solved real business problems. We were able to do fraud detection. We were doing demand forecasting with regression. We were doing recommendations with KNN and a few other things. Even in those days, we were able to solve that. This MySQL setup helped us a bit. As data grew large, we needed something more. Hadoop came to the rescue. In 2011, we actually built two on-premise clusters. This was a configuration that was there. It was redundant clusters. The setup looked like this. There was MySQL on bare metal. Then there was this classic Hadoop stack, HDFS, YARN, MapReduce. Then we layered it with Oozie for orchestration, Spark for workflows, and Hive for SQL, and Sqoop for moving data between Hadoop and MySQL.
On top of it, we had some self-serve tooling, a classic setup. Data came into Hadoop via two means. From MySQL, it came as nightly jobs into Hadoop. Then from Kafka, it was Kafka Connect that was bringing in data. This data was used for machine learning purposes. This is how prediction training was happening back then. What you see is two workflows, the training workflow on the top and an inference workflow. A scientist would actually write a workflow where they would train a Python model. Then they call it as pickling the model, which is just serializing the model, storing into Hadoop. Then another workflow loads that model, does the prediction that it wants. Then it actually stores it into MySQL in some cases, but not in all cases. Basically, the whole prediction was happening completely offline. In some cases, we want real-time. In those cases, what we did was we just faked it.
This is how we faked it. The top is the offline workflow, and the bottom is a web request. We wanted the real-time prediction to happen in the web request. All we did was we trained the model. I'll give you an example how we did it. Let's take an example of a model that we want to train, like device and country is the feature, and probability to book is the output that we want to do. In those cases, what we did was we just enumerated all the input features. We just created all possible devices, all possible countries. Then we just predicted on that upfront. That gave us a table. All we did was store that table into the MySQL. Then when the request came in, we just queried the table as if we were predicting, and then went on to do our job. Obviously, it doesn't work for most cases, but that was our earlier real-time prediction with faking it with lookup tables.
That worked for us in most cases. Hadoop powered for us most of our pipeline for many years, but there were some problems. One was it was a shared environment, so every training, production workloads, everything was running in a single cluster. There was mono-version. If you are a data scientist, you cannot use a version that you want. You just have to use a version that is possible, like now it is shared. The second thing was there was no GPU support. That limited our ability to train a bigger model, larger model. We were using two different DCs for redundant setup. Then you need to keep the data in sync between this, and that was becoming a headache. Capacity issues, like at peak times, we were operating very close to max capacity. Noisy neighbors, like some NOOB who's writing a query can actually clog the entire production cluster.
Most importantly, there was no discovery or ownership, even though people depended on each other's data. That was the biggest headache for us. This is what it looked like. Like now somebody might think that this is a Rorschach psychological test, but it is just a dependency graph for our workflows. If you zoom in closely, you can see Hadoop screaming in binary there.
2011, we introduced Hadoop. 2018, we realized the limitation of Hadoop, but then it took us until 2022 to put it into maintenance mode, and another three years to go into sunset. Like now what was going wrong? Why did it take so long, that hairball that you saw earlier? Why was it difficult? We were operating with hundreds of petabytes of data. We had about 190,000 Hadoop tables, 7,000-plus workflows, hundreds of teams, and then we want to keep everything up and running. Our goal was move everything, stop nothing, align everyone. Everybody knows that that last part is already a moonshot. We were like, why pick one impossible thing? Pick three. We had four problems to solve. One was, we wanted to actually modernize our compute and scale it, obviously, because we were operating at max capacity. Then we want segregation of workflows, because we wanted isolation at least between dev and production.
Governance and ownership, which was a mess, we wanted to fix that. The last was, we wanted to enable discovery of workflows and datasets so that people can reuse things. Saying goodbye to Hadoop was hard, and this is why. This is what happened in those gap years. 2018, when we realized the mistake, or realized the problem, we actually attempted to move into one of the cloud providers. Quickly, the product got shelved. The reason was, depending upon who you ask, it is either cost or a strategy shift. We quickly pivoted to building something internally to help us. Like now we actually built assistant application along with Hadoop to have a data catalog. Then we also had built Kubernetes clusters to do Spark. That eased us a little bit, so we could continue on. A short bit later, we started the modernization project, where we focused on three things, like quality, ownership, and governance of data.
We were trying to fix that with that modernization project. During that time period, we actually piloted another cloud, and that showed promise, but we didn't actually make enough to move the needle to actually do a full migration. In 2023, leadership actually made the call, and they said, guys, we're going to do it all in, no plan B. That actually helped, we made progress, and we succeeded. Just within one and a half years, we migrated everything that you saw. This is how we did it. Maybe there is something in there for you. We actually built a tool that mapped every possible table, every dependency into a graph. That was our first effort, map the universe. Second thing that we did was, we looked at the usage analysis of all the tables and the workflows, and the lineage as well, and said, which of this is business critical?
Then we tried to trim it down. You'd be surprised that 92% of the workflows didn't pass the test, someone cares, it was easy. The best architectural tool is Delete key. What we then did is, we actually did graph analysis on those workflows that passed, and we actually prioritized it by centrality and impact. We took a few, and after that it was simple. Group them into batches, do the migration, and slowly phase out the legacy system.
If you look back, one key thing that made the difference was this unified command center, which held that graph data, and that became the central place for anybody to look at it during the migration. If I had a workflow that I had to migrate, but then I depended on a few other workflows, I could go in there and then see, ok, when is my dependency migrating, and when can I migrate. I could plan things easy. Anything, status, dependencies, blockers, everything was in there. This replaced spreadsheet tracking, and also it replaced tribal knowledge. Everybody knew what exactly was happening. The second thing we already saw was, we removed plan B out of the equation. Leadership said, just go in. We all know that this is not always the best plan. The best strategy is prevention. If we had a time machine, these are the four messages that we would send to our past self. First, catalog every asset that you have. Data workflows doesn't matter. Catalog it. Establish clear ownership. It can be business ownership and also technical ownership of the data. Build quality gates before you share that data. Track lineage end-to-end. That concludes our data layer.
ML Engineering Layer
Next in the ML engineering layer, I want to talk about two things. One is how we industrialized ML model serving. Second, our attempts at feature engineering and the problem that still remains. Before I do that, I want to give you a 30-second overview of evolution of our ML stack. In 2005, we actually were using Perl libraries and the MySQL, which was still doing the job. Hadoop came into the picture that brought in big data analysis and reporting, that was good. True machine learning kickstarted with the introduction of Oozie and Python, like the sklearn era, because we were able to do things easily. When Spark came in, that changed the game or changed the pace of the game. Now we were able to do more things faster and we were able to crunch more numbers. H2O took it to another level. Now we were able to do faster training.
Also, we were able to deploy models directly in any Java environment. That was a big thing. In 2017, deep learning came in. Deep learning started as a very simple hackathon project, where a group of developers wanted to improve the image stacks, which was of low quality. From then on, it is widely adopted across the company. 2023, LLM wave took off and we built a bunch of generative products, which we'll touch upon a bit later. 2025, we started laying the foundations of the agentic systems, which we'll also touch later.
Going back, if you look at the timeline, 2015, in my opinion, was a pivotal year, because we were solving two problems. One was real-time predictions. Until then, we were solving real-time predictions with fake lookup tables that you saw earlier. In a hackathon, we actually built a small Scala service, which was backed by a storage. It was actually used to do model serving. Machine learning scientists could upload the model. Back in those days, the model was just classical problems, like logistic regression, classification, and so on. Uploading a model is nothing but uploading a CSV file with all the features that was used, what type of those features, and some weights and coefficients. In real time, when a user landed on the website, some backend service collected the features necessary to invoke the model. Then they used the Perl SDK, because we were still in Perl back then, to invoke the Scala service.
Over a period of time, this Scala service has evolved into a platform. Now it supports 12-plus different model formats. You can think of all the major ones are in here. This is how the setup looks like today. That service is deployed in multiple clusters. Why multiple clusters? We have some general-purpose shared tenant clusters, some dedicated clusters for very critical workloads, and then also some clusters for batch. Either these clusters actually host their model, or they actually can interact with externally hosted models, so like SageMaker. They can also contact feature store, which we'll cover later. To hide the complexity from the end users, these clusters are fronted by a custom proxy. Every prediction that these clusters make, is logged. Then those logs go into data lake and also to our monitoring platforms. Let's take an example how a flow of machine learning scientists uploading a model and inference happens.
Machine learning scientists upload the model artifact into something like S3, and then they notify an ML portal to say, I've registered this new model. That triggers a pipeline. The coordinator goes and picks up that model that the ML scientist uploaded, and then comes back, versions it in its own storage. Also, what it does is, it finds the right cluster to deploy, and then allocates enough space, and triggers that upload. In addition, it'll also upload that, update the proxy that you saw earlier to say that the proxy knows which cluster to route to. Serving was simple. When a web request came in, backend servers just invoked the custom proxy with this client SDK. This was one of our success stories. There was no problem, and it was a clear success. Two years back, this is what that system that you just saw handled. It has 480-plus models. It can do 400 billion predictions per day. All of those predictions within less than 20 milliseconds on an average. Those are impressive numbers.
Second problem that we started solving in 2015 was feature engineering. Back then, 80% of the time was spent on just data preparation. Two pain points emerged. One was duplication. Each team was trying to build the feature by themselves in a different way. The second was there was skew. The models that behaved one way in training was behaving another way in inference. We set out to solve the problem by solving the duplication and to bring consistency. We thought, let's build reusable computations. We decided to tackle the problem separately for offline and for online, because offline was targeted at machine learning scientists. Online was targeted for engineers. I'm going to sidestep here to give you the context so you can better understand the decisions that the team made. What you're seeing on screen is just an initial dataset. You have a user ID, what the user searched and when.
Then also the label that we are predicting on to say that did the user eventually book or not. That's the initial dataset. That's how an ML scientist starts their work. What they do is they try to add more features into this dataset. They keep looking for other feature tables. Feature tables look like this, which is just a time series representation of a feature. In this case, the feature represented is what is the number of searches that the user did in the last seven days. That is the series that you're seeing. Once they found such a feature table, all they do is a point-in-wise join, wherein they take a unique ID, in this case, user ID, and some timestamp, and they do a time-wise join on it. Then they get a training set, wherein they have the feature that they were looking for, which in this case is the count of last seven days.
When we looked at this, we said, we can help in two places. One is building that feature table, and the other is doing the time-wise join. That is what we set out to achieve. That was a feature table. That feature table is built by another fact log or an immutable log. This is just the searches that have happened over a period of time. By looking at this, it is just very clear that there is one data frame and the other data frame. We figured out we can actually just use Spark ML transformer, which did the feature translation between.
This is how it looked in its entirety. There were immutable fact logs, which is just log of search events that have happened in the past. We asked people to write reusable feature encoders that converted into a feature table. Once we had that, all anybody has to do is just go look at the initial dataset and do a time-wise join on it. We tried to do something similar to online as well. There were event streams. We asked people to write feature mappers in Scala, and that became enriched streams. From there, there was a centralized team which took all these features, put it into Cassandra, and then served it via an API. There were a couple of problems with this approach. One was parity. Data was different between online and offline. The computation was different from online and offline. Then there were performance issues because of the amount of data that we were processing in offline.
Backfilling or recomputation was hard. In the second attempt, we decided, let's fix data and computational parity together. The way we fixed data parity was we introduced the concept of timelines. Timelines is nothing but a time-ordered sequence of events for a user. User searched, user clicked, user booked, things like that. The idea was, let's build this timeline equally or approximately in the same way for both online and offline. Then that way, once we have that, we can just write computation once and then use the timeline. That was a big picture. This is how the timelines were built. Those are the search, clicks, and immutable events. They got materialized into Hadoop. We built timeline builders separately. It's a duplicate effort, but it was managed by a central team. That timeline was operating separately for online and offline. They synced the data or the timelines into Cassandra and HDFS. The only difference between these two timelines were the Cassandra timelines were trimmed. Unlike the MVA, TVA, we actually didn't trim timelines for saving the universe. We trimmed timelines in Cassandra for saving the space.
This is how we used timelines for computational parity. We had a full timeline in HDFS, a trimmed timeline in Cassandra. We asked people to write centralized shared feature libraries. These are things that can be used to compute features, things like sum, count, large scale, and all those typical things was written by a centralized team. It also allowed extension. Anybody could come in and write in the feature that is not already there. In online or in real time, when an application wanted some inference, they would go to a feature store API and ask, can you give me this feature? What it would do is go into Cassandra, pick up the timeline for that specific user or use case, and then build that feature on the fly with these shared libraries. The same happened on the training side or on offline. That stack was Python, because scientists were using Python.
We had a wrapper, which had a feature computation library wrapper. What it did was, whenever the scientist wanted a feature, it submitted a Spark job. In that Spark job, we actually did the same thing. We typically achieved what we wanted to do, both data and feature parity. The problem was, ML scientists were not familiar with writing features in Java, and that created a dependency between engineering and ML science. Secondly, in the previous one, the Cassandra timelines, computing features on the fly was costly, expensive, because it took more than 90 milliseconds or so to actually just fetch the data. It was not suitable for most of the use cases. Then we said, ok, third attempt. Forget feature computation, we'll just focus on feature storage and serving. Let people deal with feature computation. We didn't care how features are computed, as long as we knew where to pick the features from.
If it was pre-computed, ok, we'll go to a data lake of sorts. If it is real time, we'll go to Kafka. Then we built a feature store. In the feature store, there was an ingestor component, which knew about these multiple data sources, and pulled that data, and stored it into an online store, and served it via an API. In this API, there was no on-the-fly computation. It was just a simple lookup, because features were already computed. The same pipeline, what it also did was sync data into offline, so that MLS can use it for retraining purposes, and for also other analysis. This feature store also had other benefits, like it had feature registry, feature monitoring, and so on. In essence, after three attempts, this is what we learned. It's a multidimensional problem, and we don't have an answer. Currently, for the pre-computation and real time, we currently have three systems, and we are always looking for one more system. That wraps the second layer.
Domain Intelligence Layer
Now in that third layer, we are moving away from infrastructure to business impact. I want to give you a high-level tour of all the ML platforms that we have, and then dive into one of them. This is the platform that we have. One is GenAI platform. It's the newest kid in the block. What it does is it enables any team to actually safely build generative AI experiences. It provides tools and infrastructure and foundational capabilities like guardrails, evaluation, orchestration out of the box. Things like PII detection, PII masking, everything comes out of the box. The product teams can focus just on product innovation and not on LLM plumbing. Let's look at a few use cases there, what we have. The trip planning, which is just a conversational experience where someone can go talk in natural language and get recommendations, that's powered by GenAI. We have smart filters.
If you were ever on Booking.com, you would see hundreds of filters on the left, and it is hard for anyone to know which to pick. We have a text box where you can type it, and that translated into the right filters and sorters. The third is review summaries. That provides, based on the last reviews, a quick snapshot of pros and cons. The next is property Q&A. This actually enables instant answers to any property-specific questions, and it is grounded on reviews, past Q&A, and that is also powered by GenAI. We also have a booking support, wherein we have AI that can do basic customer support on payments, cancellation, and things regarding your booking. These are the use cases. There are many interesting things under the platform, but we are not going to cover it today.
GenAI is good, but to generate data, we actually want good content. That's where content intelligence comes in. What it does is it provides surfaces like good, high-quality content that are usable. This platform analyzes every image and text. It actually adds metadata or enriches that metadata. For example, if it is images, it adds themes, tags, and looks for any harmful content. If it is text, it looks for, for example, sentiments or topics that have been discussed. This also supports the reviews. Because most of the things happen in the background, like fraud detection is also taken care of by this content intelligence. One example that you see, anytime you see a gallery on Booking.com, it is probably powered by this content intelligence. Picking up the right photo to put up front and the order, which photos to highlight and so on. The other thing is, it autogenerates all text for screen readers.
There's a platform for that. It also does reviews. It detects topics on the reviews and summarizes it at the property level. This is what it enabled was, not just getting intelligence at content level, but going one level higher. For example, if property had all the images and all the summaries, we can actually create intelligence at the property level to see what is happening. That kind of aggregation level, this platform enabled. The third is ranking. Ranking's responsibility is to order millions of products so that any time a customer comes in, they see the most relevant results for them, like something personalized. This is a platform that we are going to dig in, so I'll park it here. Recommendations is a self-serve platform wherein you can build any kind of recommendations across the funnel, from discovery to post-booking. It has more than 40, 50 use cases. I picked a few to give you a flavor of what it looks like.
The pushcards that you might see on Booking.com is powered by recommendations. There's multi-vertical recommendations. When I say multi-vertical, I'm referring to accommodations, flights, attractions, and so on. Those kinds of recommendations come from this platform. Unique stays, team-based recommendations for you, and attraction carousels that you might see on the page, and any flight recommendations. All of these are examples that are powered by recommendations platform. The last platform is value intelligence. The responsibility of this platform is to measure and optimize promotions. By promotions, I mean anything like vouchers, discounts, things like rewards that's being optimized by value intelligence. The goal of this platform is to say, maximize value for travelers, partners, and the business. That wraps all the platforms.
Let's jump into ranking platform. Ranking is a three-way optimization problem. We need choice and value for customers. We need exposure and growth for the partners. We also need efficiency and revenue for business. If we show irrelevant results, the travelers are going to be annoyed. If we show poor visibility, partners are going to be frustrated. If any one of them is annoyed for too long, I'm going to get my salary re-ranked. It's a three-way optimization problem. Back then in 2005, we had the formula for ranking hotels look like this. It was simple. It was just a simple function, which took bookings and views, and a random tiebreaker in case there were two hotels which had the same rank. The formula evolved over time. We introduced cancellations. It was taking consideration of seasonality. What is the distance of the hotel from the center? What is the number of views the hotel is getting?
Availability of the hotel. The average ranking in the locality. What is the visitor traffic? Guest reviews. These are just some flavors of what are the factors we considered. Back then, ranking actually was computed offline using simple Perl cron scripts every night, and then the scores were dumped into MySQL, and we used it in real time. Around 2016, we actually tried to replace the ranking formula with machine learning, and we failed miserably. The handcrafted formula was undefeatable. We could not beat it for a long time, like one and a half years or so. This formula cannot be beaten. The reasons were many fold. The primary reason was that the ideal model that we wanted to train the model on, and the massive amount of data that we had was not actually helpful when Spark kept exploding. The memory of Spark was not sufficient. What we did was we cut corners, we made some approximations, and we succeeded. In true Booking sense, we ran an experiment, and it was successful.
Next, we wanted to tackle personalized ranking, and there was a problem. This is what it looked like. The ranking scores was calculated offline until then. It was put into MySQL, and an availability engine read that MySQL data, loaded it into memory. The responsibility of this availability engine was that it needs to search the availability and prices of millions of properties. Because of the amount of data that this engine had, it used a scatter-gather pattern. It had a coordinator and 24 shards. Each of those shards actually worked on a subset of the data. When a request came in from the user, it came to the availability engine via a search orchestrator, and the request landed there. The request contained something like this. Where does the user want to search on? When? Then, what is the party size? Then, what are the filters and preferences of the user?
The coordinator accepted that request and then distributed the work to the workers. Workers went on to do their job. They actually looked into the subset of the data that they had, took the data out, and then they used the ranking scores that were preloaded into memory to do the sorting. After they did the sorting, they supplied the results back to the coordinator. Coordinator aggregated all the information from the workers and re-sorted the results and gave the results back to the search. This is what was happening. If you wanted to personalize, meaning that every user gets a specific set of results, what we had to do was take the ranking logic out of this availability engine, get rid of those static scores at the bottom, and then replace it with a service. Then have that service invoke actually a model which is deployed in the model serving platform that we saw earlier.
That's what we wanted to do. There were two problems. The first problem was, if there were 1,000 requests for the availability engine, it meant that the new service is going to get 24,000 requests because it was sitting behind the fanout, behind the shards. Secondly, the availability engine was operating at super low latency, and that also meant that this new service plus the network hop to the model and the model's time all needs to be well within the time of that service. It's basically a high throughput, low latency problem, and we managed to crack it. These are the numbers from 2024. That ranking service that you saw in the previous slide, that green box that was introduced new, is able to solve 100,000 requests per second with a p99.9 latency of 100 milliseconds. The average is way low. It's like 40, 50 milliseconds or so.
I want to share one more thing before I wrap up the evolution story. Experiments at Booking typically run for two to four weeks, but this meant that we couldn't actually train or run models. We were limited in the number of models that we can run every year, because we just had 53 weeks. We wanted to move faster, knowing well that if we actually put in a bad ranking model upfront, it is going to cost all of us, like travelers, partners, and business. What we did was we introduced interleaving. This is how it worked. Typically, for an A/B testing, we actually take the users and split them across two groups, and then we show different search results for them, which was coming from different ranking models. In interleaving, what we did was we didn't show two groups, we didn't split the groups, we just showed the same results for all users.
Those results were coming from merged data, meaning we would train a couple of models, in this case, two models, red and blue. We trained the model, and each of these models gave a list of results. Then we would somehow need to merge it. One simple example could be, take the top one from here, top one from here, merge it. Then keep alternating it. It's just a team draft approach. Then once you have done, you present that to all users across the service. Then you check offline, ok, from which list did the user interact more? Was it from model A or from model B? That gives us the answer. Why it was useful was we could suddenly run more variants. On the right side, it doesn't have to be two. We can even run eight different models that are actually interleaving the results for search. That is, we can run more variants that was like 10 times speed-up than what we are used to with A/B testing.
We could use it with less traffic because interleaving is super sensitive to customer preferences, and we can get signals faster. The way we use it now, interleaving and A/B, is that we train a bunch of models, we pre-select it with interleaving, we pick up a winner, and then we take the winner and then do proper A/B testing. We have optimized both speed, while not losing scientific rigor.
I started the talk by saying that experiment laid the foundation in general for data-driven decision-making. You can see that, still, it continues to underpin what we do every day. With that, that concludes the evolution story.
What's Brewing?
Next, I want to tell you where we are going. These are the five platforms that you saw. What we started doing last year is that we started building the foundations of agentic systems. By agentic systems, think about memories, all kinds of memories, episodic, semantic, procedural, and think about agent serving, like access control for those agents, delegation controls for the users to those agents, agent-to-agent communication. Those are the things we started working on last year. Parallelly, what we are also doing is unifying all these platforms under a single umbrella and then having a single orchestration layer. Why? Because we foresee a possible fragmentation and we wanted to avoid it earlier. Like for cross-domain use cases, we want a single, centralized, unified experience for the customer, and this platform can do that. Secondly, we wanted to centralize all kinds of AI-related governance, security, quality, and all those things. We wanted to centralize that.
See more presentations with transcripts

articles.title: Reson8 releases Rumble-2-Flash speech model as a free open-weights download - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Reson8 releases Rumble-2-Flash speech model as a free open-weights download
Amsterdam-based speech recognition startup Resonate Labs B.V. today released its Rumble-2-Flash transcription model as a free download with open weights.
Designed for fast transcription of prerecorded audio, the 500 million-parameter model supports more than 40 languages. Reson8 is pitching the release at developers and researchers who need speech recognition built for languages other than English.
According to the company, the leading speech models are trained primarily on English, even though only about one in 20 people speak it as a first language. Specialist terms such as medication names are where accuracy is said to fall furthest once speech moves outside English. Reson8’s models are said to be in production use for meeting notetakers, artificial intelligence receptionists, customer support voice agents, medical transcription and captioning.
“Generic speech models are built for English and make noticeably more mistakes in other languages,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Raoul Ritter, who started the company with Thomas Kluiters and Jarno Verhagen. “Languages like Dutch, Swedish and German are spoken by millions, yet they’re an afterthought.”
Reson8 describes Rumble-2-Flash as one of the smallest models on Hugging Face Inc.’s Open ASR Leaderboard. In the company’s own runs of the leaderboard’s multilingual tests, the model averaged a word error rate of 7.09% across seven languages, including German, French and Dutch. Its average error rate in English is claimed to be about 5%.
On a separate test covering 10 lower-resource languages such as Maltese and Basque, Rumble-2-Flash is said to have posted a mean word error rate of 17.6%. OpenAI Group PBC’s Whisper Large V3 had a mean word error rate of 39.82% on the same test, according to Reson8.
Beyond benchmark sets, Reson8’s models are said to be trained for noisy settings, including phone-line audio. The real world “doesn’t happen in a recording studio,” said Kluiters, the company’s head of AI.
Today’s open-weights release follows the model’s Nov. 3 debut in Reson8’s application programming interface, a week before the company launched its flagship Rumble-2 model. Custom vocabulary support, which lets customers add up to 50,000 terms as text without fine-tuning, remains exclusive to Rumble-2.
Hosted on the company’s own graphics processing units in the Netherlands, Reson8’s service is said to retain no audio or transcripts. The company also claims ISO 27001 certification and compliance with the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation and the bloc’s AI Act.
Available free under an Apache 2.0 license, Rumble-2-Flash can also be accessed through Reson8’s API at prices starting from €0.01 ($0.001) per hour of audio.
Reson8 raised €5 million ($5.5 million) in pre-seed funding in March. Balderton Capital led the round, with NP-Hard Ventures also participating. Speech is “quickly becoming a default interface across software,” according to James Wise, a partner at Balderton.

articles.title: Unity is offering $50,000 to indie developers without asking for revenue share or IP ownership
articles.text:
In a nutshell: Unity Technologies has launched a new initiative called Unity Fellowship, offering ten indie game developers up to $50,000 in cash to build games using the Unity engine. The offer comes with no apparent catch, as the company is not asking for recoup, revenue share, creative control or even IP ownership in exchange for the money.
According to an announcement by the company on Reddit, applicants seeking the grant must meet multiple criteria in addition to the obvious Unity engine requirement. First, the game must already have a playable build or demo at the time of application and should be scheduled for release within a year of joining the program, even if only in early access.
All applicants must be at least 18 at the time of submitting their application, but they won't need to own, operate, maintain, or be affiliated with a registered business entity. The post states that the company will actually prioritize unpublished developers, although developers with existing publishers will still be able to apply if they disclose this at the time of application.
Selected teams will be entitled to receive a number of perks in addition to the money. These include a dedicated Unity partner for development guidance and troubleshooting; meetings with experts in development, game design, and promotion; industry connections such as pitch preparation and introductions to publishers; a presence at Unity events; and PR and marketing support when needed.
Clarifying its policy on AI use, Unity said that it doesn't bar developers from using the technology but applicants "must own or hold the rights to everything in your game, including any AI-generated content." Unity's liberal approach to AI use is unsurprising, given that it recently jumped on the AI bandwagon with the launch of the Unity Spark AI tool designed to build games with user-generated prompts.
Developers from around the world can participate in the program as long as they're not living in countries currently under US sanctions, such as Russia, Iran, and Cuba. Unity is also restricting developers based in Brazil, Italy and the Canadian province of Quebec, citing "local regulations." For people outside those areas, submissions will close at 5 pm ET on December 18, 2026.
The program will start in March 2027, and Unity says it will notify all selected applicants by the end of February. Interested developers and indie studios can check out the full terms and conditions, FAQs, and other information on the official Unity Fellowship portal. The application forms are on the same website.
