articles.title: Nvidia created a weird bit of intrigue by not filing a routine SEC report | TechCrunch
articles.text:
During Nvidia’s quarterly call on Tuesday, CFO-turned-interim-CEO Colette Kress dropped this little oddity: She said Nvidia wouldn’t be immediately filing its quarterly results report, known as a 10-Q, with the SEC. “We plan to file our 10-Q in the coming weeks.” And she offered no reason why.
The delay was widely noticed. Among the many comments on X about it, economic and investment analyst Edward Dowd called it a “red flag.” Nvidia has typically filed the 10-Q the same day it reports results.
The 10-Q offers far more detail about a company’s operations than an earnings press release, including sections that disclose “legal proceedings,” which include lawsuits that could affect the company; and “risk factors,” which cover other potentially business-impairing items.
The announcement of the delay was so unusual that UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri asked about it after the public earnings call. Nvidia told him the delay was related to whether the company would need to disclose additional information about its ongoing investigation into Huang in the 10-Q.
“The company announced that the 10-Q will be filed ‘in the coming weeks’ – later than usual. When queried on our callback, management indicated this was related to the ongoing investigation and whether any additional risk factors would need to be added to the filing,” Arcuri wrote in his research note. (Arcuri still rates the stock a “buy” by the way, although he did lower his price target to $220 from $240. The stock is now trading around $150).
Notably, on the same day that Nvidia reported earnings, The Wall Street Journal reported that the SEC is investigating Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors.
So the mystery thickens: What will Nvidia disclose? We’ll have to wait and see. (Nvidia has not yet responded to our request for comment.)
The delay suggests the company may have more to say about its mounting legal troubles. Nvidia is now facing multiple federal investigations over allegations that its partners were selling restricted Nvidia AI chips to China. So far, the scrutiny has come from a number of congressional committees; the Department of Justice looking into Megaspeed, the company run by a woman with whom Huang had an affair and who is also suspected of being a Chinese spy; and now, reportedly, the SEC.
Additionally, Nvidia is conducting its own internal investigation into Huang after he admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang (the Megaspeed executive), and allegations surfaced that he also had affairs with other Nvidia employees.
There’s little doubt that Wall Street will scrutinize that 10-Q once it’s finally filed. The intrigue brings to mind the old saying: “Doctors bury their mistakes. Lawyers put theirs in prison. And accountants hide theirs in the footnotes.”

articles.title: Waymo pulls cars off U.S. highways following California ban
articles.text:
Autonomous driving company Waymo has temporarily pulled all its driverless cars from U.S. freeways following a ban from California.
The California Department of Motor Vehicles ordered the driverless vehicles to stop driving on all of the state’s freeways on Nov. 11, citing what it called an “imminent hazard to public safety.”
In a statement provided to the New York Times, the department cited an incident in which three Waymo vehicles entered a construction closure on Highway 101, and another in which the vehicles tried to get around a police blockade on Interstate 280 in San Francisco.
“Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state,” said Waymo spokesperson Chris Pappas. “In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance.”
The DMV says that the restrictions in California will remain in place until the company makes “effective corrective actions” to fix the problem.
Now, this ban comes just as Waymo cars are starting to hit Toronto streets, with a planned launch for 2028. Hopefully Waymo can improve its highway performance before vehicles hit the busiest highways in North America.
From my perspective, this is not a good look for the self-driving automotive industry. If one of the industry’s leaders is scaling back operations after multiple dangerous incidents, then other companies could have trouble gaining trust with local authorities, the public, and the federal government. However, for now, it is only a temporary ban.

articles.title: ‘People will ask, agents will act’: Workday CEO outlines how AI is coming to help unleash “an incredible world of work”
articles.text:
‘People will ask, agents will act’: Workday CEO outlines how AI is coming to help unleash “an incredible world of work”
Workday wants to get AI doing your heavy lifting
The CEO of Workday has outlined his belief that AI will “augment people, not replace people,” as the technology becomes an ever-more integral part of key business functions.
Speaking at the opening keynote of Workday Rising EMEA, Aneel Bhusri outlined the potential AI can bring to HR and finance teams, automating manual or time-consuming tasks to free workers up for more important work.
“AI is probably the most important technology of our lifetime - it's a massive opportunity,” Bhusri noted. “How do we put Workday AI to work? Agents are going to start handling heavy lifting, chase approvals, connect data...people will ask, agents will act - it's going to be an incredible world of work where we unleash humans to do what humans are really good at - think, be creative, and solve problems."
A new work day for Workday
Bhusri’s view was shared by Gerrit Kazmaier, President, Product & Technology at Workday, who laid out “our vision of how work should be.”
“The question isn't whether we should embrace AI,” Kazmaier noted, “it's how do we harness its power and make it safe, reliable and trusted.”
“Most importantly, AI is not a game of quantity - the winners won't be the ones with the most AI...but the ones who apply it the best.”
“Some of you may think of AI as an efficiency game....(but) if you stop there, you're going to miss out on a real opportunity - real AI transformation is about driving real growth, faster, better, more, new…and unlocking new market opportunities.”
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
We’ve all heard a lot about the potential of AI, but in highly regulated industries such as those Workday exists in, how comfortable will companies be in handing over such vital data?
“HR and finance have zero margins for error,” Bhusri noted, “the work is tough, you handle critical systems, you pay people, you close books, you have to do this securely, reliably, the data is sensitive, highly regulated - there's zero room for error.”
The issue, he said, was that as powerful as AI is, it is often probabilistic, as it tries to anticipate and predict outcomes. However HR and finance IT systems are deterministic, he pointed out, as they are built on rules, controls, and reliable outcomes - and you wouldn’t want to run payrolls on probabilities.
“The future is marrying these two technologies together,” Bhusri declared, with the aim of building deterministic business process platform with governance security, stated outcomes that are 100% accurate paired with AI
“AI is really powerful, but if you don't have the deterministic guardrails...you really can't get value,” he added, noting the distinction between what Workday calls “lawful” and “lawless” data.
“We're grounded in trust," Bhusri concluded, "trust is everything in the world of AI - you have to trust the data, you have to trust the applications - and at the heart, AI should augment people, not replace people - that will be the way of the future.”

articles.title: Voyager 1 spacecraft crosses milestones distance of one-light day from Earth 49 years after launch — now 16.09 billion miles away, signal takes full 24 hours to travel home
articles.text:
Voyager 1 spacecraft crosses milestones distance of one-light day from Earth 49 years after launch — now 16.09 billion miles away, signal takes full 24 hours to travel home
It has been traveling for nearly 50 years to reach this milestone and continues into the unknown.
NASA has confirmed that Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach one light-day's distance from Earth, passing the milestone today. A countdown at Orbital Radar confirmed that Voyager cruised past the threshold at a leisurely 37,844 mph just after 5 am ET on Wednesday, November 18. It means that Voyager is now more than 16 billion miles away, and that a signal from the spacecraft now takes fully 24 hours to travel the distance.
There are many astronomical numbers behind what is an extraordinary feat. Sci-fi shows casually mention light-years as if they are like a trip to the local convenience store. One light-day isn’t a distance to be derided, though. Over the last half century, hurtling through space at a cruising speed of 38,000 mph, the Voyager spacecraft has clocked about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers).
These are probably bigger distances than you are used to fathoming. So NASA has kindly provided some context with the distances of various heavenly bodies in miles and light-speeds. For example, the Moon is 238,855 miles distant, or about 1.3 light seconds away from Earth. Due to Mars’ independent orbit around the Sun, it can take between three minutes and 22 minutes for light to travel between the red and the blue planet. Meanwhile, the Sun’s rays reach Earth, about 93 million miles away, in 20 light seconds. Now let us remind you that Voyager 1 is on the brink of being a whole light-day away.
On Wednesday, with this major milestone passed, Voyager 1’s journey will be far from over. NASA says that it is on course for an obscure star called Gliese 445, now in the constellation Ursa Minor. We’ll have to keep the champagne on ice for another 40,000 years to celebrate the fly-past of that star, though.
Voyager 1 carries a copy of the Golden Record. Like sending a message in a bottle, NASA scientists launched Voyager with the hope that someone, somewhere will eventually read the message. Moreover, the receiving aliens will need to source tech to play the record, which contains sounds, music, and the data needed to reconstruct photos that showcase the diversity of life and culture on our planet.
If an alien got hold of the record on Wednesday and managed to rustle up a gramophone player to listen to it, a message sent to Earth via radio waves would take a full 24 hours to be received.
Space enthusiasts are also invited to participate in a global event “by creating a wave of golden light.” It sounds rather pointless, but enthusiasts are asked to flash the three-letter call sign for NASA's Voyager mission, VGR, into the night sky - Morse Code style - using their phone flashlights. There’s a website you can open to flash your screen appropriately.

articles.title: Las Wachowski quieren recuperar los derechos de 'The Matrix': ¿Problemas para Skydance?
articles.text:
Skydance, el imperio que controla David Ellison, podía sufrir su primer gran bofetón. Según un reporte de Puck, las cineastas Lana y Lily Wachowski pretenden recuperar el control sobre los derechos de la saga The Matrix, una de las propiedades intelectuales icónicas de Warner Bros.
De acuerdo con el citado medio, las Wachowski habrían notificado al estudio que pretenden ejercer su derecho de rescindir el acuerdo de licencia que existe por The Matrix. Si su reclamo funciona, las hermanas podrían recuperar el control sobre la IP a partir de febrero de 2029.
Claro que la historia podría no resolverse con tanta facilidad. Siendo The Matrix una de las franquicias más prolíficas de Warner Bros (a pesar del fiasco de la cuarta película), tiene sentido pensar que la compañía no la soltará con tanta facilidad. A esto hay que sumarle que existe una quinta entrega en marcha de la mano de Drew Goddard, el guionista de Cloverfield, Guerra Mundial Z, The Martian y Proyecto Salvación.
Tanto las Wachowski como Warner Bros tendrían argumentos para tratar de torcer la resolución a favor. Por el lado de la dupla de directoras, pueden esgrimir que escribieron los guiones de The Matrix antes de que el estudio les ofreciera un contrato por múltiples largometrajes, allá por los años noventa.
Por el lado de Skydance, podrían aseverar que The Matrix fue, en realidad, un trabajo por encargo. Si la compañía tiene evidencias para probarlo, la creación de la saga recaería sobre Warner Bros y no sobre las Wachowski. Por ende, la dupla de cineastas no podría reclamar el control sobre la propiedad intelectual.
Las Wachowski aspiran a recuperar el control sobre The Matrix
Si Skydance y las Wachowski no se ponen de acuerdo por el futuro de The Matrix, no se descarta una extensa (y costosa) batalla legal para definirlo. En todo caso, se especula con que el pedido de las directoras no busque quitar la saga del catálogo de Warner Bros, sino forzar a David Ellison a negociar un nuevo acuerdo para licenciar la IP bajo condiciones económicas más suculentas.
Sea como sea, el reclamo de las Wachowski podría complicar el desarrollo de The Matrix 5. La nueva película tiene a Goddard como guionista y director, pero su idea es tener la bendición de las responsables de las entregas previas para seguir adelante. En septiembre pasado, Lily Wachowski reconoció que no quería volver a involucrarse en la saga: "Warner Bros quiere hacer otra. Siempre van a querer hacer otra. En lo personal, ya no quiero seguir con eso. Ya tuve suficiente".
Recordemos que The Matrix Resurrections, la cuarta película de la franquicia que debutó en 2021, fue dirigida por Lana Wachowski en solitario. La cinta fue apaleada por la crítica y los fanáticos, y protagonizó una batalla legal entre Warner Bros y Village Roadshow por su estreno en simultáneo en cines y HBO Max.
Con este panorama, la concreción de The Matrix 5 es incierta. Tampoco se sabe qué idea tendrían las Wachowski si obtuviesen el control sobre la franquicia que las lanzó al estrellato mundial.

articles.title: Las asociaciones de guardias civiles de Tráfico denuncian que les proponen cobrar más por poner multas que por hacer controles
articles.text:
Los guardias civiles creen que la DGT les quiere premiar por multar. Simple y llanamente. Es, al menos, lo que aseguran después de haber asistido a una reunión del grupo de trabajo en el que se estudian las propuestas para la nueva normativa sobre productividad y, por tanto, el extra a cobrar a final de año.
¿Qué ha pasado? Señalan nuestros compañeros de Motorpasión Moto que la Agrupación Unificada de Guardias Civiles (AUGC) rechaza lo propuesto en el nuevo borrador de productividad que se está debatiendo para la Agrupación de Tráfico. El motivo es que, según su criterio, la DGT les premiaría por multar y no tanto por vigilar las carreteras.
A preguntas de Xataka, la Asociación Española de Guardias Civiles (AEGC) tiene el mismo sentir. Señalan que con la nueva propuesta se prioriza el número de personas controladas por un radar y no tanto por la vigilancia preventiva en las carreteras pese a que el exceso de velocidad no es el primer problema en los accidentes de nuestro país.
"La bufanda". Nos explica la AEGC que a final de año, la Agrupación de Tráfico recibe un extra de dinero por productividad. Es lo que se llama "la bufanda", como coloquialmente se refieren a este añadido a la nómina. Ese dinero se reparte en función de los objetivos de productividad conseguidos.
Lo que denuncia AUGC en un comunicado es que el nuevo borrador premia las sanciones y la vigilancia con radares pero no tanto el control por seguridad preventiva en la carretera. Aseguran que con los cambios propuestos en la última Instrucción de la Jefatura de la Agrupación de Tráfico de la Guardia Civil a este respecto, el peso de las denuncias aumenta en un 35 % y el de la prevención se reduce en un 38 %.
¿Por qué? Para entender cómo se consigue "la bufanda", hay que entender cómo funciona. El complemento de productividad se consigue en función a si se han conseguido diversos objetivos que tienen diferente peso en el dinero final que se recibe. Así, las sanciones por denunciar elementos de seguridad que no se llevan puestos correctamente o infracciones generales de seguridad vial tienen menos peso que el de los controlados por radar o en en controles de drogas y alcohol.
Y es que ese complemento no se entrega sólo por el volumen de vehículos "pillados" por exceso de velocidad, se prioriza el número de coches vigilados. Esto quiere decir que las unidades de Tráfico que vigilan nuestras carreteras tienen más alicientes para poner un radar móvil en un punto estático de una carretera muy concurrida que por otra por donde pasen menos coches aunque sea menos peligrosa. O que realicen menos kilómetros de vigilancia en coche o moto por las carreteras.
¿Qué se propone? Desde la AUGC consideran que se debería eliminar el complemento por controlados por un radar o en un control de alcoholemia y/o drogas. Y es que, con el nuevo borrador, los resultados negativos en uno de estos últimos controles no suma pero el positivo puede contar doble si además de la infracción el conductor está cometiendo un delito.
Aseguran, por tanto, que el peso de la vigilancia por prevención se reduce de 73 a 45 puntos sobre el máximo de productividad que se puede conseguir mientras que el de delitos crece de 128 a 173 puntos sobre los 413 puntos como máximo que se pueden conseguir sumando todas las variables.
En un comunicado de la AEGC al que Xataka ha tenido acceso, esta agrupación también propone que se mantengan las puntuaciones en los controles de droga que han dado negativo porque se considera que es un ejercicio de prevención en carretera. Pero, en este caso, abogan por mantener el criterio de controlados por radar tal y como está, no de suprimirlo.
La vigilancia. Es el punto clave, ambas asociaciones lo defienden aunque creen que se debería atender de diferente manera. AUGC propone, como decimos, eliminar los controlados por radas y AEGC lo mantendría (aunque no aumentaría su peso). Sin embargo, ambas tienen claro que hay que hacer más vigilancia en la carretera.
"No puedes dedicar el 80% del servicio a los excesos de velocidad cuando hay otros problemas tan graves como el teléfono móvil", nos señala Fernando García, de AEGC. Y es que las distracciones son el principal causante de los accidentes de tráfico en España.
García asegura que buena parte de esa vigilancia se debería hacer con más kilómetros en carretera patrullando, algo que va bajando porque, como él mismo nos ha asegurado a Xataka en otras ocasiones, no está lo suficientemente valorado en la nómina, especialmente los kilómetros en moto que son más peligrosos.

articles.title: Zink-Luft-Akku statt Lithium: Warum ausgerechnet Vitamin B12 ein altes Ladeproblem löst
articles.text:
Vitamin B12 im Stromspeicher: Forscher:innen machen Zink-Luft-Batterien wiederaufladbar
Ein Team aus Forscher:innen der spanischen Universität Córdoba hat einen wiederaufladbaren Zink-Luft-Akku entwickelt, der mithilfe von Vitamin B12 arbeitet. Wie in einer im britischen Fachmagazin „Journal of Materials Chemistry A“ veröffentlichten Studie zu lesen ist, überstand der Prototyp im Labor bis zu 250 Lade- und Entladezyklen.
Entgegen manchen Schlagzeilen liefert der auch als Cobalamin bekannte Nährstoff dabei nicht selbst die Energie, sondern wirkt an der Luftelektrode als Katalysator, der die chemischen Prozesse beschleunigt. „Vitamin B12 hat bewiesen, dass es die notwendigen Voraussetzungen erfüllt, um als guter Katalysator zu fungieren: Beim Entladen katalysiert es die Reduktion von Sauerstoff zu Wasser, und beim Wiederaufladen fördert es die Bildung von Sauerstoff“, erklärt der beteiligte Studienleiter Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero, wie Scitechdaily unter Berufung auf die Hochschule berichtet.
Warum Zink-Luft-Batterien bisher meist Einwegprodukte sind
Zink-Luft-Batterien erzeugen elektrischen Strom, indem metallisches Zink im Inneren mit Sauerstoff reagiert, der direkt aus der Umgebungsluft in die Zelle strömt. Weil dieser Sauerstoff nicht im Gehäuse gespeichert werden muss, sind solche Batterien deutlich leichter als herkömmliche Akkus und erreichen rechnerisch eine Energiedichte von 1.218 Wattstunden pro Kilogramm.
Zudem ist Zink reichlich verfügbar, lässt sich recyceln und kommt in der Zelle mit einer Batterieflüssigkeit auf Wasserbasis aus, die weder brennen noch explodieren kann. Im Alltag stecken Zink-Luft-Zellen bisher trotzdem überwiegend als Einweg-Knopfzellen in Hörgeräten, weil sich der chemische Prozess beim Aufladen ohne passende Hilfsstoffe nur sehr träge umkehren lässt.
Die Arbeitsgruppe an der Universität Córdoba hatte für diese Aufgabe in früheren Versuchen bereits natürliche Stoffe wie den roten Blutfarbstoff Hämoglobin und das Enzym Katalase getestet, konnte diese Batterien wegen des darin enthaltenen Eisens jedoch nicht wieder aufladen. Vitamin B12 besitzt in seiner Mitte hingegen ein Kobalt-Atom, das die Reaktion in beide Richtungen antreibt, also sowohl die Aufnahme von Sauerstoff beim Entladen als auch dessen Freisetzung beim Aufladen.
Kohlenstoffnanoröhrchen verhindern das Auflösen von Vitamin B12
Bei der Konstruktion der Elektrode mussten die Wissenschaftler:innen zunächst ein praktisches Problem lösen, denn Vitamin B12 löst sich leicht in Wasser auf und würde in der Batterieflüssigkeit nach kurzer Zeit weggespült. Um den Nährstoff dauerhaft an seinem Platz zu halten, heftete das Team die Vitaminmoleküle an mikroskopisch dünne Röhrchen aus Kohlenstoff.
Diese Kohlenstoffnanoröhrchen leiten nicht nur den elektrischen Strom, sondern gehen mit dem Vitamin eine feste chemische Verbindung nach demselben Prinzip ein, das in der Natur auch die Bausteine von Proteinen zusammenhält. Während herkömmliche Kobalt-Katalysatoren bei der Herstellung oft auf 700 bis 1.000 Grad Celsius erhitzt werden müssen, läuft diese Verknüpfung bei Raumtemperatur ab, bevor das Material bei 40 Grad Celsius trocknet.
In der Lauge im Inneren der Batterie klappt das gebundene Vitaminmolekül teilweise auf, sodass der einströmende Luftsauerstoff direkt an das Kobalt-Atom im Zentrum gelangt. Dadurch funktioniert der Ladungsaustausch ohne störende Zwischenschritte, bei denen in früheren Versuchen mit nur lose aufgetragenem Vitamin B12 noch unerwünschte Nebenprodukte die Reaktion bremsten.
Leistung im Labor und die Schattenseiten der Zink-Luft-Technik
„Wir haben uns die Eigenschaften angesehen, die wir in natürlich vorkommenden Materialien finden können, um sie in neuen Batterien einzusetzen“, sagt der Mitautor Manuel Cano Luna zur Motivation hinter dem Experiment. Im Labortest hielt die rund einen Quadratzentimeter große Testzelle mit einem leitfähigen Gel im Inneren bis zu 250 Ladezyklen durch, während eine baugleiche Zelle ohne Vitamin B12 schon beim zweiten Aufladen ausfiel.
Trotz dieser Ausdauer zeigen die Messdaten der Studie, dass bis zu einem alltagstauglichen Stromspeicher noch deutliche Hürden bestehen. Die von den Forscher:innen berechnete Kapazität von 199,4 Amperestunden pro Gramm bezieht sich nämlich allein auf die hauchdünne Vitaminschicht und schrumpft auf 4,13 Amperestunden pro Gramm, sobald das Gewicht der gesamten Elektrode mitgezählt wird.
Hinzu kommt, dass auch ein biologischer Stoff wie Vitamin B12 im Kern nicht ohne das Schwermetall Kobalt auskommt, wenngleich hier nur kleinste Mengen nötig sind. Nach rund 250 Ladezyklen verliert der Akku zudem an Leistung, weil gelöste Zinkteilchen vom Gegenpol und Salze aus der Batterieflüssigkeit eine Kruste über dem Vitamin bilden und die Luftzufuhr verstopfen.

articles.title: Inside Helium Health’s difficult year
articles.text:
On November 4, employees at Helium Health, a Lagos-based healthtech startup, received an email from its People & Culture team thanking them for staying with the company through what the company described as “challenging moments.”
That same day, a picture of Dimeji Sofowora, its current CEO, standing beside Babajide Sanwo-Olu, the governor of Lagos State, and Olumide Balogun, Google’s director for West and East Africa, was published as they announced a ₦3.4 billion ($2.5 million) grant from Google.org, tech giant Google’s philanthropic arm. The funding will finance artificial intelligence tools that flag pregnancy risks and improve maternal care in four Nigerian states.
While Sofowora said the timing of both events was “coincidental,” together they signal a return to normalcy for the startup after a turbulent year marked by a leadership change and months of unpaid staff salaries.
“There were delays to salary payments during a period of the year,” he told TechCabal in an emailed response on Friday.
In the email sent to employees, the startup described the delays as “a difficult experience.”
“The November 4 communication was an internal email from our People & Culture team intended to recognise and thank employees for their commitment and to confirm that outstanding allowances had been settled,” Sofowora said.
For nearly a decade, Helium Health worked to digitise the operations of African hospitals. It raised at least $40 million, said it had worked with over 1,000 healthcare facilities, and lent money to hospitals.
Sofowora, who took over as chief executive in August, said the salary delays came from “temporary cash-flow timing” and that the company kept staff informed. Helium Health declined to disclose the number of affected employees or confirm how long the delays lasted. Former employees say they were owed salaries for at least six months.
Nigeria’s difficult healthtech sector
Helium Health’s troubles show the difficulties of running a healthtech startup in Nigeria’s healthtech sector, which saw 40 startups become inactive between 2020 and 2025. Founders and investors point to infrastructure challenges, the difficulty of making money servicing hospitals, and a funding slowdown as reasons why many early healthtech startups struggle to survive.
Spurred by sudden demand for digital health services after COVID-19, funding into Nigerian healthtech startups grew from about $5.5 million in 2019 to nearly $55 million in 2023, and Helium Health’s $30 million Series B round that June was more than half of 2023’s total. Healthtech funding later fell to about $18 million in 2024 and about $3 million in 2025. Helium Health has not announced an equity round since.
Helium Health pitched that round mainly as fuel for HeliumCredit, its lending arm for hospitals, clinics and pharmacies. These healthcare providers were already under pressure from inflation, which drove up the cost of running a hospital sharply in 2023.
After the 2023 currency float, health inflation rose from 20.5% in May 2023 to 24.1% a year later, according to an analysis of the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) data, and four listed drug makers saw their cost of sales rise 88% between early 2024 and early 2025.
In 2024, the Health Care Providers Association of Nigeria said about one in five small and medium private hospitals had shut down because of operating costs. By 2024, half of all private hospitals had shut down, according to Dr Raymond Kuti, the former president of The Guild of Medical Directors, while existing ones struggled to survive due to operating costs.
Despite this contraction in Nigeria’s health care industry, HeliumCredit’s lending period grew longer, from three to six months in 2020 to 12 to 24 months by 2023, so cash came back more slowly. The currency float also added another layer.
Since its 2023 Series B round, the naira has lost about two-thirds of its value against the dollar. Every naira loan the company facilitated and recovered is worth far fewer dollars than it was when it last raised money. Sofowora did not answer questions about who funds its loans, what Helium Health earns from them, or how they have performed.
“In cases where healthcare facilities default on the payment of loans, we will offer a full cycle of monitoring of the facility and provide support to them, whether it is capacity development through education or financial training,” Olubusi, the former CEO, told TechCabal in 2023.
How Helium Health got here
Founded in 2016 by Adegoke Olubusi, Tito Ovia, and Sofowora, Helium Health launched with an electronic medical records (EMR) system to replace paper records in hospitals. That EMR ended up as the base of everything that followed; the hospital data it collected became the credit-scoring engine for its loan products in 2020.
When Helium Health raised its $10 million Series A in May 2020, it planned to expand beyond digitising hospital records and start lending to healthcare businesses in Nigeria and across Africa. Adegoke Olubusi, then CEO, told TechCabal a week after the round that hospitals struggled to grow because few were run as proper businesses, and most had never raised outside funding.
Helium Credit was meant to fix that with zero-collateral loans, and its 2023 $30 million round used the lending business as the main draw for investors in the second-largest Series B for an African healthtech company.
By 2023, HeliumCredit’s loan book had grown from $250,000 to more than $3.5 million, spread across over 200 Nigerian health facilities. It lent on behalf of financing partners, including banks. In 2023, the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), the American government’s development lender, disclosed a $10 million loan to Helium Health to fund new loans to healthcare businesses at a $46,000 average each.
The following year, as inflation rose and hospitals closed, the customers Helium Health earned from through software and lending were squeezed. That likely shaped the startup’s new direction as it focused more on consumer-facing tools, especially in maternal healthcare, and as more of its funding came from donors like Google.
Delayed salaries, leadership change
From January, Helium Health owed salaries, at least seven months before Olubusi stepped down, one employee said.
Three current and former employees told TechCabal that Helium Health owed them salaries, in some cases for six months. One former employee, who asked not to be named to avoid retaliation, said in June they were owed more than ₦2 million ($1,470).
“At this point, I’m unsure if or when I’ll receive the outstanding amount, as my follow-up emails are no longer being responded to,” they said in August.
“Former employees whose final entitlements were still being processed when we responded in August have since completed their exit processes, as well as received those entitlement payments,” Sofowora told TechCabal.
In August 2026, Olubusi stepped down as chief executive after nearly a decade, leaving Sofowora as the only co-founder still running the company.
“A decade of belief, courage, sacrifice, and turning a simple conviction into reality; healthcare in Africa could work better, and technology would play a meaningful role in making that happen,” Olubusi wrote in a public farewell message.
Sofowora declined to discuss the reasons for his exit, calling them “private personnel matters.” He said the transition “is being managed in an orderly manner and does not change the company’s core strategic priorities.”
For the four states rolling out Helium Health’s maternal health tools with Google, Helium Health’s finances now matter as much as its technology. For now, Helium Health says its business remains on track. The company continues to operate across its markets and business lines and says Olubusi’s departure has not disrupted its daily operations or changed its strategic priorities.
“We remain focused on expanding our healthcare technology business,” Sofowora said.

articles.title: Beyond Pass/Fail: Characterizing Silicon Margin With PVTW
articles.text:
Determining not only whether a device meets specification, but how far it is from the boundary, helps inform product robustness and future design decisions.
Production test is necessarily built around decisions. PASS. FAIL. Bin 1. Bin 2. Ship. Do not ship. Characterization has a different objective. It asks not only whether the device meets specification, but how far it is from the boundary.
That distinction becomes increasingly important as processors integrate compute, memory, high speed interfaces, multiple power domains and advanced packaging into increasingly complex systems.
Suppose five devices all pass the product specification, but under the same controlled workload their minimum stable operating voltages are:
0.70 V | 0.71 V | 0.73 V | 0.76 V | 0.79 V
Production test sees five passing devices. Characterization sees five different levels of margin. That changes the engineering question from “Why did this device fail?” to something potentially much more useful:
What is consuming product margin?
PVTW (process, voltage, temperature, workload) gives us a framework for exploring that question.
Take the same device and establish its voltage and frequency boundary using conventional ATE content. Then establish another boundary while running a deterministic compute workload. Repeat with SRAM, memory, PCIe and combined workloads. We may discover that the boundaries are different.
That difference can tell us which workload is exposing the limiting condition and where deeper characterization should begin.
Rather than testing at one nominal operating point, deliberately approach the boundary. Sweep voltage at fixed frequency, temperature and workload. Sweep frequency while the other conditions remain fixed. Repeat across temperature. Then manipulate individual power domains.
A compute workload may be characterized while the core rail is swept and memory and I/O rails remain fixed. A memory-intensive workload can be characterized while a memory-related rail is swept. PCIe traffic can be maintained while relevant electrical and thermal conditions are changed.
Now we are not simply determining whether a subsystem functions. We are measuring how much margin it has under a defined workload.
Population analysis makes this more powerful. Take known good devices and devices showing reduced SLT margin. Characterize both populations under identical PVTW conditions. Instead of asking only which devices fail, compare the shapes of their operating envelopes.
Does the marginal population show a consistent voltage shift? Does the difference emerge only at high temperature? Does it appear only under simultaneous compute and memory activity? Is there a particular rail or frequency transition where the two populations separate?
The shape of the margin distribution can provide clues to the physical mechanism.
Suppose a particular system workload requires 45 minutes before marginal devices begin generating errors. That is useful for learning, but expensive as a production screen.
PVTW characterization can help determine why that workload exposes the problem. Once the mechanism is better understood, the ATE capability can search for a shorter electrical, structural or functional signature correlated with the same marginality.
Perhaps a voltage and frequency corner exposes it in seconds. Perhaps a targeted functional pattern reproduces the condition. Perhaps a particular power rail response or interface measurement predicts it.
If the correlation is strong enough, the shorter test can potentially move into Final Test or even Wafer Sort. The learning flow becomes:
SLT discovers → PVTW characterizes → ATE correlates → Production test screens
The goal of deeper SLT characterization is therefore not necessarily more SLT. In some cases, its greatest value may be teaching us how to screen the risk earlier and faster.
This is why I believe we should preserve margin data rather than reducing everything immediately to PASS and FAIL. Minimum operating voltage, maximum stable frequency, thermal margin, interface margin, power margin and workload margin can all become continuous characterization parameters. Those measurements can be compared across device populations, process corners, assembly conditions and eventually manufacturing history.
A device with 100 mV of margin and a device with 10 mV of margin may both satisfy the production specification today. But they may tell us very different things about process variation, product robustness and future design decisions. Characterizing those differences can help answer a more fundamental question:
Where is the product operating boundary, and what moves it?
That question does not end at the silicon. The package surrounding the silicon has its own manufacturing history, materials and process variation.
In Part 3, I will explore how 2D ID and unit level traceability could connect PVTW margin all the way back to wafer X,Y and substrate panel X,Y.

articles.title: Odaia raises $15-million Series C round, inks deal with US health agency | BetaKit
articles.text:
Predictive AI firm Odaia has closed a $15-million USD ($21-million CAD) Series C funding round that includes a commercial agreement with a US health media agency.
The news: Odaia announced the funding on Wednesday, saying financing was led by multinational firm Monograph Capital and anchored by an investment and agreement from Publicis Health Media (PHM). The Series C round included participation from returning investors from Odaia’s Series A and B financing rounds, including BDC Capital, Flint Capital, Innospark Ventures, Graphite Ventures, Threshold Ventures, and Wittington Ventures.
From the source: “This round lets us go deeper with the enterprise customers we already serve, and, with PHM, bring that infrastructure to more of the industry, faster,” Odaia CEO and co-founder Philip Poulidis said in a press release.
The context: Odaia’s platform utilizes AI to provide predictive commercial intelligence for the pharmaceutical and life sciences industries. Founded in 2018, the company’s platform compiles data from across information streams and can help marketing and sales teams better advertise their products by identifying physicians whose patients are likely to need a therapy, automating healthcare provider engagement by determining which physicians a team should prioritize and with what messaging.
Under Odaia’s commercial agreement with PHM, PHM will become Odaia’s exclusive agency partner in the US. Meanwhile, PHM has announced plans to integrate Odaia’s platform into the health, pharma, biotech, and wellness companies it partners with.
Final thought: As AI has accelerated both drug development and clinical trial processes, one area has remained sluggish: commercialization. The process of getting therapeutics, drugs, and other treatments into the market has been historically time-consuming, relying on lengthy data analyses by consulting firms. Odaia is applying the same principles used to speed up treatment options to speed up accessibility.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.

articles.title: How Nigerian startup PeoplePulse is helping SMEs digitise HR with AI - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian startup PeoplePulse has developed an affordable, AI-powered workforce management platform designed to help African small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) manage their people and automate routine HR processes.
Founded in June 2025, PeoplePulse grew out of HR and business consultancy Bridgemead Consulting, which has worked with SMEs on recruitment, HR outsourcing, employee management and training.
The platform brings employee records, onboarding, leave and attendance management, payroll support, performance management, workforce analytics and compliance into one place.
“Many growing African businesses still manage their HR operations using spreadsheets, WhatsApp, paper records and disconnected tools. At the other end of the market, enterprise HR platforms can be too expensive or complicated for smaller organisations,” Adetola Abolarinwa, co-founder and chief product officer, told Disrupt Africa. “PeoplePulse is designed to bridge that gap: it is accessible enough for an SME but robust enough to support a growing workforce.”
The startup, which has an 11-strong team, competes with the likes of SeamlessHR and BambooHR, but believes its combination of affordability, simplicity, localisation and AI-powered automation sets it apart.
“We did not begin by making assumptions about what SMEs needed; we had already spent years working directly with them and understanding their operational problems,” Abolarinwa said.
Funded by its founders and a friends-and-family round, PeoplePulse piloted its platform with around 280 employees across eight companies between May and July 2026, with all eight converting into paying customers. It was also selected as one of the top 11 finalists for Cycle 7 of the Women in Tech Accelerator Nigeria.
The startup charges between NGN2,000 (US$1.5) and NGN3,500 (US$2.5) per employee per month across three subscription tiers.
“Our focus is not simply on acquiring registrations. We are concentrating on successful onboarding, active usage, retention and expanding adoption within each customer organisation,” Abolarinwa said.
PeoplePulse is focused on building a strong customer base in Nigeria, with Bridgemead’s network of more than 80 businesses providing a warm pipeline, before expanding into other African markets.
“We see PeoplePulse as a pan-African opportunity, but we intend to build a strong foundation in Nigeria before expanding aggressively,” said Abolarinwa.

articles.title: Loblaw is the first Canadian retailer to connect to Muse
articles.text:
Loblaw has become the first Canadian retailer to partner with Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent.
With this functionality, Canadians can have Muse plan meals and order food accordingly from participating Loblaw brands. Meta says Muse is smart enough to remember details like brand preferences and food allergies to make the process smoother.
This comes alongside the recent launch of Muse voice support in Canada, allowing you to have real-time conversations with the agent on mobile, web and Mac.
Personally, I would never have an AI handle shopping for me, especially as Canadian banks like CIBC, RBC and TD block AI agents amid concerns related to unauthorized purchases. Not to mention that Muse itself has had some serious security issues, including most recently accessing people’s encrypted messages. But hey, knock yourself out.
In general, Muse is billed as your sort of personal virtual butler, integrating with apps like Gmail and Google Calendar to handle tasks like scheduling, trip planning, filling out online forms and, yes, making purchases for you.

articles.title: The quantum computing race is becoming a deployment race
articles.text:
The quantum computing race is becoming a deployment race
The conversation is moving from theoretical potential toward practical application
For the past decade, success in quantum computing has been measured through research breakthroughs, investment, and technical milestones. This is beginning to change. Across industries, organizations are focusing on viable quantum solutions, shifting the conversation from theoretical potential towards practical application.
This acceleration presents a strategic challenge for governments. As commercial markets increasingly focus on real-world use cases, there is a risk that governments’ ability to adopt quantum technologies will fail to keep pace. Businesses can experiment with emerging technologies in quick iterations, but governments must navigate long procurement cycles and stringent internet security requirements.
This challenge is compounded by the need for governments to identify priority use cases and communicate them to the commercial market at an appropriate level of sensitivity. Without sufficient visibility into these requirements, systems may be developed in ways that do not align with, or are not appropriate for, government use cases.
Executive Vice President, Capabilities at IQT.
Keeping pace is also made harder by the fact that quantum technologies can’t be developed in isolation. Progress relies on international supply chains, access to specialist infrastructure and facilities, and a highly skilled workforce capable of developing and deploying these technologies.
As quantum’s breakthrough moment approaches, competitive advantage will depend not simply on who develops or invests in the technology first, but on who has the capabilities in place to operationalize it and make it useful.
Quantum in action
Financial services is one industry already experimenting with how quantum computing could be incorporated into its technology stacks. For example, NatWest joined Digital Catapult’s Quantum Technology Access Programme to explore quantum computing for fraud detection, with the aim to move beyond concept to practical application.
The same can be said of the cybersecurity industry. The prospect of Q-day, a hypothetical future moment when quantum computers become powerful enough to break standard public-key encryption, is influencing strategies. Likewise, the arrival of post-quantum cryptography means organizations can begin protecting information against future quantum attacks before powerful quantum computers exist.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Microsoft is accelerating its quantum-safe security roadmap to replace encryption standards vulnerable to future quantum computers. Progress like this will be critical to ensuring the US and other nations are not left exposed if Q-day arrives, with governments playing an important role in setting standards and supporting the widespread implementation of quantum-safe security across critical systems.
The defense sector is also putting quantum technologies into practice. Quantum sensing solutions, which provide highly precise positioning, navigation, and timing when satellite navigation is denied or jammed, have moved to testing and early deployment stages. Examples include atomic clocks, magnetometers, and quantum inertial sensors.
Taken together, these developments demonstrate an important shift, where technologies that have spent years in research and development are now moving towards testing and early deployment.
Closing the government deployment gap
But unlike commercial organizations, public-sector adoption must navigate procurement, security, regulation, and integration with existing systems. The risk is that commercial capabilities develop faster than governments build the institutional capacity to absorb them. By the time a technology is mature enough to deploy at scale, beginning the preparedness process will already be too late. And right now, the timeline to get prepared is only a couple of years.
Earlier this year, the UK government announced £2 billion to establish the UK as a world leader in quantum, including programs to accelerate the development, manufacturing, and procurement of quantum computers. The challenge now is ensuring that funding translates into operational readiness, which is a distinction every government, not just the UK, will need to manage. As quantum computing matures and increasingly works alongside traditional systems, governments can’t afford to wait until commercially viable capabilities materialize before asking where they might be useful.
This also matters beyond the public sector. Governments act as both investors and early customers. By identifying priority use cases and, where appropriate, communicating those requirements to industry, governments can give companies greater clarity on the capabilities they will need. Procurement and testing can then help companies validate those solutions against real-world challenges and accelerate adoption. In a nascent industry like quantum, speed matters. Companies that scale early can gain an outsized role in shaping technical standards, informing regulatory frameworks, and influencing how the wider market develops.
Governments need to anticipate national security implications and opportunities, identify which applications matter most, provide training for their workforce, and create mechanisms to bring commercially developed technology into government quickly. They must also guide responsible development and adoption by establishing safeguards and governance frameworks.
The quantum race is an ecosystem race
Beyond preparedness, quantum is a global technology, increasingly dictated by physical resources, supply chains, and human talent. Governments must also be building resilient supply chains into their quantum strategies, while businesses need to understand how policy decisions could shape the technologies, suppliers and skills available to them.
In the UK, 85% of quantum companies import elements of their supply chain. At the same time, quantum supply chains are at risk due to heavy reliance on sole suppliers for key components, such as cryogenic refrigerators. These dependences create potential points of vulnerability. A country may possess world-leading quantum research but be constrained by physical resources and materials.
Addressing this will require investment in critical areas such as cryogenics and lasers. Governments can help create clearer demand by supporting testing, procurement, and adoption. As the market scales and technology requirements become clearer, manufacturers will have greater incentive to invest in the capacity needed to build more resilient supply chains.
Then there is talent. The UK Quantum Skills Taskforce has highlighted that the UK is at a “pivot point”, emphasizing that having the skills to develop and adopt quantum technologies will be critical to future growth. Developing the technology requires deep scientific expertise but deploying it requires a much broader workforce capable of engineering systems, developing software, and integrating quantum into existing organizations.
With specialist talent limited and in high demand, countries must consider how they can attract and retain these skills. Universities are critical to this pipeline, but governments and industry must ensure that expertise can move beyond academia and into deployment.
Preparing for the deployment race
Ultimately governments and businesses are not just competing for the next quantum breakthrough, but to build the ecosystem around it. For businesses, this means identifying potential applications and building the skills and infrastructure needed for adoption.
Governments, meanwhile, must strengthen supply chains, invest in talent, and create pathways that help emerging technologies move towards commercial deployment.
The quantum race is becoming a deployment race. Leaders in the industry will increasingly belong not simply to those that make the breakthroughs, but to those prepared to turn them into capability when the moment arrives.

articles.title: Guerre spatiale : face à l’urgence, l’OTAN se tourne vers les fusées commerciales
articles.text:
L’Organisation du Traité de l’Atlantique Nord (OTAN) veut réserver des places sur des fusées commerciales pour envoyer ses satellites militaires en orbite. Un virage clair, qui montre à quel point l’espace est devenu un enjeu crucial.
Un incident survenu récemment a prouvé à quel point les satellites sont vulnérables, alors que l’engin russe Kosmos 2612 s’est dangereusement rapproché d’un dispositif occidental. Le besoin de sécuriser les satellites est désormais primordial, à tel point que le Royaume-Uni a commandé un essaim de « gardes du corps » pour protéger ses systèmes en orbite. C’est maintenant au tour de l’OTAN d’entrer en scène.
Des satellites exposés
Ce 17 novembre, lors de la conférence NATO EDGE 26 d’Izmir en Turquie, l’instance a dévoilé deux initiatives : Starlift et la Global Data Marketplace. Leur point commun : s’appuyer davantage sur les entreprises privées pour accéder à l’espace, qui est considéré comme l’un de ses domaines opérationnels depuis 2019, indique Bloomberg.
Car l’Alliance possède de nombreux satellites assurant les communications, la navigation, le renseignement et la défense antimissile. Or, ces derniers sont exposés au brouillage de leurs signaux et aux cyberattaques. Dans ce contexte, la plateforme Starlift doit regrouper les besoins militaires des pays participants et leur réserver des places sur des fusées commerciales, à la manière d’un courtier. Elle est financée par 11 pays, à savoir la Corée du Sud, la Belgique, le Canada, la Finlande, l’Allemagne, l’Italie, les Pays-Bas, la Norvège, la Suède, la Turquie et le Royaume-Uni.
Objectif : s’entraîner aux lancements en urgence, au cas où une crise obligerait à remplacer un satellite du jour au lendemain, en s’appuyant sur les spatioports des États membres de l’Alliance et de la Corée du Sud.
Ne plus dépendre d’un seul lanceur
Car jusqu’ici, l’OTAN traitait les spatioports comme des laboratoires civils ou des aéroports commerciaux, mais ils doivent aujourd’hui être considérés comme des infrastructures stratégiques. Concrètement, un site de lancement devient aujourd'hui une cible potentielle, au même titre qu’une base aérienne : il faut donc le protéger et prévoir des solutions de repli.
C’est aussi pour cela que l’Alliance privilégie des sites répartis dans plusieurs pays, ainsi que la possibilité d’avoir recours à des fournisseurs divers. Plus on dispose d’accès à l’orbite, moins on risque de se retrouver bloqué.
En parallèle, la Global Data Marketplace, en collaboration avec l’US Space Force, permettra aux membres d’acheter des données et des services spatiaux auprès d’entreprises commerciales. Plus de 200 sociétés y sont déjà référencées, et les premières commandes sont attendues d’ici la fin de l’année.
Pour rappel, une attaque depuis, vers ou dans l’espace pourrait déclencher l’article 5, la clause qui considère l’agression d’un membre comme une agression contre tous.

articles.title: „Das geht auf meine Kappe“: KI-Agent bestellt 72 Eier ohne Grund
articles.text:
72 Eier und gelöschte Mails: Wenn KI-Agenten eigenmächtig handeln
KI-Agenten sollen den Alltag erleichtern. Dafür können sie selbstständig Entscheidungen treffen und Aktionen ausführen. Oft sind sie allerdings noch nicht in der Lage, das gewünschte Ziel zufriedenstellend zu erreichen. Von einem solchen Fall hat Matt Smith kürzlich in einem Beitrag auf X berichtet: Er wollte, dass sein KI-Agent seinen Wocheneinkauf erledigt – und dieser orderte 72 Eier zu ihm nach Hause.
„Ich habe keine gute Antwort“: KI-Agent findet keinen Grund für 72 Eier
Smith ist als Analyst und Partner bei Rebellionaire tätig. Er sagt, der auf X geschilderte Fall sei das erste Mal, dass er die Halluzination eines großen Sprachmodells selbst erlebt habe. Im selben Beitrag fragt er nach Rezepten, mit denen er mehrere Dutzend Eier verbrauchen könnte. Er hat das Missgeschick seines KI-Agenten also mit Humor genommen. Interessant ist allerdings, wie dieser auf sein Fehlverhalten reagiert hat. Anstatt eine haushaltsübliche Menge zu wählen, bestellte er vier Packungen mit je 18 Eiern. „Ich habe keine gute Antwort darauf“, heißt es in dem Screenshot, den Smith geteilt hat. Er hatte den Agenten zuvor um eine Erklärung gebeten. „Ich kann keine Notiz finden, die erklärt, warum ich vier ausgewählt habe.“
Die KI suchte daraufhin nach möglichen Erklärungen. Sie vermutete, dass sie die Zeile für Eier auf einem Foto der von Smith bereitgestellten Liste falsch gelesen habe. Allerdings gab es hier gar keine Zeile für Eier. „Dann habe ich sie ohne Grund hinzugefügt, und das geht auf meine Kappe“, so der KI-Agent laut dem Screenshot entschuldigend. Der Fall verdeutlicht, wie fehleranfällig die Technologie noch immer ist – und dass sie selbst nicht immer genau erklären kann, warum sie tut, was sie tut. Trotzdem ermutigen KI-Anbieter die Nutzer:innen dazu, ihren Modellen Zugriff auf sensible Informationen zu geben, einschließlich des Zugriffs auf ihre Bankkonten.
Openclaw-Agent löscht E-Mails einer Meta-Forscherin
Es ist nicht das erste Mal, dass Nutzer:innen berichten, dass sich KI-Agenten ihrer Kontrolle entzogen haben. So erregten beispielsweise die Schilderungen der Meta-Forscherin Summer Yue Anfang des Jahres größeres Aufsehen. In einem X-Post schildert sie, dass sie ihr Postfach von einem Openclaw-Agenten verwalten lassen wollte. Aber anstatt ihr Arbeit abzunehmen, begann er, alle E-Mails zu löschen. Auch auf mehrfachen Befehl per Smartphone habe er nicht reagiert, so die KI-Forscherin.
Metas KI-Agent Muse teilt Adresse: Käufer stehen vor der Tür
Auch Metas eigene KI-Agenten sollen schon mehrfach außer Kontrolle geraten sein. So berichtete unter anderem der Youtuber Matt Robb, dass sich sein Muse-Agent falsch verhalten habe. Er wollte ihn eigentlich nutzen, um gebrauchte Gegenstände auf Facebook Marketplace zu verkaufen. Dabei habe der KI-Agent allerdings ohne Zustimmung seine Adresse geteilt. Daraufhin seien Käufer:innen bei ihm zu Hause aufgetaucht, als er gar nicht da war.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 16.11.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.
Das wird so witzig, wenn alle meinen, mit KI Agenten shoppen zu gehen und dann Kühlschränke bekommen.
LLMs sind random Text Generatoren, die haben kein Wissen und keine Logik.
Nutzt Klassische Bots oder lasst euch welche Vibecoden. Die tun das, worauf sie programmiert sind und mehr nicht.

articles.title: AI Accelerators Drive Changes In Power Delivery Networks
articles.text:
Moving voltage regulators closer to processors can reduce power loss, but adds challenges for advanced packaging, thermal management, and system-level design.
Key Takeaways:
Power delivery is now a significant performance limiter in data center chips. The demands of AI and high-performance computing chips running near 0.7 V for a 600W GPU are forcing current to rise to 1,000 amps and beyond, compounding resistive losses and voltage droop across the PDN. Multi-chiplet constructions only compound these issues by further increasing current density and signal congestion.
To solve these challenges, designers are turning to vertical power delivery networks, where the voltage regulator modules are relocated much closer to the processors from their position on the device periphery — to the PCB landside (under the PCB), inside the accelerator package, or inside the silicon interposer. Together with the growing customization of AI accelerator modules, there are many approaches on offer with varying design and manufacturing complexity.
The vertical PDN trend began nearly a decade ago with the integration of backside power delivery networks (BPDNs) on the wafer backside, enabling fine-tuned power delivery more directly to the transistors while reducing IR drop across the tens of interconnect levels on-chip. That approach is being extended with increasingly sophisticated on-die decoupling capacitors (DCaps) formed in deep trenches as part of the BPDN. While this addresses high-frequency decoupling at the chip level, recent changes inside packages, interposers, substrates, and across data center racks are becoming just as important.
Add to that recent developments in the design of compact passive devices, like high-performance inductors, and new architectural solutions become possible, moving the VRMs and DC-DC converters into the interposer or package.
But these architectural changes are neither straightforward nor simple because they involve system co-design of the PDN, interposer, power management ICs (PMICs), integrated voltage regulators (IVRs), DC-DC converters, capacitors, and other passive devices, alongside custom HPC, memory devices, and interconnects that perform today’s elaborate AI tasks.
“In the most advanced semiconductors, people are moving from discrete PMICs to distributed IVRs. Those IVRs are great because they are placed much closer to the chip, which reduces the IR drop to the chip’s own power delivery network, so it is way more efficient. In addition, closed and fast control loops between the chip power management unit to the IVR reduce the reaction time to voltage droop events from milliseconds to microseconds. Because this reaction is so fast you can tune voltage very accurately, with a high degree of granularity even on different areas of a chip,” said Nir Sever, senior director of business development at proteanTecs.
Reconfiguring the PDN is part of a much larger drive to improve energy use. “Energy efficiency becomes the most important performance index for AI-infused platforms moving forward,” said Lipen Yuan, senior director of TSMC’s Advanced Technology Business Development, during a 2024 IEDM short course.
Power delivery challenges are most important at points of load. “AI systems are placing unprecedented demands on board-to-chip power delivery, making the final stage of voltage regulation increasingly important,” said CP Hung, vice president of corporate R&D at ASE.
Fig. 1: By regulating voltage at the point of load, OSATs enable fine-tuned voltage control. Source: ASE
“The move to multi-die architectures is bringing power integrity to the forefront, alongside thermal, stress, and warpage challenges. But the underlying power-delivery problem already existed in advanced single-die designs,” said Sojan Philips, principal product manager of Redhawk-SC at Synopsys. “AI accelerators are now operating at currents approaching the kiloampere range, where even milliohm-level resistance in the power-delivery network can result in significant IR drop. That loss of voltage margin can directly affect performance and power targets, particularly maximum operating frequency and Vmin.”
Several developments illustrate these trends:
As a result, OSATs are playing an increasing role in system co-design, electrical validation, and power integrity (PI) simulation. “The OSAT sits where die, substrate or interposer, passives, and board meet, so we are brought in earlier to model the package-level PDN and co-simulate it with the customer’s die power data,” said Alex Kizeev, technical director of signal and power integrity at Amkor’s design optimization team.
Kizeev breaks down the supply chain and responsibilities among different companies. “The best results come from a PDN budget partitioned across the die, package, and board. The foundry and fabless teams own the on-die PDN, including the die power map and the bump-map allocation. The substrate supplier defines what stackup and via/plane technology is possible. The OSAT optimizes the package-level pieces, including stackup choice, via and ball assignment, DCap selection and placement, warpage and reliability, and validation.”
“Backside power delivery can significantly improve power delivery by reducing IR drop and freeing up frontside routing resources for signals, but it doesn’t eliminate power-integrity challenges,” said Philips. “It also changes the thermal landscape. As power delivery and other structures move to the backside, the paths available for heat removal become more complex. This makes co-optimization of power integrity and thermal management increasingly important.
The overall trend is moving toward closer integration in advanced packages and dies, including the integration of inductors, capacitors, and power-conversion components into substrates and interposers.
Why power losses scale with increasing power
A simple illustration shows how the power efficiency drops as the industry scales from a 1kW GPU to a 5kW GPU (see figure 2). While losses from the voltage regulator itself stay constant at around 13%, resistive losses jump from 8% to 31%, and voltage droop rises from 17% to 31%. As a result, increasing power levels must be supplied to meet all the chip-level needs.
Fig. 2: At higher power levels, the PDN efficiency using motherboard voltage regulators degrades significantly due to VR losses, resistive losses, and droop. Source: Intel Foundry
With this lateral power delivery approach, power integrity (PI) becomes increasingly difficult to maintain as compute loads rise. As AI accelerators integrate increasing levels of compute, HBM, and interconnects between devices, the low supply voltage (0.7-0.9V) of devices means multiple kiloamp levels of current are needed to meet the high-power needs of modern GPUs. As if managing kiloamp currents is not enough, fast workload transients tend to magnify voltage droop, so designers apply voltage guardbands that further increase power consumption and reduce system efficiency. [1]
Next-gen data centers pull in 800V
For next-generation data centers built to meet AI demands, 800V DC power delivery is starting to replace traditional AC power distribution. The 800V DC power distribution coexists with multiple distributed regulators located much closer to individual loads.
To lower transmission losses from the grid to the microprocessor, next-generation PDNs begin at 800V DC and are stepped down in stages using DC-to-DC converters to 48V, 12V, and then 0.7V, for instance. One of the most critical junctures occurs at the point of load, where integrated voltage regulators supply the AI multi-chiplet package. By limiting the number of power conversions, system-level efficiency can improve while reducing thermal cooling requirements.
The voltage regulator module can be positioned underneath the PCB, a logical first step that is commonly referred to as vertical power delivery. However, chipmakers are embracing recent developments that shrink the size of various voltage regulator components, especially capacitors and inductors, to move voltage regulation inside the main processor package and below the SoC, called integrated power delivery. Finally, integrating voltage regulator components into the interposer itself is called fully integrated power delivery.
One step at a time
The approach companies take to voltage regulation integration depends on the company’s expertise, its partners, and the complexity of the system involved.
For this reason, companies are introducing suites of solutions. For example, ASE is offering a range of power delivery capabilities to enable PCB backside integration, which considers the limited space inside computer trays. [2] The company’s PowerSiP options can include double-sided connected capacitors sandwiched between coreless substrates; substrateless designs, solder-free cap array modules with exposed terminals for embedded substrate or PCB solutions; high-aspect-ratio 4:1 copper pin integration for lower packaging impedance; and high-density active and passive component integration using single- or double-sided molding.
“Power efficiency is becoming a defining challenge for next-generation AI systems,” said Harrison Chang, vice president of corporate R&D at ASE. “By shortening the high-current transmission path, our solution can reduce parasitic routing losses by 50% or more, translating directly into meaningful power savings at the system level,” he said in the release.
In June 2025, Marvell introduced its Package Integrated Voltage Regulator (PIVR) technology for AI and HPC. The PIVR replaces the conventional arrangement of discrete voltage-regulator components, often several inches away on the PCB, with compact silicon power converters and passive components tightly coupled to the processor. It’s designed to reduce the amount of low-voltage, high-current routing between the regulator and the processor. The PIVR can sit on the underside of the processor package, shortening the path from voltage conversion to the processor’s power connections. It also can sit next to the processor’s package or inside the advanced package.
Marvell is partnering with multiple companies on integration, including Infineon, which makes power semiconductors and packaged devices; Ferric, which specializes in designing integrated voltage regulators using thin-film magnetic inductors; Monolithic Power Systems, a developer of high-current-density power modules; and Empower Semiconductor, a developer of compact integrated power converters.
In July of this year, Analog Devices completed the acquisition of Empower Semiconductor, expanding ADI’s AI compute power delivery capabilities with integrated voltage regulators and silicon capacitors. “By enabling power conversion closer to the processor, the combined solution shortens the power delivery path and improves efficiency to support higher-performance, higher-density systems. Building on its leadership in high-performance power management, ADI is investing in its system-level platform to deliver a step-change in performance, density, and efficiency from grid to core.” [3]
In addition, on Nov. 2, onsemi announced it will acquire the assets of Ferric, which develops integrated voltage regulators, for up to $775 million. [4]
To understand these important acquisitions, it helps to take a closer look at IVRs.
What is an IVR?
An integrated voltage regulator is typically a 3D stack arrangement that replaces off-chip voltage regulator modules and bulky capacitors and inductors on the PCB with integrated magnetics and passives mounted onto the silicon or package using thin-film technology.
“The IVR is implemented as a 3D stack, bringing together the deep-trench capacitor, PMIC, and inductor, and embedding them directly into the substrate or interposer,” said Veshal Sridhar, product engineering architect, 3D IC at Synopsys. “Companies are moving it closer to the SOC for obvious reasons such as reduced signal parasitics between IVR and SOC die, but that introduces new thermal effects and stress effects because you’re bringing another 3D stack in and embedding it inside an interposer. There’s also potential noise coupling into the other dies from the IVR, because even for a simple 3D stack you are going to have noise coupling.”
In what Intel Foundry refers to as a Super High Density MIM (metal-insulator-metal), capacitance density can be improved by 10× compared to conventional MIM capacitors. [5] This may offer response times on the order of nanoseconds. As part of Intel’s collaboration with UMC for 12nm finFETs, the capacitors feature three metal layers for routing in a scalable design. “This broad adaptability highlights the HDMIM as a universal, highly scalable passive component, capable of heterogeneous integration with logic and power chips manufactured across diverse process nodes from various foundries.” [5]
Inductors have traditionally been one of the greatest passive bottlenecks due to their large footprint, but by integrating them into the package using copper-plated through-hole technology and advanced magnetic materials (see Figure 3), Intel is touting a high resistance-to-capacitance ratio while minimizing stray magnetic fields that could adversely affect surrounding circuits. [5]
Fig. 3: This in-package inductor uses copper-plated through holes embedded with high-permeability magnetics to improve the resistance-to-capacitance ratio and limit magnetic parasitic effects. Source: Intel Foundry
Intel’s FIVR platform uses switched-capacitor voltage regulators and hybrid buck converters to accommodate nanosecond transient spikes by computing cores without exacerbating voltage droop. FIVRs that allow a continuous switching range are superior to fixed SCVRs when it comes to delivering low-voltage inputs (e.g., 1.8 to 3V).
Finally, Intel’s low-voltage GaN MOSHEMT-on-CMOS devices are designed for >12V applications, where high density and high efficiency are essential, while minimizing the overall number of power conversions. By integrating both low voltage and high voltage MIM capacitors with active devices, it minimizes PDN impedance from VR to load. By monolithically integrating the GaN power switches with GaN nMOS drivers, the company can achieve even faster response to transients along with aggressive power density.
“Integrated voltage regulators provide unprecedented speed and granularity in voltage control, but realizing their full power-saving potential requires equally precise visibility into the silicon itself,” said proteanTecs’ Sever. “Traditional power management methods leave significant timing margin untapped. By continuously measuring timing margins across the full chip, cycle by cycle, under actual operating conditions, our embedded monitoring technology identifies where performance is truly limited and where voltage can be safely reduced. Combined with the fine-grained control of IVRs, this enables more aggressive power optimization without compromising performance or reliability.”
Can the system handle the power?
Multiphysics simulation plays an important role in power delivery planning. “A designer may have a simple stack in mind, interposer, base die, top die, and substrate. And it starts with a prototype grid and listing the power required for each die,” explained Synopsys’ Sridhar. “So there is a power budget that comes from the devices, and number of C4 bumps, number of microbumps, TSVs, etc. You want to determine whether your power delivery system can deliver the power needed from the C4 bumps through the top of the stack. Starting with a simple static IR-drop analysis, we can then leverage 3DIC Compiler together with signoff solutions like RedHawk-SC to help bridge the gap between early bump planning and PSE (power sourcing equipment) planning.”
In cases where the PDN cannot handle the power required of the system, design changes such as increasing the interposer size may come into play.
Sridhar noted how one customer brought system-level PI (power integrity) analysis into the early architecture stage, closing the loop between implementation and system analysis using 3DICC plus RHSC, turning iterations that once took days into hours and giving designers more freedom to explore before the architecture is frozen.
At the same time, the package assembly design kits that OSATs compile are becoming more detailed. “Kits are moving beyond geometric design rules to include electrical models, material properties, and validated reference designs. Teams now must consider bump pitch against current density, metal layers against cost, and DCap placement against thermal path early in the design,” said Amkor’s Kizeev.
Conclusion 
Power integrity and power efficiency have already become key differentiators in advanced AI accelerator-based data center designs. Companies are racing to incorporate leading power delivery solutions, including integrated voltage regulators, in positions closer to the GPU or AI accelerator modules where they can be most effective. Advanced power delivery began with the integration of wafer backside PDNs, but package-level and interposer-level solutions are coming fast.
Coordination among major companies in the supply chain is critical during early-stage PDN design. “Some of these design houses are not building the entire system, for instance, like HBM, where even the base die and the stack may be coming in from other design houses,” noted Synopsys’ Phillips. They want to make sure that the grid they’re designing in-house works with the other models. So they want a model exchange between these two, which is performed as part of a feasibility analysis.”
