articles.title: Waymo has stopped its robotaxis from driving on the freeway—here’s why
articles.text:
Waymo is currently restricting its fleet of robotaxis to surface streets after getting into hot water with California over its cars’ driving behavior on highways. Specifically, the software tends to drive into construction zones at speed. As first reported by the San Francisco Business Times, this behavior actually drew the ire of California’s DMV earlier this month, which ordered Waymo to stop driving on Californian highways immediately and until it can convince the DMV that its cars no longer “pose an imminent hazard to public safety.”
This is not Waymo’s first run-in with this problem. In Arizona, Waymo robotaxis did not recognize ramp closure signs on six occasions in Phoenix in April and entered construction zones. A month later in California, seven Waymo robotaxis entered lanes with active construction. In June, Waymo recalled the almost 3,800 robotaxis capable of highway driving. That problem led Waymo to stick to surface streets only in California after the May incidents until late July, when the robotaxis resumed highway operations.
In early July, Waymo told the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration that it began updating the robotaxi software to a version that “improve[s] the recognition of freeway construction zones, more appropriately prioritize[s] construction zones over other freeway hazards, and reduce[s] speed when the AV detects that it may be in a construction zone.”

articles.title: How Virtual Twins And Machine Learning Optimize DRAM Yield
articles.text:
Model process variation, detect multiple failure modes, and evaluate solutions with less wafer experimentation.
As memory technologies continue to scale, manufacturing processes are becoming increasingly complex.
Additional process steps, tighter process windows, and new sources of variation are making it progressively more challenging to reach acceptable yield.
Systemic failures are emerging as a source of yield loss during yield ramp. Unlike random defects, these failures are often driven by complex interactions between multiple process modules.
Rapid root-cause identification of these systemic defects is critical to quickly improving yield and accelerating time-to-market.1 But conventional failure analysis relies heavily on wafer experimentation and statistical analysis, which can be slow and costly as manufacturing complexity increases.
That’s where calibrated virtual twins and machine-learning optimization can help.
Fig. 1: Systemic failures are a key bottleneck during yield ramp. Faster identification and reduction of these failures can accelerate the yield ramp and shorten the time required to reach a targeted manufacturing yield.
Process engineers use virtual manufacturing models (SEMulator3D) with machine learning (ML) optimization (Fabtex Yield Optimizer) to predict process failures.
Using this technique, engineers can evaluate potential yield improvements, all with limited need for wafer-based experimentation.
As an example of this technique, we built a SEMulator3D model (virtual twin) of a DRAM manufacturing process sequence. During this model-building, we established virtual metrology measurements throughout the process sequence (Figure 2).
Fig. 2: Building and calibrating a DRAM virtual twin using process integration, virtual metrology, and silicon data.
ML was then used to calibrate the model against silicon data, enabling the virtual environment to better reproduce observed manufacturing behavior and serve as the foundation for downstream failure analysis and optimization.
For our specific case study, we built a calibrated virtual twin for our DRAM memory device that contained eight known systemic failure mechanisms.
Figure 3 displays examples of these failure mechanisms, including shorts, opens, and overlap-related defects between critical DRAM structures.
Fig. 3: Reproducing systemic DRAM failure modes and detecting them using virtual metrology.
We also specified (in the virtual twin) the virtual metrology needed to detect these failures. By translating each failure into a measurable geometric condition and monitoring it through virtual metrology, we were able to automatically detect and simultaneously analyze multiple failure mechanisms within a single study.
Using the calibrated virtual twin, ML was then applied to help us understand the impact of process and structural variations on the eight predefined failure modes.
We then searched for an optimized manufacturing solution (specific process changes) that provided the lowest failure rate across our eight predefined failure modes. Instead of addressing each failure mode independently, the optimization routine evaluated the impact of multiple process changes simultaneously and searched for process targets that improved the overall pass ratio.
As shown in Figure 4, the optimized process settings significantly reduced all eight systemic failure modes.
Fig. 4: Simultaneous reduction of multiple systemic failures through ML-based optimization and retargeting analysis. A sample retargeting plot for SNLP (storage node landing pad) open/short failures is highlighted.
Under the nominal process conditions used in the study, the predicted total yield was 0.1%. Following optimization, the predicted yield increased to 78.5%, with lower failure rates across all eight failure mechanisms.
This analysis also translated the optimized solution into actionable inline fab targets that can be directly applied in the real process, helping engineers identify which process and structural parameters should be adjusted to further reduce systemic failures.
This work demonstrates how the combination of process models and ML can be used to accelerate yield improvement during DRAM device development. By reproducing process variability in a calibrated virtual environment, and performing simultaneous optimization and retargeting, engineers can detect multiple device failures and investigate a broad solution space without the time and cost of extensive silicon experimentation.
1 I. Tirkel, “Yield Learning Curve Models in Semiconductor Manufacturing,” IEEE Transactions on Semiconductor Manufacturing, vol. 26, no. 4, pp. 564-571, Nov. 2013.

articles.title: Meet two Mississauga founders rethinking the way money moves | BetaKit
articles.text:
Two FinTech founders in Mississauga are taking aim at the complicated infrastructure behind international payments.
Gharsa Amin, founder and CEO of Kavodax, and Gezim Ramabaja, founder and CEO of Zpayd, are approaching the problem from different corners of the financial industry. One is using blockchain technology to speed up international transfers, while the other is building the connections that allow financial institutions to offer bill payments globally.
Both companies have tapped into Mississauga’s startup ecosystem for mentorship, industry connections, and support in bringing their products to market.
BetaKit spoke with the founders about what it takes to break into the financial industry, bring new payment technologies to market, and build a business in Mississauga.
Taking international transfers from days to minutes
When Gharsa Amin’s grandmother fell ill in Germany, she sent money from Canada to help support her. The transfer took five days, passed through multiple banking clearances, and incurred foreign exchange fees of approximately three to four percent. Her grandmother also had to visit the bank in person to access the funds.
“Having worked in digital banking, compliance, and technology, I knew there had to be a better way,” Amin said.
“You don’t necessarily need to build the next major financial institution. Sometimes the biggest opportunity is building the infrastructure that allows those institutions to do more.”
She founded Kavodax in 2025 to tackle the delays and costs of international payments, particularly for small and medium-sized businesses that regularly pay overseas suppliers and contractors.
Kavodax uses blockchain-based settlement and stablecoin technology to move money between countries. Customers fund payments through their bank accounts, and recipients receive funds in their local currency. Kavodax aims to complete transfers in under 30 minutes, avoiding some of the intermediaries involved in conventional international banking.
Amin said customers are generally less concerned with the technology itself than the cost and reliability of the service.
“We don’t lead with blockchain; we lead with the business problem,” she said. “Most business owners care about how much a payment costs, how quickly their supplier receives it, and whether they can trust the process.”
Conversations with prospective customers revealed frustration with foreign exchange fees of three to five percent, long settlement times, and difficulty tracking international transfers.
Kavodax has expanded its payment capabilities to more than 70 countries and 30 currencies. It has also secured approximately $400,000 in non-dilutive funding and $100,000 in investment. The company has turned its attention to getting businesses onto the platform, particularly those making regular payments to overseas suppliers and contractors. It’s also pursuing partnerships with other FinTech providers that could integrate Kavodax’s technology into their own services.
Kavodax has secured registrations with FINTRAC and the Bank of Canada, and is pursuing further security and compliance certifications as it expands its banking relationships.
Amin also sought help with the business side of Kavodax. She participated in IDEA Mississauga’s 2025 EmpowHER Tech Launchpad, a 12-week accelerator delivered in partnership with York University’s YSpace, that helps women-led tech companies grow through mentorship, business training, and investor-readiness support.
The program helped sharpen Kavodax’s customer focus, validate market demand, and identify where to concentrate its efforts. “One of my biggest takeaways was that commercialization cannot wait until product development is finished,” Amin added.
Mississauga’s international business community has also helped Amin better understand her prospective customers. Companies that rely on overseas suppliers face precisely the payment problems Kavodax is trying to address.
Kavodax’s next priorities include increasing transaction volumes, strengthening banking partnerships, and closing a $2-million financing round.
“Longer term, our ambition is to help businesses save billions in unnecessary international payment costs and expand access to financial services for 500,000 people,” Amin said. “We want to build globally relevant financial infrastructure right here in Canada.”
A borderless bill payment network
Gezim Ramabaja was just 18 when he opened his first business: a coffee shop in his native Kosovo. By the time he found his way into FinTech, he had also run a restaurant and a construction company in Canada.
It was through those latter businesses that Ramabaja stumbled across the problem that would inspire Zpayd. Many of his employees were students who relied on their parents for help paying bills. For international students in particular, arranging payments from overseas could involve technical difficulties and high fees.
“While the financial world had become increasingly connected, bill payment remained fragmented,” he said. “Payment networks, billers, and financial institutions operated largely within their own domestic ecosystems, making it difficult to pay bills across borders or access billers outside a particular country.”
He began developing Zpayd in 2021 with the goal of helping people pay bills across borders.
“I knew there had to be a better way.”
Gharsa Amin,
Kavodax
Zpayd initially offered the service directly to consumers, and finding interest wasn’t the problem. At one point, Zpayd was attracting as many as 20 sign-ups a day, and the demands of onboarding and supporting individual customers were beginning to stretch the business.
At the Money20/20 FinTech conference in Las Vegas, Ramabaja met executives who suggested offering Zpayd’s services directly to their companies. Through a single institutional relationship, Zpayd could potentially reach thousands of existing customers.
“This changed our business model but not our underlying vision,” Ramabaja said.
Today, Zpayd provides the infrastructure that allows financial institutions to offer domestic and international bill payments through their existing services. A customer could, for instance, pay a utility bill overseas through a participating payment provider, with Zpayd handling the connections to the local biller and payment network behind the scenes.
The company also supports creditor payments and loan disbursements. A lender could use Zpayd to send money directly to a creditor, for example, without relying on cheques or manual processing.
But getting banks and other financial institutions to adopt new technology is no small undertaking. Ramabaja said prospective partners have lengthy procurement processes and want assurances around security, compliance, reporting, and settlement.
“We’ve learned that credibility in this industry is built through execution,” Ramabaja said. “You have to demonstrate reliability, security, and consistency before institutions are comfortable making you part of their financial infrastructure.”
Ramabaja has been involved with IDEA Mississauga since 2023 and is an alumnus of ICUBE, the startup incubator at the University of Toronto Mississauga. He credits both organizations with helping him connect with mentors, industry professionals, and other entrepreneurs during Zpayd’s development.
Ramabaja also sees Mississauga’s proximity to Toronto’s financial sector as an advantage for a company seeking relationships with banks and payment providers.
“I also think it’s important to recognize that successful technology companies don’t need to be built exclusively in traditional technology hubs,” he said. “Mississauga has the talent, business community, and resources to support companies developing solutions for global markets.”
Ramabaja is now looking at opportunities to expand Zpayd’s services into new markets and payment categories, including loan repayments and emerging payment methods such as stablecoins. His longer-term goal is to build a global network that financial institutions can use to offer bill payment services, wherever their customers need them.
“You don’t necessarily need to build the next major financial institution,” he said. “Sometimes the biggest opportunity is building the infrastructure that allows those institutions to do more.”
PRESENTED BY
Mississauga’s startup ecosystem offers opportunities to access mentorship, develop industry connections, and work through the challenges of commercialization.

articles.title: GTA 6 head of development says the biggest lessons Rockstar learned from Red Dead Redemption 2 involved ‘the emphasis on interactivity’ — ‘Giving players the ability to attempt to approach situations non-violently is also another feature that we have carried over and continued to try and evolve’
articles.text:
GTA 6 head of development says ‘the emphasis on interactivity’ adds ‘friction’ to almost every facet of gameplay — ‘It means you have to think a little bit more about what you want to do and when and why you want to do it’
- Grand Theft Auto 6 head of development Rob Nelson discusses the lessons Rockstar Games learned from Red Dead Redemption 2
- Nelson says the studio evolved "interactivity" to make every gameplay decision matter
- He explains, "When your actions may have unintended consequences, when they may affect how your story plays out—will you consider a different approach?"
Rockstar Games has explained how it evolved interactivity from past games to make almost every gameplay choice in Grand Theft Auto 6 responsive.
In response to questions sent directly to Rockstar by TechRadar Gaming, head of development Rob Nelson discussed the biggest lessons the studio learned from Red Dead Redemption 2 that it used to build GTA 6, touching on the importance of improving in-world reactivity to make choices more meaningful.
"The emphasis on interactivity and adding friction intentionally to cause the player to have to think more, to act with more intention, to make choices and have those choices affect the ways in which the world responds to you were some of the major elements we carried over from RDR2," Nelson said.
The developer added the team also took what in previous GTA games were "relatively simple actions," and "adding a degree of friction" to them, like pulling out any weapon or stealing a car at any time.
In GTA 6, players will now need to call for their car through Scooter Bros, or go to a gun store, or search the world to find a new weapon, which Nelson said: "creates a need for (and adds value to) your vehicle, the phone and its apps, the gun store, exploring the world etc."
This means players will need to "think a little bit more" about what, when, why, and how they do things in the world.
"Similarly, if the population now reacts more believably to you as the player walking around with a large weapon—you may think twice about when and why to do it—this in turn helps to support our narrative about being fugitives on the run," Nelson explained.

The head of development continued, saying Rockstar has provided players with the ability to approach situations non-violently, which is another feature that the team carried over "and continued to try and evolve from RDR2."
"When your actions may have unintended consequences, when they may affect how your story plays out—will you consider a different approach?" Neslon said. "All these new approaches do is add choice for the player and how they want to approach the game, and that is one of our favourite aspects of this medium—it has been a great but rewarding challenge to try to weave these elements into GTA 6."

articles.title: 'GTA VI' es monumental y ya hay quien dice que es el mejor juego de la historia. Un juego de 1998 acaba de levantar la ceja
articles.text:
A las horas de escribir estas líneas, ya han salido los análisis de 'GTA VI', y la crítica lo tiene claro: 153 reivews publicadas para una media de 99. Es la más alta de la historia en cuanto a media teniendo en cuenta la cantidad de análisis de los medios que puntúan en Metacritic y si lees los análisis de los principales medios, no tarda en aparecer la reflexión que no sólo es el juego más ambicioso de la historia: es el mejor.
Y, si sólo nos fijamos en la media, así es, pero hay algo que hay que tener en cuenta: 'GTA VI' no es 'The Legend of Zelda Ocarina of Time'. Sígueme en esto porque te prometo que tiene sentido.
El reflejo de Metacritic
La media es apabullante porque, a estas alturas, 'GTA VI' no es sólo un videojuego: es un evento. Tengo colegas que se pillaron la PS5 de salida pensando en jugar al nuevo 'GTA' (y viendo cómo han subido los precios, creo que les ha valido la pena esperar seis años desde el lanzamiento de PS5 y Xbox Series X).
A nivel publicitario, el título de Rockstar no tiene parangón, y en esos análisis sale a la palestra el hecho de que esos 13 años se sienten reflejados en el título. Puede que no te guste el 'GTA' por los motivos que sean y es perfecto, pero la salida de este juego es un acontecimiento. Mis compas de 3DJuegos se han explayado en su análisis, pero para mí hay otros dos hechos notables:
- Digital Foundry, medio especializado en el apartado visual de los juegos, lo llama "El juego de la generación", alabando un apartado técnico excepcional.
- HobbyConsolas le ha cascado el primer 100 de su historia.
Y mira, puedes estar de acuerdo con los análisis o no, ya que al final son algo subjetivo, pero ocurre lo mismo que con el propio 'GTA VI': es innegable que ha revuelto algo.
Como digo, esta media de 99 ya está haciendo que se hable del mejor juego de la historia y se da por hecho que va a arrasar en unos The Game Awards en los que parte con ocho nominaciones y donde el público ya puede votar por él... sin haberlo jugado.
Pero pese a todo, pese a que un 99 de 153 análisis sea más que un 99 de 22 análisis como el de 'Ocarina of Time' de 1998, ocurre una cosa: 'GTA VI no es 'Ocarina of Time'.
El problema de Metacritic
A nivel de ambición, técnico (algo con fecha de caducidad), magnitud, situación de la industria y casi todos los parámetros que quieras, sí: 'GTA VI' es mastodóntico. Rockstar ha construido inmunerables pisos sobre las bases tan sólidas y ambiciosas que ya tenían en casa como 'GTA V' y, sobre todo, 'Red Dead Redemption 2'.
Es un "más, más, más" y, además, mejor, una expansión 3D como pocas se han visto en este medio, pero una expansión, en definitiva, partiendo de una base que ya estaba ahí. Afirmar que es "el mejor juego de la historia" basándonos sólo en las notas pues sí, no es una mentira, pero ahí es donde vuelvo a mencionar el 'Oracina of Time' de 1998.
En un año en el que la industria seguía peleando con el 3D y el paso a tecnologías extremadamente nuevas, Nintendo parió algo que se convirtió en el estándar de... bueno, de los videojuegos. Había cosas que no tenían referente y que no construían sobre unos cimientos, sino que fueron inventando sobre la marcha y resolviendo problemas que aparecían por el camino.
El modo de seleccionar un enemigo para orbitar a su alrededor en los combates es un ejemplo, pero también el botón contextual que cambia en función de la acción y la situación, la escalada y salto contextuales, el ciclo de día y noche y los eventos asociados a cada etapa, el montar a caballo en un mundo 3D, una guía por el mundo para no depender del minimapa o la vibración del Rumble Pak.
Hubo cosas que pulió de ideas anteriores, claro, pero también mucho que, como digo, fue inventando para resolver los problemas que encontraron a medida que el desarrollo avanzaba. Hay un poco de 'Ocarina of Time' en casi cualquier juego 3D y, rejugando el excepcional remake, me he dado cuenta de todo lo que bebe 'Dark Souls' del juego de Nintendo.
Al final, 'GTA VI' es construir sobre lo que ya existía y llevarlo a una escala monumental, pero 'Ocarina of Time' tuvo una influencia en los videojuegos que es imposible encapsular en una nota. Y lo bueno es que no tenemos que pelear por absurdeces, y este fin de año podemos disfrutar casi a la vez del mejor juego de la historia por nota y del remake del juego que hizo historia.

articles.title: Google Wallet arrive sur l’iPhone, mais pas pour tout le monde
articles.text:
C’est désormais officiel : Google Wallet est disponible sur iOS. Le portefeuille numérique de Google, bien connu des utilisateurs sous Android, dispose donc désormais d’une application sur l’iPhone.
Comme le propose déjà l’appli native Apple Cartes, Google Wallet doit permettre aux possesseurs de l’iPhone d’accéder à leurs cartes de fidélités, titres de transport et autres reçus. Synchronisée automatiquement avec Gmail et les autres services Google, Google Wallet est capable d’importer automatiquement vos informations ou encore de suivre vos colis.
Pas de paiement sans contact et une disponibilité limitée
Concrètement, la version iOS de Google Wallet vous permettra de numériser vos cartes physiques et autres documents en utilisant l’appareil photo de l’iPhone. Vous pourrez y gérer les cartes bancaires associées à votre compte Google pour payer plus rapidement vos achats en ligne depuis Chrome, les services Google ainsi que sur les sites acceptant Google Pay.
L’appli iOS de Google Wallet s’architecture autour de deux onglets, une page d’accueil regroupant les livraisons à venir, les cartes d’embarquement et les cartes de fidélité, et un onglet dédié aux transactions et aux passes qui consigne l’historique de vos transactions récentes, ainsi que les cartes enregistrées et les passes épinglés.
Ceci étant, Google Wallet sur l’iPhone est amputée d’une fonctionnalité majeure. Restrictions d’iOS oblige, Google n’a pas pu y intégrer Tap to Pay, son système de paiement sans contact. À moins que Google et Apple ne conviennent d’un accord, les utilisateurs d’iPhone devront donc toujours s’en remettre à Apple Pay pour régler leurs achats sans contact avec leur iPhone dans les boutiques physiques.
Autre limitation, et pas des moindres, l’appli iOS de Google Wallet n’est pour l’instant disponible qu’aux États-Unis. Google n’a pour l’heure donné aucune indication quant à une éventuelle disponibilité de son application sur l’iPhone ailleurs dans le monde.

articles.title: Apache warns of Roller RCE vulnerability exploited in attacks
articles.text:
Apache has released security updates to address a critical Roller flaw that threat actors are exploiting to gain code execution on vulnerable servers.
Apache Roller is an open-source, Java-based group-blogging server with a much smaller market share than modern content management systems and blogging platforms.
However, while this is a niche product, Apache has flagged the flaw (tracked as CVE-2026-129448) as actively exploited in the wild.
Apache has not yet provided details about these ongoing attacks, including who is responsible and how many servers have already been compromised.
"Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code. The XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester," Apache explained in a Tuesday security advisory.
"This is the same vulnerability as CVE-2026-82384, which listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected. This issue is being actively exploited."
To block ongoing attacks, Roller users should immediately upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later, which disables the extension types and rejects malicious XML-RPC requests after turning off the XML-RPC feature.
Admins who can't immediately upgrade can also temporarily mitigate CVE-2026-129448 by setting "enabledForExtensions" to "false" in WEB-INF/web.xml, removing the "/roller-services/xmlrpc" servlet mapping, and restarting Roller.
According to Apache, disabling XML-RPC in the administration user interface is not enough to block attacks because older versions deserialize the request before checking whether that setting is toggled on.
In April, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) also flagged a 13-year-old Apache ActiveMQ vulnerability (CVE-2026-34197) as exploited in attacks and ordered federal agencies to secure their systems within two weeks.
More recently, earlier this month, Apache fixed a critical vulnerability in the HTTP/2 module of Apache HTTP Server that an unauthenticated attacker could exploit to gain remote code execution on unpatched servers.
Since November 2021, CISA has added 41 Apache flaws to its catalog of vulnerabilities exploited in the wild, eight of them also abused by ransomware gangs.

articles.title: L’agent IA de Gemini peut désormais appeler le garagiste et prendre rendez-vous à votre place
articles.text:
Google ouvre gratuitement l’accès à son agent Gemini dans six pays, où il peut mener des recherches ou préparer votre briefing du matin en arrière-plan. Aux États-Unis, le déploiement va plus loin avec la possibilité de passer des appels et de régler des achats via Google Pay.
Un voyant s’allume sur le tableau de bord. Il faut trouver un garage près de chez vous, appeler, patienter, puis vérifier que le créneau proposé colle avec votre agenda. C’est cette petite corvée que Josh Woodward, responsable de l’application Gemini, dit avoir confiée à l’IA. Dans le récit publié par Google, Gemini a repéré deux garages sur Maps, les a appelés en parallèle en se présentant comme une IA, puis a inscrit le rendez-vous dans Google Agenda. Le tout en moins de cinq minutes, selon Woodward.
Spark change de nom et devient accessible sans abonnement
Présenté en mai sous le nom de Gemini Spark, l’agent s’appelle désormais « Tasks in Gemini », à ne pas confondre avec l’application Google Tasks. Un bouton sur l’écran d’accueil permet de basculer du chat vers le mode Tâches. Une fois la demande envoyée, on peut passer à autre chose. Gemini poursuit le travail en arrière-plan, accepte de nouvelles consignes en cours de route et vous prévient quand le résultat est prêt.
L’intérêt du mode Tâches se voit aussi dans les routines. Vous pouvez demander à Gemini de croiser chaque matin vos e-mails et votre agenda pour faire ressortir ce qui mérite votre attention avant la première réunion. L’agent peut également préparer un itinéraire de voyage ou prendre en charge une recherche qui demande plusieurs étapes.
Le déploiement gratuit a commencé le 17 novembre aux États-Unis, au Canada, en Australie, en Inde, au Japon et en Corée du Sud. L’agent tourne sur Gemini 4 Hydrogen, le modèle que Google vient aussi d’intégrer à son moteur de recherche. Comme c’est souvent le cas lorsqu’il s’agit d’intelligence artificielle, aucune date n’a été annoncée pour la France et il faudra sûrement attendre plusieurs mois avant de voir apparaître cette fonction chez nous.
Jusqu’où peut-on laisser Gemini agir ?
Aux États-Unis, il est aussi possible de confier une tâche à Gemini par message ou en lui transférant un e-mail. Google donne l’exemple de messages de l’école dont l’agent récupère les dates pour les ajouter au calendrier familial. The Verge relève que Gemini peut aussi se connecter à certains sites via le gestionnaire de mots de passe de Google.
Pour les achats, l’utilisateur peut fixer un plafond de dépenses. Google indique que l’agent est conçu pour demander une validation avant de passer commande, avec la possibilité de donner son accord à l’avance. Le degré d’autonomie dépend aussi du site. Dans l’exemple des courses chez Instacart, Gemini ajoute les produits demandés au panier, puis rend la main à l’utilisateur pour terminer la commande.
Google affirme que chaque compte dispose d’un environnement isolé où l’agent exécute ses tâches. Les applications connectées peuvent être retirées dans les réglages, et les commerces peuvent refuser les appels automatisés. Si votre garage les accepte, Gemini pourra patienter à votre place. Pour le prix de la révision, vous aurez encore votre mot à dire.

articles.title: Plus grande, plus puissante, rechargée en 5 minutes : BYD veut vendre sa nouvelle citadine électrique en Europe avec un nom déjà connu — Frandroid
articles.text:
La Seagull est la voiture électrique la moins chère de BYD : environ 10 000 euros en Chine. On la connaît en Europe sous le nom de Dolphin Surf, et ailleurs dans le monde sous celui de Dolphin Mini.
Avec plus de 245 000 exemplaires écoulés à fin septembre, c’est la plus vendue des BYD 100 % électriques, et l’une des électriques les plus populaires au monde cette année.
Sa remplaçante change nettement de gabarit. Elle mesure 4,21 mètres de long pour un empattement de 2,65 mètres, soit 42,5 cm et 15 cm de plus que l’actuelle. Elle accueille désormais 5 passagers au lieu de 4, passe à la propulsion avec un moteur positionné à l’arrière, gagne une suspension arrière multibras et un coffre avant de 94 litres.
Son moteur grimpe à 85 ou 95 kW (116 ou 129 ch) selon les versions, contre 55 kW (75 ch) auparavant. À l’intérieur, on trouve un écran central de 15,6 pouces et quelques boutons physiques de retour.
Pourquoi la Dolphin, et pas la Surf ?
Cette nouvelle Seagull pourrait arriver en Europe, mais remplaçerait la Dolphin, la compacte électrique de la gamme, et non la Dolphin Surf.
L’information vient du média espagnol TestCoches, pas directement d’un communiqué de presse de BYD. Elle tient toutefois la route sur le papier. La Dolphin Surf mesure 3,99 mètres, la Dolphin 4,29 mètres : avec ses 4,21 mètres, la nouvelle Seagull se rapproche nettement de la seconde. La Surf resterait au catalogue en Europe.
La vraie inconnue, c’est le prix. En Chine, la Seagull de deuxième génération démarre à 65 900 yuan (environ 9 000 euros) et monte à 99 900 yuan (environ 13 650 euros). En France, la Dolphin Surf 5 places débute à 24 490 euros et la Dolphin à 34 990 euros. Si la nouvelle venue s’installe dans la case de la Dolphin, il faudra voir où BYD place le curseur.
Transport, homologation et droits de douane sur les électriques chinoises ne permettront pas de transposer les tarifs chinois tels quels. L’écart avec la Surf, lui, pourrait compter pour les acheteurs qui comparent.
Encore faut-il que la nouvelle venue soit plus aboutie que la Dolphin qu’elle remplacerait. Celle-ci, l’un des premiers modèles BYD lancés en France, souffrait de quelques lacunes majeures, que nous avions soulignées dans notre première prise en main.
La recharge rapide, à regarder de près
L’argument principal de cette nouvelle Seagull est la recharge « Flash » : de 10 à 70 % en 5 minutes, de 10 à 97 % en 9 minutes. Ces chiffres sont impressionnants, mais ils viennent du constructeur et ont été mesurés en Chine. Cette recharge n’est d’ailleurs pas livrée sur les deux versions les moins chères. Il faudra aussi vérifier si les bornes européennes pourront en tirer parti, chose qui n’est pas forcément acquis à l’instant où nous écrivons ces lignes.
Côté batteries, la voiture reçoit les fameuses Blade 2.0 avec une chimie LFP de 30,1 ou 39,2 kWh. Elles promettent 320 et 420 km en cycle chinois CLTC. En cycle européen WLTP, les chiffres seront plus bas (entre 270 et 350 km environ). Même remarque pour l’aide à la conduite DiPilot 300 avec Lidar, proposée en option en Chine : rien ne dit qu’elle passera l’homologation européenne.
Sur ce point, la future Dolphin risque de reculer. L’actuelle annonce jusqu’à 427 km WLTP avec sa plus grosse batterie de 60,4 kWh. Pour reprendre ce nom sans perdre en autonomie, BYD devra soit greffer une plus grosse batterie à la Seagull, comme il l’a fait pour la Surf, mieux dotée en Europe qu’en Chine, soit garder un temps l’actuelle Dolphin au catalogue pour les longs trajets, comme le suggère TestCoches.
Pour l’instant, BYD n’a rien annoncé sur le calendrier, les versions ou les tarifs européens. Cette nouvelle Seagull pourrait tout à fait être produite dans l’usine hongroise de la marque ou dans la seconde, qui n’est pour le moment qu’à l’état de projet.
    Pour aller plus loin
« Très prochainement » : surprise, BYD pourrait installer une usine en France
            
Reste à savoir si l’équation tiendra une fois les taxes européennes ajoutées et si elle saura faire face à la future Peugeot e-208 entre autre, ou encore les futures versions améliorées de la Renault 5 E-Tech prévues l’an prochain. Mais à ce petit jeu technique et technologique, les constructeurs chinois ont désormais une sacrée longueur d’avance.

articles.title: ABAN partners African Angel Academy to boost angel investor capacity - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
The African Business Angel Network (ABAN) has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the African Angel Academy (AAA) to expand access to practical investment education for angel investors across the continent.
Established in 2015, ABAN is the largest pan-African organisation of angel investors on the continent. Active in 38 African countries and the diaspora, it brings together over 75 member networks and more than 5,000 angel investors committed to fuelling early-stage innovation.
The AAA, meanwhile, is an African-led initiative that trains and supports angel investors and early-stage investors to actualise their investment objectives through training, coaching, networking, and showcasing of investment opportunities.
The partnership between the two organisations will give ABAN’s investor community access to structured learning, practical tools and peer connections designed to support more informed participation in early-stage investing.
To put the partnership into action, the AAA is launching the Angel Investing Learning Programme, a five-week programme open exclusively to members of the ABAN community. Running from February 8 to March 10, 2027, it covers four core modules from the AAA curriculum – due diligence, deal structuring, valuations and negotiations – combining expert instruction with practical exercises and peer learning.
Participants who complete the programme will receive an AAA certificate and retain access to course materials for two months. ABAN members enrolling in groups of at least 20 will get a 20 per cent discount on the US$350 programme fee.
“Building a stronger angel investment ecosystem requires more than increasing the number of investors. It requires giving investors the knowledge, tools, and networks to make informed investment decisions and support the companies they back,” said Fadilah Tchoumba, CEO of ABAN.
“Africa’s early-stage ecosystem grows when more Africans are ready to invest, and ready to invest well,” said Fiona Kiruja, CEO of the African Angel Academy. “That means more Africans backing the founders building on this continent, more professionals and operators finding their entry point into early-stage investing, and more high-net-worth individuals mobilising the capital that already exists here.”
Applications for the programme are open here.

articles.title: Why Tobi Oyewole took a pay cut to build a software career
articles.text:
In 2020, Tobi Oyewole had a company car, an official apartment, and two sponsored trips to China behind him. Then he left for a new job that paid less.
“I wasn’t really satisfied with the kind of work I was doing,” he says.
For Oyewole, a petroleum engineering graduate turned software engineer, taking the pay cut was a first in another sense. Until then, someone else had made most of his career decisions for him.
As a boy, he daydreamed about playing football professionally and even won a prize in secondary school. He also wanted to become a pilot. But his father had other plans, teaching his son maths himself in the hope that he would pursue engineering.
“I’m just going to do what they wanted. I am going to be a good child,” Oyewole remembers thinking.
He initially applied to the University of Lagos (UNILAG) in south-west Nigeria to study electrical engineering, but eventually settled on petroleum engineering, another course his father approved of.
“Oil and gas is not that bad either,” he says. He enrolled in 2011.
Yet the oil and gas job he had trained for never materialised. Despite sending out applications, he heard nothing back.
“Trying to get an oil and gas job was not very easy,” he says. “I still think about it now. Maybe I didn’t try hard enough.”
Oyewole’s interest in technology and coding began in his second year at UNILAG, when he started building websites in Adobe Dreamweaver and teaching himself HTML and CSS along the way.
“I’d just be learning a few things, just to see what’s happening in this tech thing,” he says. “At the time, I wasn’t even into tech, and it wasn’t tech the way we see tech now. We just had some guys who came to teach about building stuff on the Internet.”
His growing interest in programming soon began to affect his academic performance.
“My 200-level GPA [grade point average] was the worst I ever had, because I was really inquisitive about programming and I was concentrating on it badly,” he says. By his third year, however, he had set aside his coding interest to focus on his petroleum engineering degree.
He would eventually return to programming, a decision he says he has never regretted. Today, he is also helping secondary school students discover opportunities in technology, giving others an introduction to a path he once found for himself.
Dumping oil and gas
After graduating from UNILAG in 2016, Oyewole said he had hoped to work in the oil and gas industry. However, he joined MOJEC, an electrical company, instead. The company, which builds smart electricity metres gave him his first real shot at paid employment after tertiary studies.
“I didn’t really have much experience. It was just time to put the body to work. Anything they threw at me, I was ready to do it,” he says.
He spent much of his time programming meters at the factory, supporting the information technology (IT) team, and fixing the office Internet. MOJEC also gave him room to explore other areas of the business. He describes it as “a canvas you can paint your life however you want,” where employees could take on projects with few restrictions. One such project involved renewable energy and took him to China twice on company-sponsored trips, he says.
“It was a place where you could give yourself out, and they were ready to pour back into you,” he says.
His experience gradually drew him towards the technology side of the business, prompting him to consider what he could build rather than simply fixing existing problems. He enrolled at New Horizons, an information and communication technology (ICT) training institute that offers professional certification programmes, to develop his skills, studying programming languages C# and .NET.
Although he still had his sights on oil and gas, seeing colleagues receive technology job offers and leave MOJEC about three years into his employment made him reconsider.
“I knew that I had to take this tech seriously,” he says. “I don’t think I can be putting my eyes out on oil and gas stuff anymore. This is the time for me to get fully focused on building a career in software engineering.”
In 2020, he left MOJEC and decided to spend time strengthening his programming skills through YouTube tutorials and other learning resources.
Building software
After spending time at home developing his coding skills, Oyewole joined Reliance Infosystems, an IT consulting firm and Microsoft partner, in November 2020.
Placed on the company’s customer relationship management (CRM) team, he worked with Microsoft Dynamics 365. Although his role involved learning to use and administer the platform, he was far more interested in understanding how to build software himself.
“The thing with Dynamics 365 and the likes is that these are apps that have already been built. You have to know how to use them well. But I was much more interested in building those apps myself,” he says.
He likened this curiosity to using Microsoft Excel while wanting to understand how the spreadsheet was built.
“It’s one thing to know how to use Excel well, but there are also people who built Excel from scratch,” Oyewole said.
That curiosity led him to build applications that integrated with Dynamics 365. When a client needed a custom application that no one else on the team could develop, Oyewole says he took on the project and built it from scratch.
“That was one project that really boosted my skills,” he says.
He left Reliance Infosystems in October 2021 and joined Softcom, a technology company building digital solutions, in 2022. There, he worked on Kwiksell, a product that helped merchants sell online, manage inventory, and track sales.
Working with experienced engineers introduced him to more structured development practices, including daily stand-ups, sprints, and customer validation sessions. He also began to understand how engineering decisions connected to customer needs and business goals.
“At Softcom, I started seeing systems that scale and engineers offering really smart solutions to problems,” he says.
The job also gave him the opportunity to move beyond tutorials and personal projects, deploying software to real customers, observing how they used it and learning what it took to build and maintain production software.
He also learnt to balance his interests as an engineer with the needs of the product and to work at a faster pace.
But his time at Softcom was short-lived. Financial difficulties eventually led to layoffs.
“It was my first experience of being laid off,” he says.
The experience was particularly difficult because he struggled to tell his parents, who had been sceptical about his decision to pursue software engineering.
“My layoff from Softcom was not funny at all. It was so bad I could not even tell my parents,” he says. “I was scared because my parents weren’t really okay with me venturing into software. It wasn’t something they saw potential in.”
It was one of the lowest points in his career. He began questioning his decision to pursue software engineering but knew he had to keep applying for jobs and find another opportunity.
Working with a global engineering team
In 2023, Oyewole persisted and eventually joined Andela, a Nigerian-founded talent marketplace that became a unicorn startup in 2021 after raising $20 million at a $1.5 billion valuation.
“I applied to Andela like four times before I finally got in,” he says. “After getting into Andela, I went for a couple of client interviews.”
One led to an engagement with Science Corporation, a US-based biotech startup, marking his first international role. Working with colleagues in Egypt, Pakistan and the United States, he gained experience collaborating across time zones and adapting to a more demanding engineering culture.
“It was an awesome experience because at Science, it was much more core engineering, being able to think critically about what you write,” he says.
According to Oyewole, the company’s head of engineering often reminded the team that “the best kind of code you write is no code,” encouraging engineers to keep solutions simple and think carefully before making changes.
This also pushed Oyewole to expand his skills beyond frontend specialisation; it allowed him to learn how to fix issues on the company’s Ruby on Rails server and make design decisions in the absence of a dedicated designer, he told TechCabal.
“But it was an eye-opener into global standards for technology. Being able to write code the right way, not just writing code as usual, but writing it to work,” he says.
Science was developing software to help scientists digitise experiments and track their findings. As the company grew, it shifted towards having engineers work alongside scientists in person to better understand their challenges. The change ultimately led to Oyewole’s layoff.
“We got laid off from Science because they were moving to a model where they needed engineers to be physically at the company,” he says. “They needed people who could interface with those scientists themselves to understand the pain points that the scientists were facing.”
His second international role was with Mars, best known for its chocolate brands. He joined the company’s Petcare brand as a frontend engineer on the Kinship team. The experience introduced him to a market with a very different attitude towards pets from what he was used to in Nigeria.
“When I joined Kinship US, I was the only Nigerian on my team. There was lots of culture shock, talking to different people, especially about pets,” he says. “Coming from Nigeria, where people don’t really care about pets as much as they do out there, joining the company meant you literally had to care for pets.”
His team built digital products for pet owners, including platforms connecting them with veterinarians and animal shelters, as well as tools for purchasing pet food and publishing pet-care content.
Kinship also gave Oyewole room to expand beyond frontend development. During regular check-ins, his manager encouraged him to discuss his career ambitions, and he expressed an interest in understanding the full software development lifecycle, from frontend and backend development to deployment.
“I might not be an expert at everything, but I wanted enough knowledge as an engineer to know how this works,” he says.
His manager responded by assigning him backend tasks, giving him opportunities to build features, review code, and work alongside backend engineers.
He also took on his first team leadership role, managing engineers across time zones and leading projects from start to finish.
“At that point, it was not just about writing code, but also being able to manage people,” he says. “It’s one thing to build for yourself. It’s another to manage people and scale quickly while you’re also building.”
He left the company in June 2026.
Beyond writing code
Over the years, Oyewole has come to see technology less as an end in itself and more as a tool for solving problems, a perspective shaped by his experience working across industries.
“I see technology as an enabler. I think of technology as something that could help your process,” he says. “It’s nice if you are building something cool, but what’s best is something that makes money for you.”
He believes engineers must look beyond the technical appeal of what they build to consider the value it delivers to businesses and their customers. That perspective also shapes the projects he explores outside his regular work.
Towards the end of 2025, as interest in artificial intelligence grew, Oyewole began experimenting with Model Context Protocol (MCP), a way of connecting AI applications to external tools and information. He built a tool that allowed AI assistants to search Nigerian e-commerce platforms and compare product prices, according to him. Inspired by his own experience of trying to find the most affordable options online, he built it to work with existing AI chatbots, such as ChatGPT, rather than as a standalone application.
He also explored how MCPs could improve his work as a frontend engineer, experimenting with connecting Figma, a design tool, to his team’s codebase to reduce the manual work involved in translating designs into code.
His interest in the wider tech community led him to open-source. While reading the MCP documentation, he came across an issue involving the addition of agent skills and joined the team working on it. This allowed him to contribute to the technology’s development while collaborating with engineers from companies including Amazon and Google, according to him.
He hopes to continue contributing to open-source projects and speaking at technology events, particularly those aimed at helping younger developers. He is also planning talks at secondary schools around Lagos to introduce students to technology careers, explain how the websites and applications they use are built, and highlight the opportunities available in the industry.
Beyond these interests, Oyewole’s next career goal is to take on greater responsibility for how software products are built and managed. Having spent most of his career as an individual contributor, he is increasingly interested in the decisions that go beyond writing code: choosing which features to build, balancing business priorities with technical constraints, and ensuring products solve customers’ problems.
“Over the past six years, I’ve come to realise that building great software goes beyond writing code,” he says. “There’s also the people, planning, decision-making and coordination required to turn an idea into a product.”
He hopes to take on more leadership responsibilities, from mentoring engineers and leading technical discussions to participating in product planning.
“I’d love to be remembered as someone who was always about solving problems in any industry,” he says. “I believe impact goes beyond the software we write.”

articles.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
articles.text:
Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
- Date:
- November 17, 2026
- Source:
- University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto
- Summary:
- A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.
- Share:
An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.
The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.
The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.
These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.
To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.
More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills
One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.
Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.
The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.
"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.
"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.
Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently
The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.
Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.
Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.
Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.
The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.
Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity
The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.
Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.
One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.
This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.
"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.
"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."
What the Eight-Year Study Revealed
The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.
The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.
Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.
To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.
Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.
Nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.
The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.
Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.
The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

articles.title: Humyn Labs raises $47M to bridge the gap between AI training and real-world robotics - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Humyn Labs raises $47M to bridge the gap between AI training and real-world robotics
Humyn Labs, a company turning human experience into training for robots and artificial intelligence, today announced it has raised $47 million in early-stage funding to accelerate intelligent robotic deployment readiness in real-world environments across Brazil, South Korea and India.
Accel led the $26 million equity portion of the round, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Finserv Intelligence through Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton and Jump Trading LLC. Lighthouse Canton led the remaining $21 million in venture debt, with participation from Trifecta Capital.
Founded in early 2026, Humyn’s proposal is that AI models for humanoid robots don’t learn dexterity from staged demonstrations; they must learn by observing how humans move in real environments. This provides actual behaviors showing how hands work on objects, reach, touch, handle and recover without explicit instructions.
Unlike generative AI models that learn from vast amounts of text, images and video, physical AI models must learn how to interact with the world around them. That means understanding not only what objects look like and where they are, but also how to manipulate them, how much force to apply and how to respond when something goes wrong.
“The results can be very, very, very dramatic and catastrophic,” co-founder and Chief Executive Manish Agarwal (pictured) told SiliconANGLE in an interview.
Agarwal pointed out how mistakes that might be inconsequential for a chatbot can have serious consequences for a robot operating alongside people. That makes access to diverse, high-quality data about how humans physically interact with their environments critical for training robots to work safely and reliably in the real world.
To address this, the company built a video corpus captured from head-mounted cameras as participants performed everyday household tasks, comprising up to 200,000 hours of intentional human motion. The company also shipped a dataset of 120,000 faces across five regions for facial recognition, including adjustments in lighting, pose, expression, glasses, hairstyle, facial hair, accessories, age and locale.
That’s combined with more than 50,000 hours of representative speech data for underserved language markets, including Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Odia, Assamese, Korean, Tagalog, Arabic, Vietnamese and Portuguese. Voice AI models that understand natural language already have vast amounts of data for widely spoken languages such as English, Mandarin or Spanish, but real-world customer support within South and Southeast Asian markets lacks routine coverage.
Humyn’s engine uses sound, sight, motion and touch as data inputs, which it curates, normalizes and labels so that AI models can understand the kinematics of motion, force and environmental factors. Together, this provides training patterns for physical AI models, world models, general foundation models, and audio and voice AI.
Bringing diversity to robotic data
Geographic diversity is also important because robots must understand the environments and cultural practices where they will operate. “Diversity gets you in the room. The quality ensures that you stay in the room,” Agarwal said.
To make this point, Agarwal emphasized the importance of geographic and cultural diversity in collecting training data. A household robot trained in the United States may struggle with tasks in an Indian home, where everything from cooking utensils and kitchen appliances to laundry practices and room layouts can differ. These regional differences mean that robots need experience with the specific environments and practices of the people they will eventually serve.
By collecting data across more than 20 countries, Humyn can train models on data that more closely resembles their intended deployments, potentially accelerating readiness for real-world work.
Agarwal added that the company is seeing interest from customers building household robots for domestic tasks and elder care, alongside industrial applications involving object manipulation and movement through factories, warehouses and commercial environments.
“The next phase in the deployment cycle is about how well these models perform in the wild,” Agarwal said.
In the end, data is only the beginning. Humyn wants to measure where robots fail in real-world conditions and use that to feed the AI flywheel and build better models. That means using virtual simulations, physical replicas and partnering with the enterprise and researchers to have field deployment labs to identify the differences between expected and actual performance.
The company said it intends to use the new funding to build deployment-readiness infrastructure in Brazil, South Korea and India, develop its hardware and enrichment engine, and expand its on-the-ground presence in San Francisco, London and Seoul. Agarwal said this will also involve testing robots in real-world environments to identify gaps between their expected performance and actual behavior, feeding those results back into model development.

articles.title: Sam Altman says his life is so weird that he's unfazed by Andrew Garfield portraying him in upcoming movie | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Hollywood has found plenty of material and cinematic inspiration from a string of Silicon Valley scandals and power struggles in recent years.
“You Can See Everything,” the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, smashed box office expectations, and Netflix’s limited series “The Altruists” comes out Thursday to tell the story of Sam Bankman-Fried and the downfall of FTX.
As the founder and CEO of OpenAI, one of the most influential companies of the century, Sam Altman isn’t going to escape the Hollywood treatment, either.
In “Artificial,” a biographical comedy-drama opening in theaters on Christmas, the lauded actor Andrew Garfield will portray Altman in a film that chronicles OpenAI’s rise and the internal turmoil that erupted when he was briefly ousted in 2023.
“If you had told me 20 years ago that someone was going to make a movie about me, I think that would have struck me as … that would have been a very weird thing,” Altman said onstage at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. “Now it doesn’t feel like it’s in like the top 10 weirdest things about my life.”
Garfield is best known for his role as Spider-Man, but his big break came in 2010, when he played Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in “The Social Network” alongside Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg. (That film also had a sequel of sorts this year called “The Social Reckoning,” but it bombed at the box office.)
So, if Altman isn’t fazed by the looming release of “Artificial,” what’s actually the weirdest thing in his life?
“The fact that we are ushering in this technology that we have all of these very real concerns about, and that we have, we find ourselves in a role of such significance and such responsibility to make that go well,” Altman said. “That’s a crazy situation to find yourself in.”
Sure, that is pretty weird, Sam. It’s also weird that you use ChatGPT for parenting advice and don’t respect olive oil. But I’d wager to say it’s even weirder that there’s an upcoming film about the time your colleagues briefly ousted you because they were concerned that you can’t be trusted.
Say what you want about Mark Zuckerberg (I certainly have), but at least he’s honest about what he thinks about “The Social Network.”
“It was weird, man,” Zuckerberg reflected on a podcast last year. “They got all these very specific details of what I was wearing, or these specific things correct, but then the whole narrative arc around my motivations and all this stuff were like, completely wrong … The whole arc is like, I’m somehow motivated by trying to find a girlfriend, [but] I was dating Priscilla [Chan] before I started Facebook.”
Zuckerberg said he knew his employees would be tempted to see the movie, so he organized a company outing when it was released, even though the film hardly paints a flattering portrait of him.
Zuckerberg even had enough of a sense of humor to buy a prop from the film at auction. He owns an Ardsley High School T-shirt that Eisenberg wore in the movie and even wore it himself in a video with YouTubers Colin and Samir.
Eisenberg hasn’t been particularly complimentary of Zuckerberg, saying that he doesn’t want to think of himself as “associated with somebody like that.” And while “Artificial” hasn’t hit theaters yet, Garfield doesn’t seem to have a much more favorable opinion of the tech founder he portrays.
“I don’t know Sam Altman. I’ve never met him,” Garfield told Esquire. “But I think anyone who takes on that level of responsibility for a company or technology that you know is going to do a hell of a lot of damage to the soul of humanity [must have] a certain ability to dissociate.”

There’s already loads to like about this 3D printer, and thanks to an early Black Friday sale it’s now available for $549 rather than $899.
Today’s best Creality K1 Max deal

The Creality K1 Max has a 300 x 300 x 300mm build volume and reaches speeds of 600mm/s. Its 300°C hotend supports materials including ABS, ASA, PETG and carbon-fiber-reinforced filaments.
AI monitoring, LiDAR calibration and automatic bed leveling simplify setup.

articles.title: One UI 9.5 ya está aquí: principales novedades y primeros móviles compatibles
articles.text:
Después de una larga espera, Samsung por fin está abriendo el acceso a One UI 9.5, la próxima versión de la capa de personalización que ejecuta sobre Android. El fabricante coreano ha puesto en marcha la beta del nuevo software, que desde hoy se encuentra disponible en sus móviles más importantes y que llega con características bastante interesantes.
Como no podía ser de otra manera, la beta de One UI 9.5 llega primero a los Galaxy S26, S26+ y S26 Ultra. Los usuarios interesados en sumarse al programa tienen que apuntarse a través de la aplicación Samsung Members. La actualización estará disponible inicialmente en un puñado de países, aunque se espera que su alcance se expanda con el correr de las semanas.
Respecto de novedades, One UI 9.5 trae adiciones para destacar en el inicio de la beta. Lo primero para mencionar es que el software incorpora un nuevo modo Pro tanto para la captura de fotos como para la grabación de vídeos. Este llega para ofrecer un control más granular sobre los ajustes de la cámara, algo que tanto entusiastas como creadores de contenido llevaban tiempo reclamando.
Otra característica importante que llega primero a los Galaxy S26 de la mano de One UI 9.5 es el bloqueo de apps con un PIN o datos biométricos. Si bien esta función dice presente en móviles Android de otras marcas, Samsung todavía no la había implementado de forma nativa en su capa de personalización. Esto significa que en adelante será posible blindar el acceso a una aplicación instalada a través de la huella dactilar o un código.
One UI 9.5 inicia su beta en los Samsung Galaxy S26
La beta de One UI 9.5 también introduce cambios en las funciones de salud a través de Samsung Health. Dicha app ahora incluye un apartado dedicado a medicamentos, con recordatorios y un registro para las tomas diarias. Asimismo, introduce una suerte de diario personal enfocado en el bienestar emocional.
El apartado de accesibilidad también se ve mejorado con One UI 9.5. La beta permite, por ejemplo, acceder a los controles para audífonos desde el panel de notificaciones. El software de la firma coreana también implementa los nuevos atajos flotantes, destinados a brindar acceso rápido y con un solo toque a controles de uso esencial.
Todavía no se sabe cuándo se expandirá la versión de pruebas de One UI 9.5 a otros dispositivos que no sean los Galaxy S26. No obstante, Samsung suele ser bastante ágil para abrir su software a un mayor número de modelos cuando la beta ya está en marcha. Los primeros países en recibir el software son Estados Unidos, Reino Unido, Polonia, Alemania, India y Corea del Sur, pero se expandirá a otros mercados con el paso de los días.

articles.title: Robotaxi-Premiere in München: So kommst du jetzt in ein selbstfahrendes Uber
articles.text:
Robotaxi-Premiere in München: So kommst du jetzt in ein selbstfahrendes Uber
Im Rennen um selbstfahrende Taxis in Deutschland liefern sich zwei Regionen – München und Berlin – einen spannenden Wettlauf. Während der US-Elektroautohersteller Tesla vor den Toren Berlins eine Milliardenfabrik für künftige Robotaxis hochziehen will, rollen in der bayerischen Landeshauptstadt bereits die Testflotten durch den Stadtverkehr: Heute starteten der Fahrdienstvermittler Uber und der chinesische KI-Spezialist Momenta in München ein gemeinsames Pilotprojekt für autonome Fahrten.
Bei der Premiere an der Straße „Am Oberwiesenfeld“ nördlich des Münchner Olympiaparks gaben die Partner den Startschuss für den Testbetrieb für Kunden mit Sicherheitsbegleitung. Fahrgäste in München können sich ab sofort über die Uber-App auf eine Interessentenliste setzen lassen.
Ausgewählte Nutzerinnen und Nutzer, die im Münchner Norden eine Fahrt über die Optionen UberX, Electric oder Comfort buchen, können nun ein autonomes Fahrzeug vermittelt bekommen – Ein- und Ausstieg erfolgen an festgelegten Haltepunkten.
Das Angebot ist zunächst kostenlos, bei jeder Fahrt sitzt eine Sicherheitskraft mit an Bord, die aber nur in Ausnahmen steuernd eingreift. Grundlage sind Level-4-Erprobungsgenehmigungen des Kraftfahrt-Bundesamts.
München ist Europas Testlabor – im Raum Berlin entsteht die Fabrik
Mit dem Start festigt München seine Rolle als wichtigstes europäisches Testlabor für den praktischen Einsatz autonomer Fahrzeuge. Neben Uber und Momenta erprobt Uber in der Stadt bereits ein zweites Robotaxi-System mit dem KI-Unternehmen Autobrains und dem Chipkonzern Nvidia.
Zudem kartiert die Google-Schwesterfirma Waymo seit dem Herbst das Münchner Stadtgebiet, um Ende 2027 einen regulären fahrerlosen Fahrdienst in Betrieb zu nehmen. Und im öffentlichen Nahverkehr sind im Rahmen des Projekts MINGA bereits erste Testfahrgäste auf der regulären MVG-Buslinie 178 in einem autonom fahrenden Elektrobus unterwegs.
Während in München der Alltag im komplexen Stadtverkehr trainiert wird, setzt die Hauptstadtregion einen industriellen Kontrapunkt: Am Montag hatte Tesla angekündigt, drei Milliarden Euro in den Ausbau seines Werks im brandenburgischen Grünheide bei Berlin zu investieren. Dort soll ab 2029 das eigene, komplett lenkrad- und pedallose Robotaxi «Cybercab» in Großserie vom Band rollen – mit einer Zielkapazität von bis zu einer Million Fahrzeugen pro Jahr.
Technik-Wettstreit: Teure Laser-Sensoren gegen Kamera-Systeme
Hinter den Projekten steht zugleich ein grundlegender Systemstreit der Entwickler, wie sich ein Auto überhaupt sicher durch den Verkehr navigieren lässt: Sowohl Momenta als auch der US-Pionier Waymo setzen auf maximal abgesicherte Technik. Ihre Fahrzeuge kombinieren hochauflösende Kameras und Radarsensoren mit sogenannten Lidar-Sensoren, die die Umgebung mit Hilfe von Laserstrahlen dreidimensional und zentimetergenau abtasten.
Momenta verknüpft diese Technik zudem mit Daten aus mehr als 1,4 Millionen Serienfahrzeugen von Herstellern wie Mercedes-Benz, BMW, Audi und Volkswagen, für die das Unternehmen bereits Fahrerassistenzsysteme liefert.
Einen radikal anderen und deutlich günstigeren Weg verfolgen Tesla sowie Ubers zweiter Münchner Partner Autobrains. Beide verzichten komplett auf teure Lidar-Sensoren. Während Tesla bei seinem «Cybercab» ausschließlich auf acht Kameras und neuronale Netze setzt, nutzt das System von Autobrains lediglich sechs Kameras und gleicht deren Bilder in Echtzeit mit Luftbildern ab.
Internationaler Wettlauf: USA, China und Golfstaaten sind voraus
„Deutschlands strenger Regulierungsansatz, bei dem Sicherheit an erster Stelle steht, hat einen der weltweiten Maßstäbe für autonomes Fahren gesetzt“, sagte Momenta-Manager Shuo Xie zum Start in München. Während hierzulande allerdings noch mit Sicherheitsfahrern geprobt wird, gehören komplett fahrerlose Taxis in anderen Teilen der Welt längst zum regulären Straßenbild.
Vorreiter sind die USA und China: In US-Metropolen wie San Francisco, Phoenix, Los Angeles und Austin betreibt vor allem die Google-Schwester Waymo kommerzielle Flotten ohne Sicherheitsbegleitung.
In chinesischen Millionenstädten wie Peking, Wuhan oder Guangzhou bieten Tech-Konzerne wie Baidu (mit dem Dienst Apollo Go) sowie Spezialisten wie Pony.ai und WeRide längst reguläre App-Fahrten ohne Mensch am Steuer an.
Auch am Persischen Golf schreitet die Kommerzialisierung rasant voran: In den Vereinigten Arabischen Emiraten, insbesondere in Abu Dhabi und Dubai, sind bereits vollautonome Robotaxis – teils ebenfalls in Kooperation mit der Uber-Plattform – im regulären Fahrgastbetrieb unterwegs, um den öffentlichen Nahverkehr zu ergänzen.
Innerhalb Europas sorgte zudem ein Projekt in der kroatischen Hauptstadt Zagreb für Aufsehen: Dort bietet das vom Elektro-Supersportwagen-Pionier Mate Rimac mitgegründete Start-up Verne seit diesem Jahr über Uber erste kostenpflichtige Robotaxi-Fahrten an und erprobt auf einer Teststrecke zum Flughafen bereits Fahrten komplett ohne Sicherheitsfahrer – greift dafür nach Verzögerungen bei der eigenen Fahrzeugentwicklung allerdings auf umgebaute chinesische Elektroautos und Software des Anbieters Pony.ai zurück.
