articles.title: Amazon Family arrive en France : partager Prime avec un adulte de son foyer, sans supplément ni partage de mot de passe
articles.text:
Recevoir un mail qui promet des avantages Amazon Prime gratuits a souvent l’air d’un piège. Au printemps 2025, des escrocs ont ainsi envoyé de faux messages Amazon Prime contenant l’IBAN des abonnés de Free, récupérés lors d’une fuite de données. Cette fois pourtant, l’offre est bien réelle.
Amazon a lancé ce mardi 17 novembre 2026 Amazon Family en France, une fonction qui permet à un membre Prime d’inviter un second adulte de son foyer sans payer de supplément. Autrement dit, une seule personne paie l’abonnement Prime, à 6,99 euros par mois ou 69,90 euros par an, et deux adultes en profitent.
Chacun garde son propre compte, avec son historique de commandes et ses recommandations, sans partager de mot de passe. L’invité récupère la livraison Prime gratuite sur les articles éligibles, Amazon Music Prime, le jeu vidéo en streaming d’Amazon Luna et les promotions réservées aux membres, comme le Prime Day. Prime Video fait partie du lot, mais seulement avec publicités et pour le catalogue inclus dans l’abonnement.
En revanche, la liste officielle ne cite pas les offres partenaires, comme les 120 euros qu’EDF rembourse aux membres Prime qui souscrivent chez elle un contrat d’électricité.
Comment activer Amazon Family en 3 étapes
Tout se passe depuis le compte de l’abonné Prime, comme le détaille Frandroid :
- Ouvrez « Votre compte » sur Amazon.fr, puis la rubrique « Votre Amazon Family » ;
- Indiquez le nom et l’adresse e-mail de la personne ;
- L’invité recevra un mail, et devra accepter l’invitation pour accéder aussitôt aux avantages partagés.
Avant d’inviter quelqu’un, sachez que l’abonné qui envoie l’invitation, appelé administrateur Amazon Family, doit choisir un moyen de paiement à partager. L’invité peut s’en servir, mais il n’en voit que les quatre derniers chiffres, le nom du titulaire, la date d’expiration et l’adresse de facturation.
L’administrateur reçoit une notification avec le montant de chaque achat payé de cette façon. « Chaque membre d’Amazon Family reste libre de payer une commande avec le moyen de paiement partagé ou avec le sien », précise le communiqué d’Amazon.
Méfiez-vous d’une invitation qu’aucun proche ne vous aurait annoncée. En cas de doute, ne cliquez jamais sur le lien d’un mail et passez directement par votre compte Amazon ou par la page d’aide d’Amazon Family.

articles.title: From Metrology To Autonomy: Scaling Yield, Quality, And Innovation
articles.text:
Operationalizing intelligence across the manufacturing stack begins with trusted data.
With the growth of increasingly complex devices, improving yield, quality, and manufacturing speed requires a new approach. Across 14 presentations and posters presented at SEMICON West 2026, Intel Foundry leaders and engineers shared research and emerging solutions for the AI-ready foundry of the future. By combining end-to-end metrology, intelligent analytics, and industry-wide standards, we can unlock scalable innovation for our customers.
Semiconductor manufacturing is shifting from isolated optimization to connected intelligence, according to Intel Foundry’s Lalitha Immaneni, vice president of semiconductor research and development, advanced packaging technology and manufacturing (APTM), in her keynote at the conference. Factory autonomy will not emerge from AI alone. It requires a system-first mindset based on a common foundation of trusted measurements, interoperable platforms, and advanced test infrastructure.¹
For decades, metrology has served as a critical manufacturing checkpoint. Today, it is evolving into a control layer for proactive yield management. Modern semiconductor manufacturing demands more advanced metrology and defect control to address rising contamination risks, process sensitivities, and defectivity challenges. Hidden interactions among materials, equipment, chemicals, packaging polymers, and fab environments can undermine yield and often go undetected until late-stage manufacturing, increasing costs and slowing production. Rather than reacting to failures after they occur, semiconductor manufacturers like Intel Foundry are using predictive process control supported by continuous measurement and monitoring.²
The requirement for end-to-end visibility does not stop at wafer fabrication. The industry’s transition toward heterogeneous integration has introduced increasingly complex architectures built on chiplets, hybrid bonding, high-bandwidth memory, and advanced 2.5D and 3D packaging technologies. These innovations are blurring the traditional boundaries between front-end manufacturing and back-end assembly. Today’s advanced packaging environments require the same level of process intelligence found in leading-edge wafer fabs, such as nanometer-scale precision, process control discipline, and quality assurance capabilities.³
Test operations increasingly represent the final extension of this measurement strategy. Intel Foundry’s Advanced Chiplet Test services provide wafer-to-system test coverage designed to identify issues early, enable known-good die selection, and optimize back-end yield before expensive assembly operations begin. Through predictive die classification, intelligent die pairing, integrated optical testing, and closed-loop yield analytics, test data becomes a critical input for manufacturing intelligence.
Our work on automatic defect classification (ADC) illustrates how AI can help accelerate yield learning and turn complexity into productivity. Managing thousands of classification recipes across multiple technology nodes and manufacturing sites is increasingly difficult, so engineers developed a human-in-the-loop agentic workflow to assist with log analysis, knowledge retrieval, root cause investigation, and recipe reviews. AI-generated recommendations, combined with human approval checkpoints, speed investigations while maintaining auditability and engineering oversight.⁴
We’re also exploring new approaches to thermal intelligence. Our research combines AI with heat-transfer physics to predict how heat moves through semiconductor devices more accurately and with less training data.⁵ This research complements Intel Foundry’s broader investments in advanced test and reliability methodologies, including system-level testing, burn-in, and precision thermal control for increasingly power-dense AI and heterogeneous computing devices. Together, these capabilities help engineers identify yield limiters earlier, reduce manufacturing variability, and make faster, more reliable decisions across the production flow.
Precision measurements and intelligent analytics are key components, but scaling in high volume manufacturing requires a modern digital infrastructure. Traditional vendor-locked automation systems often create data silos that limit operational visibility and slow decision-making. By adopting hardware-independent automation architectures, connected data systems, and AI-enabled edge computing, manufacturers can reduce engineering cycles, lower operating costs, and enable predictive maintenance and AI-driven quality inspection.⁶
Finally, autonomy cannot be achieved by technology innovation alone. Industry standards will play a pivotal role. The Semiconductor Assembly Test Automation and Standardization Research Association (SATAS) consortium brings together more than 40 organizations to develop open standards, interoperable architectures, and automation frameworks that can be adopted across the global semiconductor industry, helping to move semiconductor manufacturing from highly automated operations toward true factory autonomy.
SATAS is a multi-year industry initiative sponsored by Japan’s New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO) and the Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry (METI). Intel Foundry is helping advance interoperable architectures, automation frameworks, material-handling standards, and collaborative pilot environments that can accelerate back-end manufacturing transformation. By enabling a more connected and interoperable semiconductor ecosystem, Intel Foundry is making it easier for customers and partners to integrate processes, automate workflows, and adopt next-generation manufacturing capabilities.⁷
Operationalizing intelligence across the manufacturing stack is getting closer to reality. It begins with end-to-end metrology and trusted data. It extends through explainable, physics-informed AI and advanced failure analysis methodologies. It relies on resilient automation, edge computing, and advanced packaging platforms. And it scales through ecosystem-wide standards and interoperability. Together, these capabilities help customers lead in the next era of manufacturing.

articles.title: Cristina Bayés, consultora e ingeniera industrial: "Decir que dejar la calefacción constantemente encendida sirve para ahorrar es falso"
articles.text:
Apagar la calefacción cuando vamos a pasar muchas horas fuera de casa ahorra energía, y mantenerla encendida mientras no hay nadie para no tener que volver a calentar la vivienda no compensa, salvo en algún caso concreto. Eso es lo que contó la ingeniera industrial Cristina Bayés, de la consultora Anthesis, en el pódcast ‘Futuro sostenible’ de BBVA en enero de 2024.
Cuándo conviene apagarla. La recomendación principal de Bayés es apagar los sistemas de climatización si vas a pasar muchas horas fuera, porque mantenerlos en marcha durante ese tiempo implica gastar energía en calentar una casa en la que no hay nadie. Pero la ingeniera hace una excepción con la calefacción por suelo radiante, que aconseja dejar encendida a una temperatura baja debido a su inercia térmica. Vamos, que este sistema tarda bastante en calentarse y también en perder el calor que ha acumulado, de modo que no se puede regular igual que unos radiadores convencionales.
Según explica en el mismo pódcast, la eficiencia de la climatización depende en buena medida de lo eficiente que sea el equipo que tengamos en casa, y el aislamiento de la vivienda también pesa a la hora de elegirlo. Además, no todas las casas ni todas las instalaciones responden igual cuando apagamos la calefacción y la volvemos a encender.
El termostato, entre 19 y 22 grados. Para los meses de frío, Bayés recomienda tener la calefacción entre los 19 y los 22 grados, un margen con el que se puede estar a gusto sin que el consumo se dispare, y calcula que bajarla un solo grado permite ahorrar en torno a un 8% de energía. Se trata de una estimación orientativa, y de hecho el Instituto para la Diversificación y Ahorro de la Energía (IDAE) sitúa ese ahorro aproximado en un 7% por cada grado de variación.
En verano pasa algo parecido con el aire acondicionado, que la ingeniera aconseja mantener entre los 25 y los 27 grados. En este caso, según sus palabras, “cada grado de más supone un ahorro de energía de alrededor del 10%”.
Ventilar sin tirar el calor. Ventilar sigue siendo necesario en invierno, pero hacerlo con la calefacción funcionando significa perder parte de la energía que estamos pagando mientras entra el aire frío de la calle. Por eso Bayés prefiere que las ventanas se abran con los sistemas de climatización apagados y, si están encendidos, considera que con cinco o diez minutos es suficiente.
A eso se suma otro consejo, el de aprovechar los periodos de mayor temperatura exterior para abrir las ventanas. Así se reduce la diferencia de temperatura entre el interior y el exterior de la vivienda.
Aislamiento, rendijas y radiadores. Más allá de lo que cuenta Bayés, hay otros gestos que ayudan a gastar menos, empezando por mejorar el aislamiento, que la guía práctica de la energía del IDAE señala como una de las vías para ahorrar en calefacción. Cuando el frío se cuela por las rendijas de puertas y ventanas, la misma guía propone taparlas con medios sencillos y baratos, como los burletes.
También echan una mano las cortinas y las alfombras en las habitaciones más frías, que según la OCU ayudan a subir la temperatura, y en el caso de las alfombras también mejoran el aislamiento. Y en cuanto al mantenimiento, el IDAE recomienda en su lista de consejos purgar los radiadores al menos una vez al año, al empezar la temporada de calefacción, para que el agua caliente circule bien, además de limpiar de forma periódica los filtros del aire acondicionado.
Sol de día, persianas de noche. Otro truco que no cuesta nada es dejar las persianas subidas durante el día en las fachadas donde da el sol, tal y como aconseja la misma OCU, para que su calor entre en casa de forma natural. Cuando anochece toca hacer lo contrario, porque el IDAE recomienda cerrar persianas y cortinas por la noche para evitar pérdidas importantes de calor a través de los cristales.
Por último, abrigarse un poco dentro de casa antes de tocar el termostato es otra manera de mantener el confort sin aumentar el consumo, algo que el mismo organismo también recoge cuando menciona la ropa adecuada entre sus recomendaciones.
En cualquier caso, el ahorro final de todos estos hábitos dependerá del tipo de vivienda, de las temperaturas que haga fuera y del sistema de climatización instalado.

articles.title: 10 polite ways to set boundaries with family and colleagues
articles.text:
10 polite ways to set boundaries with family and colleagues
Discover 10 polite ways to set boundaries with family and colleagues while protecting your time, energy, personal space and emotional well-being.
Setting boundaries is an important part of maintaining healthy relationships, but it is not always easy. Saying no to a family member, declining an extra task at work or asking someone to respect your personal space can sometimes feel uncomfortable. Many people worry that setting boundaries will make them appear rude, selfish or uncooperative.
However, boundaries are not about pushing people away. They help establish mutual respect and make relationships more balanced. Whether you are dealing with family expectations or workplace demands, learning to communicate your limits calmly can protect your time, energy and well-being.
Here are 10 polite ways to set boundaries without creating unnecessary conflict.
1. Say no without giving lengthy explanations
You do not have to justify every decision with a detailed explanation. If a family member asks you to attend an event or a colleague requests help when you are already busy, you can politely decline.
Try saying, "Thank you for asking, but I won't be able to manage it this time." A short and respectful response communicates your decision without making the conversation unnecessarily complicated.
2. Be clear about your availability
Constant calls, messages and last-minute requests can make it difficult to protect your personal time. Let people know when you are available and when you need to focus on other responsibilities.
For example, you could tell a colleague, "I usually respond to work messages during office hours. I'll get back to you tomorrow morning." Similarly, let family members know when you need uninterrupted time for work, studies or rest.
3. Avoid taking responsibility for everyone's emotions
It is natural to care about how others feel, but you cannot make every person happy all the time. Sometimes, people may feel disappointed when you decline a request or express a different opinion.
Instead of changing your decision out of guilt, acknowledge their feelings while maintaining your position. You can say, "I understand that this is important to you, but I still need to make the decision that works for me."
4. Keep work and personal life separate
Workplace communication can easily extend beyond office hours, especially when colleagues expect immediate responses. However, being responsible at work does not mean being available around the clock.
Politely communicate your working hours and avoid responding to non-urgent requests during your personal time. You can say, "I'd be happy to discuss this during working hours tomorrow." This creates a professional boundary without sounding unhelpful.
5. Speak up when someone makes uncomfortable comments
Family gatherings and workplace conversations sometimes involve personal remarks about appearance, relationships, salary or lifestyle choices. Even when people claim they are joking, repeated comments can become uncomfortable.
Instead of ignoring your feelings, communicate your discomfort calmly. Try saying, "I know you may not mean it negatively, but I'd prefer not to discuss this topic." Being respectful does not mean you have to accept every comment.
6. Stop agreeing to tasks beyond your capacity
Taking on every responsibility may make you seem dependable, but it can eventually lead to stress and exhaustion. Before accepting an additional task, consider your existing commitments and available time.
At work, you can say, "I can take this up, but I'll need to revisit the timeline for my current tasks." With family, try saying, "I would like to help, but I already have a few responsibilities to manage today." This communicates your limits while keeping the conversation constructive.
7. Ask for privacy and personal space
Healthy relationships also require respect for individual privacy. Family members may sometimes expect access to personal conversations, belongings or decisions, while colleagues may ask questions that feel too personal.
You can politely communicate what you are comfortable sharing. For example, say, "I'd prefer to keep that matter private" or "I need some time to myself right now." You can value your relationships while maintaining personal space.
8. Avoid discussing sensitive topics when you are uncomfortable
Not every conversation needs to happen immediately. If someone brings up a sensitive subject when you are tired, upset or unprepared, it is reasonable to ask for another time.
Try saying, "I'd rather discuss this when we both have more time" or "I'm not comfortable talking about this right now." This helps prevent emotionally charged conversations and gives everyone an opportunity to communicate more thoughtfully.
9. Be consistent with the boundaries you establish
Setting a boundary once may not be enough if people are used to you always agreeing. They may need time to understand that your response has changed.
For instance, if you have communicated that you cannot take work calls after office hours, try not to repeatedly make exceptions for non-urgent matters. Consistency helps others understand your expectations and reduces confusion over time.
10. Communicate your expectations before problems arise
Boundaries are easier to maintain when people understand your expectations early. Rather than waiting until you feel overwhelmed, have open conversations about your availability, responsibilities and personal preferences.
You might tell your family that you need a specific period for uninterrupted study or let your colleagues know how much time you need to complete an assignment. Clear communication can prevent misunderstandings and make everyday interactions smoother.
Final thoughts
Setting boundaries with family and colleagues does not mean being distant, unkind or difficult to work with. It means understanding your limits and communicating them in a respectful way.
You may not always receive an immediate positive response, and some people may need time to adjust. However, you do not have to abandon your needs simply to avoid disappointing others.
Start with small changes, use calm language and remain consistent. Healthy boundaries allow you to maintain meaningful relationships while making enough room for your own priorities, personal space and well-being.

articles.title: Los siete fundadores de Anthropic que están a punto de volverse multimillonarios con la salida a bolsa de la empresa
articles.text:
Anthropic, la empresa de inteligencia artificial que desarrolla Claude, prevé debutar el jueves en el Nasdaq bajo el símbolo “ANT”. Según The Wall Street Journal, cada uno de sus siete cofundadores posee participaciones valuadas en torno a USD 18.000 millones, tras obtener USD 250 millones en ganancias.
La compañía se constituyó formalmente en enero de 2021, después de que un grupo de exintegrantes de OpenAI la abandonara en diciembre de 2020 ante diferencias sobre los riesgos del desarrollo acelerado de la inteligencia artificial. En menos de seis años, creció hasta convertirse en uno de los laboratorios más influyentes del sector.
Sus siete cofundadores son todos millennials e incluyen dos hermanos, tres doctores, un experiodista y un estudiante que abandonó la universidad, con intereses que van desde la biología hasta el punk rock y la teología.
Dario Amodei, el CEO con doctorado en biofísica que dejó OpenAI para fundar Anthropic
Dario Amodei, de 43 años y director ejecutivo de Anthropic, es doctor en biofísica y realizó estudios de posgrado en la Facultad de Medicina de Stanford con foco en oncología. Pasó por Baidu y Google antes de que Sam Altman lo reclutara para OpenAI en 2016.
Con el tiempo, ambos discreparon sobre los riesgos del desarrollo acelerado de la IA, lo que derivó en la salida de Amodei y en la fundación de Anthropic, según The Wall Street Journal.
Daniela Amodei, presidenta y directora de la junta que aprendió a negociar con su hermano desde la infancia
Daniela Amodei, de 39 años y presidenta de Anthropic, estudió literatura en la Universidad de California en Santa Cruz y trabajó en política y en Stripe antes de sumarse a OpenAI, donde se desempeñó en gestión y como vicepresidenta de Seguridad y Políticas.
Hoy encabeza el enfoque en seguridad de la empresa, con especial énfasis en evitar que sus sistemas sean utilizados para desarrollar armas químicas o biológicas, según el diario.
Christopher Olah y la interpretabilidad: entender qué ocurre dentro de los modelos de IA de “caja negra”
Christopher Olah, de 34 años, lidera la investigación sobre interpretabilidad, la disciplina que busca comprender por qué los sistemas de IA —llamados de “caja negra” por la opacidad de sus procesos internos— funcionan de determinada manera. Abandonó la universidad sin graduarse y se convirtió en una referencia del campo.
Su trabajo lo llevó a organizar encuentros con líderes religiosos para debatir la posibilidad de que los sistemas de IA tengan alguna forma de conciencia, y a reunirse con el papa León XIV, quien advirtió que la tecnología podría generar nuevas formas de esclavitud.
Tom Brown, el arquitecto de acuerdos que conecta a Anthropic con el Pentágono y Silicon Valley
Tom Brown, de 39 años y director de computación de Anthropic, es graduado del MIT y codesarrolló junto a Dario Amodei uno de los conceptos técnicos que permite a los sistemas de IA comunicarse de forma conversacional. Su rol actual abarca la negociación de acuerdos de chips, la representación informal de la empresa en Washington y el manejo de vínculos institucionales delicados.
Según el diario, aprovechó su afiliación republicana para desactivar tensiones con la administración Trump y negoció directamente con el Pentágono para evitar que Anthropic quedara excluida del mercado estadounidense.
Jack Clark, el experiodista de tecnología que hoy define la política de IA en el Instituto Anthropic
Jack Clark, de 38 años, llegó a la inteligencia artificial desde el periodismo: fue reportero de tecnología en Bloomberg Businessweek antes de trabajar en comunicaciones de OpenAI y luego dirigir las políticas de Anthropic.
Hoy encabeza el Instituto Anthropic, un centro de estudios dedicado a comprender las consecuencias de los sistemas de IA potentes. Según The Wall Street Journal, Clark definió su posición con claridad en una conferencia en Bangkok: “la singularidad ya está aquí”.
Jared Kaplan, el físico de Harvard que escribió las leyes que gobiernan el crecimiento de los modelos de IA
Jared Kaplan, de 42 años y director científico de Anthropic, es físico teórico y docente en la Universidad Johns Hopkins desde 2012, donde sus intereses de investigación van de la gravedad cuántica al aprendizaje automático. Estudió física y matemáticas en Stanford antes de doctorarse en física en Harvard.
En 2019, como consultor de OpenAI, coautoró “Leyes de escalado para modelos de lenguaje neuronal”, artículo de referencia que establece cómo la capacidad de procesamiento, los datos de entrenamiento y las variables matemáticas de un modelo influyen en el desempeño de un sistema de IA: a mayor tamaño y entrenamiento, mejores resultados.
En Anthropic, Kaplan amplió este trabajo y desarrolló formas de gobernar sistemas de IA con una “constitución”: reglas predefinidas que orientan el comportamiento del modelo y limitan respuestas para evitar que se descontrolen.
Sam McCandlish, el arquitecto jefe que define los parámetros de los nuevos modelos de Claude
Sam McCandlish, de 36 años y arquitecto jefe de Anthropic, supervisa el desarrollo de los parámetros de los nuevos modelos: las variables matemáticas internas que determinan cómo aprende y responde un sistema de IA.
Doctor en física por Stanford, comparte con Kaplan la autoría del artículo sobre las leyes de escalado. Su trabajo define el núcleo técnico de cada nueva versión de Claude, según el diario.

articles.title: Han pesado la Vía Láctea con una precisión nunca vista: 1,19 billones de veces la masa del Sol
articles.text:
Pesar la Vía Láctea no es sencillo. Se pueden hacer estimaciones analizando el brillo de las estrellas que la componen. Están bastante bien cartografiadas, así que sería algo alcanzable. Sin embargo, la mayor parte de la masa de nuestra galaxia está compuesta por la enigmática materia oscura, de modo que toda esa masa se quedaría fuera. La alternativa es analizar el movimiento de las estrellas del halo galáctico, ya que este está perturbado por la influencia gravitatoria del conjunto total de la galaxia. Hasta ahora, se habían hecho algunas estimaciones al respecto, pero contaban con un porcentaje de error bastante alto. Sin embargo, una nueva medición, llevada a cabo con datos de DESI y Gaia, ha aportado una cifra muchísimo más precisa.
El equipo perfecto. DESI (Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument) es una colaboración internacional que se encarga principalmente de cartografiar el Universo en 3D para estudiar la energía oscura. Entre sus instrumentos destacan los espectrógrafos, capaces de descomponer la luz proveniente de las estrellas y analizar tanto su composición como parte de su movimiento. Según el efecto Doppler, si la estrella se aleja de nosotros su espectro se desplaza hacia el rojo, mientras que si se acerca lo hace hacia el azul. Por su parte, Gaia es un telescopio europeo que mide con precisión las posiciones de las estrellas a lo largo de los años.
Al poner en común los datos de ambos proyectos se puede analizar el movimiento de las estrellas de una forma muy precisa. Con Gaia analizamos su desplazamiento por el cielo y con DESI se ve si se alejan o se acercan. Todo esto, en conjunto, es lo que ha servido a estos científicos para pesar la Vía Láctea.
Más preciso que nunca. Los autores del preprint que se acaba de publicar analizaron más de 10.000 estrellas distantes observadas por DESI durante sus tres primeros años. Estas se encontraban a distintas distancias, entre unos 30.000 y 310.000 años luz del centro galáctico. Después, combinaron estos datos con los movimientos en el cielo medidos por Gaia de las mismas estrellas.Las estrellas eran de dos tipos: estrellas de la rama horizontal azul (BHB) y estrellas RR Lyrae (RRL). Ambas son estrellas viejas, típicas del halo galáctico, que se encuentran en una fase tardía de su vida, y son muy útiles porque su brillo intrínseco es conocido o muy predecible. Si sabes cuánta luz emite realmente una estrella y mides cuánta luz te llega, la diferencia te dice a qué distancia está.
Con toda esta información sobre las posiciones y velocidades de las estrellas, utilizaron cuatro modelos, previamente calibrados con galaxias simuladas desde cuatro puntos de vista. Esto permitió extrapolar el movimiento de las estrellas a la masa total de la galaxia de una forma bastante precisa.
Los datos. Se calculó que la masa de la Vía Láctea sería de 1,19 billones de masas solares, con una incertidumbre de en torno al 11%. Esto incluye tanto materia oscura como ordinaria. Además, para la materia situada a menos de unos 260.000 años luz del centro, la incertidumbre baja al 8%.
No tan redonda. Los cuatro métodos que se usaron para analizar los datos de las estrellas de la Vía Láctea tienen en cuenta una conformación esférica de la galaxia, ya que eso simplifica mucho los cálculos. Sin embargo, las seis galaxias con las que se calibró eran realistas y, por lo tanto, no esféricas. Dado que las galaxias se habían simulado para la ocasión, los científicos sabían cuál es su masa. Al pasarlas por los modelos, no obtuvieron esa masa, ya que contemplaban una galaxia redonda, por lo que obtuvieron un error. Esa calibración permitió establecer el error que se debe eliminar para obtener los datos realistas cuando se analice la Vía Láctea.
Eso es lo que les ha permitido analizarla con más precisión que nunca; pero, además, les ha dado información útil para futuras investigaciones. De aquí en adelante, nuestra propia galaxia debería contemplarse en los modelos de una forma más realista y, por lo tanto, menos esférica.
En el futuro. Estos científicos esperan afinar la masa del halo exterior con estrellas aún más lejanas y más datos de Gaia. Además, el segundo conjunto de datos de DESI, a partir del que se ha hecho este estudio, será de dominio público pronto, así que cualquier astrónomo podrá contribuir a los cálculos. Quizás en un futuro tengamos mediciones aún mejores. De momento, la que han obtenido ahora es mucho mejor que cualquiera que se haya obtenido jamás.
Imagen |PHILIPPE SERRAND

articles.title: AMD teases mystery CES 2027 announcement: Zen 6, RDNA 5, or yet more AI?
articles.text:
What just happened? CES 2027 is a little over a month away, and AMD has already teased an announcement it has planned for the event. But the mysterious A-shaped/peaked motif that the company published doesn't give much away. It could be the RDNA 5 GPUs, the upcoming Zen 6 processors, or maybe even new laptop CPUs. Sadly, it could also be another AI-related announcement that almost nobody cares about.
Jack Huynh, AMD's SVP and GM of Computing and Graphics, posted the teaser on his official X account. He's certainly building up the reveal as something special, talking about "the next era of computing" and "creating a future filled with possibilities we once only dreamed of."
 – Jack Huynh (@jackhuynh) November 17, 2026
A lot of speculation points to this being an RDNA 5 announcement. That presumes that the A-shaped image is a reference to AT, or Alpha Trion, the codename for AMD's next-gen graphics chips: AT0, AT2, AT3 and AT4.
But most people think the post relates to Olympic Ridge, the codename for the Zen 6-powered Ryzen desktop CPU. That does seem possible, given that AMD announced general availability of the Zen 6 EPYC SP7 processors only a few weeks ago.
It could be that AMD is hinting at an unveiling of the new Zen 6 laptop processors. The way the line in the video swings around and opens like a hinge does suggest this is the case, and AMD is developing Medusa Point and Gator Range mobile processors that are expected to arrive next year.
Then there is the final, and sadly most likely, explanation. The symbol in the clip does start as a single line, like an "I," before opening into an "A." Yes, this could be yet another AI-related announcement, possibly something to do with AI agents. The language Huynh uses in his post certainly aligns with the hyperbole we so often hear when companies talk about AI, unfortunately.
AMD certainly had plenty to say about AI at CES this January. Alongside the Ryzen AI 400 chips for Copilot+ laptops, the company showed off Ryzen AI Halo, a mini PC that AMD said could run AI models with up to 200 billion parameters locally. Lisa Su also gave attendees a look at Helios, a server rack pairing Instinct MI455X GPUs with Zen 6 Epyc processors.
AMD's recent financial report showed its gaming revenue had crashed 40% while data center revenue jumped 97% to $8.5 billion, prompting CEO Lisa Su to declare that "we are a data center-first company." A few days later, AMD Gaming posted a message asking gamers to remember Radeon loyalty.

articles.title: Tesla’s $30,000 Cybercab comes with a $299 monthly catch
articles.text:
There is always a catch. Or in the case of Tesla’s self-driving Cybercab, several.
Last Friday night, Tesla said it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs. The two-seat, gold vehicle is unlike any other on the market: It lacks a steering wheel and brake pedals, and is primarily driven by software. (Other autonomous vehicle companies, including Alphabet’s Waymo and Amazon’s Zoox, offer self-driving rides on ride-hail networks, but don’t let people buy their cars.) Tesla’s “limited release” will supposedly offer some people (unclear how many) the opportunity to pay $29,900 to take delivery in December.
From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road.
The business model raises questions about what people will actually get when they buy a Cybercab. “You’ll never really own the car,” says Ivan Drury, the director of insights at Edmunds. “It’s more like $30,000 to buy into a franchise.”
According to documents posted on Tesla’s website, the vehicle “will not operate” without what Tesla is calling an “autonomy subscription,” a monthly fee that will start at $299. If owners don’t pay on time and in full, their self-driving cars won’t work. If they try to operate the vehicles in areas that don’t support the service—right now, they’re restricted to portions of cities in Florida and Texas—their self-driving cars won’t work. (That area can expand, contract, or “relocate” at any time.)
If owners do anything that Tesla deems “unauthorized or inappropriate,” the company says it can suspend or cancel the subscription—and their self-driving cars won’t work. If the vehicle loses connectivity, the self-driving cars won’t work. (“Tesla is not responsible for carrier, spectrum, environmental, or other external outages,” its “autonomy agreement” says.)

articles.title: Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution
articles.text:
Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution
- Date:
- November 16, 2026
- Source:
- University of Innsbruck
- Summary:
- Scientists have developed a new way to determine whether quantum simulations can be trusted, solving a growing problem as quantum computers become too powerful for conventional machines to check. Demonstrated on a 51-qubit system, the technique measures uncertainty and provides verifiable error margins that could help unlock the full potential of quantum computing.
- Share:
As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising new method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.
The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.
Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.
A New Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy
The breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.
Quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can quickly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.
But quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," says Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties."
Rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the new approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify important interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.
"From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy."
Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator
To evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.
After this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, showed that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.
This represents an important step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.
Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems
The next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.
"This is particularly important because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important."
The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.
Looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.
"After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," says Peter Zoller.
This shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how quickly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.
The findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Innsbruck. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Tristan Kraft, Manoj K. Joshi, William T. Lam, Tobias Olsacher, Florian Kranzl, Johannes Franke, Lata Kh Joshi, Rainer Blatt, Augusto Smerzi, Daniel Stilck França, Benoît Vermersch, Barbara Kraus, Christian F. Roos, Peter Zoller. Bounded-Error Quantum Simulation via Hamiltonian and Lindbladian Learning. Physical Review X, 2026; 16 (3) DOI: 10.1103/s96t-n8tx

articles.title: PHP Readies Critical Security Updates to Patch Another RCE Flaw
articles.text:
PHP is readying a new batch of critical security updates, four weeks after patches for the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities landed.
Scheduled for November 19, between 14:00 and 14:30 UTC, the refreshes will fix critical-severity issues that can be triggered in non-default configurations or uncommon setups.
“These releases are part of PHP’s regular four-week release cycle and will address security vulnerabilities affecting all supported PHP versions. The highest severity is Critical,” PHP’s maintainers noted in a pre-release announcement.
One of the security defects expected to be resolved is CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution (RCE) defect in the file-upload progress tracking functionality. The vulnerability was publicly disclosed two days after PHP2Shell made headlines.
PHP’s maintainers warned at the time that the security flaw can be triggered only under an unusual combination of configuration and code.
“An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(). Session upload progress must also still be enabled,” PHP said last month.
Noting that patches would be released as part of the regular update cycle, PHP developers recommended disabling session upload, a setting also listed as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619, one of the two RCE bugs tracked as PHP2Shell.
“Users are strongly encouraged to prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available. Technical details and fixed version numbers will be published alongside the releases,” PHP’s pre-release notice reads.
The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities have been widely exploited. Attacks began days before the patches were published.

articles.title: From Olympic figure skater to entrepreneur: Sportlogiq’s Craig Buntin is back to help automate homebuilding with Rise | BetaKit
articles.text:
Since retiring from figure skating in 2010, Craig Buntin has not lost his edge or stopped to catch his breath. Entrepreneurship was an obvious next step for the three-time Canadian national champion and former Olympic pairs skater, who is not one to rest on his laurels.
Buntin’s first foray into business was a coffee-tea fusion company named Teabean that he managed to get into 100 cafes across Montréal before eventually selling out to his distributor.
Craig Buntin’s mom taught him how to chase his dreams. His latest one involves helping Canada build homes faster with robots.
His second, a Montréal-based AI-powered hockey analytics software startup called Sportlogiq, raised the stakes and stoked his interest in technology. He co-built Sportlogiq into a platform that helped nearly every NHL team track, analyze, and optimize on-ice performance, culminating in an exit to larger US peer Teamworks earlier this year.
After that, Buntin immediately began working on another AI startup, Rise Automation, to tackle what might be his biggest challenge yet: putting a dent in Canada’s housing crisis by helping custom millwork, cabinetry, and precast concrete factories deploy robots.
The Montréal-based Mila spinout closed $2.4 million CAD in previously unannounced pre-seed funding in July—from BDC Capital’s Industrial Innovation Venture Fund, Developer Capital, and Cycle Capital—to build the AI-powered software “coordination layer” that small shops need to automate parts of the homebuilding process. That simple agreement for future equity financing, Rise’s first round to date, was supported by undisclosed angels and clients.
In an exclusive interview with BetaKit, Buntin unpacked his journey from figure skating to repeat entrepreneurship, and talked about where he plans to go from here as co-founder and CEO of Rise.
Finding his edge
Buntin, a Kelowna native, began figure skating when he was 10 because he wanted to learn how to play hockey. Despite being late to the party—most of his peers had started at six or seven—he quickly demonstrated a knack for the sport. After successfully landing his first jump on one foot in hockey skates as a small crowd of coaches, peers, and parents cheered, he was hooked.
Buntin and his older brother Jamie were raised by a single mother with limited means. A week into his figure-skating career, his mom, Jan, who worked as an office manager, sat him down after receiving her first bill to gauge his passion. According to Buntin, she said, “‘Look, if you really love this, I’ll support you. We’ll pay the bill, we’ll keep going. If not, there’s 100 other sports that are way less expensive that we could manage.’”
“I told her right there that I wanted to go to the Olympics, and that was it for me,” he said. “I never had a Plan B … That’s what I was in love with, and that’s what I was immediately dedicated to doing.”
Buntin struck a deal with his mom that, for as long as he worked hard and loved the sport, their family would make the necessary sacrifices to support his ambitions. Over the next 20 years, that’s exactly what they did. He put everything he had into achieving that goal; to help finance his efforts, his mom sold her house and his brother took on three jobs. During high school, Buntin spent his spare time working as a bus boy, washing trucks, and serving as the mascot of the local major junior hockey team, the Kelowna Rockets.
“We pushed so that I could do it, and I think she taught me how to chase my dreams and to focus on that massive north star,” Buntin said. He is grateful to have had the chance to travel the globe and represent Canada at seven World Championships and the 2006 Winter Olympics, and is glad that he retired feeling like he left nothing on the table.
Buntin sees many parallels between competitive sports and entrepreneurship. Both require setting a mission and relentlessly pursuing it “no matter how many times you fall down.”
RELATED: Teamworks, the “operating system for sports,” buys hockey analytics platform Sportlogiq
“When you go to the Olympics, you’re standing at center ice and you’re either going to win and become a hero or lose and nobody’s going to remember you,” Buntin said. “[The] idea of entrepreneurship is you’re going to work hard, make good decisions, and win, or you’re going to lose it all. It always felt really natural.”
During the final months of his figure-skating career, Buntin began toying with the idea of building a company. He began working on Teabean full-time a day after hanging up his skates. Despite lacking an undergraduate degree, he simultaneously managed to gain entry into and complete McGill University’s MBA program, which led to him focusing on Sportlogiq, which was officially founded in 2015.
From sports to sports tech
Sportlogiq’s first investor was local venture studio TandemLaunch. An old YouTube video of one of Buntin’s 2008 figure-skating performances helped convince TandemLaunch founder, managing partner, and CEO Helge Seetzen that he was a good bet.
That video showed a Paris competition where his partner Meagan Duhamel’s skate accidentally sliced the back of Buntin’s hand mid-routine. He returned minutes later, bandaged but still visibly bloodied, and the duo finished their dance to a standing ovation, ultimately securing bronze. “He’s like, ‘Yeah, this is the guy that I’m backing … Regardless of what tech, I know that this founder will bleed and keep going,’” Buntin said.
“Clearly he was not somebody who would give up easily,” Seetzen told BetaKit over email, adding that “his level of drive can go a long way.”
RELATED: TandemLaunch closes $37-million Fund IV to create and back deep tech startups
Sportlogiq uses a patented combination of AI and computer vision to pull player movement and activity data directly from standard video feeds, make it easy to parse, and derive deeper insights that coaches can use to scout, strategize, and improve performance, and broadcasters can leverage for storytelling. The startup’s tech, which has become ubiquitous in professional hockey, is also used at the college and amateur levels, and in football and soccer.
The company, which raised approximately $28 million to fuel its efforts, had a near-death experience during the early days of COVID-19, when the pandemic temporarily shut down the sports world and its sales cratered. “This is where I earned my grey hairs,” Buntin said. That stretch came post-Series B, shortly after Sportlogiq had made some big investments in expanding beyond professional hockey, forcing the firm to kill those initiatives in an effort to conserve cash. Buntin credits Sportlogiq’s team for pulling together and quickly adjusting during this period.
RELATED: AI investment firm DevCap closes $5 million as it eyes public listing
Sportlogiq was able to weather this storm and find its footing once again as a profitable, 80-person firm with more than $10 million in annual recurring revenue and a particularly attractive data-capture engine.
While the financial terms of Sportlogiq’s January 2026 acquisition by Teamworks were not disclosed, Buntin claimed it was a “sizeable” win for the firm’s founders, staff, and investors by Montréal ecosystem standards.
Tackling the housing crisis with robots
During Sportlogiq’s final days as an independent company, Buntin started working on Rise. He noted that building homes in Canada, let alone buying them, is an expensive and time-consuming process. “It’s a massive societal crisis right now,” Buntin said, and it’s one he’s particularly passionate about.
His mom selling her house to support his dream is certainly a factor. “I’ll never forget her pride in knowing it was hers, a home that would appreciate over time,” Buntin said. “You can’t underestimate how empowering that is after decades of living paycheque to paycheque.”
Buntin is also motivated by the chance to make homeownership more affordable for the next generation of Canadians, and thinks Rise offers his best chance yet “to make the most meaningful impact.”
He initially set out to help by developing sustainable building materials like carbon-negative drywall and robots to install them, but while those components can be expensive, he said that price pales in comparison to the cost of labour; Canada’s residential construction sector currently faces a severe shortage of workers.
“Homes are a manufacturing problem: the cabinets, millwork, and concrete that go into them are made in factories, and in the shops we work with, the machines sit idle about 90 percent of the week,” Buntin said. “Running them three shifts would take triple the workforce, but [there] are only about 40,000 open manufacturing jobs today. Intelligent robots close that gap.”
This led the startup to refocus on retrofitting existing shops. He co-founded Rise with chief scientific officer Liam Paull and chief innovation officer Charlie Gauthier, two researchers connected to local AI research institute Mila (Paull is an associate professor at the University of Montréal, while Gauthier is a student at Mila under him). Gauthier is developing Rise’s core tech as her PhD thesis. Buntin described it as an AI memory and mapping software system that enables robotic orchestration.
“[The] idea of entrepreneurship is you’re going to work hard, make good decisions, and win, or you’re going to lose it all. It always felt really natural.”
Craig Buntin, Rise
Mila’s managing director of AI ventures, Stéphane Marceau, said Buntin was the AI research institute’s first founder-in-residence. “What stood out early was his empirical and humble approach to building the business,” he told BetaKit over email. “He spent significant time with manufacturers, observing their operations and understanding their problems in detail before jumping to solutions.”
Most of the factories that Rise has set its sights on are not currently using robots. They have lots of unused capacity and could also stand to gain by automating some of their core daily tasks, Buntin said. But after spending a few months embedded inside some of these sites, he quickly realized that industry was “nowhere near ready for automation.”
Buntin said many factories contain “the same type of chaos as hockey,” with operations that are heavily reliant upon the institutional know-how of longstanding staff. By either setting up video cameras of its own or leveraging existing feeds inside these facilities and deriving insight from them using its tech, Rise sees room to help floor managers better understand what’s happening in their shops and the potential return on investment of automation.
“I think of it a little bit like Sportlogiq for your factory,” Buntin said. That pitch has begun resonating, as the now six-person startup is set to install its tech at its fifth factory by the end of November. That marks the first step in Rise’s game plan. The next step is connecting these factories with partner third-party robotics firms like Laval, QC-based Omnirobotic and providing the “human-robot interface” or “coordination layer” necessary to retrofit their sites for these robots. While it has begun doing the latter, its progress on this front remains early.
A scarcity of egocentric data remains a key barrier to more widespread deployment of robots capable of consistently executing real-world tasks. Buntin is betting another firm will win that race, and positioning Rise as not only an infrastructure player that other manufacturing robotics firms can plug into but a potential sales channel for them.
For the shops Rise is selling to, the pitch is simple: the chance to boost their capacity and reduce their costs. With Rise, Buntin hopes to help Canada tackle some huge challenges, from housing costs to construction timelines, while also trying its best to bring workers along for the ride, rather than displacing them.
“We’ve got a mountain in front of us,” Buntin said. He’s excited to embark on another climb.
Feature image courtesy Rise Automation.

articles.title: China threatens "countermeasures" on the face of new AI GPU rental and export restrictions — Beijing threatens retaliation ahead of Thursday's Xi Jinping meeting, Sino-American trade war may be renewed for a new season
articles.text:
China threatens 'countermeasures' in the face of new AI GPU rental and export restrictions — Beijing threatens retaliation ahead of Thursday's Xi Jinping meeting, Sino-American trade war may be renewed for a new season
"When elephants fight, the grass suffers."
Yesterday, the Trump administration extended the reach of its existing export controls on high-end AI accelerator chips, namely, but not limited to, Nvidia's Blackwell lineup. The updated regulation now requires licenses for renting those chips in large quantities to the entirety of America's D:5 countries list (nations embargoed from arms sales). As expected, the news landed in Beijing like a lead dragon, and its Ministry of Commerce states that China "will take countermeasures to firmly safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests."
The bold move taken by the U.S. arrives at a peculiar time, as President Trump is currently visiting the nation for the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Trump is scheduled to meet President Xi Jinping on Thursday, Nov. 19, a tête-a-tête that's bound to be interesting. Both nations were recently embroiled in a bitter trade war, with ever-mounting tariffs and restrictions on both sides until a temporary truce was called in Oct. 2025. Only some restrictions were lifted, though; for example, Chinese semiconductors still face a 50% tariff when imported stateside.
A potential restart of tariff-slapping would all but guarantee an even larger amount of turmoil in U.S. stock markets. Those seas are already choppy enough thanks to Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang's romantic involvement with purported Chinese spy Alice Huang — along with mounting suspicions that the soulmates may have connived to siphon billions' worth of Blackwell chips from her Singaporean outfit Megaspeed onto Chinese AI laboratories.
Nvidia cut off about half of its Asian buyers last July, seemingly in the purview of the export controls, and told data center operators that over 50% of their business must come from non-Chinese companies. Meanwhile, both Malaysia and Singapore have intensified their scrutiny of AI hardware shipments.
China's countermeasures ammo is as of yet unspecified. The nation had restricted the sale of gallium, germanium, and antimony to the U.S. previously, and the truce shelved that bullet until Nov. 2027. Beijing may well choose to simply not renew that agreement when that day comes. Although analysts believe that the nations will be cordial enough during this summit, Trump's perceived provocation may bring China's proverbial nuclear option of restricting rare earth exports back to the loading bay.
The truce on that particular matter only has a few weeks left, expiring on Jan. 10, 2027. Likewise, super-hard materials and high-density lithium batteries, crucial for the newest generations of EVs, solar power storage, and battery installations, all have white flags that will come down early next year. Analysts also expect that Chinese firms and their government will continue to heavily invest in domestic chip production, namely, but not only, by Huawei.
Broadly speaking, the U.S.' updated chip control regulation means that Chinese firms cannot sidestep the existing control on chip sales by renting them instead, closing one of the main existing loopholes around the export restrictions. Additionally, selling chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil now also requires a license, as the U.S. Department of Commerce suspects that companies in these nations import Blackwell cards to sell to China.

articles.title: Microsoft announces Windows Server 2028 with hardened security
articles.text:
Microsoft has announced Windows Server 2028, the next major release of its server operating system, at the Ignite 2026 conference on Tuesday.
This new Windows Server version ships with a hardened Server Core configuration by default and a new security baseline that allows admins to relax specific settings.
"A hardened Server Core configuration by default and a new security baseline help reduce the work of establishing a secure baseline from day 1," said Neil Hinnant, Director of Windows Server & I/O Fabrics PM.
"Trusted Launch extends protection to virtual machines, guaranteeing boot integrity across your VM fleet, and Confidential VM support begins a journey to support integrity-protected runtimes on supported CVM hardware."
The list of hardened Server Core settings is extensive and includes:
- Identity and authentication: Credentials are hard to steal and hard to reuse: Kerberos over NTLM, LSASS protected, strong passwords and account lockout, no consumer accounts.
- Network exposure: The server talks only over signed, encrypted, authenticated channels: SMB signing and encryption, the firewall on in every profile, legacy name resolution and unauthenticated RPC off.
- Cryptography: TLS is limited to modern cipher suites, key exchange is hybrid post-quantum (ML-KEM), and stored keys are strongly protected.
- Privilege and admin access: Admins approve elevation, powerful rights stay with Administrators, Guests cannot sign in, and installers cannot elevate on their own.
- Platform and code integrity: The sign-in process runs only Microsoft-signed code. Signature validation is stricter. The paging file is encrypted.
- Remote access and observability: RDP with NLA and TLS, WinRM without Basic, Digest, or unencrypted traffic, advanced audit with command lines, PowerShell script block logging, and larger event logs.
However, the company said it's still working on adding NTLM blocking, hardware-backed platform protection, print and RPC hardening, and more to the hundreds of security settings enabled from first boot.
Windows Server 2028 also offers simplified administration and management at scale through Intune management for Windows Servers, bringing endpoint-management workflows for configuration, compliance, applications, and updates to eligible, persistent servers.
It also improves performance with native NVMe storage enabled by default, NVMe over TCP and RDMA transports, and the ability to boot from ReFS.
Last but not least, it introduces new AI accelerators, including the ability to deploy and configure inference environments, manage accelerated hardware, and support open-weight and custom models (including Windows ML, Foundry Local, vLLM, and Llama.cpp).
Admins who want to test Windows Server 2028 can register for the Windows Insider Program for Windows Server or apply to enroll in the Windows Server Technology Adoption Program (TAP) for earlier access.
"This major release raises the security and access bar, accelerates enterprise infrastructure, and simplifies management at scale," Hinnant added. "It also begins our long term investments extending Microsoft Foundry to bring AI inference to fleets of local token factories, giving customers more choices to put the right intelligence in the right place with the right cost structure."

articles.title: AI data centers delays push inference chips into existing sites - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Stalled data center buildouts send inference chips hunting for space in telco and colo sites
Demand for inference is outrunning the construction of new AI data centers, as power, capital and permitting delays push fresh capacity further out. That gap is sending chipmakers to hunt for room in existing facilities.
Many older telco and colocation sites have the space and power. But most can’t take today’s dense, liquid-cooled GPU racks without costly retrofits, which opens the door for air-cooled inference systems, according to Anton McGonnell (pictured), vice president of core product at SambaNova Systems Inc.
“We as an industry are just encumbered by the velocity of data center buildouts, and that’s been slowed down by just the physics of how long this takes, by the access to capital, and more and more by legislative hurdles — particularly in the U.S.,” McGonnell said.
McGonnell spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed AI data centers and the demand for air-cooled inference racks. (* Disclosure below.)
Reviving brownfield capacity for AI data centers
SambaNova’s fifth-generation chip, the SN50, targets the decode phase of inference, where output tokens are generated and data movement becomes the bottleneck. Its racks stay air-cooled and light enough to fit existing facilities, McGonnell explained. Newer GPU racks, by contrast, can demand reinforced flooring and 120 to 250 kilowatts of power per rack, he noted.
“On all of this stuff — the power and the cooling gear — there’s 18- to 24-month lead times to get this equipment into the data centers. Never mind all of the construction costs,” McGonnell said.
SambaNova, which investors valued at $11 billion in July, pairs its decode chips with partners that handle prefill, the compute-heavy first phase of inference. At SC26, it is demonstrating Intel’s D-Series GPUs for prefill alongside its SambaRack SN50 for decode in an air-cooled heterogeneous setup.
“They have developed a chip that has much, much better cost performance for the prefill phase of inference,” McGonnell said. “They’ve sacrificed HBM, which isn’t needed for prefill because it’s a compute-bound problem.”

articles.title: Google et Amazon vont détenir près d'un tiers d'Anthropic
articles.text:
Amazon (14,7 %) et Google (13,7%) détiendront ensemble environ 28 % d’Anthropic après son introduction en Bourse, selon de nouveaux documents déposés auprès de la SEC. Une partie de ces titres vient de billets convertibles, et aucun ne donne de droit de vote. Anthropic et ses cofondateurs pourraient lever jusqu’à 64,4 milliards de dollars.
Anthropic doit fixer le prix de son action ce mercredi 18 novembre, avant une cotation jeudi sur le Nasdaq sous le symbole “ANT”. Les derniers documents d’Anthropic, repris par Bloomberg, précisent ce que deux de ses fournisseurs cloud vont détenir.
Actions sans vote et billets convertibles : comment Amazon et Google entrent au capital
Amazon et Google passent par une catégorie spéciale d’actions, la classe N. Ces titres ne donnent pas de voix en assemblée, seulement droit à d’éventuels dividendes. Amazon en recevra 1,92 milliard (34 % de la classe), soit 14,7 % d’Anthropic. Google en aura 1,79 milliard (32 % de la classe). Ses titres viennent à la fois d’une conversion de billets et du placement privé, où il a acheté 135,1 millions d’actions pour environ 10 milliards de dollars. Le poids des fondateurs n’est donc pas touché : Nous rapportions en fin de mois dernier que ces derniers garderaient 50,1 % des voix grâce à une action de classe F unique, détenue par Founder LLC.
Pour Amazon, tout part des investissements de 2023 et 2024. Le groupe a obtenu des billets convertibles, c’est-à-dire des reconnaissances de dette qu’il peut transformer en actions à un prix fixé à l’avance, soit environ 2,09 ou 5,05 dollars selon l’année. En face, la fourchette de l’introduction en Bourse va de 70 à 78 dollars. Amazon n’a converti qu’une partie de ses billets et en garde pour des milliards de dollars. S’il convertissait tout, il détiendrait 23,8 % d’Anthropic. Selon Bloomberg, un plafond de 12 % encadre ces conversions et Amazon a promis de le conserver.
- Excellente compréhension des consignes complexes
- Très bon niveau en rédaction
- Analyse de longs documents efficace
En mars 2025, d’après des documents judiciaires obtenus par le New York Times, Google disposait 14 % d'Anthropic. Le placement privé de 26 milliards de dollars rassemble sept groupes : AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, NVIDIA et TSMC Partners. Google et NVIDIA y mettent chacun 10 milliards, un achat qui n’aura lieu que si l’introduction aboutit. Placement compris, le total devrait dépasser les 75 milliards de dollars levés par SpaceX en juin. En haut de la fourchette, Anthropic serait valorisée environ 1 405 milliards de dollars, sur une base diluée.
Ces trois groupes ne sont pas que des actionnaires. Anthropic décrit Amazon, Google et Microsoft comme à la fois investisseurs, clients, partenaires de distribution et concurrents. Concrètement, une entreprise qui utilise Claude via son compte chez l’un d’eux paie ce fournisseur, qui garde une commission avant de reverser le reste à Anthropic. Ce circuit représente environ 44 % du chiffre d’affaires des trois premiers trimestres de 2026. Anthropic s’est aussi engagée à dépenser plus de 100 milliards de dollars chez AWS d’ici dix ans.

articles.title: Ce vidéoprojecteur 4K compact signé Anker, compatible HDR10 et Dolby Vision, perd 620 € grâce au Black Friday — Frandroid
articles.text:
Filiale d’Anker, Nebula propose un vaste catalogue de vidéoprojecteurs aux formats variés. On y trouve notamment le Cosmos 4K SE, un modèle compact et facile à transporter, capable de projeter une image 4K jusqu’à 200 pouces. Il tourne en plus sous Google TV, pour ne rien gâcher. S’il vous intéresse, sachez que son prix est passé sous la barre des 900 euros à l’approche du Black Friday.
Les points forts du Nebula Cosmos 4K SE
- Une poignée pour le déplacer facilement
- Des images en UHD jusqu’à 200 pouces
- Google TV
Lancé à l’automne 2024 à 1 499,99 euros, l’Anker Nebula Cosmos 4K SE est aujourd’hui disponible en promotion à 879 euros sur Amazon.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant le Nebula Cosmos 4K SE. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Un vidéoprojecteur compact rapide à installer
Le vidéoprojecteur Nebula Cosmos 4K SE adopte un format rectangulaire assez classique, mais surtout compact (263 x 265 x 165 mm), et ne pèse que 4,5 kg. Autant dire qu’on le déplace d’une pièce à l’autre sans difficulté. Il intègre même une poignée, pour être facilement transporté. Dans son dos, on trouve par ailleurs une connectique plutôt fournie, avec deux entrées HDMI 2.1, dont une est compatible eARC pour le retour audio, un port USB-A permettant de lire directement des contenus multimédias et une prise casque, si vous voulez plonger dans votre bulle. Le vidéoprojecteur est aussi compatible Bluetooth et Wi-Fi.
Côté installation, et comme tout bon vidéoprojecteur, le Nebula Cosmos 4K SE dispose de plusieurs fonctions automatiques de correction de l’image. Évitement des obstacles, ajustement du trapèze, autofocus… On peut profiter d’images rectangulaires et nettes, même si l’appareil n’est pas placé exactement en face du mur ou de l’écran. De plus, les corrections de l’image s’opèrent à chaque fois en moins de 2 secondes. Un capteur de luminosité ambiante est aussi de la partie, de même qu’une fonction permettant de définir la couleur de la surface sur laquelle le projecteur envoie l’image : le vidéoprojecteur peut ainsi ajuster correctement sa colorimétrie.
Des images nettes et une partie audio maîtrisée
Le Nebula Cosmos 4K SE utilise une double source de lumière combinant laser et LED. Il s’appuie sur une puce DMD de 0,47 pouce avec la technologie DLP et le traitement XPR de Texas Instruments ; ce qui permet de simuler une image avec une définition Ultra HD à partir d’une matrice nativement Full HD. Il prend aussi en charge les contenus HDR10 et Dolby Vision. Voilà pour la présentation. En action, le vidéoprojecteur est capable d’afficher des images UHD jusqu’à 200 pouces (Nebula annonce plutôt 120 pouces maximum dans une pièce normalement éclairée), très flatteuses et avec des couleurs bien vives. Le contraste est toutefois un peu faible. On aurait aimé davantage de profondeur dans les scènes plus obscures. La luminosité (1 800 lumens ANSI annoncés par Nebula) est, de son côté, suffisante pour profiter des contenus vidéo même si la pièce est un peu éclairée. L’effet arc-en-ciel, caractéristique de certains vidéoprojecteurs utilisant le DLP, est présent, mais nous l’avons jugé peu gênant.
L’appareil propose également une excellente partie audio (deux haut-parleurs de 15 watts compatibles Dolby Audio) : le son est bien projeté à l’avant et donne l’impression de provenir directement de l’écran ou du mur. La puissance est ici suffisante pour couvrir une pièce moyenne. Notez aussi que via une liaison Bluetooth, vous pouvez vous servir du vidéoprojecteur comme d’une enceinte Bluetooth (il faut tout de même le garder branché au secteur, faute de batterie). Un mode Jeu est en outre disponible et permet de profiter d’un temps de retard à l’affichage réduit (mais dans ce cas, les corrections automatiques de l’affichage sont désactivées). Attention, le vidéoprojecteur n’est pas compatible avec les signaux 120 Hz et reste limité à du 60 Hz. Enfin, l’appareil est animé par Google TV, une interface toujours aussi fluide et agréable, avec une offre particulièrement riche, application Netflix officielle comprise.
Pour en savoir encore plus, n’hésitez pas à lire notre test complet du Nebula Cosmos 4K SE.

articles.title: « J'ai commis de graves erreurs » : Jensen Huang veut revenir chez Nvidia, le conseil dit non
articles.text:
L’espoir n’aura duré que quelques heures. Jensen Huang a publié sur X, hier soir, sa première déclaration publique depuis sa démission, le 12 novembre, après la révélation de plusieurs relations extraconjugales, dont l’une avec Alice Huang, femme d’affaires soupçonnée par Washington de liens avec les services de renseignement chinois. « Je n’ai pas été à la hauteur des exigences attendues de chacun chez Nvidia, et j’ai commis de graves erreurs dans ma vie personnelle », écrit-il. Il assure assumer « pleinement » ses erreurs et vouloir coopérer avec l’enquête indépendante menée par le conseil d’administration.
 Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.
I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.
Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.
Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.
Jensen
— Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) November 17, 2026
Surtout, le cofondateur de Nvidia ouvre clairement la porte à un retour. Évoquant un « déferlement d’appels » d’employés, d’investisseurs, de partenaires et de clients, il affirme que « si le conseil d’administration décide que [son] retour est dans l’intérêt de nos actionnaires, de nos employés, de l’entreprise et de l’Amérique, [il serait] honoré de répondre à ces appels et de reprendre [ses] fonctions de PDG ». Une sortie qui intervient après une semaine de mobilisation : la lettre ouverte réclamant son retour approche désormais les 200 000 signataires, et Donald Trump a déclaré lundi qu’il « ne verrait certainement pas d’inconvénient » à sa réintégration, estimant qu’il avait « retenu une grande leçon ».
« Le conseil n’a pas l’intention de réinstaller Jensen »
Le conseil d’administration n’a pas tardé à répondre. Le soir même, en ouverture de la conférence téléphonique consacrée aux résultats trimestriels, son président Harvey Jones a été limpide : le conseil « a accepté à l’unanimité sa démission et n’a pas l’intention de réinstaller Jensen au poste de PDG », rapporte Associated Press. Il a aussi refusé de répondre aux questions sur le départ de l’ancien dirigeant.
La recherche d’un successeur est lancée, avec l’aide du cabinet de chasseurs de têtes Heidrick & Struggles, selon Reuters. « Nous voulons nommer un PDG permanent aussi vite que possible, mais nous ne précipiterons pas les choses avant de trouver exactement la bonne personne », a expliqué Harvey Jones, en précisant que des profils internes comme externes seront étudiés. En attendant, Colette Kress, directrice financière depuis 2013, assure l’intérim. Le choix promet toutefois d’être délicat. Jeff Bezos, le fondateur d’Amazon, a d’ailleurs mis en garde le conseil mardi : « Si vous ne faites pas revenir Jensen, je n’embaucherais pas quelqu’un de l’extérieur. Nvidia est trop compliqué ».
Congrès, SEC et sécurité nationale
Pour Jensen Huang, l’affaire est loin d’être close et plusieurs échéances majeures approches. Les présidents de trois commissions de la Chambre des représentants ont annoncé qu’il avait accepté d’être entendu à huis clos le 1er décembre, suivi le lendemain du directeur juridique de Nvidia, Tim Teter. « Le peuple américain a besoin de réponses sur M. Huang et le rôle de Nvidia dans l’accès d’acteurs dangereux de la RPC à nos puces les plus avancées », ont-ils déclaré. Le gendarme boursier américain, la SEC, enquêterait par ailleurs sur Nvidia, selon le Wall Street Journal. De son côté, le conseil d’administration a créé un comité chargé de superviser les questions de sécurité nationale et le respect des contrôles à l’exportation, alors que Megaspeed, l’entreprise où travaillait Alice Huang, est soupçonnée d’avoir détourné des puces Nvidia vers la Chine.
Ironie de la situation, Nvidia n’a jamais aussi bien vendu. Le groupe a publié mardi un chiffre d’affaires trimestriel de 115,84 milliards de dollars, plus du double d’il y a un an, et prévoit 130 milliards pour le trimestre en cours. « Notre dynamique est réelle. Notre demande s’accélère », a assuré Colette Kress en conclusion de la conférence, avant de lancer : « On gère ». L’action a pris plus de 4 % après la clôture, mais Nvidia reste valorisé environ 2 000 milliards de dollars de moins qu’à son pic de début octobre.
