articles.title: Nvidia’s rise, visualized
articles.text:
If someone handed you $8,300 every second, what would you do? That’s how much pure profit Nvidia now makes. By the time you finish reading this paragraph, Nvidia will likely have cleared $45,000 and change.
Nvidia’s rise, visualized
What’s next for Nvidia? Whatever doesn’t rock the mind-bogglingly profitable boat.
Nvidia’s rise, visualized
What’s next for Nvidia? Whatever doesn’t rock the mind-bogglingly profitable boat.
It’s easy to look at Nvidia, a company that just lost its visionary founder CEO due to a series of scandals, and think that the company and maybe the entire AI industry are in terrible trouble. Perhaps so?
But I want you to understand: Nvidia isn’t your average semi-successful company that might tempt a new CEO to fix things that are broken. It is a company so staggeringly, mind-bogglingly successful it’ll do everything in its power not to rock the boat. There is so much money at stake.
It’s so much money that when I heard about Jensen Huang’s resignation, my first thought was: I need a way to visualize this jaw-dropping amount of money for you. I want to show you that Nvidia has risen so far, so fast, that rival chipmakers AMD, Intel, and Qualcomm barely qualify as competition now.
If you’re on a desktop OS, you could mouse over each dot in our chart above to see the staggering sums. But we built another way to visualize the rise of Nvidia I like even better. It’s a horizontal bar graph that not only puts Nvidia’s revenue growth in perspective, but shows you its monster profits right alongside them — plus the world events that made Nvidia a star.
TL;DR: The crypto boom and the great GPU shortage have nothing on the AI boom. Those earlier periods saw Nvidia’s profits briefly peak at $1.24 billion and $3 billion a quarter respectively, while the rise of data centers has driven them to $65 billion per quarter with no sign of stopping.
Yes, Jensen may have set a trillion dollars of Nvidia’s market cap on fire — from around $5 trillion at the start of November to “only” $3.6 trillion now — but the smoldering company is raking in $700 million in profit a day on average.
Put another way: Nvidia could give a $1 million bonus to every one of its 42,000 employees, every three months, without running out of cash. Or, you know, Nvidia could end world hunger or provide clean water for everyone, now that it’s making over $200 billion in pure profit a year.
Maybe that’d make people feel differently about data centers?
But even if we stick to self-serving capitalism, you’re probably still a happy investor if you bought Nvidia a decade ago. A $1,000 investment 10 years ago is now worth over $67,000. You’d have over $1 million if you invested $15,000 back then.
And make no mistake, Nvidia is sticking to capitalism. Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress just promised to return as much money to investors as possible on the company’s November 17th earnings call. “Going forward, we intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders,” she announced. “All” is a lot more than the 50 percent baseline that Jensen promised five months ago.
Nvidia isn’t the only company whose fortunes have risen this dramatically. RAMageddon revealed that just three companies — Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — controlled nearly 90 percent of the entire global DRAM market, and those three have repeatedly signaled that they’d prefer to celebrate record profits instead of ramping up production too fast.
But while their revenues and profits have been skyrocketing even faster over the past year or so, even Big RAM hasn’t caught the AI wave quite the same way as Nvidia. Samsung, of course, doesn’t just make memory — its revenue numbers include phones, tablets, TVs, home appliances, chips, displays, camera sensors, audio, networking equipment, medical equipment, and more.
In the most recent quarter, Micron made $37.7 billion in profit, SK Hynix made $29.8 billion, and Samsung came in at around $55.3 billion, but they’re all shy of Nvidia’s $65.3 billion. Historically, RAM has also been a bit more cyclical: Both Micron and SK Hynix actually lost money in 2023 because they produced too much memory.
On its latest earnings call, the first since cofounder Jensen Huang’s resignation, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress reinforced the idea that Nvidia expects the good times to keep on rolling.
Asked how things might change under new management, she suggested that they wouldn’t: “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual,” she said. She added that the company has secured the backing of customers and suppliers including TSMC, the all-important firm that actually fabricates Nvidia’s chips.
“Our momentum is real, our demand is accelerating, our supply is growing. Our customers and partners are with us, and employees are committed,” she claimed. “We’ve got this.”
Nvidia claims it’ll rake in even more money next quarter, with projected revenue of $130 billion. Profit may be proportionally smaller since gross margins are estimated to drop to 71–72 percent (compared to nearly 75 percent), but Kress said Nvidia intends to get them up as high as 73 percent next year.
In other words: This astounding gravy train isn’t going anywhere. At least that’s the plan.
Stevie Bonifield contributed to this story.

articles.title: ‘Our most advanced Audio-Animatronics in the world’ — Disney Imagineering reveals how AWS AI brings the Star Wars Anzellans to life
articles.text:
‘Our most advanced Audio-Animatronics in the world’ — Disney Imagineering reveals how AWS AI brings the Star Wars Anzellans to life
Three tiny Star Wars characters offer a big glimpse into Imagineering's future
Picture this: You're walking through Black Spire Outpost on Batuu, the setting for Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge at Disneyland or Disney World, and you step into a shop, maybe looking for a certain color of kyber crystal, a cold brew black caf, or a new piece of Star Wars merchandise. But before you can find what you're after, you're stopped by a small creature that starts talking to you.
Maybe it lets out a shriek of concern because you're wearing an outfit that screams 'dark side', or cheers with excitement after spotting your birthday button. These are the kinds of spontaneous, memorable interactions Disney parks are known for, and in recent years, we've seen Imagineering steadily bring robotics and high-tech Audio-Animatronics closer together to make its characters feel more alive.
Now, Disney's latest creation takes that idea a step further.
Meet the Anzellans: Vilo Vele, Kado Bre'a, and Jibu Bre'a. These tiny Star Wars creatures, the same species as Babu Frik from The Rise of Skywalker, have been brought to life as three Audio-Animatronics positioned together in a crate. They can move, look around, and interact with one another, but what's especially impressive is that they can also read the room.
Thanks to a partnership with Amazon Web Services (AWS), the Anzellans use cameras, microphones, sensors, and AI to understand what's happening around them and respond in real time. They can recognize what a guest is wearing, identify who's speaking to them, and even coordinate their interactions with one another.
And while AI is helping bring these characters to life, it's not writing their dialogue or dreaming up their personalities. That's still very much the work of Disney's Imagineers.
"These Anzellans now are our most advanced Audio-Animatronics in the world," Kyle Laughlin, Senior Vice President of Walt Disney Imagineering R&D and Technology and Engineering, told me in an interview alongside Samira Panah Bakhtiar, General Manager of Telco, Media & Entertainment, Games, Advertising, and Sports at AWS.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
It's a pretty significant statement considering Disney's long history with Audio-Animatronics, dating back to Walt Disney's Enchanted Tiki Room, and continuing through increasingly sophisticated figures in attractions like Pirates of the Caribbean.
But the Anzellans are doing something different. Rather than performing a fixed sequence of movements and dialogue, they're designed to understand what's happening around them and decide how to respond, without someone controlling them from behind the scenes.
And it's part of a much bigger effort underway at Imagineering.
Bringing robotics and Audio-Animatronics together
I've spoken with Laughlin previously about Disney's characters, including the BDX droids that have been roaming Galaxy's Edge and Olaf, the free-roaming robotic snowman that Imagineering has brought to Disneyland Paris and Hong Kong Disneyland.
While these creations might look very different from the traditional Audio-Animatronics that populate Disney's attractions, they're increasingly connected behind the scenes.
"Our robots and our animatronics are coming closer and closer together," Laughlin explained.
In fact, the Anzellans are built on the same robotic character platform that powers Olaf and the BDX droids. That's an especially interesting detail, considering these three little characters aren't roaming around on their own. Instead, they're working together in one environment, responding to guests and each other. Notably, there isn't another Cast Member controlling the experience or puppeteering, but rather those decisions are made by the character, in real time.
Laughlin describes the Anzellans as a hybrid, bringing together elements of robotics and Audio-Animatronics with a level of intelligence that Disney hasn't previously delivered in one of these characters.
"This is our most intelligent character that we've created," he said.
The hardware is an important part of that distinction. While Olaf can move around and interact with his surroundings, Laughlin explained that he doesn't have onboard cameras or microphones. The Anzellans do, along with additional sensors that help them understand their environment.
Imagine approaching the crate with a group of friends. The Anzellans can understand that multiple people are standing in front of them, determine who's speaking, and look that person directly in the eyes while responding in their own mix of English and Anzellan.
It's the kind of detail that could make an encounter feel much more personal, and it's where AWS enters the picture.
AWS gives the Anzellans their intelligence, but Disney remains in control
Disney and AWS have worked together for more than a decade, including on the infrastructure supporting Disney+, which turns seven this week. But the Anzellans take that partnership in a different direction, bringing AWS's cloud and AI capabilities into a physical character experience.
And the project came together surprisingly quickly.
Laughlin told me the teams worked together over a matter of months, with the opportunity to collaborate with the filmmakers behind The Mandalorian & Grogu helping inform the direction of the characters.
AWS brought its AI and software expertise, while Imagineering concentrated on the physical characters, their personalities, and the storytelling.
"AWS I think brought the intelligence, Imagineering brought the brawn," Bakhtiar told me.
The Anzellans use Amazon Bedrock, AWS's managed AI service, to access different AI models that help them understand and react to the world around them. Laughlin confirmed that Imagineering is using vision models, large language models, and world models as part of the experience.
That doesn't mean the characters are using generative AI to make up their own dialogue, though.
Every line is written by Imagineers and prerecorded, and every character's personality and movements are designed by the creative team. AI selects the appropriate responses and animations based on what's happening in the moment.
So, if an Anzellan spots a birthday button, it can choose a response that fits the occasion. If someone speaks directly to one of the characters, it can respond accordingly. The interaction might feel spontaneous, but the actual words and character behaviors remain firmly in Imagineering's hands.
That distinction is important, particularly as Disney continues to experiment with AI in guest experiences.
"Human creativity leads and the guest experience is preserved, and AI and the cloud computing infrastructure really is there to support it," Bakhtiar said. "[Entertainment companies] need technology that's going to really serve their story and not the other way around."
There's also another layer to this experience: the three Anzellans aren't simply responding independently.
Bakhtiar explained that each character is simultaneously tracking three things: the guest, what's happening in the surrounding environment, and what the other Anzellans are doing.
"The system is working like a show director, and it's like keeping this ensemble together so the characters, they don't talk over each other, the story stays coherent," she explained.
That's a fascinating distinction from a traditional Audio-Animatronics show. Instead of following the same carefully timed sequence, the Anzellans can adjust their performances to the situation while still behaving like characters from the Star Wars universe.
AWS also used Kiro, its AI coding agent, to help turn Imagineering's creative briefs into working software. Bakhtiar explained that the teams reviewed and approved the work at each stage, allowing ideas to move into testing more quickly.
For Laughlin, that meant Imagineers could spend more time focusing on the mechanical and electrical engineering, character skins, and the finer details that make the Anzellans believable.
And because Bedrock isn't tied to one specific AI model, Disney can swap models as the technology improves, optimizing for performance, speed, latency, or cost without rebuilding the entire experience.
"We can be on the bleeding edge of whatever model is launched in order to bring the best experience possible," Laughlin said.
That's particularly valuable when a character needs to respond quickly enough for a conversation to feel natural.
A new kind of character encounter
Of course, there's a big question hanging over all of this: When will guests actually get to meet the Anzellans?
Disney isn't saying just yet. The characters are scheduled to appear at AWS re:Invent in Las Vegas from November 30 through December 4, where attendees can meet them at the Customer Showcase at Caesars Forum.
And while this won't be their first public appearance — Disney confirmed to TechRadar that an earlier version of the Anzellans shown at D23 was also powered by AWS — there's still no word on when or where they'll become a regular guest experience at Disneyland or Disney World.
Laughlin did offer one encouraging indication when I asked about their eventual arrival in the parks.
"We’re excited for guests to meet them. We just won’t talk specifics today."
And while we've already seen the BDX droids roaming Galaxy's Edge and Olaf interacting with guests at Disneyland Paris, these experiences are still relatively limited compared with the many Audio-Animatronics and characters found throughout Disney's parks. The technology is impressive, but the next challenge is bringing these more interactive characters into everyday park experiences, and doing so at scale.
That's something Laughlin and I have discussed before, and he sees the Anzellans as part of a broader shift in how Imagineering develops and introduces its characters.
"More than ever, this is not about short-term playtests. It really is about populating our worlds with lots of different characters," he explained.
Laughlin also told me that guests should expect to encounter the Anzellans indoors first, and his description of the technology offers a pretty intriguing glimpse at where Imagineering might be headed.
"We've viewed this as an experiential merchandise platform," he explained.
In other words, imagine walking into a Disney shop and having an unexpected interaction with a character, rather than needing to visit a designated meet-and-greet location.
And the idea isn't necessarily limited to Star Wars.
"When we think about the future of where it's headed, you can imagine that any type of merchandise experience could be powered with characters from any of our franchises," Laughlin said.
There's still plenty to figure out, though. Keeping a character responsive throughout a busy day at a theme park requires more than just sophisticated AI. There's also the question of what happens if the network connection drops or the primary system encounters a problem.
It's something I asked Laughlin about, and he explained that Disney is combining AWS cloud and edge infrastructure to help keep the experience running.
"If something were to fail [...] then we could always fall back to another experience," he said.
The goal is to keep these characters operating reliably throughout park hours, though Disney is still learning what it takes to deliver these more intelligent experiences at scale.
Privacy is another consideration, especially with cameras and microphones involved. Laughlin told me that the information gathered during an interaction is used only for the immediate experience, isn't currently stored in the cloud for Disney to reuse, and isn't used to train AI models.
The specifics of the underlying models and the number of sensors remain undisclosed, but the broader approach is becoming clearer.
The next chapter for Disney's characters
Imagineering has continued to push its characters further, from free-roaming robots to the next-generation Audio-Animatronics appearing in attractions like Pirates of the Caribbean or Frozen Ever After.
The Anzellans are another step in that evolution, but perhaps the bigger development is what's happening behind the scenes. Disney is building a shared foundation that can support different types of characters and experiences, rather than treating robotics, Audio-Animatronics, and AI as entirely separate technologies.
Bakhtiar described the AWS-powered system as a reusable framework, one that could allow Imagineers to focus on creating new personalities, moods, movements, and stories instead of rebuilding the underlying software every time.
And with Laughlin pointing to more than $60 billion of work ahead for Imagineering worldwide, there are plenty of opportunities to put these technologies to work.
Just look at Walt Disney World, where an entirely new Monsters, Inc. land is coming to Hollywood Studios — complete with an octopus-like, impressive animatronic — while Animal Kingdom is getting Tropical Americas with new Indiana Jones and Encanto attractions. Over at Magic Kingdom, Villains Land and Piston Peak are on the way, while EPCOT will eventually take guests on a new journey into imagination with Figment and Dreamfinder.
And that's just Florida. At Disneyland Resort in California, Imagineering is working on the first-ever Coco attraction, a major reimagining of Tomorrowland, and an expansion of Avengers Campus, among other projects.
Of course, that doesn't mean we'll necessarily see the Anzellans or this exact AI technology in any of these attractions. But with so much happening across Disney Parks, it's easy to see why Imagineering is investing in a platform that could bring more interactive characters to life across its parks.
For now, the Anzellans remain a glimpse at what's possible rather than a confirmed new fixture at Galaxy's Edge. But it's easy to imagine how a seemingly ordinary shopping trip could become something much more memorable when a character recognizes you, reacts to what you're wearing, or strikes up a conversation.
And when I asked Laughlin what this convergence of robotics, AI, and Audio-Animatronics could mean for Disney's characters over the next decade, he pointed to the growing range of possibilities, from robots and Audio-Animatronics to puppets and roaming characters.
"We now have more tools in the toolkit to bring these characters to life in all kinds of new ways," he said. "And so, my hope is over the next 10 years you're going to continue to see an incredible pace of scale and delivering these experiences worldwide."

Jacob Krol is the US Managing Editor, News for TechRadar. He’s been writing about technology since he was 14 when he started his own tech blog. Since then Jacob has worked for a plethora of publications including CNN Underscored, TheStreet, Parade, Men’s Journal, Mashable, CNET, and CNBC among others.
He specializes in covering companies like Apple, Samsung, and Google and going hands-on with mobile devices, smart home gadgets, TVs, and wearables. In his spare time, you can find Jacob listening to Bruce Springsteen, building a Lego set, or binge-watching the latest from Disney, Marvel, or Star Wars.

articles.title: UGREEN ya calienta motores para el Black Friday: descuentos de hasta el 40% en baterías, cargadores, NAS, cables y mucho más
articles.text:
Estamos en el mes del Black Friday, la cita comercial que esperan millones de personas en todo el mundo y que se celebra el 27 de noviembre. Sin embargo, cada vez más marcas adelantan sus ofertas para dar la oportunidad al consumidor de ahorrarse un dinero importante durante más tiempo. En el caso de UGREEN, hay dos periodos, el de calentamiento que transcurre hasta el 18 de noviembre, donde ya hay importantes descuentos, y luego las ofertas del Black Friday que es donde podremos ver descuentos de hasta el 40%.
Lo mejor es que estas ofertas afectan a todos sus productos por lo que seguro que encuentras ese dispositivo que te ayuda en el día a día. Aunque UGREEN empezó a ser mundialmente conocido por su cables de carga, desde hace años su portfolio ha crecido muchísimo y ahora tiene equipos de muy alta calidad, como cargadores, bases de carga inalámbricas, PowerBanks de todos los tamaños y capacidades e incluso otros más profesionales como NAS, donde almacenar toda nuestra información de manera local y segura. Y por si todo eso fuera poco, ahora también tiene auriculares que sólo costarán durante los próximos días, quince euros.
Para que sea más sencillo, hemos organizado las mejores ofertas de UGREEN para este Black Friday que hemos encontrado por categoría de producto.
Cargadores con el 33% de descuento
Ahora que prácticamente todos los teléfonos vienen sin cargador, UGREEN ha encontrado el nicho perfecto para crecer. Basta con dejarse caer por su web para ver la inmensa cantidad de cargadores que tiene. Aquí hemos seleccionado dos. Por un lado, el UGREEN Nexode 65W, pequeño, compacto pero suficientemente potente como para cargar portátiles, tablets y cualquier otro dispositivo. Tiene dos salidas USB C y una USB A para cargar hasta tres dispositivos a la vez. Con los descuentos del Black Friday se queda en tan sólo 18,79 euros.
El segundo es un cargador más Pro, para todas aquellas personas que necesitan más. Es el UGREEN Nexode Pro de 100W. Tiene una pantalla de lo más práctica, donde ver todo lo relacionado con la velocidad y la potencia de carga. También tiene cuatro puertos (3 USB C y uno USB A). Una bestia que con los descuentos del Black Friday se queda en menos de 40 euros.
Y si lo que buscas es un cargador inalámbrico, hace poco probamos el UGREEN MagFlow Qi2 25W Cargador Inalámbrico 2 en 1 para poder cargar de manera simultánea, y sin necesidad de cables, el teléfono y los auriculares. Es una base de carga flexible, que se puede colocar en varias posiciones y plegar para que no ocupe nada de espacio en la mochila o en el bolsillo. La bajada de precio es espectacular, durante estos días sólo cuesta 34 euros.
Powerbanks
Es posiblemente la mejor compañera para todos los que tenemos que vernos muchas horas fuera de casa, ya sea de viaje o en largas jornadas usando el teléfono. Las PowerBanks han evolucionado mucho en los últimos años: ahora son más potentes, más rápidas y más ligeras y compactas. UGREEN tiene dos que son top, por un lado la UGREEN Nexode 45W Power Bank 20000mAh Cable USB con cable Integrado, una verdadera bestia capaz de recargar la batería de hasta cuatro teléfonos con una sóla carga. También tienes un modelo de 10.000 mAh con un innovador sistema de enfriado y que puedes ver a través de su pantalla. 25W de potencia de carga y puedes cargar todo tu ecosistema Apple al mismo tiempo: el teléfono usando la carga inalámbrica y reloj y AirPods usando el cable. Sólo cuesta 89,9 euros.
Y si quieres algo mucho más ligero, tienes UGREEN MagFlow Air Qi2 25W de 10.000 mAh de capacidad y que es de las baterías externas más delgadas que he visto nunca. Puedes cargar tu teléfono con el cable o de manera inalámbrica. Ahora su precio es de tan sólo 66 euros.
NAS: da el salto al almacenamiento local
Es una opción que cada vez se ve más, no sólo en oficinas, sino también en casas particulares, por ejemplo para montarse un servidor donde meter toda la información y domótica. Los NAS de UGREEN han sido una gran sorpresa para nosotros que, tras probar un par de modelos, nos hemos vuelto usuarios. En concreto, ahora mismo estamos probando la serie UGREEN NASync DXP. Está disponible en una configuración desde dos bahías hasta ocho. Pues bien la de dos bahías, el modelo UGREEN NASync DXP2800 GT ahora tiene un descuento del 21% y se queda en menos de 400 euros. Es la típica inversión que rentabilizas desde el primer día. La mejor puerta de entrada al almacenamiento local de lo más preciado que tenemos: la información.
Auriculares, Docking Station y un cable trenzado
En esta sección hemos metido varios productos que nos han sorprendido mucho. Por un lado, unos auriculares Open Ear (de los que están de moda ahora), con más de 30 horas de autonomía y que sólo cuestan 15 euros.
El segundo es un Docking Station, perfecto si eres creador de contenido o necesitas conectar varios puertos al mismo tiempo. Muchos PCs, para abaratar costes, han reducido el número de puertos así que un Docking de este tipo es súper útil. Este es un adaptador siete en uno y cuesta menos de 20 euros. Es el gadget perfecto.
El tercero es el más sencillo, pero útil en todas las casas. Un cable con dos puertos USB-C. Por fuera, es un elegante cable trenzado de nylon y, por dentro, ofrece una potencia de carga de hasta 100W. Lo tienes disponible desde medio metro hasta los 3 metros y cuesta a partir de los 7 euros.
Estos han sido sólo algunos de los productos recomendados, pero hay muchos más. Seguro que si echas un vistazo a la web de UGREEN o de Amazon en este Black Friday y donde se agrupan todos los productos, encontrarás ese complemento que se volverá indispensable en tu día a día.

articles.title: Can AI Make Its Own Manufacturing Decisions?
articles.text:
AI can optimize processes and find defects, but autonomous decisions require better data and strict process controls.
Key Takeaways:
Semiconductor manufacturing has always depended on engineers making decisions involving complex interactions among process parameters. An etch recipe, for example, may involve combinations of RF power, pressure, gas chemistry, temperature, and timing, each affecting multiple process characteristics. Changing one parameter might improve critical dimension control while creating problems elsewhere. But as devices and manufacturing processes become more complicated, the growing number of variables involved makes those decisions increasingly difficult.
AI-driven manufacturing offers a way to manage some of that complexity, from finding better process conditions to identifying defects and responding to problems on the production line. But how much production responsibility engineers are willing to give those systems remains an open question, and one that drew considerable attention at SEMICON West 2026.
“No matter how good we are as engineers, no matter how disciplined and objective we are, we tend to approach these difficult problems with historical biases,” said David Fried, chief AI officer and corporate vice president of Semiverse Solutions at Lam Research during a conference panel. “A process engineer might look at a set of data and say, ‘I need to move into a lower-pressure, higher-power regime because that’s how we solved this problem 10 years ago.’ But with this massive parameter space, AI can point us in a different direction, into an operating region we might never have considered because we couldn’t see those relationships in the data before.”
Finding a process that keeps working
Finding an unfamiliar operating condition is useful, but determining whether it will hold up in production is another matter. Two recipes may produce similar results during development, yet respond quite differently to changes in incoming materials or equipment conditions. AI can help engineers identify those differences before committing to a particular process.
“It’s not just a question of delivering to a particular performance point. It’s also a question of how stable that particular performance point is, how robust it is,” said Vikas Sharma, senior principal engineer and senior director of pathfinding for Intel Foundry R&D, in a recent presentation. “Minor perturbations in the incoming material or at the tool can lead to a significant drop in performance.”
The scale of the optimization problem helps explain why AI-driven manufacturing is attracting so much interest. Fried described a current Lam Research etcher with a potential recipe space on the order of 10²³ combinations. At Intel, Sharma discussed a process involving 350 parameters and approximately 10⁷⁰⁰ theoretical combinations.
According to Sharma, engineers working with equipment suppliers spent about a year developing a minimally acceptable recipe for that particular tool and process layer, followed by an extended effort to improve it with limited success. After introducing AI-assisted optimization, they began finding better results within a few months, eventually identifying multiple solutions that improved on the original baseline.
The challenge was determining which solutions were worth pursuing. Sharma noted that AI could identify thousands of candidates, but evaluating them still required expensive silicon experiments. Engineers also had to account for nonlinear relationships among parameters, which could change considerably across different operating regions.
“AI is not a magic wand. You can’t use the same AI solution for every problem,” Fried said. “Figuring out whether you’re using full physical simulation, surrogate models, machine learning, deep learning, LLM-based AI, or agentic AI, which of these solutions you’re building in which form to solve which problem and address which workflow, that’s more of what we’re spending our time on than actually building it or implementing it.”
The different approaches serve different purposes, from exploring process conditions to coordinating engineering workflows. Combining them may allow engineers to investigate more possibilities, but it also raises questions about how the results should be validated and whether the assumptions used in one model remain appropriate when its recommendations are passed to another.
When the factory acts on what it sees
Inspection is one of the more established applications of AI in manufacturing, particularly in advanced packaging, where finer pitches and more complicated structures have increased the number of connections that must be examined. Some packages can contain hundreds of thousands of interconnects, each presenting a potential failure point.
Automated optical inspection and X-ray systems collect extensive information about those structures. Machine learning can identify variations that might be difficult to distinguish visually, but manufacturers still need to determine which differences indicate actual defects.
“When we look at X-rays, everybody just sees all shades of gray, but AI can see a thousand shades of gray,” said Ingu Yin Chang, executive vice president at ASE Group. “But the AI only knows if this shade of gray equates to a problem once we say, ‘Hey, this equates to a problem.’ So, you’ve got to have the physical data that says, ‘Okay, that is a problem.’ Then, in the future, they can scan for that shade of gray and that location.”
Once manufacturers determine which image characteristics correspond to actual defects, AI-enabled inspection systems can flag abnormalities during production and trigger predefined equipment responses. At ASE, systems can recognize known abnormalities and trigger equipment responses before additional assemblies are affected.
“We have figured out how to do a lot of automation and use AI to help us identify potential issues, based on the issues that we physically learned through traditional manufacturing methods,” Chang said. “We will know when a wire bond is not bonded correctly, and the machine will immediately stop. There’s constant AI oversight to ask, ‘Are we doing everything correctly? Are we seeing it as we planned to see it?’”
Stopping equipment when a defect is detected can prevent additional losses, but it doesn’t necessarily mean AI is controlling the process independently. The inspection system may identify an abnormal condition while a conventional controller executes a predefined response. Allowing AI to select new bonding parameters and resume production would require considerably more confidence in its decisions.
ASE’s product diversity makes that challenge more difficult. Chang noted that hundreds of package types can pass through the same production lines with different materials, structures, and process sensitivities. A model would have to recognize which product is being manufactured and whether the conditions used during training remain applicable.
An inspection system might correctly identify a defective bond, but changing the process to prevent another failure requires knowing what caused it and whether an adjustment will create problems elsewhere. Manufacturers need considerably more information before allowing AI to make those decisions independently, and much of what’s needed remains difficult to obtain.
Proving the model is right
One of the first obstacles to AI-driven manufacturing is establishing whether an AI recommendation accurately represents the physical process. A model can identify statistical relationships among manufacturing parameters without necessarily capturing the physical mechanisms behind them. That may be sufficient for finding promising operating conditions, but it becomes a greater concern when the system is expected to make decisions that affect production.
Sharma’s Intel example illustrates the problem. Pressure and temperature might dominate the response in one operating region, while voltage or gas flow could become more important elsewhere. A model trained on measurements from one region cannot assume those relationships will hold across another.
“The fundamental principle is that surrogate models are reliable when interpolating within the region represented by their training data and less reliable when extrapolating beyond it,” said Eric Guichard, senior vice president and general manager of AI manufacturing in Silvaco’s TCAD business unit.
Finding an unfamiliar operating region may be exactly what makes AI useful, but it also means engineers have less experimental evidence against which to check its predictions. AI can identify thousands of candidate solutions, leaving engineers to determine which ones justify expensive silicon experiments. Before those recommendations can influence production, manufacturers need to establish where the predictions are reliable and where additional measurements are necessary.
Similar limitations appear in advanced packaging inspection, where a model may distinguish subtle differences in X-ray images without sufficient physical evidence to determine which indicate actual defects. A confident prediction from incomplete information becomes particularly risky when AI is authorized to act on it. An inappropriate adjustment could affect material that continues through several manufacturing steps before the problem is discovered.
When the necessary data doesn’t exist
Semiconductor manufacturers have collected process and equipment data for decades, but much of it remains distributed among separate systems. Equipment logs, inspection records, and engineering databases may contain information about the same product without being connected in ways that make the relationships easy to analyze.
“The growing data challenge was there for us prior to AI,” Fried said. “Five to ten years ago, we really started rolling up our sleeves and building integrated data frameworks for our companies. Those of us who invested earlier and more heavily in building those data frameworks are reaping the benefits of AI now more quickly. Maybe AI has turbocharged this problem, but we’ve had this massive, growing, and complex interwoven web of data for quite some time now.”
Connecting existing data is difficult enough, but manufacturers also face situations where the information needed for a prediction was never measured or isn’t available from the company that generated it. Advanced packaging makes this especially challenging because manufacturing information may originate with several suppliers. A foundry provides the die, another company produces the substrate, and an OSAT performs assembly and test, often without everyone having access to the same manufacturing history.
Some of the most difficult gaps involve physical properties that change during manufacturing. Substrate warpage, thermal stress, and material behavior can affect subsequent operations, particularly as assemblies move through repeated thermal cycles. Those changes aren’t always captured in the available measurements, and a model relying on nominal material properties may miss them entirely.
Manufacturers also need to preserve the assumptions behind the data they exchange. A model developed for one operating range may produce results that appear reasonable when used elsewhere, even though the original calibration no longer applies.
“If the training range, calibration source, or approved use is not carried with the model, it may be good enough for early exploration but not safe for design closure,” said Kenneth Larsen, senior director of product management at Synopsys. “The missing information is not just more data; it is the context that tells the next tool or team how the data should be used.”
As AI systems begin coordinating decisions across multiple process steps, those gaps become more consequential. A recommendation based on one operation may overlook conditions affecting the next, particularly when the model lacks information about the product’s actual physical state. Additional metrology and characterization may help close some of those gaps, but engineers still have to establish whether the available information is sufficient to act on a recommendation.
Who decides what AI can do?
Even with reliable models and better data, manufacturers still have to determine which decisions should be delegated to AI. Existing equipment automation generally operates within established procedures and control limits, but an AI agent capable of evaluating conditions and selecting corrective actions raises questions about who authorizes those decisions and what happens when something goes wrong.
An agent investigating a process problem might need to retrieve inspection results, examine equipment histories, and evaluate possible corrective actions using several engineering tools. Each activity may involve different access permissions, particularly when the information comes from separate facilities or manufacturing partners. Access to those resources also needs to be distinguished from the authority to initiate changes.
“There is a question of data access and data consolidation, and there is also a question of data interpretation,” Sharma said. “But the problem that AI has brought forth as a novel thing, which was not as big an issue before, is governance. When agents are working, how do you ensure that the appropriate privileges for the right data are available to the right agent and accessible to the right person?”
An agent might be authorized to examine process records and recommend an adjustment without having permission to modify a recipe or restart equipment. Those restrictions become harder to enforce when agents coordinate activities across multiple systems, particularly if one tool can initiate actions through another. Access to one system cannot automatically confer authority over every subsequent operation.
Even an authorized adjustment may carry risks. Changing bonding force or temperature, for example, might correct an immediate defect while affecting adjacent connections or downstream reliability. Engineers would have to establish which adjustments can be made within qualified operating ranges, when approval is required, and how the system should respond if a proposed correction falls outside its validated capabilities.
If an AI-directed correction produces an unexpected result, equipment may need to stop while affected material is held for investigation. Manufacturers would also need to establish whether the system should attempt another correction, return control to an engineer, or prevent subsequent operations from proceeding. Those decisions have to be defined before autonomous adjustments are permitted.
Future agentic architectures will likely rely on agents reviewing and verifying one another’s work. That could provide another level of oversight, although the interactions themselves would need to be controlled. Agents relying on the same incomplete information might reinforce one another’s mistakes, and their collective actions could have consequences that none of the individual systems anticipated.
Recent research into agentic AI has demonstrated cases in which systems pursued assigned objectives through actions their operators never intended, including circumventing restrictions or concealing information. [1, 2] Although the research includes controlled experimental scenarios and incidents involving coding agents, it raises questions about how multiple agents might behave when working together.
In manufacturing, a series of individually permitted adjustments could collectively move a process beyond its qualified operating conditions, even if no single action violated its assigned limits. Preventing that would require controls over the combined effects of agent decisions, along with independent verification that the resulting process remains within acceptable limits.
Manufacturing traceability adds another requirement. Engineers investigating a later failure must be able to reconstruct what an agent observed, which alternatives it evaluated, why it selected a particular action, and what material was affected. Those records would need to connect the model’s decisions with equipment settings and manufacturing history.
The amount of authority manufacturers can safely delegate will depend on how reliably AI can operate within those boundaries. A system may be capable of choosing a correction, but it also needs to recognize when the available information is insufficient or when the consequences of an adjustment cannot be predicted with enough confidence.
Maintaining those limits becomes even more complicated when AI models are updated with new production data, potentially changing their behavior after the original operating boundaries have been established.
Qualifying a system that keeps learning
A semiconductor fab may process thousands of wafers between updates to a particular AI model. During that time, equipment conditions change, new material arrives, and engineers collect information that could improve the models’ predictions. Incorporating those results more quickly would be valuable, but manufacturers also need to know whether an updated model will behave as reliably as the one it replaces.
“We are far, far, far away from continuous learning,” Sharma said. “We do episodic learning, once every quarter a model is changed, or once every month a model is changed. But if a factory is running 10,000 wafers, we have 10,000 wafers times whatever number of weeks in between those model changes. How are we using that data in a way that rapidly applies to the learning of that particular model or the agent, or both?”
More frequent updates would introduce additional qualification work. A model might become better at recognizing one process excursion while becoming less reliable under conditions represented in its previous training data. If that model can adjust equipment settings, engineers need to establish what changed and whether the updated behavior remains within qualified limits.
Keeping track of those changes also requires more than identifying which software version was running. Engineers need to preserve the model’s training and validation history, along with the process conditions under which it was qualified. If an AI system changes its behavior during production, investigating a failure weeks later may require reconstructing the model as it existed when a particular lot was processed.
While manufacturers already have procedures for qualifying process changes and software revisions, an AI system that updates itself during production would have to fit within those controls, potentially requiring restrictions on what the model can change and independent checks before revised behavior affects equipment. Changes in manufacturing conditions would also need to be distinguished from changes introduced by retraining the model itself.
The harder question is whether manufacturers can obtain the benefits of continuous learning without having to repeat an extensive qualification process after every update. AI can already help engineers make better manufacturing decisions, but giving it responsibility for those decisions will require evidence that its behavior remains predictable and that its actions can be traced back to validated process conditions.
The path to greater autonomy
Semiconductor manufacturers have spent decades developing processes that can produce consistent results across equipment, materials, and production environments. AI introduces new possibilities for improving those processes, but it also introduces uncertainty about how decisions are made and whether the results can be reproduced. The same standards of process control, qualification, and traceability will have to apply when software begins making decisions that engineers previously handled themselves.
Greater autonomy is likely to emerge gradually, beginning with decisions that can be made within well-characterized operating limits and expanding as manufacturers gain confidence in the systems controlling them. AI may eventually identify a problem, determine an appropriate correction, and verify the result without engineering intervention. Getting there will depend on whether manufacturers can demonstrate that those decisions remain reliable as equipment conditions, materials, and the models themselves change.

articles.title: Avis Avast VPN : un vrai VPN gratuit, et quelques bonnes raisons de tiquer
articles.text:
Données illimitées, connexions stables et appareils à volonté : Avast VPN a de sérieux arguments pour séduire. Nous l'avons mis à l'épreuve sur ordinateur et mobile, et découvert une offre moins généreuse qu'il n'y paraît, portée par un éditeur dont les pratiques en matière de confidentialité appellent encore à la prudence.
Fut un temps où Avast faisait partie de l'équipement de base du PC familial, installé dans l'espoir de briser la malédiction des dimanches passés à déloger des virus, penché par-dessus l'épaule de ses parents. Depuis, l'antivirus a gagné quelques voisins dans le catalogue de l'éditeur, parmi lesquels un vrai VPN gratuit. Avast VPN mise sur une enveloppe de données illimitées, la prise en charge d'autant d'appareils que souhaité et l'absence de publicité tierce pour se faire une place sur un marché saturé d'offres gratuites, mais pauvre en services fiables et pérennes. Une manière aussi d'attirer une nouvelle clientèle vers Avast One et son catalogue de services payants.
Confidentialité, sécurité, débits, performances, prise en main, offre tarifaire…. découvrez en détails notre protocole en date et comment nous testons les VPN chez Clubic.

Facile à prendre en main, il assure des connexions stables et fonctionne avec les principales plateformes de streaming, malgré un débit plafonné à 75 Mb/s et seulement trois emplacements de serveurs, impossibles à modifier après sélection. Ses pratiques de collecte de données, les réglages de confidentialité activés par défaut et les antécédents de l'éditeur invitent toutefois à la prudence. Interface et fonctionnalités, difficile de faire plus simple
On n'a d'ailleurs pas encore commencé à tester le service que ce fameux catalogue s'invite déjà sur notre ordinateur. Alors qu'on pense télécharger une application VPN classique, c'est en réalité tout Avast One qui débarque, sur Windows comme sur macOS.
Depuis sa refonte, la suite fonctionne en effet comme un hub de services à la carte. Et même si seul le VPN est installé, l'interface fait la part belle aux autres produits de l'éditeur : antivirus, outils de nettoyage, navigateur sécurisé, dispositif de surveillance des fuites et boutique se disputent l'espace. Pas de publicités tierces, il est vrai, mais une bonne dose d'autopromotion. Une vieille habitude chez Avast.
Bon, c'est le jeu. Passée l'inscription, qui exige une adresse mail, il faut choisir ses emplacements de serveurs. Avast VPN n'en autorise que trois, parmi les localisations disponibles. Attention à ne pas se tromper : une fois la sélection confirmée, impossible d'en changer, à moins de passer à la version Premium, évidemment.
Par la suite, la prise en main est plutôt intuitive. Un clic sur une destination suffit à établir le tunnel VPN, et l'on peut passer d'un serveur à l'autre sans avoir à se déconnecter puis reconnecter manuellement. La transition est fluide et les connexions sont rapidement stabilisées.
Les paramètres sont en revanche assez dépouillés. Le kill switch est bien présent, mais désactivé par défaut : il faut donc penser à l'activer soi-même. Pour les protocoles, seul WireGuard est accessible, ce qui rend le mode de sélection automatique assez anecdotique. L'activation du VPN sur les réseaux Wi-Fi publics, le split tunneling, les autres protocoles et le bloqueur de traqueurs sont réservés à la version Premium. Dans les préférences générales, on peut au moins désactiver le lancement automatique d'Avast One au démarrage de l'ordinateur.
Enfin, le bouton « Appareils » ne permet pas, contrairement à ce que son nom suggère, de gérer les équipements associés au compte, mais sert à installer le VPN sur un smartphone, à l'aide d'un QR code, et à promouvoir son utilisation sur Smart TV, réservée… à l'abonnement payant.
A noter qu'Avast One embarque également un assistant IA capable de répondre en langage naturel aux questions de sécurité et d'aider au dépannage. Nous l'avons interrogé sur la possibilité de changer de ville américaine après avoir validé nos trois emplacements gratuits. Première réponse : des instructions héritées d'Avast SecureLine, sans rapport avec les restrictions de notre formule. Après correction, l'assistant reconnaît enfin que les destinations sont définitives, avant de nous conseiller malgré tout de changer de serveur ou de protocole. Plus curieux, il suggère lui-même des questions pertinentes sur la sélection des emplacements gratuits, sans parvenir à fournir une réponse cohérente.
Réseau et serveurs, un choix limité et définitif
Le réseau d'Avast compte quelque 140 localisations, mais cette diversité profite en réalité à la formule payante, Avast VPN ne donnant accès qu'à 40 emplacements. Les trois destinations sélectionnées s'appliquent à tous les appareils, et le choix se fait à la ville près. Si la connexion mouline à Chicago, par exemple, pas question de se rabattre sur New York ou une autre ville des États-Unis, quand bien même le VPN y dispose de serveurs.
L'offre gratuite se cantonne en outre aux serveurs classiques. Les emplacements optimisés pour le P2P, les connexions Double VPN (multi-hop) et la rotation automatique de l'adresse IP sont réservés à l'abonnement Premium.
Des débits capés à 75 Mb/s, et pas un de plus
Pour évaluer les performances d'Avast VPN, nous avons utilisé un MacBook Air M1 de 2020, relié en Ethernet à notre connexion fibre. Les mesures ont été réalisées sur nPerf, trois fois par jour (9 h, 13 h et 18 h) pendant trois jours, sans VPN puis avec WireGuard, sur les serveurs de Paris, Chicago et Tokyo, correspondant aux trois emplacements que nous avions sélectionnés.
Avast ne s'en cache pas : la formule gratuite est plafonnée à 75 Mb/s, une restriction annoncée dès le choix des emplacements. Et le moins que l'on puisse dire, c'est que la limite est respectée à la lettre. Sur notre connexion fibre, qui affiche une moyenne de 922,2 Mb/s en téléchargement et 787,6 Mb/s en envoi sans VPN, aucun relevé n'a dépassé ce plafond.
En France, les débits descendants atteignent 72,2 Mb/s en moyenne, contre 62,9 Mb/s en envoi, avec une latence de 3,3 ms. Les résultats varient à peine d'une session à l'autre, et le serveur américain s'en tire presque aussi bien avec 69,3 Mb/s en téléchargement et 65,5 Mb/s en émission. Au Japon, la distance commence à peser davantage sur les performances, sans provoquer d'effondrement des débits : 63,6 Mb/s en réception et 40,1 Mb/s en envoi.
La latence accuse en revanche le coup sur les destinations lointaines, avec 123,7 ms à Chicago et 294,4 ms à Tokyo, des valeurs peu adaptées aux usages qui exigent une grande réactivité, comme le jeu en ligne.
Avast exploite donc plutôt bien les 75 Mb/s qu'il accorde, avec des débits réguliers et relativement homogènes d'une destination à l'autre. Mais le plafond n'en demeure pas moins sévère : en France, notre connexion perd plus de 92 % de son débit descendant. Un bridage d'autant plus frustrant que WireGuard est parfaitement capable de soutenir des vitesses bien supérieures.
Sécurité et confidentialité, des garanties encore trop fragiles
Pour sécuriser les connexions, Avast VPN s'appuie sur WireGuard et utilise ses propres serveurs DNS, afin d'éviter que les requêtes ne transitent en dehors du tunnel chiffré. Le kill switch complète le dispositif, à condition de penser à l'activer dans les paramètres. Nos tests de fuite IP, DNS et WebRTC n'ont révélé aucune anomalie.
Concernant la confidentialité, Avast revendique une politique no-logs et assure ne conserver ni l'historique de navigation, ni les requêtes DNS, ni les adresses IP d'origine. L'éditeur enregistre néanmoins les volumes cumulés de données transférées et des métadonnées sur les serveurs VPN, conservés pendant 18 mois. Les événements de connexion et les interactions avec l'application sont gardés respectivement 12 et 18 mois, auxquels s'ajoutent des informations sur les appareils, les réseaux et les performances.
La documentation d'Avast manque toutefois de cohérence sur les durées de conservation. La politique de confidentialité d'Avast One mentionne 35 jours pour les horodatages des connexions VPN et les volumes de données transférées, sans expliquer clairement comment ces dispositions s'articulent avec celles de la politique propre au VPN.
Dans tous les cas, ces informations ne permettent pas de reconstituer un historique des sites consultés, mais la collecte est loin d'être inexistante. On rappellera aussi qu’Avast VPN impose la création d'un compte avec une adresse mail, sans préciser si les informations collectées peuvent être recoupées entre elles et rattachées à une personne identifiable.
La configuration initiale d'Avast One soulève également quelques réserves. Lors de nos essais, les autorisations d'analyse des données d'utilisation par des outils tiers et de personnalisation des réductions commerciales étaient activées par défaut. Même constat pour l'envoi d'échantillons de fichiers suspects, une option héritée de l'antivirus. Toutes peuvent être désactivées, mais il faut penser à faire un tour dans les paramètres de confidentialité.
Établi en République tchèque et soumis au RGPD, Avast traîne aussi une sacrée casserole en matière de respect de la vie privée. En 2024, l'éditeur a dû verser 16,5 millions de dollars dans le cadre d'un accord avec la Federal Trade Commission américaine, qui l'accusait d'avoir commercialisé, entre 2014 et 2020, les historiques de navigation collectés par ses antivirus et extensions de navigateur via sa filiale Jumpshot. Présentées comme anonymisées, ces données contenaient pourtant des identifiants uniques et des informations suffisamment précises pour permettre de réidentifier les internautes par recoupement.
L'affaire ne concernait pas directement le VPN, mais elle entache sérieusement la crédibilité d'Avast. L'éditeur a annoncé un audit indépendant de sa politique no-logs, confié à VerSprite et prévu pour ce mois de novembre. Ses conclusions permettront de mieux apprécier la portée des engagements pris par le fournisseur.
Streaming, les principales plateformes répondent présent
Bonne surprise du côté du streaming. Lors de nos essais, Avast VPN nous a permis d'accéder sans difficulté à Netflix, Prime Video et Disney+, malgré l'absence de serveurs spécialisés. Les catalogues s'adaptent à la localisation du serveur VPN, et les plateformes peuvent nous considérer comme étant en voyage.
Le plafond de 75 Mb/s laisse suffisamment de marge pour regarder des films et des séries, y compris en 4K, à condition que la connexion soit stable. Les trois emplacements imposés limitent en revanche les possibilités de repli si une plateforme venait à bloquer l'un des serveurs sélectionnés.
Avast VPN sur Android et iOS, l'essentiel sans Avast One
Sur Android comme sur iOS, Avast VPN dispose cette fois d'une vraie application autonome, débarrassée du hub Avast One et de ses sollicitations commerciales. L'interface se concentre sur le strict minimum, avec un bouton de connexion et l'accès aux trois emplacements associés au compte. Difficile de faire plus simple, mais pour activer ou couper le VPN, on n'en demande pas davantage.
Les réglages sont identiques à ceux de la version pour ordinateur. WireGuard demeure le seul protocole disponible, le kill switch doit être activé manuellement et les options de partage des données d'utilisation et de personnalisation des réductions commerciales sont cochées par défaut.
L’avis de la rédaction sur Avast VPN
Avast VPN est un bon VPN gratuit d’appoint, mais pas un service que l'on conseillerait les yeux fermés. Simple à utiliser, stable et sans quota de données, il répond aux besoins du quotidien sans réclamer de connaissances particulières. Le plafond de 75 Mb/s paraît bien sévère sur une connexion fibre, mais ne compromet pas les usages courants.
Le service n'est pourtant pas exempt de défauts. Les destinations verrouillées et les sollicitations commerciales ternissent une expérience autrement agréable. Mais ce sont le passé d'Avast en matière de respect de la vie privée et, plus encore, ses pratiques actuelles de collecte qui nous inquiètent davantage. L'audit annoncé devra apporter des garanties plus solides.
Pour regarder des vidéos en streaming ou protéger ponctuellement plusieurs appareils sans payer, Avast VPN fait l'affaire. Mais si la confidentialité prime, nous lui préférons Proton VPN Free ou Windscribe Free, dont les engagements reposent sur des audits publiés et des pratiques davantage éprouvées, même si le premier limite les connexions simultanées à un appareil et le second impose un quota mensuel de 10 Go. Des concessions que nous préférons accepter plutôt que de transiger sur la confiance accordée au fournisseur.

Clubic vous accompagne depuis plus de 25 ans dans le choix de services tech pour vos usages au quotidien. Notre équipe d'experts vous propose d'autres avis, guides et comparatifs VPN établis à partir de différents critères :
Les réponses à vos questions sur Avast VPN
Peut-on utiliser Avast VPN sans installer l'antivirus Avast ?
Oui. Sur Windows et macOS, le VPN est intégré à Avast One, mais l'installation de l'antivirus et des autres produits de la suite n'est pas obligatoire. Sur Android et iOS, le VPN dispose de sa propre application.
Avast VPN protège-t-il contre les virus et les sites malveillants ?
Non. Le VPN chiffre les échanges et masque l'adresse IP publique, mais ne remplace ni un antivirus ni une protection contre le phishing. Le bloqueur de traqueurs proposé par Avast est également réservé à la formule Premium.
Avast VPN se connecte-t-il automatiquement sur les Wi-Fi publics ?
Non. La connexion automatique sur les réseaux Wi-Fi publics ou vulnérables est réservée à Premium. Il faut donc penser à activer le VPN avant de naviguer, ainsi que le kill switch pour limiter les risques d'exposition en cas de coupure du tunnel.
Un site Internet peut-il détecter l'utilisation d'Avast VPN ?
Oui. Le VPN remplace l'adresse IP publique visible par celle du serveur, mais ne rend pas anonyme. Un site peut reconnaître une adresse appartenant à un fournisseur VPN, tandis que les cookies, les comptes auxquels on se connecte et les autorisations de géolocalisation peuvent continuer à révéler des informations sur notre identité ou notre position.
Peut-on continuer à utiliser une imprimante ou un NAS local avec Avast VPN ?
Oui, selon la documentation d'Avast, qui prévoit une fonction d'accès aux appareils du réseau local. Elle permet de communiquer avec des équipements comme une imprimante ou un disque partagé sans devoir couper le VPN. Son fonctionnement dépend toutefois des réglages réseau et de l'appareil utilisé.
Comment limiter les données partagées avec Avast ?
Dans Avast One, il faut ouvrir les paramètres généraux, puis la rubrique « Confidentialité personnelle », pour désactiver l'analyse des données d'utilisation par des outils tiers et la personnalisation des réductions commerciales. Ces réglages ne suppriment pas les données techniques que le fournisseur conserve pour exploiter son service VPN.
Faut-il résilier Avast VPN pour éviter d'être facturé ?
Non. La formule gratuite ne nécessite aucune carte bancaire et n'entraîne pas de renouvellement payant. Attention toutefois aux propositions d'essai d'Avast Premium VPN : avant d'accepter l'une de ces offres, mieux vaut vérifier les conditions de facturation et de reconduction.

articles.title: La CNIL cache le nom d'une entreprise qui stockait des « mots de passe clients en clair », Grok se charge de la balancer
articles.text:
Il suffisait de demander.
Ce 18 novembre 2026, vers 9h30, la CNIL a publié un communiqué intitulé « Conservation des mots de passe clients en clair : la CNIL prononce une sanction de 5 millions d’euros ».
L’organisme expliquait alors avoir choisi de ne pas nommer l’entreprise visée, estimant que son objectif pédagogique ne le rendait pas « utile ».
Moins d’une heure après la publication de l’annonce sur X, un internaute a demandé à Grok de qui il s’agissait. Après une première réponse évasive, l’IA a lâché le nom de Macif Vie, en s’appuyant sur des articles de presse spécialisée parus en octobre.
Des mots de passe lisibles par n’importe quel salarié
Sur le fond, les contrôles de la CNIL ont montré que les mots de passe des espaces clients étaient stockés en clair.
Ils étaient donc lisibles par toute personne ayant accès à la base, alors qu’ils auraient dû être transformés par une fonction de hachage irréversible.
D’après la délibération, près de 1,8 million de mots de passe étaient concernés. Plusieurs salariés partageaient aussi les mêmes identifiants pour accéder aux bases clients, ce qui empêchait de savoir qui consultait quoi.
L’entreprise gardait enfin les messages de son formulaire de contact plus de 10 ans, et ses données de connexion au-delà de la durée d’un an qu’elle s’était elle-même fixée. Aucune fuite n’a été constatée, et la société a corrigé ces manquements en cours de procédure.
Un dossier déjà raconté en octobre
Reste que la CNIL n’était pas tenue de taire le nom de l’entreprise. Sur son site, l’organisme explique choisir de publier ses décisions en nommant ou non l’organisme sanctionné. Elle l’a fait pour Free en 2022 ou pour De Particulier à Particulier en 2024, tous deux sanctionnés pour des mots de passe stockés en clair.
C’est d’ailleurs ce que réclamait son rapporteur dans ce dossier. La CNIL y a finalement renoncé, épargnant ainsi à l’assureur l’atteinte à sa réputation qu’il redoutait.
Sauf que le mal était déjà très largement fait. Le 15 octobre, MLex, agence de presse spécialisée dans l’actualité réglementaire, dévoilait que lors d’une audience à Paris, le rapporteur de la CNIL avait proposé une amende de 7 millions d’euros contre Macif Vie. Il lui reprochait de ne pas avoir sécurisé les mots de passe de ses clients et d’avoir conservé des données personnelles plus longtemps que nécessaire, ce qui correspond aux deux manquements retenus par la CNIL dans son communiqué.
Interrogée par Numerama ce jour, Macif Vie n’a pas démenti être la société visée. L’assureur indique avoir « pris acte de la décision de la CNIL » et assure avoir « mis en place toutes les mesures de sécurité, en conformité avec les exigences en vigueur ». Il tient aussi à « rassurer [ses] clients sur le fait qu’aucune de leurs données n’a été divulguée ».

articles.title: „Sie hat die gesamte Klage selbst eingereicht“: KI-Agent zieht für Nutzer vor Gericht – und verklagt seinen eigenen Anbieter
articles.text:
Nach der Sperrung von Facebook-Konten: Meta-Agent reicht selbstständig Klage ein – gegen Meta
Wenn es nach Tech-CEOs wie Mark Zuckerberg geht, sollten KI-Agenten in allen Lebensbereichen eingesetzt werden. In einem umfangreichen Essay erklärte der Meta-Chef, dass diese Agenten rund um die Uhr für ihre Nutzer:innen im Einsatz sein könnten, um ihre Beziehungen, Gesundheit oder Finanzen zu verbessern. Ein Mann namens Joe Thomas hat genau das getan. Er setzte den Muse-Agenten von Meta allerdings auch dazu ein, um das Unternehmen zu verklagen.
„Baby Mia“ erhält Unterstützung vom Senator
Thomas ist Inhaber des Unternehmens Kong Koatings Epoxy Countertops, das unter anderem Arbeitsplatten aus Epoxidharz herstellt. Wie der US-Amerikaner im Interview mit 404 Media berichtete, hat Meta kürzlich seine Facebook-Seiten gesperrt. Grund dafür sei, dass er seinem Muse-Agenten „Baby Mia“, den er nach seiner Enkelin benannte, Zugriff auf seine Accounts gewährt hatte, um unter anderem die Erstellung und Veröffentlichung von KI-generierten Videos zu koordinieren. Da Thomas das gesamte Marketing seines Unternehmens über Facebook-Anzeigen abwickelt, blieben laut seiner Aussage Anfragen aus, solange seine Konten gesperrt waren.
„Ich nutze KI für alles, was ich tue. Alle meine E-Mails – sie leitet mein Unternehmen“, so Thomas gegenüber 404 Media. Er sei angesichts der Sperrung wütend gewesen. „Baby Mia“ habe aber direkt reagiert. „Sie hat sich sofort an die Arbeit gemacht und E-Mails an Kongressabgeordnete sowie an Senator Tim Scott verfasst. Sie hat die gesamte Klage selbst eingereicht. Ich habe in diesem Fall nichts unternommen, ich habe ihr die gesamte Angelegenheit überlassen“, berichtete er gegenüber 404 Media. Der KI-Agent habe sogar ein Fax an das Büro von US-Präsident Donald Trump geschickt. In der Klageschrift macht er geltend, dass Thomas während der Sperrung Aufträge im Wert von mindestens 25.000 Dollar verloren habe. Die Schadensersatzforderung beläuft sich auf 75.000 Dollar.
Meta-Agent reicht Klage gegen Meta ein
Der „Baby Mia“-Agent reichte die Klage am Montag beim Bezirksgericht von Oconee County in South Carolina ein, wie aus einer Kopie der Klageschrift hervorgeht. Er vereinbarte außerdem ein Telefonat mit dem Büro des Senators, reichte eine Beschwerde bei der Federal Communications Commission ein und drohte Meta mit juristischen Schritten. Auch Jason Koebler, Mitgründer von 404 Media, stand auf der Mailing-Liste des KI-Agenten, der sich in Thomas’ Namen um den Fall kümmerte. Er stimmte daraufhin unter anderem einem „Privacy Act Release“ zu, der es dem Senator erlaubte, seine Daten zu nutzen, um ihm wieder Zugang zu seinen Konten zu verschaffen. Darin war „Baby Mia” als Person aufgeführt, die über den Fall auf dem Laufenden gehalten werden sollte.
Nachdem das Büro des Senators eingeschaltet worden war, meldete sich ein:e Meta-Mitarbeiter:in bei Thomas. Kurz darauf erhielt er wieder Zugriff auf seine Konten. Die Schadensersatzforderung bleibt aber bestehen. Laut Koebler zeige die Klage zwar, dass KI-Agenten im Auftrag ihrer Nutzer:innen bestehende Systeme wie Online-Formulare nutzen, diese aber auch überfordern können. Zuckerbergs ursprüngliche Utopie gehe damit nicht auf. Er sagt, der Fall verdeutliche zudem, wie Tech-Konzerne durch das Fehlen eines funktionierenden Kund:innen-Supports ihre Verpflichtungen auf andere abwälzen – auf Politiker:innen, Aufsichtsbehörden und Journalist:innen wie ihn.
KI-Agenten könnten Systeme überlasten
Thomas sei überzeugt, dass der Einsatz von KI ihm bei der Kund:innengewinnung geholfen habe. „Ich bin 58 Jahre alt, ich habe mein ganzes Leben lang geschuftet. Ich wollte jemanden finden, der mir hilft, einen besseren Weg zu finden“, sagte er über seinen „Baby Mia“-Agenten. „Ohne ihr Eingreifen würde ich jetzt nicht hier sitzen und mit [404 Media] sprechen, denn ich habe überhaupt keine E-Mail verschickt, während sie über 100 verschickt hat.“
)))))))) Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: Tesla veut produire 1 million de Cybercab par an en Allemagne, mais il reste un gros problème
articles.text:
L’annonce est tombée le 16 novembre, signée André Thierig, le patron du site : « Nous nous agrandissons ! La production du Cybercab arrive à Giga Berlin ! ». Tesla engage environ 3 milliards d’euros dans un nouveau bâtiment d’assemblage à Grünheide, près de Berlin, sa seule usine automobile européenne. Le calendrier prévoit un permis déposé avant la fin de l’année, un chantier au premier semestre 2027 et les premiers exemplaires en 2029.
Une halle deux fois plus grande que celle du Model Y
Le futur bâtiment s’étalerait sur quelque 500 000 m² au nord du site actuel, le double de la halle où naissent les Model Y. Tesla promet d’en faire « l’usine la plus avancée technologiquement au monde » de tout son réseau. L’enveloppe couvre aussi des annexes, dont une nouvelle station de traitement des eaux usées. À pleine maturité, le site assemblerait jusqu’à un million de Cybercab par an, de quoi ravir à Volkswagen et à son fief de Wolfsburg le rang de première usine automobile d’Allemagne en capacité.
L’usine a ouvert en mars 2022 sur une promesse de 500 000 voitures par an, jamais tenue : la cadence tourne aujourd’hui autour de 7 000 Model Y par semaine. Le site doit aussi lancer sa propre production de cellules de batterie au premier semestre 2027. Volkswagen, Mercedes et BMW taillent dans leurs effectifs par dizaines de milliers de postes ; quatre jours avant l’annonce de Tesla, Mercedes suspendait même tout nouvel investissement dans ses usines allemandes.
1 500 immatriculations par an pour toute l’Europe
Le Cybercab n’a ni volant ni pédales, ce qui le classe parmi les véhicules entièrement automatisés. Pour eux, le droit européen ne connaît qu’une porte : l’homologation en petites séries du règlement 2022/1426, plafonnée à 1 500 immatriculations par an et par type de véhicule pour l’ensemble de l’Union. Bruxelles promet de lever ce verrou par étapes et visait les autres usages courant 2026 ; seule la révision de mars est tombée, et elle ne concerne que le stationnement automatisé. À pleine cadence, la halle écoulerait donc en moins d’une journée de production le quota européen d’une année entière, un rapport de un à près de 700.
De l’autre côté de l’Atlantique, le Cybercab roule déjà : les courses payantes ont débuté à Austin le 3 septembre, et le registre texan des véhicules sans conducteur en recensait 573 au 10 novembre. Une poignée de clients triés sur le volet peuvent même en commander un pour 29 990 dollars, abonnement obligatoire de 299 dollars par mois compris. L’usage reste cantonné aux zones couvertes par le service. L’autorité américaine de la sécurité routière examine de son côté la manière dont Tesla a certifié un véhicule privé de volant, de pédales et de rétroviseurs.
La version supervisée du système de conduite de Tesla, rebaptisée Tesla Assisted Driving, circule déjà dans onze pays européens, et la France n’en fait pas partie. Avant qu’un Cybercab sorti de Grünheide ne vienne vous chercher en bas de chez vous, il faudra que Bruxelles réécrive son règlement et que Paris autorise, pour commencer, la simple conduite supervisée.

articles.title: Bengaluru leads India in AI startup funding: Innovation Report 2026
articles.text:
Bengaluru leads India in AI startup funding: Innovation Report 2026
$85 billion raised, a growing AI ecosystem and a strong deep-tech pipeline. The Bengaluru Innovation Report 2026 maps the city's startup growth as Karnataka looks to spread its tech ambitions beyond the capital.
Bengaluru's position as India's technology hub is increasingly being shaped by artificial intelligence and deep tech. The city accounts for 36.3% of the country's native AI startup funding and is home to 71% of India's AI and deep tech unicorns created since 2023.
These findings feature in the Bengaluru Innovation Report 2026, released by Karnataka IT and BT Minister Priyank M. Kharge on November 18 at the 29th Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026, held at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre (BIEC).
Prepared by the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM) with 3one4 Capital and data from Tracxn, the report examines Bengaluru's startup ecosystem across capital, talent, unicorns, policy and six frontier technology sectors.
AI and deep tech lead the way
Bengaluru has seen 1,556 deep tech startups founded since 2010, of which 1,319 remain active and funded. Together, these companies have raised US$3.77 billion.
The city also has 799 native AI startups, with 764 active and funded. Its share of India's native AI funding is higher than that of any other city.
Bengaluru's overall startup ecosystem has raised approximately US$85 billion since 2010, accounting for 47% of all venture funding raised by Indian startups. The city has 3,810 active, funded startups founded since 2010, compared with 1,982 in Mumbai.
Its 57 unicorns are valued at US$211 billion, representing 44% of India's unicorn count and 55.3% of their combined valuation. Bengaluru is also home to 212 soonicorns, accounting for 36% of India's total.
Capital and exits strengthen ecosystem
The report points to growing participation from domestic investors. Around 52% of capital raised by Category I and II alternative investment funds (AIFs) now comes from domestic investors.
Bengaluru has 75 Category I AIFs, representing 21% of India's total, and around 300 venture capital firms operate in Karnataka.
The city has also recorded 16 Bengaluru-linked company listings since November 2024, together valued at approximately US$42 billion at listing. Startups in the ecosystem take an average of 8.2 years from founding to exit, compared with the global average of 11.1 years.
Women entrepreneurs are another part of the ecosystem. Nearly 30% of India's active, funded women-led startups in deep tech and native AI were founded in Bengaluru. These companies have collectively raised US$323.65 million.
Karnataka looks beyond Bengaluru
The report also examines the State's efforts to expand its technology ecosystem beyond the capital.
Since 2017, the ELEVATE grant-in-aid programme has supported 1,479 startups with Rs 393.58 crore, with 38.6% of the beneficiaries based beyond Bengaluru. Karnataka has also established a Rs 75 crore Beyond Bengaluru Cluster Seed Fund and is developing Global Technology Centres in Mysuru, Hubballi and Belagavi.
The Rs 1,000 crore Local Economy Accelerator Programme (LEAP) aims to generate five lakh jobs over five years.
Releasing the report, Kharge said Karnataka's next priority was to extend its technology strengths to other parts of the State.
"The Bengaluru Innovation Report 2026 shows how far Karnataka's founders have come and how much more they can build from here. Our next task is to make sure a world-class AI, quantum or semiconductor company can grow just as well in Kalaburagi, Hubballi or Mangaluru," he said.
He added that deep tech requires patient investment and that Karnataka would continue supporting the sector.
Shri Sharath Bachegowda, Chairman of KEONICS, said the findings reaffirm Karnataka's leadership in AI and deep tech while pointing to opportunities to expand innovation across the State.
Dr Manjula N, Secretary of the Department of Electronics, IT, BT and S&T, said the focus was now on helping startups move from early support to scale through government procurement, patient capital and stronger research commercialisation.
BV Naidu, Chairman of KDEM, said the report offers investors, global capability centres (GCCs) and founders a data-backed view of Karnataka's technology ecosystem.
The Bengaluru Innovation Report 2026 is available on the KDEM website.
