articles.title: First Circle Capital raises $26 million to back African fintechs
articles.text:
First Circle Capital, a female-led venture capital firm focused on African fintechs, has closed its fund at $26 million, bringing fresh capital to early-stage startups building financial services across the continent.
The fund, Africa Fund I, will invest in pre-seed and seed-stage companies developing financial products, services, and technology infrastructure, particularly businesses using artificial intelligence, automation, and data to build more efficient financial services.
The International Finance Corporation (IFC), Bpifrance, Egypt’s Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency (MSMEDA), Axian, the Dutch Good Growth Fund, Stellar Foundation, and FSD Africa invested in the fund.
The fund’s close comes as fintech continues to attract a significant share of startup investment across Africa, even as venture capital investors become more cautious and concentrate capital in fewer transactions. African startups raised $3.42 billion in 2025, with fintech attracting $1.37 billion, accounting for 40% of total funding.
First Circle Capital is betting that the next generation of African fintech companies will emerge from problems that remain unresolved despite the growth of digital payments and lending over the past decade.
“Africa Fund I is built around a clear thesis: the next generation of African fintech leaders will be those addressing the structural challenges that continue to limit access to financial services across the continent,” Selma Ribica, co-founder and managing partner at First Circle Capital, said in a statement. “We want to identify those businesses at the earliest stages and work closely with their founders as they scale.”
Ribica, a former M-Pesa executive and fintech investor, Agnes Aistleitner, and Robert Smith founded First Circle Capital in 2021. The firm operates across Kampala, Nairobi, Casablanca, and Cape Town, with a pan-African investment mandate covering markets including Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Egypt, Morocco, Uganda, Ghana, and Francophone Africa.
Its investment thesis, which it calls FinTech 2.0, focuses on insurtech, alternative lending models, interoperability and financial infrastructure, climate fintech, fintech software-as-a-service, and regulatory technology. The firm is also interested in AI-native fintech startups that build artificial intelligence and data-driven operations into their businesses from inception.
“We are particularly excited by the emergence of AI-native fintech companies,” Ribica said. “Founders now have the opportunity to build financial businesses around automation, intelligence, and software from day one, fundamentally changing the economics of delivering financial services across African markets.”
First Circle Capital says it has invested in 18 companies across African markets. Its portfolio includes TurnStay, a South African fintech building cross-border payment infrastructure for global travel merchants; Morocco-based WafR, which digitises transactions and payments through neighbourhood retailers; Scale, a card-as-a-service infrastructure company; and Orca Fraud, an AI-native fraud prevention platform for financial institutions. The firm added that it works with founders on securing follow-on funding, strategic investors, commercial partnerships, and business development opportunities
“We see a significant opportunity to back the founders addressing these challenges: making payments cheaper, expanding access to credit and insurance, strengthening fraud and risk management, improving financial operations through software, and developing innovative financial solutions for sectors such as agriculture and energy,” Aistleitner, co-founder and partner at First Circle Capital, said.
The $26 million close adds to a growing number of African-focused venture capital funds that have raised or secured new commitments this year. In August, Ventures Platform, the Nigerian venture capital firm, closed its second pan-African fund at $84 million, attracting new institutional investors including the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, Norfund, Alphatron, and Ashesi University Foundation, alongside existing investors such as the IFC, British International Investment, Proparco, AfricaGrow, and Nigeria’s iDICE programme.
In October, DPI Venture Capital, Development Partners International’s venture capital platform, announced the final close of its Nclude Fund at more than $112 million. In November, Enza Capital, a multi-stage venture capital firm, announced a $21 million first close for its AI Africa Fund, targeting $60 million to invest in AI-native and AI-enabled startups across Africa.
For First Circle Capital, Africa Fund I is designed to back founders before their businesses become established players. African startups raised just $46.5 million across 281 pre-seed deals in 2025, accounting for 1.5% of total venture investment, even as the broader VC market grew by over 40%. The funding gap means early-stage founders might struggle to secure the capital needed to reach the point where larger investors are willing to back them.
“Our ambition with Africa Fund I is to build a portfolio of companies that become fundamental to how financial products are delivered across Africa,” Smith, partner and head of operations at First Circle Capital, said. “We believe the next generation of African fintech will combine deep local market understanding with increasingly sophisticated technology, including AI-native solutions that can fundamentally improve the economics and accessibility of financial services.”

articles.title: Sèche-cheveux haute vitesse et brosse à dents connectée : Laifen lance son Black Friday jusqu'à -27 % — Frandroid
articles.text:
Des moteurs de 110 000 à 115 000 tours par minute, une température de sèche-cheveux régulée en temps réel, des brosses à dents réglables depuis un smartphone : l’objectif de Laifen est de mettre de la tech dans la salle de bain. Fondée en 2019, la marque développe ses propres moteurs haute vitesse de sèche-cheveux pour souffler fort et sécher vite, tout en gardant la chaleur sous contrôle.
Pour le Black Friday, trois de ses appareils voient leur prix baisser sur Amazon :
- Le Laifen Neo, sèche-cheveux haute vitesse pour toute la famille, passe de 149,99 € à 109,99 €
- Le Laifen Air Pro, sèche-cheveux ultraléger qui se glisse dans un sac, passe de 99,99 € à 79,99 €
- La Laifen Wave Pro, brosse à dents électrique connectée, passe de 109,99 € à 79,99 €
Laifen Neo : le sèche-cheveux rapide et silencieux que toute la famille peut utiliser
Le Neo est le sèche-cheveux qui résume le mieux le savoir-faire de Laifen. Son moteur maison propulse un flux d’air puissant qui réduit le temps de séchage à environ trois minutes selon la marque. De quoi rendre le brushing du matin beaucoup moins pénible, surtout quand on a les cheveux longs.
Pour éviter de trop chauffer les cheveux, le Neo est équipé d’un capteur qui vérifie la température de l’air 100 fois par seconde et ajuste la chauffe en continu. Il intègre aussi une fonction ionique : des particules chargées négativement sont diffusées dans l’air pour réduire l’électricité statique. L’intérêt ? Limiter les mèches qui se dressent et les frisottis, pour des cheveux plus faciles à discipliner après le séchage.
Avec 390 grammes sur la balance, le Neo ne fatigue pas le bras, et son fonctionnement est assez discret (59 dB annoncés par Laifen) pour sécher ses cheveux sans réveiller toute la maison. Un mode enfant abaisse la température pour sécher en douceur la tête des plus petits. Deux embouts magnétiques, qui se fixent et s’enlèvent d’un geste, complètent l’ensemble : l’un pour lisser, l’autre pour diffuser l’air et dessiner les boucles.
Le Neo est vendu habituellement 149,99 € dans ce coloris violet. Pendant le Black Friday, il perd 27 % de son prix : comptez 109,99 € seulement sur Amazon, avec deux ans de garantie.
Laifen Air Pro : un sèche-cheveux haute vitesse au format de voyage
Le Laifen Air Pro s’adresse à ceux qui veulent un sèche-cheveux à emporter n’importe où. Avec 299 grammes et un format compact, il tient dans un sac de sport ou une valise cabine, ce qui évite de dépendre du sèche-cheveux de l’hôtel ou du vestiaire.
Il fonctionne sur le même principe que le Neo, avec un moteur haute vitesse de 115 000 tours par minute et une température limitée à 70 °C. Cinq modes sont proposés, de l’air froid pour fixer une coiffure à un mode bébé à basse température, en passant par un cycle qui alterne air chaud et air froid.
Trois embouts sont fournis pour lisser ou travailler les boucles. Son poids et sa taille peuvent aussi en faire un sèche-cheveux principal pour une petite salle de bain, où un modèle encombrant trouve difficilement sa place.
Habituellement vendu 99,99 €, l’Air Pro passe sous la barre des 80 € pendant le Black Friday. Comptez 79,99 € sur Amazon jusqu’au 30 novembre.
Laifen Wave Pro : une brosse à dents électrique notée 8/10 par Frandroid
La brosse à dents Wave Pro associe deux mouvements : des vibrations à haute fréquence (jusqu’à 66 000 par minute) et une oscillation de la tête sur 60°. Les brosses électriques se limitent souvent à l’un ou à l’autre.
Avec une note de 8/10 dans le test de Frandroid, la Wave Pro est du genre convaincante. Après un mois d’utilisation, la testeuse salue des performances « bluffantes » et apprécie de pouvoir ajuster finement le brossage à sa sensibilité. Vitesse, vibrations, amplitude des mouvements : les réglages permettent de trouver le bon équilibre entre intensité et confort.
La brosse à dents intègre aussi un capteur de pression : quand on appuie trop fort, un voyant s’allume sur le manche et l’intensité diminue pour épargner les gencives. Deux têtes de brosse à dents sont fournies, l’une pour la plaque dentaire, l’autre pour la blancheur. Laifen annonce jusqu’à 70 jours d’autonomie, sur la base de deux brossages de deux minutes par jour. La recharge se fait en posant la brosse sur un socle magnétique.
Tous ces réglages passent par l’application mobile de Laifen, qui dresse aussi un bilan de chaque séance : durée du brossage et nombre d’appuis trop forts détectés. La brosse est par ailleurs certifiée IPX8, elle peut donc tomber dans le lavabo sans risque.
Habituellement vendue 109,99 € dans sa finition métal argentée, la Wave Pro perd 30 € pendant le Black Friday. Comptez 79,99 € sur Amazon.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI launches to rave reviews and will be the biggest entertainment release ever - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Grand Theft Auto VI has launched to rave reviews and is set to become the biggest entertainment release in history.
For gamers it’s a massive event with many die-hard GTA fans coordinating their annual leave so they can play the game for days on end without interruptions.
The game, which has been 13 years in the making, has launched to perfect reviews from gaming sites which are in awe of its scale and detail.
Grand Theft Auto VI is expected to generate more than $5 billion in revenue.
It will easily eclipse the highest-grossing films of all time including Avengers: Endgame ($2.94 billion), Avatar ($2.92 billion and Spider-Man: Brand New Day ($2.52 billion).
Those on the outside looking into this launch will be wondering what all the fuss about?
Firstly, most don’t appreciate the size of the gaming industry.
In Australia, revenues from computer gaming easily outstrips the box office.
In 2025, Australians spent more than $4.2 billion on video games. That’s up 12 per cent from the $3.8 billion spent in 2024.
In the same period the Australian box office totalled $970 million.
This year the Australian box office has already crossed the $1 billion mark in 2026, the first time it has done this since 2019, thanks to the success of The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day.
This year Grand Theft Auto VI will beat all those totals in Australia on its own.
The game has been available for pre-order for some time before today’s release. Rockstar, the game’s developer, even allowed users to download the 212 GB game to their system early so it would be ready to play at the stroke of midnight.
In fact, it set a download record for the NBN with a 30 per cent increase above baseline traffic and almost 8Tbps of increased load in the busy hour.
Another thing to note for planning to go into a store to buy GTA VI – is a discless game.
When you buy the game cover over the counter, there’s no disc inside, just a download code.
One common misconception around gaming is that it’s only for kids.
The average age of an Australian gamer is 35 so it’s very much an adult pastime and a popular family activity.
Getting back to Grand Theft Auto VI, why is it so popular?
The main appeal of the game is its sheer scale and scope.
This is what’s called an open-world game, where players can follow the playable character’s story but also go off and explore the world on their own.
The game is set in the fictional town of Vice City and follows the story of Jason and Lucia who find themselves on the wrong side of the law and must use their guile and ingenuity to stay alive.
Is a single-player game. It does not have an online multiplayer option.
But unlike regular computer games, Grand Theft Auto VI is a much larger sandbox.
A recent release, which we quite enjoyed, was Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.
The campaign was a remarkable mission-based story that had a beginning and end.
After completing the campaign if you decide to play the game again, it would be the same experience.
With Grand Theft Auto VI, there are tasks and missions to complete but the attraction to hardcore fans is the fact they can venture out into the world and create their own adventures.
Being called Grand Theft Auto, the earlier versions of the game were all about stealing cars, running away from the police and building your wealth.
Those elements are still at play in Grand Theft Auto VI but it is now much broader.
You can spend days and weeks in little pockets of the world, interacting with people, driving cars, steering boats, flying planes and getting you up to all sorts of mischief.
IGN has called the game precedented, unbelievable, and unmissable.
It’s review said: “As optimistic as I was about a new GTA built in the wake of everything Rockstar learnt from the majestic Red Dead Redemption 2, I was simply not ready for just how much richer, deeper, and more satisfying Grand Theft Auto VI has proven to be. After three weeks and over 120 hours playing it, I’m still hopelessly hooked, absorbing the world at walking speed like a tourist in a new town.”
GameSpot says Grand Theft Auto VI sets the bar for open worlds impossibly high.
It said: “This game is the culmination of everything the developer has previously achieved in the open-world space that pushes the genre to heights that, in all likelihood, no other developer will be able to reach. GTA VI is an astonishing open-world action game that I’d wager won’t be outdone until Grand Theft Auto VII.”
Kotaku says the game is overwhelming, exciting, and different than any past GTA game.
It said: “GTA VI is a truly remarkable game. A masterpiece of open-world design that brings forward the best parts of all of Rockstar’s past games into one billion-dollar adventure that is unlike anything I’ve played before. It’s a game I’ll be playing for years, and I can’t wait to talk about it with others.”
Grand Theft Auto VI is available now for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S.

articles.title: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
articles.text:
Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
- Date:
- November 11, 2026
- Source:
- ETH Zurich
- Summary:
- Researchers have created a quantum computer that stores information in microscopic vibrations, potentially making quantum machines smaller, more powerful, and better at preserving information. The breakthrough successfully demonstrated advanced quantum calculations and could help overcome major barriers to practical quantum computing.
- Share:
A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.
Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.
By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.
The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.
Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers
The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.
Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.
The major difference lies in how that information is stored.
"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.
Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.
Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better
One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.
In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.
Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.
However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.
Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.
Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.
New Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests
The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.
The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.
To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.
"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.
Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.
A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers
One of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.
However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.
Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.
Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.
Story Source:
Materials provided by ETH Zurich. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yu Yang, Igor Kladarić, Martynas Skrabulis, Michael Eichenberger, Stefano Marti, Simon Storz, Jonathan Esche, Raquel García Bellés, Max-Emanuel Kern, Andraz Omahen, Arianne Brooks, Marius Bild, Matteo Fadel, Yiwen Chu. Mechanical resonator–based quantum computing. Science, 2026; 392 (6801): 972 DOI: 10.1126/science.aef4139

articles.title: Cómo enfriar una habitación y gastar menos luz: el método que combina aire acondicionado y ventilador
articles.text:
Encender el aire acondicionado y el ventilador simultáneamente puede ayudar a reducir el consumo energético en casa. Aunque muchas personas consideran que utilizar ambos equipos aumenta el gasto de electricidad, los expertos señalan que esta combinación permite distribuir mejor el aire frío y evitar que el sistema de climatización trabaje a temperaturas demasiado bajas.
El ingeniero Daniel Beguería, citado por el El Español, explica que no es necesario elegir entre uno de estos aparatos. Por el contrario, utilizarlos de manera conjunta puede mejorar el confort dentro de una habitación y disminuir la exigencia sobre el aire acondicionado.
La explicación está relacionada con la manera en que el cuerpo humano percibe el calor. Un ventilador no reduce la temperatura del ambiente, pero genera una corriente de aire que favorece la evaporación del sudor y ayuda a disipar el calor corporal. Esto permite sentir mayor frescura incluso cuando el termómetro registra temperaturas elevadas.
Una habitación puede resultar confortable a 28 o 30 grados cuando existe una circulación adecuada del aire, sin necesidad de mantener el aire acondicionado a temperaturas considerablemente más bajas.
Cómo utilizar el aire acondicionado y el ventilador para ahorrar energía
La recomendación principal consiste en configurar el aire acondicionado entre 26 y 27 grados y acompañar su funcionamiento con un ventilador. De esta manera, el aire frío puede distribuirse mejor por la habitación y generar una sensación térmica agradable.
Cuando se utiliza únicamente el aire acondicionado, algunas personas suelen configurar el termostato a 22 o 23 grados para enfriar rápidamente el espacio. Sin embargo, esta práctica obliga al equipo a trabajar con mayor intensidad y puede incrementar el consumo eléctrico.
El ventilador ayuda a evitar esa situación porque permite aprovechar mejor el aire frío que ya produjo el sistema de climatización. Así, no es necesario reducir tanto la temperatura para conseguir una sensación de frescura.
Combinar ambos dispositivos puede reducir el consumo energético entre un 17% y un 73%, dependiendo de las características de la vivienda, las condiciones exteriores y los equipos utilizados.
Por qué un ventilador de techo puede ser más eficiente
No todos los ventiladores ofrecen los mismos resultados. Beguería destaca que los modelos instalados en el techo suelen ser una alternativa eficiente para distribuir el aire dentro de una habitación.
Estos dispositivos permiten mover el aire de manera más uniforme y no ocupan espacio en el suelo. Además, pueden funcionar durante periodos prolongados con un consumo eléctrico considerablemente menor al de un sistema de refrigeración mecánica.
Un ventilador de techo puede consumir alrededor de 10,4 kilovatios hora durante 800 horas de funcionamiento al año. En condiciones comparables, un aire acondicionado puede alcanzar los 392 kilovatios hora.
Esto significa que el sistema de climatización puede necesitar hasta 38 veces más energía que un ventilador de techo para proporcionar condiciones de confort similares.
Otros consejos para enfriar la casa sin aumentar el consumo eléctrico
Además de combinar ambos aparatos, existen medidas que permiten mantener una temperatura agradable sin exigir demasiado a los equipos de climatización.
Una de ellas es aprovechar la ventilación cruzada durante la noche, cuando la temperatura exterior suele ser menor. Abrir ventanas ubicadas en lados opuestos de la vivienda facilita la circulación del aire y ayuda a renovar el ambiente.
También es recomendable utilizar cortinas gruesas, persianas y elementos de protección solar para impedir que la radiación caliente directamente las habitaciones. Mejorar el aislamiento de puertas y ventanas permite conservar durante más tiempo la temperatura interior.
Por último, si el problema principal es la humedad, se puede aprovechar la función deshumidificadora del aire acondicionado. Esta característica reduce la humedad ambiental y puede mejorar la sensación de confort sin necesidad de bajar excesivamente la temperatura.
En conjunto, estas medidas permiten aprovechar mejor los equipos disponibles y reducir el esfuerzo energético necesario para mantener una habitación fresca.

articles.title: Tackling GPU Bottlenecks in Plane-Wave DFT with K-Point Batching and Mixed Precision | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Training a next-generation machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) requires ground truth: tens to hundreds of millions of density functional theory (DFT) calculations of energies, forces, and stresses across diverse structures and chemistries.
Plane-wave DFT, with VASP as its dominant implementation, is the gold standard for generating that data. It is accurate, well-validated across materials classes, and ubiquitous at the national labs and research institutions running these calculations at scale.
As MLIP training datasets have grown, so has the pressure to generate DFT data faster and cheaper. But the small unit cells and dense k-point grids common in MLIP data generation can leave significant GPU performance unused. VASP’s OpenACC implementation has delivered meaningful speedups, especially for large-system calculations. However, for smaller systems, sequential k-point processing limits GPU utilization. At the same time, AI workloads are reshaping GPU hardware development toward lower-precision data types, creating a growing gap between what modern NVIDIA GPUs can deliver and what FP64-only HPC codes are optimized for.
This post introduces two new NVIDIA capabilities that address these bottlenecks. The first, Daviator, resolves the small-system GPU performance problem through k-point and spin-batched GPU kernels. In particular, a batched Davidson solver delivers significant performance gains. The second, a new mixed precision execution layer, enables further performance gains, especially on inference-class GPUs with a high FP32:FP64 throughput ratio.
For a projected reference dataset workload, the results show up to 22x faster time-to-solution and up to 75% lower cost compared to CPU execution, depending on hardware and configuration.
The GPU bottleneck in plane-wave DFT
In periodic systems, electronic wavefunctions are parameterized by crystal momentum, a discrete set of k-points that samples the Brillouin zone. For periodic structures with small unit cells, hundreds to thousands of irreducible k-points are required to achieve well-converged results.
Each k-point solve is largely independent; for instance, no inter-k-point communication is required during the Davidson eigensolver step. Despite this independence, VASP’s OpenACC GPU port processes k-points sequentially. For large systems, the work per k-point can fully saturate a GPU, but for small systems with dense k-point grids, the hundreds of small GPU dispatches per step causes kernel launch overhead to dominate compute time. The result: a single-atom iron system with 752 k-points ran 8x slower on the more expensive GPU hardware than on CPU. Thus, researchers working at this scale were left with a manual routing decision based on the size of the job.
Additionally, plane-wave DFT traditionally runs in FP64, a conservative default that guarantees accuracy throughout the solver pipeline. But GPU hardware is no longer symmetric in this regard. On data center GPUs, FP64 throughput has held flat across NVIDIA Hopper, Blackwell, and Rubin GPUs, while FP32 throughput has continued to increase. Inference-class and workstation GPUs like the RTX PRO 6000 push this further, with a 64:1 FP32:FP64 ratio (Figure 1). As AI workloads drive hardware development toward lower-precision data types, the fraction of peak GPU throughput available to FP64-only codes is stagnating.
Daviator: Batching k-points for GPU saturation
Daviator is a library of GPU kernels developed by NVIDIA that replaces sequential per-k-point processing in plane-wave DFT inner loops with batched GPU operations. At the core of the transformation lies a batched Davidson eigensolver that replaces sequential loops that cause latency with batched FFTs, GEMMs, and custom kernels. This drops the number of GPU kernel launches drastically, enabling SM occupancy to go from a fraction of capacity to near saturation. Data stays resident in GPU memory throughout. VASP retains full ownership of the SCF loop, mixing, symmetry, and I/O; Daviator integrates at well-defined call boundaries over data already on device.
Running a calculation
Daviator will be available through the NVIDIA ALCHEMI VASP microservice by setting LDAVIATOR=True in the INCAR. Existing VASP inputs work without modification. The POSCAR, INCAR, and KPOINTS below are a standard setup for a k-point-dense metallic system.
Daviator intercepts the Davidson solver internally (ALGO = Normal) and routes it through batched GPU operations.
POSCAR:
Fe1
1.0
   2.3017038599999999    0.0000000000000000   -0.8137751999999999
  -1.1508519300000000    1.9933340200000000   -0.8137751999999999
   0.0000000000000000    0.0000000000000000    2.4413256099999998
Fe
1
direct
   0.0000000000000000    0.0000000000000000    0.0000000000000000 Fe
INCAR:
ALGO = Normal
LDAVIATOR = True
EDIFF = 5e-05
IBRION = 2
ISIF = 3
ISMEAR = 1
ISPIN = 2
NBANDS = 12
NSIM = 6
LASPH = True
LMAXMIX = 4
LORBIT = 11
LREAL = False
LWAVE = False
MAGMOM = 1*5.0
NELM = 100
NSW = 3
PREC = Accurate
SIGMA = 0.05
KPAR = 1
KPOINTS:
Gamma-centred 30x30x30 mesh
0
Gamma
30 30 30
Some of Daviator’s GPU kernels are specialized for the batch sizes they meet and may trigger a compilation on first use.
Add these lines to your job script before launching VASP to ensure efficient caching:
export CUDA_CACHE_PATH=/tmp/cudacache   # fast storage, not $HOME
export CUDA_CACHE_DISABLE=0             # make sure caching is on
Finally, run as usual:
mpirun -np 1 vasp_std
For now, VASP with Daviator is limited to single-node execution. Multi-node support, coverage of systems with non-collinear spins (vasp_ncl) and explicit gamma-only runs (vasp_gam) is expected to be released at a later stage.
Results
The benchmarks below compare Daviator against VASP 6.6.0 CPU and OpenACC baselines on NVIDIA H100s/H200s and B200s.
Daviator overcomes the OpenACC port’s limitations; a single iron atom achieves over 2x speed-ups relative to the CPU baseline (Figure 2). The gains increase for higher-accuracy functionals: the 22x Davidson speedup on LiFePO4 r2SCAN enables higher accuracy meta-GGA runs at production scale.
For mid-size systems like a 64-atom Bi-doped GaAs structure, VASP with Daviator cut execution time by more than 85%. Even at 348 atoms with a single k-point, Daviator delivers a significant improvement over the OpenACC and CPU baselines. VASP with Daviator improves the previous state-of-the-art for all system sizes, eliminating the need to route jobs between CPU and GPU based on system size.
Going further with mixed precision
Daviator eliminates the k-point bottleneck, but currently relies on FP64 arithmetic and storage. GPU hardware is shifting toward lower-precision data types, and HPC codes that adapt to mixed precision stand to recapture substantial performance from hardware they already own.
Further increasing the throughput, especially on GPUs with a high FP32:FP64 ratio, requires leveraging the FP32 units, but developing a mixed-precision Davidson solver is non-trivial. Not every kernel in the Davidson pipeline is equally precision-sensitive, but simply running each in FP32 and comparing against FP64 only yields a pass/fail result.
Additionally, the failures can be insidious. Hard failures are obvious: a solver rejects an ill-conditioned input. Soft failures are not: energy drift, incorrect convergence, diverging MD trajectories that appear valid on casual inspection. Genuine mixed precision requires knowing exactly where the precision boundaries lie.
By using a generic floating-point type with configurable mantissa and exponent bits, we can identify the minimum required bit counts for each that still produce correct results. The following section describes a general workflow for a precision requirements analysis that can be adapted for other codes as well.
Knowing the exact precision requirements for each kernel informs whether to switch it to FP32, improve the implementation to bring it into FP32 range, or keep it as an FP64 island.
Implementing this approach depends heavily on the specific code, but always requires the following building blocks:
- An instrumented version of the code that uses a generic floating point type with a configurable mantissa and exponent bit count.
- A run script that executes the code with a specific precision setting and input.
- A compare script that checks the accuracy of the results against a reference.
- A screening script that runs the instrumented code multiple times for each kernel, first with decreasing mantissa bits until the comparison fails, and then with the smallest working mantissa size and decreasing exponent bits.
Once this setup is in place, re-run the screening after each code change to track precision requirements. Measured precision requirements for different implementations of a reduction kernel vary (Figure 3).
The results depend on the input and comparison threshold. Here, all kernels would pass a simple FP32 run (Figure 4) without providing an insight into the numerical properties. The baseline is likely to fail with either a slightly larger input or a stricter comparison. The algorithm choice may also come with additional constraints.
The code instrumentation can be performed at three levels:
- The library level: Some libraries offer configurable precision, though only to a limited extent. The emulated matrix multiplications in cuBLAS, for example, allow screening the precision requirements of GEMMs by explicitly setting the mantissa bit count.
- The language level: The native floating-point types can be replaced with a generic one. NVIDIA CCCL provides such a type, with both compile-time and runtime configuration of mantissa and exponent bits.
- The compiler level: A completely non-intrusive and mostly automatic instrumentation can be achieved by replacing floating-point operations with a software implementation during compilation. The Verificarlo project takes this approach with its VPREC backend, but is limited to CPU code.
A complete instrumentation also covers dependencies and standard math functions. The instrumented code will be much slower, but the runs can be largely parallelized across HPC resources.
To move from analysis to implementation, start by adding FP64↔FP32 conversion infrastructure around your application’s hot path or a subset of it. Then create type-configurable versions of the functions and kernels in that region. For an initial implementation, keep everything exceeding FP32 requirements as an FP64 island; each subsequent iteration can reduce the FP64 footprint further.
Following this workflow, the original analysis of the Davidson algorithm, based on Verificarlo, indicated that large parts of the code could run with FP32 arithmetic and storage. The FFTs, the application of the Hamiltonian, and the orbital updates run in FP32, while the subspace eigenproblem, the tall-skinny GEMMs behind the subspace matrices, as well as the energies and convergence measures remain in FP64.
The tall-skinny GEMMs in the Rayleigh-Ritz projection were the remaining FP64 bottleneck. Pure FP32 accumulation here is insufficient as the output feeds directly into a numerically sensitive eigenvalue solver. The split-k algorithm resolves this by breaking the dot products into FP32 chunks with a final FP64 accumulation step (Figure 5).
Results
In VASP, convergence is controlled by the EDIFF parameter, which specifies the threshold for the total energy change between electronic iterations within an ionic step. Below that threshold, convergence is reached.
The default is 10-4 eV, while some calculations go down to 10-6 eV or lower. For reference, FP32 provides around 7 significant decimal digits of precision. EDIFF is an absolute threshold that varies by system and typically scales with atom count, so there is no single best setting.
The mixed-precision Davidson implementation converges to an EDIFF of 10-4 to 10-6 eV depending on the input; continuing with FP64 allows the calculation to converge below the FP32 noise floor. On GaAsBi-64, FP32 enables a 2× speed-up at EDIFF = 10-5 eV, and the combined FP32→FP64 run is 1.5× faster than pure FP64 at EDIFF = 10⁻⁸ eV (Figure 6).
On H100 and H200, where FP64 Tensor Cores match FP32 throughput, mixed precision delivers only marginal end-to-end gains. The benefit is concentrated in hardware with a high FP32:FP64 ratio such as the RTX PRO 6000, where the FP32 Davidson solver runs 3x–7x faster, delivering roughly 2x end-to-end acceleration (Figure 7).
Enabling mixed precision
Daviator’s mixed precision can be enabled by setting LDAVIATOR_MIXED_PRECISION to 1 (0 is FP64). Within an ionic step, the calculation starts in mixed precision (with FP32 storage) until a configurable threshold DAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32 or a number of SCF steps DAVIATOR_SWITCH_TO_FP64_AFTER_STEP is reached. For most inputs LAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32 works well from 10-4 to 10-5.
The following INCAR parameters are available to configure the use of mixed precision specifically for Daviator (Table 1).
| INCAR Parameter | Values | Description | 
|---|---|---|
| LDAVIATOR_MIXED_PRECISION | False = FP64 True = FP32 | Enable/Disable Mixed Precision (FP32 = mixed arithmetic and FP32 storage in Daviator) | 
| DAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32 | real number > 0 in eV | EDIFF threshold for FP32 | 
| DAVIATOR_SWITCH_TO_FP64_AFTER_STEP | Integer N >= 0, switch to FP64 after electronic step N (N=0 is FP64) -1 = FP32 only, i.e. converge to DAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32, then stop -2 = dynamic. i.e. switch to FP64 after DAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32 convergence | Selects when an ionic step switches from reduced precision to FP64. | 
The INCAR for a run that uses FP32 until EDIFF = 5-5 eV and then switches to FP64 until EDIFF = 5-7 eV would look like this:
ALGO = Normal
EDIFF = 5e-07
[...]
LDAVIATOR = True
LDAVIATOR_MIXED_PRECISION = True
DAVIATOR_SWITCH_TO_FP64_AFTER_STEP = -2
DAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32 = 5e-05
Hardware requirements and availability
A VASP user license is required. Daviator and its mixed precision option will be available on any NVIDIA GPU through the NVIDIA ALCHEMI VASP microservice; add the INCAR parameters above to activate it.
What both layers deliver at scale
The Open Materials 2024 (OMat24) inorganic materials dataset contains over 100 million VASP data points (total energy, forces, and stress) from molecular dynamics (“AIMD”), relaxation (“rattled-relax”), and static (“rattled”) calculations for MLIP training and validation.
To estimate the time and cost to compute this dataset, we extrapolated from a benchmarked sample of 13 representative inputs across the dataset’s system-size distribution. The individual benchmark runs were tuned to maximize resource utilisation and overall throughput, assuming multiple parallel runs per node. While OMat24 was generated with real-space projectors, the benchmarks and projections here use the more precise reciprocal-space projector setting in VASP (INCAR: LREAL=False).
On the same number of cloud instances, VASP + Daviator is up to 22x faster than VASP on CPU nodes, and up to 7x faster than VASP without Daviator on GPU (Figure 8). For a batch of eight small systems on one GPU, the NVIDIA ALCHEMI VASP microservice raises throughput a further 3–5x.
To estimate the price of the data set generation, we applied a geometric mean of the on-demand prices of AWS, Azure, CoreWeave and Google. On datacenter GPUs, the existing OpenACC GPU support in VASP is more expensive than the corresponding CPU computation.
However, the combination with Daviator reduces the cost to roughly 35% of the CPU cost on H100/200 and B200, with mixed precision contributing up to $200,000 in additional savings. The overall lowest price-point—around 25% of the CPU cost—is achieved on RTX PRO 6000 using VASP with Daviator and FP32 (Figure 9).
What’s next for GPU-native DFT
For standard DFT, GPUs are now the clear choice for VASP. For teams building MLIP training pipelines at the scale of OMat24 and beyond, VASP + Daviator delivers a GPU-native workflow end-to-end with cost savings of 60–75% over CPU, or approximately $5–6M USD for a dataset the size of OMat24.
For teams running RTX PRO 6000 or other NVIDIA GPUs with a high FP32:FP64 ratio, mixed precision yields a 2x speedup over FP64, with benefits beyond dataset generation. Daviator also opens up workload classes that were previously impractical at GPU scale. Meta-GGA functionals like R²SCAN are now viable for production; the reported speed-ups for LiFePO₄ may bring higher-accuracy DFT within reach for battery, catalyst, and defect datasets.
Acknowledgments
The VASP development team and Akhilesh Mishra contributed to this post.

articles.title: At Ignite 2026, Microsoft reinvents Copilot as the autonomous engine of enterprise work - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
At Ignite 2026, Microsoft reinvents Copilot as the autonomous engine of enterprise work
Business knowledge workers spend their days running a gauntlet of emails, spreadsheets, messaging platforms, meetings and productivity applications, wasting hours of their time switching from one to another to get mundane tasks done.
Microsoft Corp. is now proposing an alternative: It wants Copilot to evolve from a somewhat useful generative artificial intelligence assistant into the autonomous foundation for all business work. At Microsoft Ignite 2026 today in San Francisco, it unveiled a slate of powerful new capabilities and features for its favorite autonomous tool as part of its ongoing effort to transform Copilot into the new workplace operating system.
The company’s new vision was outlined in a blog post by Microsoft Chief Marketing Officer Jared Spataro, who pointed to its comprehensive intelligence layer for work, called WorkIQ, as the critical engine behind this shift.
Spataro explained that enterprise work is notoriously messy. Microsoft 365 stores roughly 19.5 exabytes of customer’s business data, and it’s adding billions of new files, documents, emails and messages each day. For businesses, it’s not enough to just give an autonomous AI agent access to this data and expect it to start making sense of it. It needs WorkIQ, which acts as the centralized reasoning layer for all Copilot agents, retrieving data, understanding its intent, identifying what’s important for the task it has been assigned while ignoring everything else.
While WorkIQ sits under the hood, Spataro says, the average worker’s day will soon begin in “Home,” which is the new user interface for Copilot. Home merges traditional chat with a portal called Cowork, which is where people can start delegating different tasks to AI agents. Spataro said Home is like a grounding anchor, or a place where workers can log in each day to pick up where they left off.
Home’s key element is Auto, which is an intelligent composer that dynamically routes users’ requests and prompts to the most suitable AI model. It’s the place where most people will typically begin each new task.
“Tell Copilot what you want to accomplish and it intelligently routes the work to the right models and effort for the task,” Spataro explained. “For more complex work, Auto may recommend moving from Chat to Cowork. If you agree, Copilot transfers the tasks seamlessly, helping to deliver the outcome with the right level of investment.”
Another key part of Home is called Today. It’s a “proactive command center” that’s currently available in private preview that scans a user’s email, calendar and Teams threads in order to highlight the things they have to get done that day.
Best of all, it won’t leave users feeling overwhelmed, Spataro said, because it also helps them to complete that work. For instance, it can quickly draft replies to emails, propose alterations to someone’s schedule and queue other messages for the user to review.
How Copilot gets work done
Copilot’s ability to get work done has been advanced by its deeper integration with Microsoft’s Office suite. Spataro said the company is bringing the full capabilities of Office directly into the Copilot application.
As a result, users will be able to move effortlessly from ideation on a notepad or whiteboard to conjure up a completed Word document or Excel spreadsheet based on what they just outlined. Those files will live entirely within Copilot, which gains the ability to co-author alongside human colleagues. Because Office is now native to Copilot, every document and file will be secured by Microsoft 365’s strict security and compliance controls, Spataro said.
Human-to-agent collaboration is being boosted too with the arrival of Copilot Workspaces, which is a kind of canvas that both can access, Spataro said. Within Copilot Workspaces, an agent might draft a section of a document, then notify a human to come and review it when they get the chance. The human will be able to leave comments for other agents to address.
Further aiding Copilot in work automation is a new capability called Autopilot, which dramatically enhances what the tool can now do. Autopilot is available now to subscribers who have enrolled in Microsoft’s Frontier early-access program. It’s a fully autonomous and always-on AI agent that comes with its own Microsoft Entra identity, memory and an ecosystem of productivity tools.
Autopilot is very different from standard AI agents that are programmed to wait for a user’s prompts. It’s continuously available, watching various Teams channels and the user’s email inbox for updates. It can automate recurring work processes, and it can manage entire project pipelines, such as a multistep supplier review, fully autonomously, Spataro said.
Autopilot is powerful, but safeguards are in place. Information technology teams have complete control over what it can and can’t access, and if something goes wrong they can step in and block it from doing anything else at a moment’s notice.
“Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail,” Spataro explained. “Powered by WorkIQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions. You decide what work Autopilot takes on and it will always check with you before key actions.”
More apps, more data
Coding continues to be a major focus, and now Microsoft is giving everyday knowledge workers the ability to build software that can help them get their work done even faster. With Copilot Code, launching in a few week’s time, users will be able to generate interactive dashboards, persistent desktop widgets and lightweight business applications from simple, natural language prompts.
All of these Copilot-generated apps will be hosted within Copilot Managed Runtime, which is a new, highly-secure environment that IT teams can monitor to ensure none of them pose a risk to the company’s data.
To reassure organizations that their AI agents are not only secure, but also providing real value, Microsoft has updated the Agent 365 platform to give teams more control and visibility into their AI spending. Agent 365 now comes with a Business Analytics feature that brings a FinOps-style approach to AI budgeting.
Whereas most platforms just track token consumption, it goes further, measuring each agent’s return on investment by looking at the “work completed” and the number of hours it took. According to Spataro, this will give companies a much clearer picture of the benefits of their AI investments.
Finally, there’s a lot going on in terms of business data connectivity. For one thing, Microsoft said, it’s making sure that Dynamics 365, its combined customer relationship management and enterprise resource planning platform, doesn’t live in isolation. With Dynamics 365 in Copilot, its AI agents gain more than 100 prebuilt “skills” that allow them to perform tasks in sales, service and finance.
But Dynamics 365 isn’t for everyone, and Microsoft recognizes that many of its customers prefer to use alternative CRM tools. That’s why it announced a major new partnership with Salesforce Inc. that gives Copilot unprecedented access to the Salesforce platform too.
Their new offering is called Copilotforce, and it’s enabled by two-way “Zero Copy” integrations between Microsoft Fabric and Salesforce Data 360. The idea is that Copilotforce will bring trusted context from Salesforce directly into Copilot and also productivity and collaboration tools like Teams and Office. The new platform has 38 prebuilt skills to help Copilot start automating sales-related tasks, allowing them to retrieve customer data, generate meeting follow-ups and update CRM records based on tasks they’ve just completed.
There’s a lot to digest, but the deluge of updates sends a clear message that AI agents are on the march, expanding their role as they take on much more complex enterprise work.

articles.title: David Ellison says HBO will air critical Elon Musk documentary despite his $1B investment in Skydance | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Skydance CEO David Ellison says HBO will air Alex Gibney’s documentary about Elon Musk, even after news broke that the SpaceX founder had invested $1 billion in the newly formed company following its Warner Bro. Discovery and Paramount merger.
Following news of that investment, questions emerged over how Musk’s sizable stake in the company might affect Skydance’s plans to distribute a documentary that is highly critical of him.
When asked by The New York Times editor and columnist Andrew Ross Sorkin whether HBO would still distribute the documentary even with Musk’s stake in its parent company, Ellison said, “We have a pay-one deal with A24, who produced that movie. Of course, we’re going to honor the deal.”
He went on to say, “We believe in independence. We don’t believe in censorship of any kind.”
Co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz are tasked with bringing together two major streaming platforms, Paramount+ and HBO Max, along with a portfolio of networks, including CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central, and Food Network, under a single corporate umbrella.

articles.title: Sony’s impressive Bravia 8 II OLED hits a new low price ahead of Black Friday
articles.text:
Black Friday is a great time to save on a new OLED television for your winter movie nights. Though, it turns out that you can already get a great deal on the 65-inch Sony Bravia 8 II, one of our favorite OLED televisions. It’s currently discounted by $1,100 at various retailers, including Amazon, Best Buy, and directly from Sony. That discount brings the price under $2,200, the lowest we’ve seen. You can also save $800 on the 55-inch model, which is typically $2,599.99 (Amazon, Best Buy, Sony), but now costs just under $1,800.
Sony’s impressive Bravia 8 II OLED hits a new low price ahead of Black Friday
This screen is one the best we’ve tested, and the lower price makes it more competitive with other OLED televisions.
Sony Bravia 8 II OLED TV
The Bravia 8 II was chosen as the “king of TV” by a panel of judges (including The Verge’s own Nilay Patel) in Value Electronics’ 2025 shootout. The OLED TV has excellent color accuracy, a bright panel, and a 120Hz refresh rate.
My colleague John Higgins praised the Bravia 8 II for its excellent image quality and engaging picture, though those positive traits are consistent with almost all OLED TVs. What sets this one apart is its impressive image processing, the bold colors from its quantum dot-equipped OLED panel, and that it looks great right out of the box (although he recommends using Professional mode). The screen was awarded the top spot at 2025’s Value Electronics TV Shootout, beating out similar offerings from competitors like Panasonic, LG, and Samsung.
For gaming, the panel can reach up to 120Hz at 4K, with both variable refresh rate and automatic low-latency mode to ensure that your content looks and feels good to play. The connectivity includes two HDMI 2.1 (one with eARC), and two HDMI 2.0 ports, giving you plenty of inputs for consoles and a Blu-ray player, among other gadgets. We spotted some color fringing of certain colors in dark scenes, and lamented the lack of a but it’s an otherwise excellent screen we can easily recommend.

articles.title: ‘Playing Grand Theft Auto can wait until the weekend’: As GTA 6 launch nears, schools are offering pupils prizes to attend as they battle ‘GTA flu’
articles.text:
School offers students prizes to avoid 'GTA flu' outbreak — Xbox and PlayStation gift card draw aims to avoid attendance drops
Low attendance is expected
- GTA 6 arrives tomorrow in the biggest game launch of the year
- Schools are bracing for low attendance numbers as students play the game
- Some schools are offering prizes to encourage pupils to show up
Grand Theft Auto 6 is launching tomorrow, and you can bet people across the globe will be skipping work to enjoy the game as soon as it becomes available. Some schools are worried that pupils will take a similar approach, and they’re taking some pretty unusual steps to ensure attendance, even as GTA 6 threatens to pull excited students away.
According to BBC News, Belfast Boys’ Model school in Northern Ireland is offering students prizes to attend lessons on November 19, with students who turn up on both Thursday and Friday being entered into a draw to win one of two gift cards each worth £70 (about $91) for either Xbox or PlayStation consoles. Entries for the draw will mark International Men’s Health Day and raise money for the charity.
The school sent a letter to parents saying that “activities such as playing Grand Theft Auto can wait until the weekend” and reminding “all parents and carers of the importance of ensuring that students attend school on Thursday 19th November.”
The date is important because it coincides with GCSE math exams for 15- and 16-year-olds, with the school’s letter arguing that “Good attendance is one of the strongest indicators of academic success.” The school evidently wants to avoid a repeat of the so-called “GTA flu” that saw pupils flunk out of school on the day GTA 5 launched in 2013.
Mary Montgomery, principal of Belfast Boys’ Model school, stated that the voucher idea was a “pupil-led incentive.” Students had initially suggested offering GTA 6 itself as a prize, Montgomery said, but this proposal was turned down because the game is 18-rated. Instead, a gift card for two of the best consoles on the market was suggested as an alternative.
And Belfast Boys’ Model school pupil Michael, aged 17, told BBC News that gaming can help young people to “switch off and manage some of the stress around exams, which is important with GCSE modules this week.”
How to pre-load GTA 6
Any students tempted to flunk out for a day or two are hardly alone. Research from Zety claims that one in ten workers plans to take time off to play GTA 6 and breathless headlines proclaim the release could “paralyze the working world” — although not everyone is feeling so credulous.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
There’s no need to stay home to download GTA 6 to your console — it can be pre-loaded ahead of time so that it’s ready to play as soon as it unlocks on November 19. As long as you’ve pre-ordered the game and enabled your console’s automatic update and download settings, you’ll be able to enter your activation code and start downloading the game automatically. But at a huge 212GB in size, it’ll take a while to finish, so make sure you give it plenty of time.
Of course, that doesn’t give you a full day of playing the game instead of working or studying, but it at least means that GTA 6 will be ready and waiting for you when you get back home.
With some schools offering incentives to put the controller down for a few hours, we’ll have to see if it’s enough to avoid another outbreak of the dreaded “GTA flu.”

articles.title: Microsoft Takes Perception Agentic Security Platform Out of Preview
articles.text:
Microsoft used its Ignite 2026 conference on Tuesday to announce the general availability of Perception, a product designed for coordinating teams of AI agents to handle security tasks.
Unveiled in July as Project Perception, the system has been in public preview inside Microsoft Defender since August.
Playbooks direct the agents, which are split into red, blue and green teams. Red agents play the attacker and probe for weaknesses; blue agents handle detection, alert triage, and investigations; and green agents fix problems.
The four blue team agents that are now generally available cover alert triage, attack investigation, detection authoring and threat intelligence. According to Microsoft, the Alert Triage Agent can handle roughly 80% of alerts in a typical Defender queue, based on an analysis of approximately 8 million alerts across its security products.
The Recon Agent, one of the red team agents, is also generally available, and a Web App Pen Test Agent has entered preview.
Two new green team playbooks work across Microsoft, AWS and Google Cloud. The agents behind them include Posture Prioritization, which is generally available, and Risk Reduction, which is in public preview.
The Risk Reduction Agent can recommend vulnerability shielding when a fix isn’t immediately available. This preview feature temporarily protects vulnerable assets until a permanent patch can be rolled out.
“Your team sets the guardrails and signs off on high-impact actions, and automated triggers launch playbooks when an incident meets the criteria you set,” Aleš Holeček, president and chief architect of Microsoft Security, wrote in a blog post.
Microsoft is also previewing integrations that link Perception to SIEM, SOAR and IT service management tools via MCP and APIs.
The company also addressed the risk posed by AI agents, which it views as a new kind of insider with broad access to data and tools.
In preview, Agent 365 and Entra Suite can detect 60 types of local AI agents, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and GitHub Copilot. Intune policies can keep supported agents on the device.

articles.title: CISO Conversations: Patti Degnan – Part of the Job Is Deciding What Not to Do
articles.text:
Patti Degnan’s journey is unusual. She didn’t have an early plan to become a CISO; but perhaps life events made it inevitable.
Patti Degnan’s first encounter with security shaped her future interest: her identity was stolen in 2006. “That was my first introduction into safeguarding data. It piqued my interest in how to better protect my own information. I wanted to understand what had happened, so I tried to discover what information about me was held by different agencies. The intent was seeing if my personal data was safe – but the effect was learning the concepts of privacy and personal data protection.”
It wasn’t until joining Symantec in 2012 that this underlying interest began to rise to the surface. “I was in internal audit, focusing on the operational and IT perspective, and began to focus on data privacy.” This was pre-Snowden and years before GDPR. She was combining audit knowledge, PCI understanding and privacy knowledge at a time its importance was growing.
Symantec had made several acquisitions. “We probably had close to 60 different backend infrastructure components that were all payment gateways. I worked hard trying to figure out what that complex environment looked like, and how we were deploying controls around it – and that was my first serious foray into security.”
She left Symantec in 2015, having become IT audit and compliance manager, and moved to LendingClub as senior manager in IT compliance and assurance. She was now seriously immersed in security. By 2018 she was senior director, information security GRC at Informatica. She then led security teams at Looker through its acquisition by Google, and by 2023 she was CISO at Notion. In 2025 she became an operating partner with the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz but returned to full-time cybersecurity in 2026 as CISO at Glow, an AI-powered endpoint security company that came out of stealth in July with $180 million in funding.
During this 20-year journey she evolved from a security victim to a security leader. Noticeably, however, it wasn’t a career plan to become a CISO – cybersecurity leadership simply grew from increasing interest and concern over personal privacy.
Leadership is a complex subject. Not everyone can be a leader, but you must be a leader to be a CISO. Where does that ability come from? Are you born with it or without it, or is leadership a quality you can learn?
The most common suggestion is that you learn as you journey. Nobody leaves high school and jumps straight into being a CISO. The journey begins with excelling in a position within a small team, being promoted to lead that team, and progressing to lead a larger team. As time passes, you learn more leadership skills by leading teams. But this still doesn’t explain why some people can be excellent at their job, but don’t seem able to become a leader.
“Philosophically, I don’t think anyone cannot learn to be a leader. But I think you must want it. I think inherently everyone has the capability to become a leader in their own way,” says Degnan. The implication is that everyone is born with the potential to be a leader, but the potential can only be activated through individual desire to do so. If, for whatever reason, you want or need to be a leader, you can learn the skills necessary to be one.
Since Degnan’s early stolen identity, adversarial activity has grown from ‘simple’ identity theft to any credential theft that can be used as an entry point into enterprise networks. The threat is more sophisticated, and the risk is more damaging. It is no longer a simple threat to individuals but a threat to entire businesses. As this threat has widened, so have CISO responsibilities also widened – CISOs must now have increased business understanding to protect the business. Cybersecurity has become a business enabler rather than simply a threat preventer. The modern CISO needs to be a businessperson as well as a technical security expert; and the former is slowly increasing in importance over the latter. So, today, can a CISO be purely a businessperson without a background of technical expertise?
“I think you can,” she says, “although you must at least have some understanding of how technology works. But ultimately, it’s entirely dependent on the business you’re in. If you’re in a tech company, you should understand how technology works because you have to translate across different stakeholder groups. I’ve worked with a guy who has primarily worked in manufacturing, and his landscape of what he would have to secure is entirely different from what I’ve had to secure in my career; so yes, I do think you have to have some level of technical understanding. Do I think you need to be a hands-on keyboard developer to understand it? No.”
CISOs do not work alone. They either inherit an existing security team, add personnel to that team, or recruit a new one. So, what does Degnan look for when recruiting her own security team members? Are, for example, security certifications important?
“To me, no. I know that’s controversial because some people spend their whole life getting a million certifications. I believe some people are great at applying theory to how things work in reality, but you don’t need to have a certification to do that. I’ve had multiple certifications over the years that I haven’t maintained, but they are a good foundation and a way to understand how things work in different areas of security, you know, in the different departments. But I don’t think it necessarily makes you a better practitioner.”
What she does look for, however, is proof of ownership and understanding of any claimed achievements. If a candidate’s resume claims to have built a specific process, she might ask for details. “Walk me through the thought process that got you there, and how did you do it?” she said. The purpose is not directly to challenge the candidate’s claim, but to discover how well they understand the cause of the need and the solution they created for it.
This approach could but does not exclude keen newcomers who haven’t yet had any opportunity to build anything. “I would never exclude that type of person. But it’s not always possible to include them. It largely depends on the size and maturity of the team you’re building. Large teams can advocate for more junior people that you can grow and shape. Small teams tend to be super lean, and you need to concentrate on acquiring a candidate that can immediately shore up one or more of the domains you need to cover.”
Regardless of the method and reasoning behind recruiting individuals, she keeps one eye on the end product: a single team with a single culture of cooperation. “It is important,” she explained, “to have the right people on the team that are not simply curious and qualified for their own position but will also work together for the team. That’s very important because we’re all in the trenches together, pushing the same rock up the same hill.”
In this process, she doesn’t specifically seek diversity in team member selection. Diversity is likely to come naturally within a team built for functionality. Gender, background, and whether someone is neurodivergent or neurotypical are irrelevant to the purpose of building the best possible cooperative team, and she neither seeks nor rejects any candidate on diversity reasoning.
One issue that faces every security practitioner is ‘burnout’. The dictionary definition is ‘mental or physical collapse caused by overwork or stress’. Working in security embraces both causes: the work is always-on, crises occur at any hour of any day, and failure to remediate any crisis could adversely affect the company and everyone working for it. Burnout is often described as rampant within cybersecurity, with some surveys suggesting it affects between 50% to 70% of practitioners.
Recovery is possible, but it takes time. But then, what? A return to the same conditions that caused the burnout in the first place: overwork and stress? Preventing future or recurring burnout can only be achieved by improving the working environment of overwork and stress. Stress cannot be eliminated because it is caused by adversarial third parties over which we have no control. Overwork could be reduced by increasing the staffing levels; but it is rare for any CISO to have the budget to adequately do so. And, ironically, the more successful the CISO, the less likely they are to receive funding for more staff.
The cause of burnout is cybersecurity itself. The CISO cannot eliminate it. All a CISO can do is attempt to manage the symptoms as they become, or before they become, apparent. Today, AI can help.
“I think burnout comes from everything being urgent,” explains Degnan. “Everything’s on fire all the time, and obviously in security, there’s an infinite amount of work. Part of the role of the CISO, or any leader, is deciding what not to do. So, I try to give very clear priorities. Automate the work you know machines should be doing in this day and age. Reserve humans for judgment and creativity in the problems where context really matters. And I’ve always been a big advocate for telling people to take time off. If you feel you need an extra day, take the day, especially now when we have the ability to build redundancy into workloads with AI. AI is pretty exciting. It gives you greater flexibility in reducing burnout.”
She goes further in time off. “My philosophy has always been that everybody should work wherever they’re going to do their best work. If someone is having a rough week and can’t come in to work, they shouldn’t. I would be happy to take the heat for it in that scenario.”
To be a successful CISO, she believes the two most important character traits are personal resiliency and communication skills. For the first, “In the face of the constantly evolving and changing concerns that are always there, you must be able to pick up the stick and keep walking every day.” That’s not just for yourself; it’s the image of strength you need to convey to your team.
Communication skills include the ability to receive information from one source and translate and deliver that information to a different destination. “You’re sitting between different levels of technical understanding among teams, executives, customers, and in some cases regulators. The board, if you report to it, is a prime example. You must have the communication skills able to translate the potential effect on the business of subtle and technical security issues into language the non- or less-technical business managers can really understand.”
For the CISOs with a planned career path, advice from mentors along the journey is common and important. Degnan had no visible path and received no specific advice. Instead, she learned from her own experiences. “The best lesson I ever learned was to never underestimate yourself,” she explained. “There will always be someone who can go deeper or be more technical in any domain, but you can still understand the strategy and the programs better than you credit yourself.”
But while she had no mentors, she is now a mentor for her security team. So, what advice would she give them in their career path? In specifics, it varies between individuals. “More generically, I have two pieces of advice. Firstly, always dive as deep as you can and know your domain, so you are comfortable when talking about it with other people. Secondly, understand the importance of communicating and partnering across the aisle. We’re not here just to look busy; we have to partner with other teams in the business to add the value of security understanding to what they are doing.”
This is perhaps the single greatest lesson to be learned from Patti Degnan’s philosophy. Security is not an island – it is a partnership with the entirety of the business. Deep understanding of the domain, and constant cooperation within the security team, and from the team to the entirety of the business, is what leads to successful cybersecurity.
Related: CISO Conversations: Noopur Davis – The Accidental Global CISO at Comcast
