articles.title: L'IA trouve les failles vraiment trop vite : Anthropic et Google sonnent la fin des 90 jours de grâce avant la divulgation
articles.text:
Depuis des années, le milieu de la sécurité informatique suit une règle tacite : un chercheur qui trouve une faille prévient discrètement l’éditeur, puis lui laisse 90 jours avant de la rendre publique. Ce délai de trois mois doit permettre au correctif d’arriver chez tout le monde avant que les pirates ne connaissent la faille, et s’en servent.
Or, dans un billet publié ce lundi 16 novembre, Anthropic, l’entreprise derrière l’intelligence artificielle Claude, a décidé de ramener ce délai à 30 jours pour les failles de gravité élevée ou critique, et à 45 jours pour les autres. Les nouvelles règles valent pour les signalements faits à partir du 1er janvier 2027.
Et la raison profonde de ce bouleversement dans les principes de divulgation coordonnée et responsable ? L’IA.
Une faille ne reste plus secrète trois mois, estime Anthropic
Anthropic justifie ce changement par les progrès rapides des modèles d’IA, devenus bien meilleurs pour dénicher des failles. Selon l’entreprise, une brèche repérée par une IA a de plus en plus de chances d’être retrouvée par une autre, bien avant le délai des 90 jours, ce qui augmente fortement le degré de risque en sécurité informatique.
Anthropic dit d’ailleurs constater déjà davantage de redécouvertes. Google part du même constat.
Le 13 novembre, Project Zero, l’équipe de chasseurs de failles de Google qui avait popularisé la règle des 90 jours, a annoncé passer à 60 jours le 2 février 2027, puis à 30 jours le 3 janvier 2028, que le correctif soit prêt ou non et quelle que soit la gravité de la faille. L’équipe supprime au passage les 30 jours supplémentaires qu’elle accordait depuis 2021 pour déployer un correctif.
Ce rythme pèse surtout sur les mainteneurs, qui entretiennent les logiciels libres, et Anthropic le reconnaît. Elle rappelle qu’elle joint déjà un correctif à ses signalements quand c’est possible. Elle propose aussi aux mainteneurs de projets libres critiques OSS Scanner, un service gratuit qui passe leur code au crible de ses modèles régulièrement.
En somme, l’entreprise dont les modèles accélèrent la chasse aux failles propose aussi de les mettre au service de ceux qui doivent les corriger. Les logiciels difficiles à mettre à jour, comme ceux des infrastructures critiques, auront un calendrier négocié au cas par cas.
Les failles déjà exploitées par des pirates gardent leur régime : elles restent soumises au même délai de sept jours qu’avant. Les nouveaux délais ne s’appliquent pas non plus aux trouvailles d’OSS Scanner qu’aucun humain n’a encore relues.

articles.title: Gravierende Sicherheitslücke in Java entdeckt: Wie eine KI für nur 200 Dollar einen Exploit fand
articles.text:
Gravierende Sicherheitslücke in Java entdeckt: Wie eine KI für nur 200 Dollar einen Exploit fand
Java gehört zu den beliebtesten Programmiersprachen und hat eine Vielzahl von Anwendungen hervorgebracht. IBM berichtete noch im Oktober 2025 zum 30. Geburtstag der Programmiersprache, dass Java in über 90 Prozent der Fortune-500-Unternehmen zum Einsatz kommt – darunter Amazon, Apple und Google-Mutter Alphabet. Diese Beliebtheit gerät jetzt durch eine Sicherheitslücke ins Wanken.
Sicherheitslücke in Java: Was der Fehler bewirkt
Das amerikanische Cybersecurity-Startup Calif hat in einem Beitrag eine Sicherheitslücke in Java offenbart. Diesen Fehler haben die Sicherheitsexpert:innen mit dem Namen „Java4Shell“ versehen. Laut ihren Untersuchungen lässt sich der Fehler in zahlreichen Java-Anwendungen wie Jira, Confluence und Keycloak auslösen. Dienste, die auch eine Reihe größerer Unternehmen nutzen.
So kann ein Fehler im Base64-Decoder ausgenutzt werden, um Arbeitsspeicher zu manipulieren. Wie Calif dazu schreibt: „Base 64 ist ein sehr geläufiger Weg, um binäre Daten als Text darzustellen. Es wird in Authentifizierungsprotokollen, bei Datei-Uploads und beim Senden von Netzwerknachrichten genutzt. […] Wir haben einen Fehler im Code gefunden, der den manipulierten Input angrenzenden Speicher überschreiben lässt. […] Die Korruption kann schon mit 64 A‑Zeichen mit einem nachfolgenden ‚=‘ ausgelöst werden.“
Laut den Sicherheitsforscher:innen kann der Fehler dazu führen, dass sensible Teile des Speichers offengelegt werden und Angreifer:innen potenziell aus der Ferne Schadcode auf betroffenen Systemen ausführen können. Calif betont, dass es allerdings keinen universellen Exploit gibt, um die Lücke ausnutzen zu können. Abhängig davon, wie Base64 genutzt wird und wie die Java-Anwendung funktioniert, sind andere Schritte nötig, um den Fehler auszunutzen.
Wie eine KI eine Sicherheitslücke entdeckt
Calif hat sich auf die Fahnen geschrieben, Cybersecurity mit KI voranzutreiben. Dafür nutzen sie GPT-6 Cyber von OpenAI. Die Künstliche Intelligenz soll mithilfe des zuständigen Sicherheitsforschers etwa eine Stunde gebraucht haben, um den Fehler in Java zu entdecken. Nach zwei weiteren Stunden war ein erster Exploit entwickelt. Die Token-Kosten beliefen sich dabei auf etwas weniger als 200 US-Dollar.
Dass die Lücke ernste Konsequenzen haben könnte, hat auch Oracle erkannt. Das Unternehmen hinter Java hat mittlerweile Updates veröffentlicht, die mehr als zehn Sicherheitslücken schließen. Dazu zählt auch „Java4Shell“. Laut Calif sollten alle Java-User:innen ein Update durchführen, um sich gegen mögliche Exploits zu schützen.
~ Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: Este es el valor de la criptomoneda ethereum este 18 de noviembre
articles.text:
Ether, comúnmente llamada como ethereum, es la moneda digital #2 en cuanto a términos de capitalización de mercado, por lo que se trata de una de las divisas digitales que más despierta el interés entre los mineros (creadores de las criptodivisas).
Ethereum es una plataforma de blockchain de código abierto que se ejecuta con el uso de su moneda nativa, llamada ether o ETH, por lo que a pesar de que la gente usa estos nombres como sinónimos son cosas distintas.
Ether es un token que se utiliza específicamente en la blockchain ethereum para pagar transacciones. Este token es responsable de impulsar casi todo lo que ocurre en la red, misma que puede ser usada por cualquier persona para crear y ejecutar contratos inteligentes, que son programas de software que se ejecutan de manera autónoma y sin la intervención del usuario.
De acuerdo con el portal de Binance, la moneda digital solana actualmente cuenta con 122.2M de unidades creadas.
El valor de la criptomoneda ethereum para este día a las 14:05 horas (UTC) es de 1793.1 dólares. Esto quiere decir que el activo digital reportó un cambio de -1.55% en el último día, así como un movimiento de 0.0% en la última hora.
Por su nivel de capitalización, esta moneda digital ocupa la posición #2 entre las más populares.
Cotización de la criptomoneda Ethereum
Ethereum 2.0: las claves
Tras varios meses de retraso y con el temor de que ya nunca pasaría, finalmente el 15 de septiembre de 2022 Ethereum llevó a cabo su tan ansiada fusión o actualización al nuevo nivel 2.0 con la promesa de mejorar la experiencia de los usuarios de esta criptomoneda.
“The Merge”, inglés para “La Fusión”, es una transformación en la forma en que Ethereum procesa las transacciones y en cómo se crean nuevos tokens de Ether.
Esta fusión se trata de la combinación de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum con una nueva cadena de bloques separada conocido como proof-of-stake, el cual reduce el consumo de energía de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum en un 99,9 %, según sus propios desarrolladores, lo que la vuelve más “amigable” con el ambiente al tiempo que las transacciones serían más baratas.
Sus defensores creen que la fusión hará que Ethereum resulte favorecido con respecto al máximo rival, Bitcoin, pues podría aumentar su uso.
En el proceso Proof Stake los propietarios de Ether bloquearán cantidades establecidas de sus criptomonedas para verificar nuevos registros en la cadena de bloques, ganando nuevas monedas además de su criptografía “participada”.

articles.title: IKEA, ASOS, Zoom… Plus de 175 sites piratés ont peut-être tenté de voler vos données bancaires
articles.text:
Comme le révèle l’entreprise de cybersécurité Report URI, les sites de 178 entreprises et organisations ont été exposés à un malware ce lundi 16 novembre 2026, entre 5 h 21 du matin et 22 heures environ (heure de Paris). Parmi les sites compromis, nous pouvons notamment citer GitLab, Transavia, Air France-KLM, IKEA, ASOS, HSBC ou encore la plateforme de visioconférence Zoom. Pour être plus précis, ce ne sont pas les sites en eux-mêmes qui ont été compromis, mais un outil externe baptisé Optimizely, qui permet à ces sites de tester plusieurs versions de leurs pages web.
Un malware capable de voler des informations bancaires
Durant environ 15 heures, les sites web compromis ont chargé sans le savoir un malware. Les internautes de passage ont donc été exposés à ce malware durant ce laps de temps. Pour y parvenir, les pirates ont injecté des scripts JavaScript malveillants dans les projets de leurs clients, en passant par la plateforme Optimizely.
Le malware, défini par Report URI comme « un kit multifonctionnel », était capable de récupérer les cookies et les numéros de carte saisis dans les formulaires de paiement du site, mais aussi de remplacer les adresses des portefeuilles de cryptomonnaies par celles de l’attaquant. Il était également capable d’installer des kits d’exploitation sur des iPhone et des iPad non mis à jour. À noter toutefois que le malware n’aurait pas pu avoir accès aux paiements effectués via des modules externes comme Stripe ou Adyen.
La faille aurait été comblée, mais la prudence reste de mise
Optimizely, la plateforme qui a été victime de cette cyberattaque, a confirmé l’incident, tout en assurant que la faille a maintenant été comblée et le code malveillant supprimé. En théorie, visiter les sites mentionnés plus haut ne représente donc aujourd’hui plus de risque.
Si vous avez consulté l’un de ces sites ce 16 novembre, Report URI conseille de surveiller vos relevés de compte et de contacter votre banque immédiatement à la moindre détection de transaction suspecte. Veillez également à mettre votre iPhone ou votre iPad à jour. Précisons au passage que Report URI estime que sa liste de sites compromis est sans doute incomplète, et donc plus importante. Nous avons ici cité les plateformes compromises les plus utilisées en France, les autres sites concernés étant peu visités sous nos latitudes (la chaîne CNN, la plateforme de streaming Peacock, Levi’s Japan, etc.).
Cet épisode nous rappelle qu’il faut faire attention à notre comportement en ligne, même lorsque l’on visite des sites réputés pour être fiables. Un site web peut être très bien sécurisé, mais rester vulnérable à cause d’un outil externe qu’il utilise et qui aurait été compromis.

articles.title: Bull Shows Intel Xeon Diamond Rapids Package at SC26
articles.text:
Intel is doing a mini launch of its next-generation server CPU (or something thereabouts at SC26). There are many systems on the floor, but one, the Bull Sequana XH31600, actually showed Diamond Rapids packages.
Bull Shows Intel Xeon Diamond Rapids Package at SC26
Starting off, here is the Bull compute blade with blind mate power and liquid at the rear, networking in front, and four Intel Xeon Diamond Rapids packages up front.
Just ot be clear about what you are seeing, these are two dual-socket compute nodes with Intel Diamond Rapids, each with 16-channel memory.
Here is a view of the package. We have already seen the LGA9324 socket covered in the ASRock Rack DMRD16-2L+ from OCP Summit 2026.
You can see that in the Bull platform, the CPUs are on fairly wide motherboards because of all of the memory on either side.
The idea is that these blades are liquid cooled, so you can see how everything has heatpipes and liquid cooling blocks.
The other node had the liquid cooling blocks as well as the cabled connections to the networking.
On the networking, Bull had its BXI technology for interconnect. In its booth, Bull showed a BXI switch with 64x 800G OSFP ports, but the BXI NICs were shown as QSFP-DD and PCIe Gen5 x16. It actually looks like Bull is doing something similar to what we did with the NVIDIA ConnectX-8 C8240 800G Dual 400G NIC Review This is a SuperNIC when we managed to use two PCIe Gen5 x16 links to get 800Gbps from the ConnectX-8.
What stood out a bit is that there was an NVIDIA ConnectX-8 SuperNIC as well in an OCP NIC 3.0 form factor. It’s interesting that Bull has its own interconnect, with a 51.2T switch and a PCIe Gen5 NIC in a platform with a Gen6 CPU, but right next to it is NVIDIA’s high-volume PCIe Gen6 NIC competitor.
What is very cool about this platform is that it is incredibly bespoke.
For years, Bull has had one of the better-looking blade designs, largely because they liquid-cool everything. Probably worth pondering, however, is that with NVIDIA pushing the industry with ORv3, and AMD now with the double-wide. It feels like there is a high-volume standard for high-density racks in the industry if you want power and cooling. Maybe the more interesting part is that Bull’s design does not have a copper-cabled backplane in the rear.
Overall, this was very neat to see.
Final Words
What has been interesting at SC26 is that this type of platform would have been mind-blowing years ago. Now, with the NVIDIA Vera Rubin designs in ORv3 racks, the Bull systems fit in with the higher-volume AI infrastructure bits. What Bull has, however, is SiPearl, Intel Xeon Diamond Rapids, NVIDIA, and AMD Venice nodes on display in a common form factor.
Many other vendors are showing off Diamond Rapids systems with neat designs, including 32DIMM/ socket 2DPC configurations at SC26. For its part, Bull is the only one we have found that has a package. Diamond Rapids seems to be in the sampling phase. The best guess is maybe we start to see a launch in Q2 2027, but if that slips past June (or it becomes a split launch with 1P platforms and 2P platforms), the next real launch window for Intel is early September 2027.

articles.title: Microsoft Agent Framework Releases Poisoned With Credential Stealer
articles.text:
Hackers distributed two malicious versions of Microsoft’s Agent Framework Python package through PyPI in a November 17 supply chain attack, potentially exposing cloud and CI/CD credentials belonging to users who installed them.
Microsoft Agent Framework is designed for developing AI agents and multi-agent applications. The affected package, agent-framework, has approximately 190,000 downloads per month.
The malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were released roughly 33 minutes apart. Both have since been quarantined on PyPI, where version 1.26.0 remains the latest clean release.
Microsoft has acknowledged the incident, with an Agent Framework maintainer confirming in a GitHub discussion that the compromised releases were removed from PyPI and that an investigation was underway.
The malicious distributions retained the legitimate framework components while introducing additional code that attempted to steal credentials. This allowed applications to continue functioning normally despite the compromise.
Researchers at OX Security, Wiz, Endor Labs, and SafeDep independently analyzed the malware, which exploits a Python startup mechanism to execute automatically in an affected environment.
The malware runs whenever the Python interpreter starts, even if the application doesn’t explicitly import the compromised package.
Its targets include secrets stored in environment variables and configuration files, as well as credentials belonging to other running processes. It also attempts to obtain Azure managed identity tokens and Azure DevOps authentication tokens that could provide access to cloud resources.
The second malicious release expanded the credential-stealing functionality to GitHub Actions.
The method used to publish the malicious packages remains unknown. Unlike legitimate releases, which included both built and source distributions, the malicious versions contained only built packages. Wiz also found no corresponding releases or malicious code in Microsoft’s main source repository, suggesting the packages may have been uploaded outside the normal release process.
SafeDep identified a PyPI maintainer account named vibiret, created on the day of the attack, with publishing permissions for the affected package and five related projects. However, the account’s involvement in the malicious uploads has not been confirmed.
Organizations are advised to check developer environments, CI/CD pipelines, and container images for the compromised versions, and replace affected installations with verified packages. They should also rotate potentially exposed credentials, investigate suspicious cloud activity, and rebuild affected environments.
Microsoft’s Agent Framework repository on GitHub is inaccessible at the time of writing. Several other Microsoft repositories, including ONNX Runtime projects, have similarly disappeared, but it is unclear whether the incidents are related.

articles.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
articles.text:
A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
Scientists have developed a promising new method that could read quantum information with 99.85% accuracy while barely disturbing the qubit itself.
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo
- Summary:
- Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.
- Share:
One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.
Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.
The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.
Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult
Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.
This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.
"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.
To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.
The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.
Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.
"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.
A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal
The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.
Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.
These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.
"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.
The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.
The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.
Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.
"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.
How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information
To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.
One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.
The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.
According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.
"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.
This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.
A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage
Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.
Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."
The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.
"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.
This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.
That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.
Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor
The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.
Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.
Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.
The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.
Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.
"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."
The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.
Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance
In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.
This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.
The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.
"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.
The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.
This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.
Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy
To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.
These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.
The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.
According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.
The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.
However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.
Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?
Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.
The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.
What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.
"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.
This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.
The research offers two potentially significant advances.
From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.
From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.
If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.
More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo. Original written by José Tadeu Arantes. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Xian-Peng Zhang, Chuanchang Zeng, Zhen-Biao Yang, Jose Carlos Egues, Yugui Yao. Andreev qubit readout from dynamic interference supercurrent. Physical Review B, 2026; 114 (8) DOI: 10.1103/6gkt-hghj

articles.title: Sony's updated turntable is an easy entry into the world of vinyl | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Record players and other retro tech are making a strong comeback, and I’ve recently rejoined the world of vinyl collecting. Lately, I’ve noticed myself turning to Spotify less frequently, so it felt like the perfect time to start using a record player again.
Choosing a turntable can be quite overwhelming, especially for beginners. That’s where Sony’s new PS-LX3BT turntable comes in.
Since 2019, Sony’s PS-LX310BT has been a go-to choice for vinyl newbies. Now that it has been discontinued, the PS-LX3BT emerges as its successor, keeping the same beginner-friendly approach while adding a few modern upgrades.
Currently priced at $399.99, the PS-LX3BT is designed for people who want to enjoy vinyl without getting too caught up in the technical side of things. It’s also a good option for those looking to upgrade from their first inexpensive turntable without having to learn how to set up or customize a more complicated audio system.
One of its biggest selling points is how easy it is to use. The PS-LX3BT features automatic playback, so you simply press start and the tonearm lifts, moves into position, and drops onto the first track for you. There’s no need to manually position the needle or worry about getting everything just right. It’s a small convenience, but one that makes the experience much less intimidating for newcomers.
Sony has also made a few welcome changes compared with its predecessor. The PS-LX3BT now uses USB-C for power and supports Qualcomm’s aptX Adaptive Bluetooth codec, allowing it to transmit audio at up to 24-bit/96kHz. It also has a traditional phono output alongside Bluetooth, so you can choose between a wired speaker setup and listening wirelessly.
One slightly strange design decision, however, is the repositioning of the start, stop, and tonearm buttons. On the older model, these were placed outside the dust cover. Now they’re underneath it, meaning you’ll have to lift the cover just to press start. It’s not a huge inconvenience, but still kind of annoying.
The turntable also offers USB connectivity for digitizing your vinyl collection. Connect it to a computer, and you can convert your records into digital audio files, which is useful if you want to preserve older records or listen to your collection on the go.
My biggest disappointment is the lack of a built-in speaker. It would have been nice to have everything included for someone just getting started. You’ll need to buy speakers (and possibly an amplifier) or compatible Bluetooth headphones separately, so keep that added cost in mind.
If you’re searching for a more affordable and beginner-friendly automatic record player, there are cheaper options, such as this $179 option from Audio-Technica. But overall, Sony’s PS-LX3BT is a solid choice for anyone ready to dive into the world of vinyl for the first time.

articles.title: The leaked Lenovo Legion Go Beam could be the affordable handheld we need
articles.text:
For a while there, it seemed like Lenovo had given up on selling handheld gaming PCs, hiking the price of its Legion Go 2 and Legion Go S far higher than other RAM-starved competitors. A decent one can easily cost $1,000 if not $2,000 now. But it looks like Lenovo might be about to announce a relatively cheap handheld once again— the Legion Go Beam.
The leaked Lenovo Legion Go Beam could be the affordable handheld we need
It looks comparatively cheap — and that might be a good thing in this economy.
Windows Latest has leaked images of the handheld, and there’s no question it’s designed to be a value alternative to even the company’s least expensive Legion Go S variant. While it’s got the same big stippled grips and triggers for comfort, there’s only one USB-C port on the top instead of two, a comparatively cheap-looking D-pad, no touchpad, and only a single tiny intake and exhaust for its fan.
There’s no SteamOS logo where that would go, so it likely runs Windows instead… but then there’s that name, “Beam.” Perhaps you’ll “beam” your games to it because it’s a streaming and cloud gaming handheld, instead of one that primarily plays games on its own chip? Maybe that’s why it doesn’t need as much airflow as previous handhelds?
Perhaps there’s a partnership with Xbox Cloud Gaming specifically, and that’s why it’s all lit up in Xbox green?
But it might just be green because it looks nice with white, which has been the “value” color for handhelds so far (see: ROG Ally, Xbox Ally, and the Windows-based Legion Go S). And it might be “Beam” because there’s a literal beam of light on the bottom, even though the first thing I do with most handhelds is turn any and all distracting RGB lighting off. Or maybe it’s “Beam” just because it sounds like a friendly, fun, value-oriented name, instead of something “S” or “Pro.”
I won’t begin to speculate on the Legion Go Beam’s price, except to say that “cheap” may be relative. The Legion Go S was originally supposed to cost $499, but wound up costing far more except on the occasional sale. The Legion Go 2 was supposed to start at $1,099 but wound up costing $1,500 and up after RAMageddon. Streaming-first handhelds have been far cheaper, though, like the $249 Sony PlayStation Portal.
Lenovo has a history of announcing its new gaming devices at CES in January each year, including previous Legion Go handhelds, so I’m expecting to see an official announcement of the Lenovo Legion Go Beam then. Even if so, that doesn’t mean it’ll be available in January — there’s often a many-month lag.

articles.title: 5 Life-changing lessons from It's Okay by Jaya Kishori
articles.text:
5 Life-changing lessons from It's Okay by Jaya Kishori
Discover 5 meaningful lessons from It's Okay by Jaya Kishori on accepting emotions, overcoming self-doubt, letting go and finding inner peace.
Life rarely unfolds exactly as we imagine. Sometimes, despite our best efforts, things fall apart. Relationships change, plans fail, people disappoint us, and situations arise that leave us questioning ourselves.
In such moments, we often feel pressured to stay strong, hide our emotions and pretend that everything is fine. But what if we allowed ourselves to admit that things are not okay?
In It's Okay: A Book of Inspirational and Mystic Thoughts, Jaya Kishori offers a comforting perspective on dealing with life's challenges. Rather than encouraging readers to ignore their struggles, the book reminds them that problems, emotional setbacks and difficult experiences are natural parts of being human. It encourages readers to acknowledge their circumstances, develop a healthier perspective and find ways to move forward.
Drawing on personal experiences, spiritual teachings and stories passed down through generations, Jaya Kishori explores how people can approach life's uncertainties with greater understanding and emotional strength.
5 Life lessons from It's Okay by Jaya Kishori
1. Accepting your reality is the first step towards healing
One of the most important things we struggle with is accepting situations that do not go according to our expectations. We spend days questioning why something happened, wishing things had turned out differently or comparing our present circumstances with the life we once imagined.
However, constantly resisting reality does not change what has happened. It only makes it harder to find peace. The book encourages readers to understand that accepting a situation does not mean being happy about it or agreeing with everything that happened. It simply means acknowledging the truth instead of exhausting yourself by fighting something that is already beyond your control.
For instance, if you experience failure, lose an opportunity or go through a difficult phase in a relationship, accepting the situation allows you to understand what happened and decide what to do next.
The takeaway: You cannot always control what happens in life, but you can choose how you respond to it. Accepting reality gives you the clarity to stop dwelling on the past and start working towards a better future.
2. It is okay to acknowledge your emotions
Many people believe that being strong means never crying, feeling disappointed or expressing vulnerability. They hide their sadness behind smiles, tell everyone that they are fine and avoid discussing what is actually troubling them.
But ignoring emotions does not make them disappear. An important lesson to take from the book is that experiencing difficult emotions is a natural part of life. You do not have to feel happy every day, and you do not need to pretend that nothing affects you. Whether you are feeling lonely, anxious, disappointed or overwhelmed, acknowledging those emotions is an important step towards understanding yourself.
Instead of judging yourself for feeling a certain way, give yourself the space to understand what is causing those feelings. Sometimes, talking to someone you trust, taking a break or simply allowing yourself to process an experience can make a difference.
There is also a difference between acknowledging your emotions and allowing them to control your decisions. You can accept that you are hurt without letting that hurt define your entire life.
The takeaway: Emotional strength does not mean suppressing your feelings. It means understanding them, accepting them and learning how to deal with them more healthily.
3. Stop allowing other people's opinions to define you
We live in a world where people constantly have something to say about our choices, appearance, careers, relationships and personal lives. Sometimes, even a small comment from someone can make us question our abilities or feel inadequate.
Over time, we may start making decisions based on what others expect from us rather than what genuinely matters to us. This creates unnecessary pressure and takes away our ability to appreciate our own journey. The lesson here is to understand that everyone sees life through their own experiences, beliefs and expectations. What works for someone else may not necessarily work for you. Similarly, someone else's opinion about your life does not automatically make it the truth.
It is important to listen to constructive feedback, but there is no need to carry every criticism or allow every comment to affect your self-worth. You deserve to make decisions that align with your values and aspirations, even when everyone does not understand them.
The takeaway: Your worth should not depend on how others perceive you. Learn to value your own decisions, recognise your strengths and stop seeking approval from everyone around you.
4. Let go of what you cannot change
One of the biggest reasons people struggle to find peace is their attachment to things that are no longer within their control.
We revisit old conversations, regret decisions, think about missed opportunities and wonder what would have happened if we had chosen differently. While reflecting on the past can help us learn, constantly living in it prevents us from appreciating the present.
Letting go is not always easy, especially when something or someone has been an important part of your life. It takes time to accept certain endings, forgive yourself for past mistakes and make peace with experiences that did not turn out as expected.
However, holding on to every disappointment does not bring back what you have lost. Sometimes, moving forward requires accepting that certain chapters have ended.
This does not mean forgetting your experiences. It means taking the lessons from them without allowing them to become a permanent source of pain.
The takeaway: You cannot rewrite yesterday, but you can decide how you want to live tomorrow. Let go of unnecessary emotional baggage and give yourself the opportunity to experience life beyond your past.
5. Choose faith and a positive perspective during difficult times
Life can be unpredictable. There will be moments when you work hard but do not see results, when your plans fall apart or when you cannot understand why certain things are happening.
During such phases, it is easy to lose hope and believe that things will never improve. The book brings attention to the importance of spiritual understanding, faith and maintaining a positive outlook when dealing with life's challenges. Having faith does not mean expecting everything to happen exactly as you wish. Instead, it means developing the strength to face uncertainty without losing hope.
A positive perspective also does not require you to ignore your problems. It encourages you to look for possibilities, learn from difficult experiences and believe that your present circumstances do not have to determine your entire future.
For readers who find comfort in spirituality, prayer, reflection and faith can also become meaningful ways to navigate emotionally challenging periods.
The takeaway: Not every difficult experience will make sense immediately. Have faith, keep making sincere efforts and remind yourself that one challenging phase does not define your whole life.
Final thoughts
It's Okay by Jaya Kishori offers a reassuring reminder that life does not have to be perfect for us to find happiness and peace. We all experience difficult days, unexpected disappointments and moments when we feel lost. What matters is how we understand these experiences and allow ourselves to grow through them.
The five lessons from the book encourage us to accept reality, acknowledge our emotions, value ourselves, let go of the past and maintain faith during uncertain times.
Perhaps the most meaningful message is that saying "It's okay" should not become an excuse to ignore problems or tolerate situations that hurt us. Instead, it should give us the courage to acknowledge what is happening, face it honestly and take steps towards finding a solution.
Because sometimes, the first step towards changing your life is accepting that you do not have to have everything figured out right now.

Black Friday 2026 – La liseuse Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition à 199,99 € (-30%)
La liseuse Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition passe sous les 200 € chez Amazon soit une baisse d'environ 30% sur le prix habituellement constaté. C'est actuellement l'un des meilleurs produit de notre comparatif.
Après une excellente Kindle Paperwhite 2024, Amazon signe avec la Kindle Colorsoft sa première liseuse à écran couleur. Ce modèle promet une expérience autrement intéressante pour les amateurs de bandes dessinées, magazines et autres contenus graphiques en couleur.

Points forts
- Contraste de l’écran couleur et luminosité.
- Légère, étanche et rechargeable sans fil.
- Interface claire, à défaut de novatrice.
- Réactivité (tant que vous ne zoomez pas dans les images).
Points faibles
- Fidélité des couleurs très perfectible.
- Zoom trop lent dans les contenus en couleur.
- Absence de mode sombre.
- Autonomie très correcte, mais moins importante que pour la Kindle Paperwhite 2024.
Pour sa première liseuse couleur, Amazon a réussi à éviter quelques-uns des écueils rencontrés par les concurrentes de la Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition. Ainsi, l’écran de cette dernière est très lumineux et bien contrasté, ce qui est un progrès notable. Néanmoins, il n’est pas parfait pour autant et souffre comme la concurrence d’une colorimétrie très perfectible. Toutefois, même s'il n’est pas indispensable sur une petite diagonale, cet afficheur en couleur est un vrai plus. La lecture sur la Kindle Colorsoft s’avère très plaisante au quotidien, que ce soit en couleur ou en noir & blanc. Nous n'avons finalement pas grand-chose de sérieux à lui reprocher. Son plus grand problème vient d’une adversaire interne redoutable, l’excellente Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (2024), qui ne dispose certes pas d'un écran couleur, mais est vendue (à date) 100 € moins cher !

articles.title: Tesla peut déployer sa conduite autonome en Finlande, mais la France résiste toujours
articles.text:
Tesla franchit une nouvelle étape dans le déploiement de son système de conduite autonome en Europe. Le constructeur américain vient d’obtenir le feu vert de Traficom, l’agence finlandaise des transports et des communications. Il pourra prochainement commercialiser son système Tesla Assisted Driving auprès des propriétaires d’environ 6 500 véhicules compatibles. La Finlande rejoint ainsi les dix autres pays européens ayant reconnu l’homologation provisoire délivrée aux Pays-Bas en avril. Mais la France reste encore à convaincre.
Tesla Assisted Driving : ce qui change pour les automobilistes finlandais
Le FSD (Full Self-Driving) de Tesla change de nom et devient Tesla Assisted Driving. Une évolution réclamée par plusieurs responsables politiques européens, qui jugeaient l’ancienne appellation trompeuse pour un système nécessitant toujours la surveillance du conducteur. « Le changement de nom aide les utilisateurs et le marché à comprendre la vraie nature du système », explique Jukka Juhola, expert principal chez Traficom.
La Finlande autorise son déploiement avant même le vote européen. L’agence justifie sa décision par ce changement de nom, mais aussi par les modifications apportées à la gestion de la vitesse. Jusqu’à présent, le FSD pouvait autoriser un dépassement de 50 % de la limitation. Cette marge est désormais réduite à 10 % et revient à zéro à chaque démarrage du véhicule.
L’arrivée de l’hiver a également pesé dans la décision. Traficom préfère laisser aux propriétaires le temps de découvrir le système avant les premières chutes de neige et l’apparition du verglas. Les caméras peuvent en effet être perturbées par la neige, la neige fondue ou les saletés. L’agence recommande notamment de garder les mains sur le volant face à une plaque de verglas, une flaque de profondeur inconnue ou de fortes rafales de vent.
Car, malgré son nouveau nom, le Tesla Assisted Driving ne rend pas les voitures autonomes. Le conducteur reste responsable de la conduite et doit pouvoir reprendre le contrôle à tout moment, y compris en cas d’excès de vitesse.
La France toujours réticente face au système de Tesla
En France, le constructeur américain est encore loin d’obtenir une autorisation. En juillet dernier, le ministre des Transports, Philippe Tabarot, avait notamment critiqué la possibilité de dépasser jusqu’à 50 % la vitesse autorisée, mais aussi le manque de garanties concernant la vigilance du conducteur lors des changements de voie, aux intersections et dans les ronds-points.
En septembre, une visioconférence avec Elon Musk a toutefois permis d’ouvrir le dialogue. Le gouvernement a depuis autorisé des essais sur route avec deux véhicules Tesla, sans pour autant s’engager sur une reconnaissance de l’homologation néerlandaise.
Tesla encore loin de convaincre l’ensemble de l’Europe
Le dossier doit désormais passer devant le comité technique des véhicules à moteur (TCMV), qui réunit les représentants des 27 États membres. Un vote était initialement attendu le 6 octobre, mais le comité ne devrait finalement pas se réunir à nouveau avant décembre.
Pour obtenir une reconnaissance européenne, Tesla doit réunir au moins 15 États représentant 65 % de la population de l’Union. Malgré onze pays favorables, le constructeur ne rassemble pour l’instant qu’environ 70 millions d’habitants sur 450 millions, soit un peu plus de 15 %.
L’Allemagne pourrait apporter son soutien après avoir obtenu les modifications réclamées à Tesla. Mais même avec Berlin, les pays favorables ne représenteraient qu’environ un tiers de la population européenne. Le constructeur devra donc encore convaincre plusieurs grands marchés, dont la France, l’Italie et l’Espagne. La généralisation du Tesla Assisted Driving en Europe n’est donc pas encore pour demain.

articles.title: Flipper One sur Kickstarter : prix, date de fin et précommande — Frandroid
articles.text:
Décidément, les campagnes de financement participatif sont plutôt favorables à Flipper Devices. Déjà à l’époque du Flipper Zero, l’entreprise avait récolté près de 5 millions de dollars sur les 60 000 demandés. Et l’histoire semble se répéter, note le média It’s Foss.
Le Flipper One, nouveau gadget dédié aux pros de la cybersécurité et autres hackers en tout genre, vient de se lancer sur Kickstarter et a déjà récolté près de 12 millions d’euros sur les 270 000 demandés.
Du 19 au 30 novembre, le Plaud Note Pro passe à 149 € au lieu de 189 € ! Il enregistre vos réunions, les transcrit et les synthétise pour vous, il suffit d’appuyer sur un bouton. Les Plaud Note, NotePin et NotePin S sont aussi à -20 %. Bref, c’est le moment d’arrêter de perdre du temps au travail !
À partir de 360 €
Lancée le 17 novembre dernier, la campagne a déjà attiré près de 25 000 contributeurs et contributrices et a donc explosé les attentes de l’entreprise avec encore 28 jours restants avant la fin de cette première phase de commercialisation. De quoi rassurer les équipes qui expliquent vendre leur premier lot d’appareils à prix coûtant pour récolter suffisamment de fonds pour démarrer la production en usine.
Les récompenses disponibles commencent à 399 $ (soit environ 364 €). À ce prix (auquel il faudra ajouter 10 à 20 € de frais de port pour l’Europe), vous aurez droit à un exemplaire du Flipper One sans aucun module supplémentaire. Les prix montent jusqu’à quasiment 700 € pour obtenir un pack avec tous les accessoires supplémentaires.
Ces tarifs restent 25 à 35 % moins chers que ceux qui devraient être affichés une fois la campagne terminée. La faute à un prix de la mémoire qui continue d’exploser. La Foire Aux Questions indique d’ailleurs que la quantité de mémoire vive peut encore changer selon l’évolution des prix. Il faudra par contre se montrer patient, les premières expéditions n’auront lieu qu’à partir de juillet 2027 si tout se passe bien.
Fin du tarif préférentiel le 17 décembre
L’entreprise rappelle tout de même que le Flipper One n’est pas un remplaçant du Flipper Zero. Le nouveau gadget est clairement plus pensé pour être un ordinateur de poche sous Linux, tandis que l’ancien est plus pensé pour exploiter les protocoles de communication hors ligne, tels que le NFC ou le RFID.
    Pour aller plus loin
Le Flipper Zero, gadgets préférés des hackers, devient encore plus puissant
            
Si vous souhaitez mettre la main sur un Flipper One à un tarif avantageux, la campagne se termine le 17 décembre prochain. Celles et ceux qui ont déjà acheté un coupon de prévente peuvent réclamer leurs récompenses en s’identifiant avec le même mail sur Kickstarter.

articles.title: Essai Linktour Alumi : j'ai conduit la voiture sans permis qui ne joue pas les voiturettes
articles.text:
Sur le marché de la voiture sans permis électrique, deux marques servent de repères. Citroën vend son Ami à 8 190 €, avec un habitacle réduit au strict minimum. En face, Aixam, le spécialiste historique, demande 13 999 € pour une e-City Pack. Linktour veut se glisser entre les deux avec l’Alumi, lancée en France le 16 juin 2026 par cette filiale de Shandong Weiqiao Pioneering, un groupe chinois du textile, de l’énergie et de l’aluminium.
Lors d’une présentation à Paris à laquelle Numerama a été conviée, la marque s’est présentée comme le « premium accessible » du segment. C’est à cette occasion que j’ai pu prendre le volant des deux versions de la gamme Linktour.
Commençons par un petit rappel des forces en présence. Il y a d’abord l’Alumi de base qui est un quadricycle léger (catégorie L6e). En raison de sa réglementation, cette version est bridée à 45 km/h et se destine ainsi aux jeunes automobilistes qui peuvent la conduire dès 14 ans avec le permis AM. Au-dessus, on trouve l’Alumi Elite, qui bascule dans la catégorie des quadricycles dits lourds (catégorie L7e). Pour la conduire, il faut le permis B1, accessible dès 16 ans, et il est possible de rouler avec sur le périphérique.
Côté autonomie, Linktour annonce 120 km pour la première et 180 km pour la seconde, selon le cycle WMTC, la norme d’homologation des deux-roues et des quadricycles. La recharge se fait sur une prise domestique (AC), en 4h pour l’Alumi et 4h30 pour l’Elite. Sans surprise, il n’existe pas de recharge rapide (DC) sur ce genre de voiture.
La Linktour Alumi fait oublier la voiturette
L’Alumi ne mesure que 2,69 mètres de long, et pourtant on y trouve étonnamment beaucoup de place. L’accès à bord est facilité par de grandes portes (sans encadrement s’il-vous-plaît), tandis que la cabine est capable d’accueillir deux grands gabarits sans que les deux se gênent ou se sentent étriqués.
Pour parfaire l’habitabilité, le coffre offre un volume très généreux de 320 litres, engloutissant pas mal d’affaires. Les grandes vitres et le toit panoramique (de série dès l’entrée de gamme) offrent une excellente visibilité, ce qui fait vraiment la différence en ville. Par ailleurs, on ne sent pas tout petit face aux autres véhicules sur la route, renforçant cette sensation de « vraie » voiture et qui rassure les occupants.
Surtout, la présentation intérieure fait toute la différence face à l’Ami et consorts grâce à des matériaux plutôt flatteurs pour le segment, toutes proportions gardées. En revanche, j’ai trouvé qu’il manquait un vrai rangement entre les deux sièges. J’aurais bien vu un bac de rangement histoire de poser un petit sac. Il y a bien un espace au-dessus de la planche de bord, mais il n’est pas très profond et les affaires peuvent aussi se balader pendant la conduite.
Facile à conduire en ville
Au volant, l’Alumi se conduit facilement, même sans direction assistée sur la version L6e. C’est seulement lors des manoeuvres qu’il faudra sortir un peu les muscles, mais une fois en mouvement l’effort est bien moindre. Le moteur électrique (8 ch sur l’Alumi, 14 ch sur l’Elite) permet de suivre le flot de la circulation avec réactivité, et on ne se traîne pas au démarrage d’un feu rouge. Naturellement, le gabarit permet de se faufiler entre les voitures sans encombre, par exemple lorsqu’un carrefour est complètement bouché.
Point notable, l’insonorisation est plutôt soignée et le système audio est correct. Le gros bémol au niveau de la conduite est finalement la faiblesse du freinage régénératif. Il est d’ailleurs tellement peu prononcé sur la version sans permis qu’on fait quasiment de la roue libre au lever de pied.
Côté construction, Linktour a choisi un châssis en aluminium au lieu du châssis tubulaire habituel, et la carrosserie est vissée plutôt que collée. Remplacer un élément abîmé devrait donc être plus simple (j’y reviens un peu plus bas).
Une voiture déjà bien équipée
La version sans permis de la Linktour Alumi démarre à 10 690 €, soit 2 500 € de plus qu’une Ami. Sur le papier, l’Alumi offre bien plus d’autonomie que l’Ami pour un prix inférieur à celui d’une Aixam, laquelle n’est pas plus endurante non plus. Pour la version Elite de l’Alumi, l’ABS et le droit au périphérique justifient une bonne partie des 4 000 € d’écart avec la version de base.
À 10 690 €, l’Alumi standard (sans permis) embarque de série les vitres électriques, un compteur numérique de 5 pouces et un chauffage simple. On trouve Apple CarPlay et Android Auto, une caméra de recul, un grand écran central de 10,25 pouces à partir de la finition intermédiaire Plus à 12 690 €. Sur la version haut de gamme Pro à 13 690 €, l’Alumi gagne la climatisation, le chauffage à deux niveaux (au lieu d’un), le volant multifonctions et un port USB-C 60W.
Dès 14 990 €, l’Alumi Elite (avec permis) reprend la dotation du modèle de base et ajoute notamment l’ABS, le démarrage sans clé ainsi que la direction assistée. Enfin, pour 16 990 €, le niveau Elite + hérite des équipements de la version Plus de l’Alumi sans permis.
| Modèle | Catégorie | Permis | Autonomie | Prix | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Linktour Alumi | L6e | AM (14 ans) | 120 km | 10 690 € | 
| Linktour Alumi Elite | L7e | B1 (16 ans) | 180 km | 14 690 € | 
| Citroën Ami | L6e | AM (14 ans) | 75 km | 8 190 € | 
| Aixam e-City Pack | L6e | AM (14 ans) | 75 km | 13 999 € | 
Un réseau encore en construction
Linktour dit avoir trouvé une centaine de clients depuis juin. 90 % des immatriculations concernent la version L6e (sans permis), et c’est la finition la plus haut de gamme qui se vend le mieux. La marque mise également sur la catégorie L7e, un marché qui va « exploser » nous explique un porte-parole. Et l’Alumi a une la place à prendre : Renault a arrêté la vente de son Mobilize Duo au 1er janvier 2026. Linktour vise aussi les flottes d’entreprise et les auto-écoles. Une auto-école du Loiret va justement servir d’ambassadrice. Une version cabriolet et des versions utilitaires, avec plus d’espace de chargement, sont prévues.
Il existe aujourd’hui 25 points de vente, surtout des revendeurs de voitures sans permis et des groupes multimarques. Linktour en promet bientôt 50. On peut aussi acheter l’Alumi en ligne et se la faire livrer à domicile. L’entretien passe par l’atelier du revendeur ou par Go Mécano, un réseau de 300 camions-ateliers. Bonne nouvelle, les pièces de rechange sont déjà stockées en France.

articles.title: Linux Foundation Newsletter: November 2026
articles.text:
Linux Foundation Newsletter: November 2026
The Linux Foundation | 18 November 2026
Welcome to the November 2026 edition of the Linux Foundation Newsletter!
LF Education’s Black Friday sale runs November 27 through December 4, with savings of up to 65% on training and certifications. Also new is the Certified Kubernetes Network Engineer (CKNE) certification and its Certification Pathway, and you can sign up to be notified when registration opens for the Secure AI Associate (SAIA) exam.
This month’s biggest announcements include a new open source project for AI agent identity and a milestone for the Agentic AI Foundation. The Linux Foundation welcomed Agent Name Service (ANS), which builds on DNS to verify and discover AI agents. AAIF added four projects (Agent Skills, Open Responses, OpenEnv, and OpenSandbox), bringing it to 10 hosted projects, and passed 300 members in its first year. The CNCF now hosts 231 projects, with KubeVirt and NATS graduating this month.
LF Research published four reports. The 2026 State of Open Source in Financial Services found a 63% year-over-year increase in GitHub commits from financial institutions. The AI impact on cybersecurity report found that 3 in 5 teams ship code faster than security reviews can keep up. A third finds that the future depends on VMs and containers running together, and the fourth, State of Commercial Open Source 2026, draws on 225 founders and leaders. LF Research and CNCF are also fielding a 3-minute survey on neocloud adoption.
You’ll also find a recap of the industry challenge LF Europe co-led at the World Open Innovation Conference in Kaunas, Lithuania, plus project news that ranges from agentic AI to telecom and embedded systems.
>> Read on for even more news, research, and opportunities from across the Linux Foundation.
Contents
Education Opportunities
Black Friday Deals Are Coming: Save Up to 65%!
Mark your calendars! From November 27 through December 4, save up to 65% on Linux Foundation Education training, certifications, and more. Whether you're building new skills or taking the next step in your career, you won't want to miss these deals!
New Certifications. More Ways to Grow. Take your skills further with the new Certified Kubernetes Network Engineer (CKNE) certification and Certification Pathway. Explore how the CARE Program makes it easier to keep your credentials current as you advance your skills. Plus, get ready for the upcoming Secure AI Associate (SAIA) certification exam. Sign up to be notified when registration opens!
LF Event Highlight
The full schedule is LIVE for Open Source Summit Japan, Automotive Linux Summit, and Embedded Linux Conference, happening December 7–9 in Tokyo!
One registration gives you access to all three events, featuring the latest in open source, automotive innovation, and embedded systems.
🎉 For the first time, Embedded Linux Conference is coming to Japan! Explore sessions on embedded Linux, real-time systems, kernel development, and more.
👉 Register by November 23 + SAVE!
LF Research: 4 new reports, and a new survey on Neoclouds!
Are you involved in your organization’s cloud infrastructure decisions?
As AI workloads drive demand for GPU capacity and specialized AI-native providers enter the market, LF Research and CNCF are fielding a 3-minute survey to capture how organizations actually run production workloads today and the extent to which neoclouds are being adopted.
We would love to hear from you! Your feedback will inform open source cloud tooling priorities and community benchmarks that help the ecosystem navigate modern infrastructure strategies more effectively.
How is finance balancing rapid AI adoption with enterprise risk? Produced by FINOS and LF Research in partnership with GitHub, Scott Logic, and sponsor BrightQuery, the annual survey-based 2026 State of Open Source in Financial Services Report delivers definitive data on industry adoption and risk management in the era of modern AI.
While AI coding tools boost security development speed by 17%, false positives from scanning tools increase workloads by 30%. Critically, 3 in 5 teams now ship code faster than security reviews can keep up, and 82% of practitioners warn that overreliance on AI tools is weakening developers’ security skills.
Yet, preparedness is possible! Download the report, produced in partnership with OpenSSF, ActiveState, and LF AI & Data for actionable recommendations on building dedicated governance, strengthening supply chain safeguards, and balancing AI speed with human oversight.
Virtual machines are anchoring modern enterprise infrastructure and the rise of agentic AI. The latest research from the Linux Foundation, in partnership with Broadcom and CNCF, reveals how practitioners are experiencing the evolution of VMs and production workloads. The future is shaping up to depend on both VMs and containers, secured and managed together. Download the report for strategic guidance on balancing isolation, utilization, and modern cloud native architectures.
Commercial open source companies are proving that community trust and developer adoption can successfully translate into durable enterprise revenue. The State of Commercial Open Source 2026, produced by LF Research and Serena Capital with sponsors AWS, CNCF, Futurewei, LF AI & Data, and Red Hat, delivers ground-up operational benchmarks and strategies from 225 founders and leaders. Download the report for strategic guidance on feature gating, enterprise sales, and sustainable scaling.
LF Europe: Community Updates
At the World Open Innovation Conference in Kaunas, Lithuania, LF Europe’s Mirko Boehm joined LF Research’s Anna Hermansen to lead an industry challenge on how open source must evolve as we work to create and sustain open ecosystems for hardware, data, and AI models, and how we can apply open innovation principles to support these more complex systems.
Linux Foundation Projects: Featured news
Formations
- The Linux Foundation welcomed Agent Name Service (ANS) as a new open source project, advancing trusted identity, verification, and discovery for AI agents across the internet. Built on existing DNS infrastructure, ANS provides an open standard for securely identifying and authenticating AI agents, enabling greater interoperability across platforms and services. Read the announcement >>
Academy Software Foundation (ASWF)
- 2026 Virtual Town Halls: Watch On Demand – Recordings from all 11 project town halls are live, including ACES, OpenColorIO, OpenEXR, MaterialX, OpenTimelineIO, and the USD Working Group. Each covers the year’s releases, production use cases, roadmap and what’s next. Watch the recordings
- Call for Papers: Open Source Forum 2027 – Our annual Open Source Forum returns to Los Angeles on February 18, 2027, for 100+ business and technical leaders, with the theme “New Technologies Impacting Studios.” The call for talks closes December 6 at 11:59 PM PT. We welcome talks on AI and machine learning, virtual production, pipeline tools, computer graphics, and immersive films. Submit your talk
- USD Collective Projects Initiative Launches – The USD Working Group, with over 1,000 contributors, has launched an open source test bed for standardizing how assets are defined in production pipelines. Its first project, built by volunteers across different DCCs, already exposed differences in how tools handle USD, including two renderers lighting the same scene differently. Read the blog
- Open Source Days 2026: 500+ attendees in Los Angeles, plus new members CIQ, Evercast, and RIT. Watch the recap and recordings
Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF)
- Four new projects join AAIF: Agent Skills, Open Responses, OpenEnv, and OpenSandbox bring AAIF to 10 hosted projects, expanding open collaboration on agent capabilities, model interoperability, training, and execution. Read the announcement.
- AAIF surpasses 300 members in its first year: New Gold Members include Ant Group, Gates Foundation, MongoDB, Nutanix, Royal Bank of Canada, Vercel, and Vultr, broadening participation in open standards for agentic AI. Meet the new members.

Open Mainframe Project
- Welcome Gait to the Open Mainframe Project – The Open Mainframe Project community welcomed Gait, a new open source Visual Studio Code extension developed with 21CS. Gait lets developers write and debug z/Architecture assembler code locally in VS Code, with no mainframe access required. They can set breakpoints and step forward or backward through instructions to see exactly what the code does. Gait also works alongside HLASM Language Support and Zowe, so learners can move from local practice to real z/OS work. 21CS announced the new project in a keynote at GS UK Forge. Read the blog.

The migration reduced operational overhead and laid the groundwork for hybrid search and AI-driven travel experiences. Read the case study >>

- Extending Inductor for the IBM Spyre Accelerator: IBM moved its Spyre compiler to an out-of-tree Inductor backend, cutting compiler code size nearly 7x.
- From KTIR to SpyreCode: An MLIR Dataflow Backend for IBM Spyre: IBM lowers kernels through the KTIR MLIR dialect into SpyreCode. The new scheduler brought up its first op about 4x faster.
- Integrating SGLang into Spyre in Under a Week with AI: AI coding agents helped integrate SGLang with IBM Spyre in under a week, reaching about 3.6× the reference PyTorch throughput.
- Muse Spark Is Now an Open-Weights Model: Meta’s natively multimodal model is now on Hugging Face. It has 816B total and 42B active parameters and a 1M-token context.
- Optimizing Muse Spark Open on TPU v7 with SGLang-TorchTPU: Covers community optimizations for serving large MoE models on Google Cloud TPU v7.

- Fast by Default: Compile-Time Heuristic for Helion Kernels: Helion now picks fast kernel configs at compile time, giving near-autotuned performance without hours of tuning.

- ExecuTorch WebGPU: PyTorch Models on the GPU, in the Browser: A new backend runs GPU-accelerated PyTorch inference directly in the browser, privately and with low latency.
- One Search, Two Layers: Compiler Controls Inside PyTorch Helion using NVIDIA CompileIQ: Helion’s autotuner now searches NVIDIA CompileIQ compiler controls, giving 2–7% gains, including 6.9% on GB200.
- Bringing Elastically Deterministic Data Loading to TorchTitan with Zephon: Keeps global batches identical across GPU counts, cutting score drift from up to 0.82 points to 0.05.
- Announcing the Special Interest Group (SIG) for Ray on Accelerators: A new SIG unites hardware vendors and Ray contributors on a vendor-neutral roadmap for accelerator support.
- Modernizing Table Batched Embeddings with FBTriton: Meta’s Python-based embedding kernels outperform legacy CUDA on recommendation workloads.

- Sylva Hackathon 2026: A Few More Days to Go!
The Sylva Hackathon 2026 is just around the corner! Taking place on November 23–24 in Bern, Switzerland, the two-day event will bring together 66 participants from 19 countries, working across eight teams to tackle real-world challenges in open source telco cloud infrastructure. Participants will collaborate on topics including Telco GitOps, Kubernetes automation, configuration validation, deployment troubleshooting, AI-powered operations, and more. - New White Paper: Trust You Can See – CNTi Test Suite and the Business Case for Cloud Native Network Functions
How can telecom operators and vendors verify whether network functions are truly cloud native? This new white paper, authored by Cédric Ollivier (Orange), Martin Matyáš (Tieto), and Philippe Ensarguet (Orange), introduces the CNTi Cloud Native badge, which makes CNTi Test Suite results continuously available and publicly visible. It explains how the badge helps open source projects demonstrate their cloud native capabilities, vendors identify issues earlier and simplify operator acceptance, and operators evaluate network functions using a common set of tests. The paper also explores how the badge complements formal certification and Sylva platform validation, providing an initial layer of evidence rather than replacing more comprehensive testing. Learn more.
- In the News: European Telecom Operators Move Toward a Common Cloud Architecture with Sylva
In a recent article published by LeMagIT, journalist Yann Serra explores how European telecom operators are working together through the Sylva Project, an open source initiative hosted by Linux Foundation Europe, to establish a common cloud infrastructure for 5G services. The article features insights from Philippe Ensarguet, VP of Cloud & Software Engineering at Orange and Sylva's strategy lead, on how a shared, Kubernetes-based architecture can reduce dependence on proprietary infrastructure solutions, simplify network function validation, and strengthen Europe's digital sovereignty. It also highlights Sylva's growing ecosystem, its network of validation centers, and future plans to support AI workloads, radio access network (RAN) functions, and potential applications in other critical sectors, including energy and aerospace.Read more.
- From Sigstore to CRA readiness: Sylva’s journey with OpenSSF
In our recent blog, Louise Grosset and François-Régis Menguy (Orange – Sylva WG03) share how Sylva is strengthening software supply chain security and working toward Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) readiness using tools and frameworks from the OpenSSF ecosystem.
The blog highlights Sylva’s use of Sigstore for artifact signing and verification, SLSA as a supply chain security framework, and OpenSSF Scorecard and the Best Practices Badge to assess and improve security practices. It also covers progress in vulnerability disclosure and CVE management, and how the OpenSSF CRA Readiness Guide helps Sylva document its security practices to support downstream integrators. The authors discuss ongoing challenges with GitLab, third-party dependencies, and complex artifacts, while sharing practical lessons for other open source projects. Read more.
