articles.title: Tech lawsuits defined 2026 — and lawmakers want more
articles.text:
With just a few weeks remaining, lawmakers are trying to pass new protections for victims of online harm before the end of 2026, targeting deepfake creators and online platforms that block users from filing lawsuits.
Tech lawsuits defined 2026 — and lawmakers want more
Congress is scrambling to provide legal recourse for deepfakes and online grooming.
On Tuesday, members of a Senate Judiciary subcommittee hosted a hearing calling for the end of forced arbitration for online harms. Their immediate target was Roblox, which they accused of evading legal complaints about children allegedly groomed on the platform by enforcing its own forced arbitration clause against users who agreed to the terms as minors, in some cases even under the age of 10. Separately, a few blocks away, Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Laurel Lee (R-FL) brought hotel heiress Paris Hilton to Capitol Hill to advocate for the Defiance Act, which would let victims of nonconsensual intimate deepfakes sue their creators.
“The best thing we can do in terms of enforcement is we can open up the courthouse doors,” Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), who chairs the Judiciary subcommittee, told reporters after the Roblox hearing. “The more I see these companies evade regulations, the more I think there is nothing as powerful as a jury.” Hawley introduced a new bill with ranking member Dick Durbin (D-IL) to render arbitration agreements unenforceable for disputes over alleged child sexual exploitation or “child cyber injury,” which could include “reputational harm, mental suffering,” or death.
“The best thing we can do in terms of enforcement is we can open up the courthouse doors”
Roblox has sought to enforce its arbitration clause in lawsuits it’s facing over allegations that users were groomed on the gaming platform as minors, despite the company’s claims of protections. Roblox is facing about 180 lawsuits in a consolidated case over its alleged role in failing to protect children. Under the arbitration process, the public would not get to see legal discovery like the kind that’s come to light under recent cases against Meta. Hawley called the jury system “corruption-proof” and “an incredibly big hammer.”
Roblox has denied that it’s trying to dodge accountability. “Safety has been central to Roblox since we launched. We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” Roblox’s global head of public policy Nicky Jackson Colaço said in a statement. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”
Congress has only a little more than three more weeks left in session before the end of the year, and a new Democratic majority will be sworn in come January. Republicans are expected to do their best to push through President Donald Trump’s nominees for judgeships and executive branch posts like FCC commissioner in the lame-duck session, as well as try to pass year-end bills like the National Defense Authorization Act, which often includes a range of other policy items. But some lawmakers are holding out hope that they can open up courthouses to new litigation over deepfake abuse and child predation.
Litigation has become one of the more successful ways for survivors of online harm to seek change. Congress has failed to pass many prominent child safety, privacy, and consumer protection bills, though it has begun to tackle the deepfake issue through the Take It Down Act. At the same time, attorneys general and individual plaintiffs have collected significant settlements and legal wins despite the broad scope of tech’s legal shield, Section 230. If bills like the Defiance Act or those seeking to end forced arbitration were to pass, tech companies and perpetrators of online harms could become vulnerable to a new wave of legal challenges.
“You will be amazed by how quickly the company will change its behavior once it is sued in public court”
In addition to Hawley and Durbin’s bill about forced arbitration, Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Katie Britt (R-AL), and Cory Booker (D-NJ) introduced a similar bill with a slightly different approach, including explicitly covering data privacy violations. At the Roblox hearing, Northwestern University law professor Myriam Gilles, an expert on forced arbitration, said she’s testified before Congress many times on this topic, but “never expected to come before this body to talk about its use against 9 year olds.” Passing either proposal, she said, would have a profound impact. “You will be amazed by how quickly the company will change its behavior once it is sued in public court.”
The Defiance Act would let victims of nonconsensual intimate deepfakes sue their creators for damages, in an attempt to raise the cost of creating these kinds of images. Hilton visited Washington earlier this year to share how an intimate non-deepfake video of her at age 19 shared without her consent impacted her life, and she used her story to advocate for the Defiance Act. At Tuesday’s press conference, she said she would come back to Congress as many times as necessary for the bill to become law. “Some people might have thought that was the end of my fight,” Hilton said. “But when I make a promise to survivors, I keep it.”
Hilton said over 50 million people have been victimized by sexually explicit deepfakes. “For me personally, strangers have created over 100,000 AI-generated explicit images and videos portraying me in the most graphic and disturbing ways imaginable,” Hilton said. “If this can happen to someone with my resources and my platform, imagine how powerless a young girl might feel facing this completely alone.”
Hilton’s comments were followed by Elliston Berry, an advocate who said a classmate made an explicit deepfake image of her friend group “from an innocent social media post” when she was 14, and distributed it throughout her school. “In a matter of seconds, my sense of security disappeared,” she said. “For me, the Defiance Act means recognition that victims deserve to be heard, that their experience matters, and that their right to seek justice should not depend on how quickly technology advances.”

articles.title: NVIDIA RTX Spark Compact Desktops Out Now
articles.text:
New NVIDIA RTX Spark compact desktops from ASUS, Dell and MSI are available today, bringing local AI agents, image and video generation, and model fine-tuning to a dedicated Windows PC.
With up to 128GB of unified memory and NVIDIA’s AI software stack, these systems provide room for larger local models alongside RTX-accelerated creative and development tools. A dedicated desktop can keep agents and scheduled tasks running while a laptop travels or handles other work.
Alongside the new desktops, an expanding software ecosystem brings more creative and development workflows to RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops.
Native Windows on Arm applications from Adobe, the NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction feature in Blender and local generation workflows in ComfyUI expand what creators and developers can do on RTX Spark — all on one Windows PC.
A Windows PC Built for Local AI
As workflows expand to include local AI models and agents, more work can continue beyond an active editing session — from generating assets to processing long renders or scheduled tasks.
RTX Spark compact desktops give developers, creators and AI enthusiasts a dedicated Windows PC for local models and always-on agents. They bring together image and video generation, model fine-tuning, creative applications and development tools in one compact system.
Running supported models locally keeps locally processed code and files on the PC and avoids per-token cloud application programming interface (API) charges for those tasks.
RTX Spark desktops are equipped with a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU, an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores and up to 128GB of unified memory, delivering up to 1 petaflop of AI performance. Ten-gigabit Ethernet connectivity enables fast transfers of large datasets, model files and creative assets between RTX Spark compact desktops and networked storage.
This advanced hardware unlocks incredible capabilities for creators, developers and AI enthusiasts, including:
- Running massive 120-billion-parameter large language models locally
- Rendering 90GB+ 3D scenes in real time
- Smoothly editing 4:2:2 video in real time
New compact desktops are available for purchase from ASUS, Dell and MSI, joining the RTX Spark family of laptops available today. Mini PCs from Acer, GIGABYTE and HP are coming soon, along with the Microsoft Surface RTX Spark Dev Box.
From Local Agents to AI Creation
Native CUDA support and Linux development tools through Windows Subsystem for Linux give developers a foundation for building and running local AI workflows. Developers can set up agents with Hermes Agent or NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and fine-tune supported models using Unsloth.
RTX Spark can run creative agents that connect familiar applications and local AI tools, helping creators move from an idea to finished work with natural-language instructions.
NVIDIA Switchyard, now available in Hermes, automatically routes agent tasks between local and cloud models. Everyday tasks can run on device, while advanced reasoning draws on cloud models, helping manage cloud costs across creative workflows.
These capabilities come together in creative workflows that connect Photoshop and ComfyUI through Hermes Agent. Using natural-language instructions, creators can turn sketches into rendered images and animations, or animate an image entirely on device — from isolating a subject and defining its motion to generating the finished video.
NVIDIA brought these workflows to life at Adobe MAX, where attendees used natural-language instructions to turn sketches into rendered images and animations for a shared digital Miami landscape.
The RTX Video Frame Generation and RTX Video HDR features, already available in ComfyUI, extend the pipeline: a generated clip can be expanded to 60 frames per second and converted to high dynamic range for color grading, all within a single ComfyUI workflow on RTX Spark.
Adobe Accelerates the Full Creative Stack for RTX Spark
NVIDIA and Adobe are expanding native Windows on Arm support and RTX acceleration across Adobe’s creative applications, helping video editors, photographers, designers and 3D artists work more efficiently on RTX Spark.
Adobe Premiere accelerates a range of AI-powered editing features through NVIDIA TensorRT-RTX, including Enhance Speech, Object Mask, Scene Edit Detection and Auto Reframe — so editors spend less time waiting and more time cutting.
GPU acceleration also extends to Film Impact transition and effects plug-ins. The update improves support for professional video formats, including Canon RAW, Red RAW, ARRI RAW, ARRICORE, ARRI HDE, H.264 and HEVC in MXF, ProRes RAW and long-GOP video. This lets editors realize more than 50% quicker turnaround on everyday H.264 video deliverables.
Adobe Photoshop adds TensorRT-RTX acceleration for the Remove Tool and ArmRTX Spark-native Camera Raw support, helping photographers remove unwanted objects faster and work with RAW images without relying on emulation. At Adobe MAX, Adobe previewed a next-generation image processing engine with extensive GPU acceleration, including interactive Gaussian blur and Light Leaks filters.
Adobe Substance 3D Painter 12.2 is now optimized for RTX Spark with native support on Arm for the first time in public beta. Artists in games, visual effects and visualization can run Substance Painter natively on RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops, with no compatibility layer required.
Adobe Illustrator and InDesign now offer native Windows on Arm versions optimized for RTX Spark. Adobe Illustrator delivers up to 30% higher performance than its emulated version, helping accelerate illustration, graphic design and page-layout workflows on RTX Spark.
Blender 5.3 Adds DLSS Ray Reconstruction to the Viewport
Blender 5.3 integrates DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction into the Cycles viewport, helping artists evaluate lighting and materials with near-final-quality ray-traced previews as they work.
The practical difference is immediate: instead of navigating a noisy, resolving preview, Ray Reconstruction delivers near-final-quality lighting, reflections and materials in the interactive viewport in real time.
DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction support requires Blender 5.3 and the latest NVIDIA Game Ready Driver or NVIDIA Studio Driver. Download the NVIDIA App to get automatic notifications when the latest drivers are available, optimize games and applications from a unified GPU control center, and discover the latest NVIDIA tools and software.
Windows Server 2028 Coming to DGX Station for Windows
Announced at Microsoft Ignite, Windows Server is evolving for organizations that need to run AI closer to their enterprise applications and data.
Microsoft is expanding hardware choice through support for the latest AI silicon, helping customers take advantage of accelerated inference and increasingly capable models in their own environments. NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows platform powered by the GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra Desktop Superchip is expanding to include support for Windows Server 2028.
New accelerator platforms and the breadth of the Windows silicon ecosystem provide customers options at different capability levels and price points for advanced AI development, local inference, and agent workloads at scale.
Windows ML Updates Give Developers More Options
Also announced at Microsoft Ignite, developers can now bring any GGUF model from Hugging Face and run it within Windows ML using the llama.cpp backend.
The DxCGC backend, now available as an experimental release, is an integration for game developers that compiles and runs machine learning models through DirectX 12, allowing them to execute AI workloads alongside graphics.
Windows APIs let applications integrate platform-provided AI capabilities adding GPU support for AION Instruct and VSR.
Developers can also build high-performance AI models for Windows ML using the command line interface.
#ICYMI: The Latest NVIDIA Local AI Updates
🦙 llama.cpp v1.0.0 marks a major milestone for building local AI apps. The open source inference engine introduces API versioning updates, alongside expanded model support and CUDA optimizations for NVFP4 inference. Learn more.
🎉 Ricursive Intelligence introduced its first open model: Ripple-65B Preview. The full-stack AI lab builds self-improving systems by co-optimizing hardware, software and models. Ripple-65B Preview was trained on NVIDIA B300 GPUs, refined using NVIDIA Nemotron post-training datasets and runs locally on DGX Spark. Download the NVFP4 checkpoint from Hugging Face.
🤖 Runway’s Praxis-1 is a newly released 27-billion-parameter world action model that predicts video and actions together. Developers can run it locally on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090, NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, DGX Spark and DGX Station, and adapt it to their own robots, cameras and tasks with LoRA fine-tuning. Download the NVFP4 checkpoint from Hugging Face.
🛠️ NVIDIA TensorRT Edge-LLM helps run AI models locally on DGX Spark with just a few commands. Read the technical blog, which walks through downloading Nemotron-3.5 Lightning, setting up optimized inference, testing prompts and serving the model through a local OpenAI-compatible API.
Subscribe to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter. Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook.

articles.title: Critical Perforce Puppet RCE Exploited in Attacks
articles.text:
Threat actors have been exploiting a critical-severity vulnerability in Perforce Puppet to execute code on vulnerable servers.
Puppet is an infrastructure-as-code (IaC) and configuration management platform that uses a client-server architecture for device management.
Tracked as CVE-2026-115731 (CVSS score of 9.4), the exploited security defect is described as a deserialization of untrusted data issue in the report processing of Puppet Enterprise and Puppet Core, leading to remote code execution (RCE).
It allows clients that have a certificate signed by the Puppet certificate authority (CA) to send reports containing malicious payloads that would be executed on the server with the service user permissions, putting managed systems at risk.
“A successful attack could expose the server’s certificate-signing key, allow an attacker to issue trusted certificates, and enable changes to software and configuration delivered to managed systems on their next Puppet run,” Perforce explains in an advisory.
Unauthenticated attackers could obtain a certificate if the CA auto-signs requests without performing strong verification. Administrators are advised to turn off auto-signing and enforce strong validation to ensure only trusted systems and authorized users can receive certificates.
The security hole was patched on November 3 alongside CVE-2026-115732, a critical issue where an attacker could use a certificate with a name that extends an approved name to bypass authorization and impersonate a managed machine.
Puppet Enterprise and Puppet Enterprise Advanced versions 2026.0.1, 2025.12.1, and 2023.8.13, and Puppet Core versions 9.1.3 and 8.22.2 contain patches for both flaws.
CVE-2026-115731 was flagged as exploited on November 4 and the US cybersecurity agency CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 17, urging federal agencies to patch it within two weeks, in line with BOD 26-04’s recommendations.
The vulnerability also affects the OpenVox configuration management platform. A proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit targeting OpenVox was published shortly after CVE-2026-115731 was patched.
